title: Mechanical reinforcement and geotechnical design of open pit mine using DEGRES program
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Fleurisson J.A.; Alonso-Garcia J.; Cojean R.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: The DEGRES program is a computational tool to help with decisions about geometrical design and geotechnical studies in open pit mining and quarrying. Firstly, it automatically provides a geometrical model of a pit from a basic contour plane. Secondly, a haul road can be inserted into the geometrical model. Finally, in association with geological and geotechnical models of the ore body, various basic failure mechanisms are analyzed for the total or partial height of each pit side. Regarding the calculated safety factors and volumes of unstable rock masses, mechanical reinforcement with tensioned anchors can be studied.

title: Analysis of braking a cylindrical boulder and application to bench blasting
authors: Szuladzinski G.; Saleh A.
abstract: The main objective of the paper is to establish the bursting pressure of a cylindrical boulder made of brittle material. The formulas found by means of a relatively simple approach are extended and applied to one of the fundamental problems in open pit mining, namely the maximum burden determination in bench blasting. While a number of such formulas is currently in use, they come from empirical observation. The expressions given here, based on (simplified) engineering mechanics of blasting processes are intended to fill the existing gap. The range of values predicted with the new expressions is consistent with experimental observations.

title: Catalogue of world wide diamond and kimberlite occurrences: a selective and annotative approach
authors: Janse A.J.A.(.; Sheahan P.A.
abstract: Kimberlites occur on every continent and the total number of known primary host rock occurrences is generally accepted as 5000, of which 500 are diamondiferous, 50 have been or are being mined and 15 are large active mines. Clifford's Rule is shown to be valid in that economic kimberlites occur only on Archons, i.e. cratonic regions underlain by Archaean basement, whereas economic lamproites occur on some Protons, i.e. Proterozoic mobile belts adjacent to Archons. These Archons are distributed world wide in twelve potentially diamond producing regions which occur on seven continents. Three of these twelve regions, i.e. North America, Europe and Antarctica do not have any diamond mines, although significant primary diamond deposits have been found on the first two which will probably be mined in the next decade. The South American continent contains several cratons including the Guyana, Guaporéand Sa ̃o Francisco Cratons which each enclose Archons. These are predominantly located in remote, tropical, heavily forested areas which have not yet been fully explored. Most kimberlites discovered so far in South America lie in Protons, i.e. Proterozoic mobile belts encircling the Archons and are not economic. Therefore almost all production from South America is from alluvial deposits. There is no commercial diamond production from the North American continent, although there are many occurrences of diamonds, kimberlites and lamproites. A great staking rush has taken place in Canada in the Northwest Territories, Alberta, Saskatchewan, Ontario and Québec and is still continuing. Two, and possibly five, diamond mines may be developed in the next decade. Diamond prospecting is proceeding at a fast pace in Canada and in a more limited way in the United States. The African continent contains three large cratons, the South African, Central African and West African cratons. The South African Craton includes the large Kalahari Archon on which the majority of the world's active major kimberlite diamond mines are located in South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe and Swaziland. They comprise 11 kimberlite pipe mines and 3 kimberlite dyke mines. Large alluvial, beach and off-shore deposits also produce a large proportion of the world's total. The Central African Craton includes the Lunda-Kasai and the Tanzanian Archons which each contain one active kimberlite pipe mine in Zaire and in Tanzania. Several large kimberlite pipes in Angola may become mines in the next decade. The craton also contains several large alluvial mining areas in Angola (Lunda and Cuango), Zaire (Eastern and Western Kasai) and in the Central African Republic. The West African Craton includes the Man Archon and the Ebumean Proton. Diamondiferous kimberlite pipes and dykes are located on the Man Archon in Sierra Leone, Guinea, Liberia and Mali. Alluvial deposits immediately downstream from kimberlites are mined in Sierra Leone, Guinea and Liberia and occurrences of pipes and alluvials are being evaluated in Mali. Lamproite dykes located on the Eburnean Proton in Ivory Coast were mined in the past and large alluvial deposits, which cannot be traced to their primary host rock, are mined in Ghana and Ivory Coast. The basement of most of Europe is not conducive to the intrusion of diamondiferous kimberlites or lamproites, although there are many vague reports and rumours about diamond finds in several countries. The East European Craton covers most of western Russia and its neighbouring states and extends into Finland and northern Scandinavia. Several diamondiferous kimberlites and lamproites have apparently been found in the Ukraine, Belorus, Russia (Karelia and the Arkhangelsk district) and probably occur also in Finland and possibly in northern Sweden and Norway. A large diamond mine may be established on five adjacent pipes in the Pomorska field, 100 km north of Arkhangel in the next decade. There is no commercial diamond production from Europe at present. The Asian continent contains at least five cratons, the East Siberian Craton in eastern Russia, the North China, Tarim and Yangtze Cratons in China and the Indian Craton in India. The East Siberian Craton is located in eastern Siberia between the Yenessei and Lena rivers and lies partly in Yakutia and partly in the Krasnoyarsk district. At least 1000 kimberlite pipes occur in this craton and seven pipes have been mined. At present only one, Udachnaya, appears to be active as the others are being developed for deepening their open pit or for underground mining. In addition, the large Yubileinaya pipe is being prepared for open pit mining commencing in 1995. Some small alluvial deposits have also been mined in the past. All diamond mines are located in Yakutia and started only in 1959. Three cratons can be recognized in China, the North China (or Sino-Korean), the Tarim and the Yangtze Cratons. Diamondiferous kimberlites appear to occur only on the North China Craton in the Liaolu Archon. Two small kimberlite pipes are mined in central Shandong and southern Liaoning. Diamondiferous lamproites apparently occur in Protons on the Yangtze and possibly on the Tarim Cratons and alluvial deposits in the Yuan River in western Hunan have been mined in the past. The Indian subcontinent is underlain by the Indian Craton which includes four Archons, separated by Mesozoic rifts and surrounded by Proterozoic mobile belts. India's only active diamond mine at Mahjgawn near Panna in northern Madhya Pradesh is developed on a lamproite pipe located on the southern rim of the Arivalli Archon. Diamondiferous, but uneconomic, kimberlite pipes and dykes occur on the Dharwar Archon in Andhra Pradesh and these may be the primary host for the widespread alluvial deposits in the Krishna River near Kurnool and Kollur. Recently diamondiferous kimberlite pipes have been discovered near Bahradih in southern Madhya Pradesh which are probably the primary host for the alluvial deposits in the Mahanadi River in Orissa. Alluvial diamonds are mined in Indonesia in Kalimantan on the island of Borneo. There are no indications of Archon, Proton or Tecton basement and no substantiated finds of diamondiferous kimberlites or lamproites. The Australian continent contains three large cratons, the West Australian, North Australian and South Australian Cratons. Diamondiferous kimberlites and lamproites occur on all cratons, but the only primary host rock mined since 1985 is the Argyle lamproite pipe which is located on a Proton, i.e. the Proterozoic Halls Creek mobile belt adjacent to the Kimberley Archon. Alluvial deposits are mined at the Bow River mine, immediately downstream from Argyle. Alluvial deposits which have not been traced to a primary host rock also occur in an orogenic belt near Copeton in New South Wales. Diamond prospecting is widespread and is focussed on the North Australian Craton in the Kimberley Archon and its off-shore areas (Cambridge Gulf) in Western Australia and in the Batten area in eastern Northern Territory. © 1995 Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

title: New casting model tracks unwanted overburden
authors: Preece D.S.; Scovira D.C.
abstract: An increasing emphasis on environmentally sound mining practices makes it necessary to be innovative in applying new technologies to open pit mining. An important challenge is groundwater acidification attributed to geologic layers, typically shales that have a higher-than-average pyrite content. Groundwater acidification is accelerated significantly in open-pit mines as the relatively impermeable shale layers are rubblized by blasting, greatly increasing the hydraulic conductivity of the material. A viable solution for mine operators is to separate the pyritic material during muck pile excavation and encapsulate it in some manner to prevent groundwater interaction. This solution depends on being able to locate the pyritic material in the muck pile. The blast-induced movement and final location of these geologic layers that may cause environmental problems can be predicted using discrete element methods. Actual field data from coal mine bench blasts at a mine in the central Appalachia - including geometry, geology, blast design, and percent-cast - were employed to simulate a pyritic shale layer's blast-induced movement and final location. -from Authors

title: Canadian experience in open pit mining
authors: Singhal R.; Collins J.; Fytas K.
abstract: More than two-thirds of the mines in Canada are surface operations. They produce the bulk of the country's iron ore, asbestos, coal, copper, lead, zinc and synthetic crude oil from oil sands. This article describes the mining methods, equipment, automation and computers, environmental issues and management associated with this type of mining. -S.E.Long

title: Czech-U.S. Epa Health Study: Assessment Of Personal And Ambient Air Exposures To Pah And Organic Mutagens In The Teplice District Of Northern Bohemia
source: International Journal of Environmental Analytical Chemistry
authors: Šrám R.; Lewtas J.; Pinto J.
keywords: air pollution | Czech Republic | mutagens | polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAH)
abstract: For over 40 years the Northern Bohemia area of the Czech Republic has been characterized by heavy industrialization, open pit mining, and utilization of high sulfur brown coal by industry and in residential home heating. These conditions have resulted in severe environmental pollution and concern over evidence of adverse health effects for residents in the region. Beginning in August 1991, Czech scientists from the Teplice District Institute of Hygiene and U.S. Environmental Protection Agency researchers from the Health Effects Research Laboratory and the Atmospheric Research and Exposure Assessment Laboratory cooperated in conducting pilot studies in the Teplice District, which is centrally located in the industrialized area. These studies determined ambient concentrations and personal exposures to airborne polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) and organic mutagens. Active personal air samplers were used in personal exposure studies of coal miners, policemen and other workers in the Teplice district. Stationary medium-volume (PM<inf>10</inf>) and high-volume (PM2.5 and TSP) samplers were also used to collect ambient air samples. Personal sampler results from 24 h sampling in January 1992 of a group of Teplice policemen showed BaP exposures averaged 40 ng/m<sup>3</sup>Ambient high-volume (HiVol) air sampling results from 12 h nighttime samples collected in Teplice between February 17 and March 27, 1992 showed particle-associated BaP averaged 12 ng/m<sup>3</sup>and ranged from 2–34 ng/m<sup>3</sup>The sixteen PAHs that were quantified averaged 131 ng/m<sup>3</sup>for the same time periods. Approximately 50% of the particle-bound PAH concentrations in Teplice air resulted from compounds that are carcinogenic in animals. Mutagen concentrations and potency were determined by the Ames plate incorporation assay. The mutagenic potency of extractable organics from ambient air particles was higher than those for U.S. residential areas that are heavily impacted by wood smoke but similar to those from U.S. cities more heavily impacted by vehicle emissions. This document has been reviewed in accordance with U.S. Environmental Protection Agency policy and approved for publication. title: Legal probleme concerning rehabilitation of mining areas and facilities for up - grading of coal with regard to the mining inspectorate
authors: Schmidt R.
abstract: The german federal mining act regulates mining, milling and recultivation of the surface by the operation schedule procedure. Several states published special laws for open pit mining of brown coal and rehabilitation of landscape. In eastern Germany some mining decrees of the former GDR concerning recultivation are still in force by the unification act.

title: Non-electric sequential blasting for open pit mining application
authors: Hanger C.
abstract: An in-depth study of sequential blasting with the use of standard non-electric shock tube down hole timing along with surface M.S connector timing is described in the present study. In addition to written representations, several illustrations intended to refine the actual direction and predicted movement of the shot involved are accounted for. The actual testing of four different systems at the Chimney Creek is also discussed.

title: Managing Risk. Proceedings 4th large open pit mining conference, Perth, September 1994
source: Managing Risk Proceedings 4th Large Open Pit Mining Conference Perth September 1994
abstract: The 44 papers deal with the various aspects of risk involved in the mining industry. The matter is examined from the technical and economic viewpoints of risk involved in exploration, mining activities and remediation. The role of governments, the legal requirements of mining companies and the liability of individuals are covered in general terms. Case studies covering areas such as geological risk, strategies to cope with unstable slopes and protocol for mine closure are presented in some detail. Examples of how management deals with specific components of risk and how systems have been developed to help with the task of environmental management are discussed. The main emphasis is on Australian gold and diamond mining but some studies from Canada and China are also included. -S.E.Long

title: Neural network pattern recognition of blast fragment size distributions
authors: Barron L.; Smith M.L.; Prisbrey K.
abstract: Neural networks have considerable potential for applications in particulate image analysis. An area of great current interest is to use image analysis techniques to characterize particle size distributions in video images of blasted rock. A simulated neural network was trained to recognize fragmented rock size classes taken from images of blasted ore in a large open pit mining operation. Size distributions were assigned to categories such as 40% and 60% minus six inches. Pattern recognition features were extracted from digitized images using two-dimensional Fourier transforms. These features were then used as a training set to enable the neural network to recognize the size category of subsequent images of blasted rock taken from the mining operation. Training sets were developed for a back propagation algorithm by hand sorting and sizing the blast fragments from photographed piles. Within the limits of this experiment, the trained network consistently recognized the size distribution categories. A trained neural network can be readily calibrated to adjust for changes in light and shadow, a problem which plagues algorithm-based blast fragmentation analysis routines. Neural network techniques may provide a solution to the problem of rapid and reliable on-line and on-site size distribution recognition and assessment. © 1994 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: Zaldivar
authors: Chadwick J.
abstract: An overview of Chile's new Zaldivar copper mine. The process design features Nordberg WaterFlush crushers, a large thickener, and new patented vertical smooth flow (VSF) SX technology. The SX-EW plant will have an annual production capacity of 125 000 t. Geology of the deposit, open pit mining operations, crushing and classifying, heap leaching, the VSF solvent extraction technology and results from a pilot test unit, the 35 m diameter Supaflo High Rate thickener, additional geological resource potential, and construction costs, are outlined. -J.M.McLaughlin

title: Risk analysis and uncertainty in open pit mine design
source: Managing Risk Proc 4th Open Pit Conference Perth 1994
authors: Read J.R.L.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: This paper examines the concepts of risk analysis and uncertainty in open pit mine design. It describes the relationship between risk analysis and uncertainty, describes methods that can be used to quantify uncertainty, and suggests ways of reducing the geological and geotechnical uncertainties that are inherent in open pit mining. -Author

title: Individual personal liability risk management in open pit mining
source: Managing Risk Proc 4th Open Pit Conference Perth 1994
authors: Williamson-Noble J.; Lawrence M.
abstract: This paper identifies the areas where such individuals in the open pit mining industry in Australia face the risk of personal liability and measures which can be used to minimise the risk or which can be used to make out a defence to legal action which could arise. -from Authors

title: Determining the maximum present value of an open pit mining operation
source: Managing Risk Proc 4th Open Pit Conference Perth 1994
authors: Crone J.
abstract: An alternative method for determining the maximum present value of an open pit mining operation is given. In this method the maximum present value is determined by working backwards from the end of the operation life, progressively asking the question of each increment "what cut-off grade maximises the present value at the start of mining of that increment?' The method allows calculations to be performed by a "spreadsheet' package. -from Author

title: Assessment of technical and financial risk through feasibility studies
source: Managing Risk Proc 4th Open Pit Conference Perth 1994
authors: West R.; Aspinall T.
abstract: This paper discusses the identification and assessment of risk for mining developments particularly for open pit mining. A distinction between sensitivity studies and risk analysis is developed, demonstrating the importance of geological and mining engineering judgement as applied by experienced practioners to the analysis and assessment of risk in such projects. Technical and financial risk analysis are discussed under: mineral resources and ore reserves; mining and processing methods; project construction; financing; and costs and commodity pricing predictions. -Authors

title: Design of compact bucket wheel excavators and spreaders - based on BG'86 design regulations for giant open pit equipment
authors: Baben R.
abstract: The BG'86 is a constant set of design rules and regulations used not only for giant open pit mining equipment for `Rheinbraun', but applied all over the world also as a standard for the design of compact bucket wheel excavators and spreaders. The special design features of the compact machine are a challenge to the responsible designer to interpret the rules on their merits and to cooperate for further development. In order to avoid any misunderstandings which may lead to problems in the execution of a contract it is therefore recommended that full clarity be established if possible at the time the contract is drawn up about all aspects of applying the BG'86 between all parties to the contract.

title: Flexowell-pylon-conveyor
authors: Paelke J.
abstract: In the areas of conveying and transshipment of bulk materials, careful attention to the cost/benefit ratio is now more important than ever. This applies equally to capital investment as well as the ongoing costs for operation and maintenance. Belt conveyors have generally been recognized as one of the most economical methods of handling bulk materials because they adapt themselves to continuous handling of ore, coal, stones etc. Belt conveyors offer benefits of reduced supervision, lower maintenance cost, minimum product degradation and downtime. With the aid of FLEXOWELL -technology and the newly developed conveying systems allowed by it, it is now possible to overcome the performance limitations of conventional conveyor belting and break through into new dimensions in conveying technology. These FLEXOLIFT -systems have already been successfully applied in practice, e.g. up to 6,000 t/h unloading capacities in self-unloading vessels or up to 203 m vertical lifts in the underground mining industry. Innovative designs combine steep inclined and vertical conveying with horizontal or inclined discharge sections eliminating the need for material transfer stations. This article introduces the so-called FLEXOWELL -Pylon-Conveyor for the use of steep inclined conveying in quarries and in open pit mining.

title: Modeling an open pit mine in a multitest statement
authors: Nazarov I.V.; Kortelev O.B.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: We describe a structure of an algorithm for modeling and evaluating a dynamically evolving open pit mine. The algorithm is implemented on a decision tree and combines step-by-step optimization and piecewise continuous development of alternatives in a system processing standard configurations (patterns). The system represents the informational environment for description of the engineering process of open pit mining. © 1994 Plenum Publishing Corporation.

title: The Sue uranium deposits, Saskatchewan, Canada
authors: Baudemont D.; Piquard J.; Ey F.; Zimmerman J.
abstract: The Sue uranium deposits occur in northern Saskatchewan, at the eastern edge of the Athabasca Basin. They were discovered from 1988 to 1989. They have been named in order of discovery: Sue A and Sue B (1988), Sue C and Sue CQ (1989). The orebodies are spatially related to the unconformity separating the Helikian Athabasca Sandstone Group from the underlying metasediments of the Wollaston Group and are clustered on the western edge of the presumed Archean Collins Bay dome, along a single 2.9 km long N-S trend. They occur at a depth of 8 m to 180 m below surface which should allow open pit mining methods. The mineralization is located along a major faulted corridor. It is associated with extensive hydrothermal transformations overprinting older alteration events. In the Sue A and B deposits, uranium oxides and silicates are associated with Ni-Co arsenides and Fe-Ni-Co-Cu sulphides. The Sue C and CQ deposits consist mainly of uranium oxides. -from Authors

title: Mortality among workers in the diatomaceous earth industry
authors: Checkoway H.; Heyer N.J.; Demers P.A.; Breslow N.E.
abstract: A cohort mortality study was conducted among workers from two plants in the diatomaceous earth mining and processing industry in California. Diatomaceous earth consists of the skeletal remains of diatoms. Exposure to amorphous (non-crystalline) and crystalline silica in the form of quartz results from open pit mining and exposure to crystalline silica (principally cristobalite) occurs in the processing of the material. Lung cancer and non-malignant respiratory diseases have been the health outcomes of greatest concern. The main study cohort included 2570 white men (533 Hispanic and 2017 non-Hispanic workers) who were employed for at least 12 months cumulative service in the industry and who had worked for at least one day during the follow up period, 1942-87. Vital status was ascertained for 91% of the cohort and death certificate information was retrieved for 591 of 628 (94%) identified deaths. The all causes combined standardised mortality ratio (SMR) was slightly increased (SMR = 1.12; 628 observed) compared with rates among US white males. The principal contributors to this excess were increased risks from lung cancer (SMR = 1.43; 59 observed) and non-malignant respiratory disease (NMRD) excluding infectious diseases and pneumonia (SMR = 2.59; 56 observed). The excess of lung cancer persisted when local county rates were used for comparison (SMR = 1.59). Internal rate comparisons by Poisson regression analysis were conducted to assess potential doe-response relations for lung cancer and NMRDs. Mortality trends were examined in relation to duration of employment in dust exposed jobs and with respect to an index of cumulative exposure to crystalline silica. The crystalline silica index was a semiquantitative measure that combined information on duration of exposure, differences in exposure intensity between jobs and calendar periods, the crystalline content of the various product mixes, and the use of respiratory protection devices. Increasing gradients of risk were detected for lung cancer and NMRD with both exposure indices. The relative risk trends for lung cancer and NMRD with crystalline silica exposure lagged 15 years were respectively: 1.00, 1.19, 1.37, and 2.74, and 1.00, 1.13, 1.58, and 2.71. Based on a review of available but limited data on cigarette smoking in the cohort and from application of indirect methods for assessing confounding variables, it seems unlikely that smoking habits could account for all of the association between exposure to dust and lung cancer. The intense and poorly controlled dust exposures encountered before the 1950s were probably the most aetiologically significant contributors to risks from lung cancer and NMRDs. The absence of an excess of lung cancer among workers hired since 1960, and the finding of no deaths attributed to pneumoconiosis as an underlying cause of death among workers hired since 1950 indicate that exposure reductions in the industry during the past 40 years have been successful in reducing excess risks to workers. Further mortality follow up of the cohort and the analysis of radiographic data will be needed to determine conclusively the long term patterns of disease risks in this industry.

title: Computerized grade control in complex porphyry copper deposits
authors: Franklin P.
abstract: Grade distribution within porphyry copper deposits can sometimes be erratic in nature. Conventional, manual grade control techniques for open pit mining have proved to be inadequate for accurately predicting mining head grades and for delineating ore and waste contacts. This paper describes a highly interactive computerized grade control system that uses a combination of geostatistical modelling and graphical techniques to perform the daily grade control operations. The software is used to improve the reliability of grade predictions and to perform reconciliation of mined materials with planned materials. The paper is illustrated with examples from operating copper open pits located in western Canada. © The Geological Society 1992.

title: Mine water risk in open pit slope stability
authors: Mandzic H.
abstract: Water pressure due to groundwater presence has a great influence on the open pit slope stability and for that reason the risk of slope instability is dependent on water level in the slope. Factor of safety could be reduced from 1,3 to 1.0 if the water level increases. In all cases in open pit mining practice more than 40% of slope instability risks depend on groundwater conditions in the slope, To prevent slope failure, effective drainage system can be installed, and other factors can remain unchanged. The importance of controlling water surface in open pit slope is emphasized. In general, increasing the open pit slope angle and decreasing the failure risks, is directly proportional to effective drainage system. © 1992 Springer-Verlag.

title: Third large open pit mining conference, Mackay, Queensland, August-September 1992
authors: ANON
abstract: Third in a series of conferences on large open pit mining. The theme was maximisation of economic benefits using state-of-the- art technology. The book contains 67 papers in sections on: open pit economics; mine design, equipment and operations; new mining techniques; blasting; rehabilitation; geotechnical problems; water management; mine scheduling and risk evaluation; man management; and includes several mining case studies. (D.G.H.)

title: High angle conveyors for surface mining in the 90s
authors: Dos Santos J.
abstract: High angle conveyor systems in open pit mining offer many advantages over the traditional, truck only, haulage systems, including: (1) superior energy efficiency (2) less dependency on petroleum products (3) less sensitivity to inflation (4) less labour (5) less excavation for the amount of ore recovered, and (6) less ramp construction and maintenance costs. This paper presents the sandwich belt high angle conveyor as the vital link to optimisation of in-pit conveying systems. High angle conveyor development to date is discussed, beginning with studies in 1979, to the first large scale prototype in 1983, through the numerous commercial installations. Discussion continues with the high angle conveyor systems to suit the various open pit mining operations and the corresponding characteristics of the system components, particularly the high angle conveyor. The range of high angle conveyor systems from the low capacity (up to 1 814 t/h), low lift (10.7 to 36.6 m), highly mobile to the moderate capacity (1 814 to 3 629 t/h), moderate lift (36.6 to 76.2 m), intermittently mobile to the high capacity (greater than 3 629 t/h), high lift (greater than 76.2 m), semi-mobile, are discussed along with some possible combinations of these.

title: Coal mining in Canada in the nineties
authors: Davies G.; Parkes D.
abstract: Mathematically, the proposed formula is: 'Human Effectiveness + Technological Improvement = Success in the Nineties'. A brief review is made of geology, level of technology, management and labour situations, and range of production costs in coal producing countries. This comparison shows keen competition for Canadian coals, especially from the People's Republic of China, South Africa and Australia. Domestic competition comes from nuclear energy, hydro-electric generation, natural gas (if permitted) and eastern United States coal. The huge increase in the size and power of surface mining equipment in the last forty years led to modern large-scale open pit mining. While conventional truck and shovel operations will continue to be widely used, more continuous mining and conveying systems will be installed as pits become deeper and haul distances longer. Computer systems will become more sophisticated and their applications more widespread, leading to higher productivity and closer control of all operations and equipment performances and to partial or complete automation of certain operations. The underground revival will be driven by a new generation of mining people, cooperating to produce over 3 million t/y from 300 m longwall faces retreating over 3 km resulting in mine productivities of over 40 tonnes per man shift, as is already achieved in several mines throughout the world. Continuous operation using on-line control systems will assist in consistent production with availabilities over 75%.

title: An application of closed queueing networks theory in truck-shovel systems
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Kappas G.; Yegulalp T.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: Primary applications of queueing networks theory have been in the area of computer systems and computer communication networks analysis and performance. The application introduced here is a steady state analysis of a generalized truck-shovel system in a typical open pit mine. The service time distributions of each activity are assumed to be of a general form. The approach used here minimizes the error of performance parameter estimates of the most saturated service center. The formulation allows one to obtain estimates of system parameters relatively fast and very close to those obtained by simulation. The relative error of the critical performance parameter estimates as compared to those obtained by simulation do not exceed 5%. The output of the model can be used within various optimization schemes for design and operational control of open pit mining systems. © 1991, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Mining with microbes
authors: Debus K.
abstract: In an effort to reduce production costs and to end the environmental degradation caused by current digging and smelting procedures, the metal mining industry in the United States is turning to biotechnology. For example, the copper industry employed a microorganism called Thiobacillus Ferrooxidans in a biochemical process to produce over 30 percent of the 1989 copper production. Referred to as biohydrometallurgy, the merger of biology and metals offers several advantages over conventional mining methods. It eliminates the environmental destruction associated with open pit mining, and it reduces the acid rain and water pollution which are by-products of current mining and smelting techniques. Technical problems, however, limit commercial feasibility. For example, biohydrometallurgical processes are much slower than conventional procedures. The United States Mining Industry needs to spend more research money on biohydrometallurgy, public policy should encourage this kind of ecological engineering, and mining engineers need additional training in biology.

title: Les Mines Selbaie story: Introduction
authors: Bryce R.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: Selbaie is located northwest of Joutel in what is known as the fourth east-west volcanic sediment group in northwestern Quebec. The main metals produced are copper and zinc, with important contents of silver and gold. Production comes from an open pit mine on the A-1 zone and from two underground mines on the B zone and the A-2 zone. Production from all sources now exceeds 7000 tonnes per day, with a workforce of 540 regular employees. Of particular interest technically is high recovery of B zone reserves underneath 40 m of overburden cover, low-cost capital development of the A-2 zone, computerized control of open pit mining, and copper-zinc separation of the A-1 zone ore. Due to the low grades of the deposits, efficiency in all aspects of the production process is essential to success of the operation.

title: Overview of open pit mines for mining technologies with high outputs
authors: Kolleth H.
abstract: The article summarizes possible methods of open pit mining from the point of view of the equipment, i.e. the different mining methods are listed according to the possible equipment configurations. Continuous mining is given particular emphasis as continuous mining and conveying systems are generally more economic than other systems. The technologies considered are digging/excavating methods, transport methods, and spreading or dumping methods for overburden or waste using. Subjects covered include combinations of technologies, methods and equipment, types of open pit operations, and the influence of the materials on the selection of mining technologies.

title: Rock mechanics: contributions and challenges. Proceedings of the 31st US symposium
source: Rock Mechanics Contributions and Challenges Proceedings of the 31st US Symposium
authors: Hustrulid W.; Johnson G.
abstract: The theme of the 31st US symposium on rock mechanics is "Rock mechanics - contributions and challenges', having as objectives the examination and quantification of the progress that has been achieved in addressing the major practical challenges facing the science of rock mechanics and mine design. The 124 papers cover areas such as experimental studies; conceptual, analytical and numerical modelling; design and construction methods. Thirty five papers deal with practical mining problems including rock reinforcement, blasting, rock bursts, open pit mining, remote sensing, borehole geophysics, mechanical fragmentation and subsidence. Areas emphasised are coal and metal mine designs. Other papers deal with computer models, instrumentation, fracture mechanics and testing techniques. -A.W.Hall

title: Engineering geology in Papua New Guinea: a review
authors: Stead D.
abstract: Papua New Guinea is a country where geology has a major impact on civil and mining engineering projects. It is situated in a geologically active region and hence is subject to earthquake- and volcanicity-related hazards. Combined with a high annual rainfall, rugged topography and intense weathering, this makes Papua New Guinea an extremeley challenging and interesting environment for the engineering geologist. Several large-scale open pit mining operations such as Panguna and Ok Tedi have involved a considerable input from geological engineers both in mine design and in the development of the necessary infrastructure. Environmental concerns have become increasingly important requiring the design of tailings dams to limit the effect of mineral extraction. The construction and maintenance of roads is an important factor in the growth of Papua New Guinea and both major and minor roads have been adversely influenced by slope instability problems. Numerous slope failures have occurred along the country's main route, the Highland's highway, on several occasions resulting in road closure. The development of hydroelectric power has also involved a significant input from geological engineers in the design and construction of dams and ancillary structures. This paper examines the influence of geology on the development of Papua New Guinea. © 1990.

title: Generating massive power
authors: Anon
abstract: An outline of the huge power generation facilities near Melbourne, Australia is given. The power plant is located at an open pit mining complex with modular construction plant, with units of 1,000 MW each. Two units are in operation, while the third is being constructed. Over 3,000 tons of brown coal are recovered per hour by a giant dredges.

title: Comparison of clay mining in underground and open pit mines
source: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Knissel W.; Schaefer W.
abstract: In an empirical investigation the mining operations for clay and kaolin in the Federal Republic of Germany are compared. Starting with a differentiation between open pit and underground mines, the mining technology in German mines is presented. For the reason of the high productivity and efficiency of the open pit mining operations with hydraulic excavators and truck transportation, the use of underground methods is limited to high quality clays. Therefore possibilities for the improvement of underground mining are proposed. The production of clay in open pit mining operations is subject to environmental regulations. By an environmentally sound design of waste dumps and the use of a new drilling method for clay production, surface use can be minimized.

title: Effective modelling for cast blasting
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Chung S.H.; Tidman J.P.
abstract: There is a need for cast bla;. ing in open pit mining. Although this type of blasting requires higher explosive consumption, the 30 to 40% saving on handling broken muck justifies application of this technique. Based on the HEAVE module built in SABREX, a computer blast simulation program developed by ICI, effective cast blasting for different site conditions can be designed and confirmed by means of high speed photography. Case studies given in the paper confirm the model's ability to make realistic predictions. © 1989, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Application of drive systems for mine haulage vehicles
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Johnson J.W.
abstract: There are many different types of open pit mining operations around the world, and the challenge for any drive system manufacturer is to produce a system or systems that will work satisfactorily in these mines. Several factors must be considered, such as vehicle speed requirements, available engine horsepower, mine rolling resistance, grades, grade lengths, payload and tire sizes. How well a particular drive system performs depends on size, weight, and available tractive/retarding effort. In addition to performance, the system must also have an operating cost that will be acceptable over the life of the equipment. Today the choice of drive systems is between mechanical or electrical and within these types there are several manufacturers. Regardless of how the power is provided to the rear wheels, the job must be accomplished reliably and at acceptable cost. This paper will cover characteristics of an electric drive system and how it is applied. © 1989, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Australian miners face up to deeper overburden
authors: Runge I.
abstract: Over the last two decades, the coal mining industry in Australia has developed into the world's largest exporter, and the mines have achieved recognition as some of the worlds most technologically advanced. Whilst Australian companies have not been slow to adopt new technologies in underground mining, the majority of growth since 1969 has been in the large scale open pit mining areas in Central Queensland and the Hunter Valley of NSW. With most operators reconciled to the changed marketing and financing positions of their coal projects, the challenge for the 1990's will be technical. Surplus capacity in overburden removal equipment no longer exists - and as the mines move into deeper areas, low cost dragline methods are increasingly less applicable. The article describes the equipment used at a number of Australian mines.

title: A mathematical programming approach for scheduling equipment in a surface coal mining operation
source: International Journal of Mining and Geological Engineering
authors: Goodman G.V.R.; Sarin S.C.
keywords: Coal mining | equipment scheduling | model simulation | surface mining
abstract: A mathematical programming model for scheduling open pit mining was developed and validated using data from a surface mining operation. A two-phase solution procedure was used involving repeated evaluations of an integer scheduling model and a simple transportation model. © 1988 Chapman & Hall Ltd.

title: Influence of blasting on open pit economics
authors: Singhal R.K.; Naidu H.G.
abstract: A survey was recently carried out to study the blasting practices used in the western Canadian surface coal mines. The economics of open pit mining is heavily dependent on the cost of overburden handling. Steeper slopes lower the volume of overburden to be handled. There is, however, a limit to which the pit slopes in any given situation can be steepened - steepening beyond this point could jeopardise the pitwall stability rendering it unsafe and might result in curtailment of pit production.

title: USE OF ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE METHODS IN OPEN-PIT MINING.
authors: Brfueggemann H.; Kade M.
abstract: This article is based on a specific application of open-pit mining - the exploitation of raw material for cement production - but its validity is not restricted to this domain. In recent years Krupp Polysius has established a software package for the computation of numerical deposit models, based on borehole samples and topograpical data. Subsequently an additional module was required to evaluate these models and deduce a suitable mining strategy, taking into consideration different constraining factors related to the process technology. All work was performed within the framework of a real, normal-scale example, but all concepts, designs and finished software components are set up to deal with general open pit mining applications - they are not restricted to this specific application.

title: OPEN PIT MINING PRODUCTIVITY - AN UPDATE.
authors: Nilsson D.
abstract: In this article the development of productivity in US open pit mining is first briefly described. The study shows that for strip coal mining, there has been a small but steady increase in productivity during the last decade. In 1986, the average productivity was some 5 tons of coal per employee-hour. For US open pit metal mines, there was a decrease in productivity during the late 70's; but during the 80's the average productivity increased again, and in 1984 averaged some 40 tons per man-hour (ore and waste). The study also shows that the yearly production level in an open pit greatly affects productivity. For US strip coal mines, productivity is twice as high in mines producing more than 1 Mt/y of coal than in smaller mines.

title: Modified tree graph algorithm for ultimate pit limit analysis. M.Sc. thesis
authors: Huttagosol P.
abstract: The use of computer models to design the ultimate pit limits during feasibility study and long range mine planning is becoming a significant practice in open pit mining. One of the limitations of determining optimal ultimate pit limits using true optimizing techniques has been a great deal of computer resources required. The maximum closure of a graph model, which is a true optimizing technique developed by Lerchs and Grossman, is extended for solving an ultimate pit limit problem. The tree configuration of the graph theory can be reduced to only connections between positive vertices. The extended method is shown to require less computer memory and processing time while yielding an optimal solution. -Author

title: Comparison of tripper-spreader combinations
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Meyer T.
abstract: In future, the volume of overburden to be dumped will further increase as mining operations have to go down to greater and greater depths in order to expose the mineral deposits to be extracted in open pit mining. For this reason, the selection of the correct spreading system is becoming increasingly important. Thus, an optimal tripper-spreader combination has to be selected with regard to the actual dumping procedure and the geometry of the dump cross section. In order to guarantee economical mining of mineral deposits, despite the increasing costs of overburden removal, the machine system selected must also be examined with regard to its costs, operational safety and availability. Because of the complexity of the subject matter and the limited size of this paper, this is a contribution only to give a brief overview of the machines more commonly combined as systems and to present their most significant features in terms of type, method of operation, mass and cost effectiveness. © 1988, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Practical considerations for developing an automatically driven open pit mining machine: Compact bucketwheel excavator
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Kolleth H.
abstract: The era of electronic revolution Is here bringing changes to mining technology. The surface mining industry Is keen to be part of this changing environment. Efforts are being directed towords developing automated mining equipment. This paper, using the compact bucket wheel excovator as an example examlnes the theoretical and practical parameters which must be considered in developing an automated machine. © 1988, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: SCIENTIFIC BASIS FOR DESIGNING A FUTURE COAL MINE.
authors: Burchakov A.
abstract: An analysis of the development of the coal industry in the USSR over the last 25 years shows that its lags behind West Germany in improving its performance. Increasing open pit mining and changeover to hydromechanization of underground mining are the two lines of advance pursued at present but they have certain disadvantages. It is proposed that the most expedient would be mechanohydraulic underground coal mining. The processes of coal extraction, its transport at the coal face and along the preparatory drifts would remain mechanical. However, its transport to the day surface would be hydraulic via pipelines. Applications of this method to a Kuzbas mine is considered. Problems of working with coal slurries are examined.

title: The dredging of lignite from beneath the Danube.
authors: Pavlovic V.; Makar M.; Matko Z.; Simic R.
abstract: The use of dredging technology for the recovery of multiple lignite seams is an extension of current dredging practice. This paper identifies the essential elements of the operating technology for the dredging of the lignite from the Kovin deposit on the banks of the Danube. The equipment required for the trial dredging programme is specified. This trial will allow complete data on the practicality of lignite mining by dredge to be gathered, which will enable the full scale mine to be designed. The mine will be planned to supply two 300 MW power generating plants with 5.5 million tons of lignite per annum. It is expected that this method of mining will reduce the environmental impact of the mine, be highly productive as it is fully mechanized, convert 300 x 166 tons of lignite from resources to reserves and reduce the cost per ton of coal mined by 60%, as compared with conventional open pit mining.

title: FUTURE DEVELOPMENT WORK IN AUSTRALIA.
authors: Thomas L.
abstract: Australia is a fortunate country with respect to resources. Large areas of the metalliferous districts are still not explored in detail, and the known reserves are far more than are needed for domestic consumption. Similarly, coal is known to exist in many inland basins. A deep coal mine in Australia is only 300 to 400 m below the surface, and there are many coal seams still available for open pit mining. Australia has a technical ability to work deeper mines, for example, North Broken Hill Mine is working Pb/Zn/Ag ore at a depth of over 1500 m. Mount Isa will be deeper than 1800 m, and the new Olympic Dam Mine at Roxby Downs will extract gold, copper and uranium ore to at least 650 m. Coal-mine shaft sinking and drainage, as well as metalliferous mining techniques are surveyed.

title: Investigation of Labour Conditions and the State of the Osteo-articular System in Excavator Machine Operators Engaged in Opencast Mining.
authors: Grigoryan E.; Druzhinin V.; Starozhuk I.; Nikombekov A.
abstract: The working conditions of excavator operators and occupation related illnesses of osteo-articular system are analyzed. The hygienic evaluation of conditions in open pit mining under general vibrations and adverse microclimate is discussed. The result of X-ray examinations of spine and arms and changes in osteo-articular system are described.

title: In-pit crushing and high angle conveying in Yugoslavian copper mine
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Santos J.A.D.; Stanisic Z.
abstract: Plans for large scale open pit mining of the low grade copper ore at Majdanpek Copper Mine began after a 1949 exploration revealed an extensive ore body. Mining operations and haulage systems have progressed in phases exploiting the most current technology. Phase I (1960–1980) haulage system was by trucks only. Phase II (1980 to present) began to exploit the favorable economics of waste haulage by conveyor from a fixed, pit perimeter crusher to the waste dump, with dumping by mobile spreader. Phase III (scheduled for 1988 operation) will expand exploitation of haulage by conveyor by Installation of in-pit portable crushers, shiftable conveyors and an elevating high angle conveyor (HAC®) to lift the ore out of the pit onto an overland conveyor system to the ore processing plant. Design of the HAC and its suitability for the severe requirements at Majdanpek (250 mm [10<sup>M</sup>] sized copper ore at 4,000 t/h [4,409 st/h] for 93.5 m [307 ft.] of lift at 35.5°) is the primary focus of this paper. The Phase III haulage system affords more in-pit flexibility and optimizes total excavation for the amount of ore to be recovered. Present plans for the future are for extending the Phase III ore haulage system deeper into the pit by introduction of a second HAC to discharge onto the first HAC. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Examples of open pit mining instability
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Brawner C.O.
abstract: Geotechnical technology for surface mining has become increasingly sophisticated as lower grade ore deposits are being developed. With larger and deeper open pits, more detailed and accurate investigation has become necessary during the past decade. Many variables influence successful open pit operations. These include ore grade, metal price, development costs, construction costs, mine design, stability and operating costs. With the great increase in the size of open pits to depths over 600 - 800 meters, the determination of pit slope angle and control of wall stability has a major influence on project economics. This paper briefly discusses preliminary considerations for pit slopes from a geotechnical standpoint to optimize economics and safety, describes recent developments in stability engineering and to illustrate a wide range of stability problems, typical examples are briefly reviewed. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Procedure and example of grade control in open pit mining
source: Pacific Rim Congress 87 Proc International Congress 1987 Gold Coast Queensland
authors: Guibal D.
abstract: Grade control plays an essential role in the good running of a mine. The factors at play are many, starting from a good analysis of the geology and a correct sampling procedure. Once this is achieved (and it is an essential prerequisite), the problem is to adequately define which is ore and what is waste. This paper tries to show, through a small example, how simple geostatistical techniques (variography, and moving average or kriging), can help in accurately defining these limits in a geologically homogeneous zone, thus allowing optimal use of the available information. -Author

title: The use of integrated geological, geophysical and remote sensing methods in the finding of economic minerals for open pit mining, southwestern Venezuela.
source: Improvement of Mine Productivity and Overall Economy by Modern Technology 13th World Mining Congress Vol 1
authors: Rodriguez S.E.
abstract: SW Venezuela is formed by Precambrian rocks, mainly complex granites, pegmatites, and alkaline intrusives. As the result of the complicated geological, metallogenic and structural history, the area, especially the Cedeno District of Bolivar State, has constituted a very important target for exploration. Since 1972 the whole area has been under research by the Geological Survey and Regional Corporations. As a result of integrated aero geophysical programs an important carbonatite body was discovered in a jungle-type terrain. Geological, geo-chemical and drilling programs defined >400 mill. metric tons of a rare earth-Th-Cb-Ba-phosphate rich ore. Apparently, this carbonatite forms part of an extensive belt of intrusives of alkaline nature. Geological and geomorphological studies carried out in the extensive plateau of the Parguaza Granite, outlined more than 300 mill. metric tons of high quality bauxite during 1977. A large open pit is under preparation in order to produce raw material for the large alumina plant of Puerto Ordaz, Bolivar State. A large concentration of diamantiferous young alluvial sediments was outlined by remote sensing methods in the Guaniamo River Area. The ore bodies are constituted by old channels covered by a thick tropical rain forest. The deposits are under open pit mining. Between 1982 and 1985, Venezuela produced >1 400 000 carats of diamonds. Very detailed geological, lithological, geomorphological and remote sensing programs carried out between 1978 and 1982 in the Cedeno District, Bolivar State, defined several important Ta-Nb-Sn rich pegmatites. The intense wathering has produced a large and thick alluvial and elluvial deposits of gravel rich in Tantalite, Columbite and Cassiterite. Some specific areas are under drilling in order to outline ore bodies for open pit methods. Parallel to these investigations, the geological survey is evaluating important high quality quartz and potassic feldspar deposits.-Author

title: PRESENT STATUS FOR DEVELOPMENT OF TAR SAND OIL RESOURCES AND PROGRESS OF UPGRADING TECHNOLOGIES.
authors: Fujita M.
abstract: Tar sand oil is one of valuable hydrocarbon resources with approximate 1. 57 trillion bbl of reserve found in Canada. Two mining methods, viz. open pit mining and insitu recovery method, are currently commercialized and the latter will predominate in future. In Japan, Research Association for Petroleum Alternatives Development (RAPAD) was organized under the sponsorship of MITI and this association has been engaged in development of upgrading technology of tar sand oil for the past 8 years, with excellent results. Problems and countermeasures in production of tar sand oil and their import to Japan are also discussed.

title: A microcomputer approach for simulating truck haulage systems in open pit mining
authors: Castillo D.; Cochran J.K.
keywords: Microcomputer | Open pit ming | Simulation | Truck haulage
abstract: A low cost microcomputer system for simulating truck haulage in open pit mining is presented. An actual analysis of a working mine evaluating computer dispatching is described. The system employs SLAM II and FITPLUS for simulating and statistically analyzing mining models. Issues concerning simulation software, statistical support software, processing times and implementation costs are addressed. Results demonstrate that with the proper tools simulation can be performed on microcomputers in an accurate, timely and cost-effective manner. © 1987.

title: Settlement observations of open pit mine backfill
authors: Thomson S.; Sonnenberg R.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: Reclaimed land from open pit mining operations must have essentially completed settling under self-weight and must be capable of supporting light structures before it can be returned to the public domain. The settlement of the spoil from one open pit mining operation west of Edmonton, Alberta, was monitored by a series of magnet extensometers installed in boreholes. Time-settlement plots indicated that self-weight settlement occurs within a 3 to 5 year period. Tests of individual small footings pointed out the necessity to place shallow foundations on beneficiated soil. The results of a second series of small footings led to the founding of an 8 m×10 m prototype instrumented, reinforced foundation on a 1 m thick soil/flyash mat. Observations to date indicated an entirely acceptable settlement pattern.

title: Open Pit Mining of Petroleum Bituminous Rocks at the Kirmaku Deposit.
source: Izvestia Vyssih Ucebnyh Zavedenij Neft I Gaz
authors: Dzhavadov A.; Sadigov A.
abstract: Petroleum bituminous rocks are a form of accumulation of hydrocarbons which are characterized by a complete or partial loss of mobility. The largest accumulations of such minerals are in the Sarmatian and Chokrakian tiers, in the Maikopian suite and in the productive formations of the Azerbaijan SSR. Some specific feature of open pit mining of these minerals are described. The plasticity of oil sands increases in summer and this creates some difficulties for excavation and transportation. The burden layer is only 2. 5 m thick.

title: LOS PELAMBRES COPPER PROJECT, CHILE.
source: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
authors: Atkinson W.; Souviron A.
abstract: The porphyry copper deposit at Los Pelambres is a resource exceeding 2 Gt (2. 2 billion st) of 0. 7% copper and 0. 02% molybdenum. It includes a high-grade zone of plus 1% copper that is amenable to open pit mining with a low stripping ratio. Metallurgical testing has recoveries of 96% for copper and 93% for molybdenum which can be obtained by conventional flotation methods. This paper summarizes the history of the prospect, the geology of the ore body and the surrounding area, and the results of exploration.

title: BENTONITE GAINS GROUND IN US MINE.
authors: Gordon C.
abstract: Bentonite, rather than synthetic liners, is the preferred ground consolidation technique in Europe. In the US it is going through a trial period in the Montana Tunnels gold mine which is one of the bigger open pit mining projects in the USA.

title: Combined Open Pit and Underground Mining Method at Aghires Mine.
authors: Muste I.
abstract: After discussing the deposit, the author indicates that in a mining field of about 50 ha seam, caolinous sand was mined by using the chamber method with abandoned pillars. An extraction of 60% sand from seam II or 20% of the overall reserves from this field was reached. Following this, after having described the physical and mechanical features of the ore seams and the host rock, a safety plate was provided over the stopes and three alternatives for the open pit mining of the remaining reserves were designed.

title: IN-PIT MINING SYSTEMS.
authors: Wood J.
abstract: As open pit mining operations go deeper because of earlier exploitation of deposits with low overburden ratios and high grade seams, mine operations must now look to more highly mechanised methods for both waste and mineral recovery and for transportation out of the pit to utilisation or ultimate disposal. Although these mechanised techniques have had wide acceptance for many years in Europe and Victoria's Latrobe Valley, for the exploitation of lignite on a very large scale for pwer generation and for bauxite mining in WA and NT, their adoption to other forms of hardrock mining has only been seriously considered during the last ten years. Mechanised methods offer an economic solution to the exploitation of mineral deposits with higher overburden ratios than have been considered feasible in the past and in pits up to 250 metres deep. Their successful application depends on a system approach to the selection of each element involved in the new mining process.

title: INCO'S NEW OPEN PIT DELIVERS LOW-COST NICKEL ORE.
authors: Anon
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open-pit mine; surface mining
abstract: Filling the processing pipeline with lowcost mined nickel ore was Inco's main motive for developing its new Thompson open pit mine in northern Manitoba, Canada. The new pit, which mines the crown pillar of the Thompson underground mine, replaces ore that was previously railed from the Pipe open-pit, located 20 min to the south. The decision to bring the Thompson open-pit mine into production rather than rejuvenate or develop any of the other underground mines was based primarily of the fact that surface mining technology, personnel, and equipment already existed at the Pipe open pit. Mining is carried out in the pit two shifts/day operating on 45-ft benches with 25-ft berms. The ultimate dimensions of the mine will be 5,100 ft along the north-south direction, 800 ft in the east-west direction, and 400 ft below surface at its deepest point.

title: OPTIMUM SCALE OF AN OPEN PIT OPERATION: DISCOUNT RATE AND RISK.
source: Bulletin and Proceedings Australasian Institute of Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Schaap W.
abstract: For a large scale open pit mining and concentrating operation on a low-grade disseminated ore body, it is possible to set an approximate lower bound on economically feasible operating scales and an approximate upper bound on economically desirable scales. The effects of infrastructural costs and the addition of a risk premium to form the discount rate for planning purposes are considered theoretically and by worked example.

title: SANDWICH BELT HIGH ANGLE CONVEYORS - HAC: EVOLUTION TO DATE.
authors: Dos Santos J.
abstract: Sandwich belt conveyors may be used to transport materials at high angles, to 90 degree , while maintaining the most positive features of conventional conveyors. The present discussion deals with the evolution and development of sandwich belt high angle conveyors (HACs) to satisfy the operational requirements of the open pit mining and materials handling industries. The relationship between conveying angle and hugging pressure by the cover belt is developed mathematically. The vertical-radius-of-curvature constraints are discussed in detail, and the constraint equations are developed. Criteria for development are established as basis for the evolutionary development of the latest sandwich belt HACs. Finally, design features of the first large-scale prototype and the latest commercial HAC units, one in coal, the other in an open pit copper mine, are described.

title: Principal Lines of Development of the Coal Industry in the Twelfth Five Year Plan Period.
authors: Shchadov M.
abstract: In the 11th FYP period 3537. 7 Mt of coal have been mined in the USSR. The annual output in 1985 was 718 Mt, i. e. 8. 7 Mt more than in 1980. Open pit mining increased by 25. 1 Mt, i. e. by 13. 2%, and its share in the total output rose from 36. 8 to 41. 1%, mainly due to the development of the Kuznetsk, Kansk-Achinsk and Ekibastuz basins. There were many shortcomings which are noted. By 1990 the plan envisages an in output in output to 780-800 Mt. Many mines will be exhausted, especially in the Donetsk basin, therefore deeper seams would have to be developed. The main increase in the output of coal is envisaged in Siberia and the Far East. By 1990 Donetsk basin is to produce 193. 3 Mt, the Pechora basin 28. 3 Mt, the Kuznetsk basin 155 Mt, and Ekibastuz basin 95-96 Mt of coal. New machinery to be developed and new facilities to be built are described.

title: Integrated open-pit planning approach and systems.
source: Mining Latin America Mineria Latinoamericana Papers Presented at the Conference Santiago 1986 Institution of Mining Metallurgy London Imm N American Publications Center Brookfield Vt
authors: Mellish M.; Preller A.H.; Tutton D.A.
abstract: Rio Tinto Corporation Zinc PLC has major open pit mining interests around the world, all of which have been planned using computerised techniques. The successful project planning and detailed operational planning of many of these has been conducted using an integrated set of computer software which has been constantly improved over the last two decades. This paper is limited to consideration of large open pits although many aspects are also applicable to other types and sizes of operation. The approach is based on a geological and mining team effort with the geological and mining aspects being considered at all times. -from Authors

title: HIGHWALL STABILITY MONITORING AT SYNCRUDE CANADA LTD. OPEN PIT MINING OPERATION.
authors: Fair A.; Isaac B.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: The Syncrude Canada Ltd. open pit mine is located approximately 40 km north of Ft. McMurray in northern Alberta. The mining operation utilizes draglines to excavate the oil sands in a single bench operation with up to 60 meter high cuts. The permit level of daily production is 129,000 barrels of synthetic crude oil, and the mine production over the 25-year mine life is in the order of 265,000 tons per day. Since production startup in June 1977, potential slope instability problems have been identified that could affect the safety of the draglines. Four main types of instability have been identified to date. Of these, shallow block slides are considered to be the most hazardous and result from the presence of adversely dipping clay beds within the upper 20 m of the highwall face. The highwall monitoring techniques currently being utilized have evolved over the past 10 years, beginning with the original Test Pit program in 1973-74. Current routine monitoring methods involve vertical slope inclinometers and visual observation. These methods are intermittent and manpower intensive. A review of currently available monitoring methods has shown that traditional surface techniques are not feasible with Syncrude's current mining configuration.

title: Selection of a Method of Open Pit Mining Protection Against Groundwater as a Function of Hydrogeological Conditions.
authors: Mrsovic D.; Radonic S.
abstract: The lignite deposit at Drmno belongs to the Kostolac Coal Basin. Extensive exploration works were completed, yielding hydrogeological relations and parameters of the Deposit. Two alternative protective solutions were proposed: well method, and a combined method (protective curtain, pre-dewatering cut, and wells). The advantage was given to the second which afforded improved operating effects and greater mining safety. Protective works were completed in three stages: preparation, opening, and full mining. The effects of the drainage system operation were monitored during all three operating stages.

title: DEVELOPMENT AND INTRODUCTION OF BOILERS BURNING KANSKACHINSK COAL AT THERMOELECTRIC POWER PLANTS.
source: Soviet Energy Technology English Translation of Energomashinostroenie
authors: Boitsov Y.; Patrikeev A.; Pavlov N.; Litinetskii V.
abstract: It is known that the fuel balance of thermoelectric power plants is undergoing major changes: the consumption of fuel oil has declined, and the proportion of solid fuel has increased, especially in eastern regions of the USSR. In recent years, the use of eastern coal in has taken on steadily increasing importance in the country's fuel-energy balance. Most of the coal beds are shallow, which creates the conditions for open pit mining using high-speed mining techniques.

title: Problems of Intensification of Transportless Burden Removal Systems.
authors: Shchadov M.
abstract: By the year 2000, more than 50% of the total coal output of the USSR is to come from open pit mining. Intensification of open pit mining can be accomplished by means of effective 'transportless' burden removal systems by means of powerful walking excavators. This also means improvement of the stability of internal dump slopes, expecially those on an inclined base. By appropriate control, explosions can be utilized to shape dumps and to stabilize their slopes. The efficiency of operation of excavators is discussed. Some recommendations are offered.

title: STATUS OF OPEN PIT MINING IN THE FEDERAL REPUBLIC OF GERMANY.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Jochums A.
abstract: The historical development of open pit mining techniques in Germany which culminated in extraordinary technical advances after the Second World War and which found widespread recognition in other countries is reported. The high degree of mechanization is obligatory in Germany to stay within economic limits: the coal is of very poor quality and ranges from 1900-2300 kcal/kg; the deposits close to the surface have been exploited and present mining activities have reached more than 350 m depth from the surface; cost of labor is in the upper most bracket comparing industrialized nations in the world. Obviously, only mechanization and to some extent automization can provide the answer.

title: ASPECTS OF ELECTRICAL EQUIPMENT FOR OPEN PIT MINING.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Streit E.
abstract: Raw materials for basic industry and power generating plants are excavated in opencast mines by two different mining methods: continuous mining, employing bucket wheel excavators; and discontinuous mining (strip mining), employing draglines and shovels. Depending upon the geological structure of the mine a combination of both methods can also be used. The main equipment-groups for opencast mining are: bucket wheel excavator, conveyor system, tripper car and spreader. Since all these equipment are driven by electric motors, an extensive range of power equipment is necessary.

title: Application Fields in Open Pit Mining, Working Technologies and Parameter Calculation of the Explosive Charges Located in Chamber Holes.
authors: Muste I.
abstract: Blasting technology with explosive charges located in chamber holes in open pit mining, its applicability, the influence of certain physical and mechanical properties of the rocks and minerals, as well as the working technology and parameter calculation of the explosive charges located in the chamber holes are presented.

title: Shock airwaves in short-delayed blasting for open pit mining
authors: Ganopol'skii M.I.; Smolii N.I.
abstract: 1. During a short delayed blasting with a delay interval between groups of 50 m/sec, a complete separation of SAW pulses produced by individual charges is observed. The weight of the charge in a group in that case can be taken equal to the weight that would be safe for an instant blasting. When the delay is 30 m/sec, the charge weight in a group should not exceed two-thirds, and for a delay of 20 m/sec a half, of the maximum admissible weight for instant blasting. These recommendations are applicable at distances not greater than 2000 m from the explosion site. 2. When blasting a linear string of charges, the delay interval at which SAW pulses are fully separated depends on the direction at which detonation propagates along the block and is defined by relations (13) and (14). With this position of charges, they should be detonated in the direction away from the object to be protected. © 1986 Plenum Publishing Corporation.

title: Conveyor technology reaches a peak.
authors: Smith A.
abstract: A review is presented on the present state of conveyor belt technology. The different types of materials and designs used are discussed: fabric belting; pipe conveying/air beds/steel; steel cord/aramid fibres; curving and incline belts. The market outlook is quoted as being bleak, but with possible demand for long distance conveying and specialised applications such as open pit mining. (A.J.)

title: APPLYING THE NEW ROBOTICS TO CONSTRUCTION AND AGRICULTURE.
source: Technical Paper Society of Manufacturing Engineers
authors: Leonard R.
abstract: Recent advances in industrial automation, artificial intelligence and autonomous planetary rovers support a synthesis of these techniques to create mobile construction robots. These machines could perform repetitive tasks such as open pit mining, hot house harvesting of vegetables or mining the moon. A developmental program which solves immediate needs is outlined.

title: Possibilities for Underground Water Quality Prediction in Areas of Open Pit Brown Coal Mining.
authors: Hummel J.; Roesch L.; Fischer R.
abstract: The article describes the development of and the computer programs' efficiencies in simulation of the underground water quality in areas of brown coal open pit mining. The drainage of the open pits and hydrology of these areas are the main components in simulations and predictions of the underground water quality to ensure the healthy water supply to the residents of these areas.

title: Bingham Open Pit Mine of Kennecott Utah Copper Division/USA.
authors: Strzodka K.
matched_open_pit_phrases: open pit mine; open pit mining
abstract: The article reviews the local geology of the copper deposits and lead-zinc paragenesis and the open pit mining at the Bingham Mine.

title: First Industrial Robots in Brown Coal Open Pit Mining.
authors: Brueckel K.
abstract: The article describes the first industrial robot used in open pit mining of brown coal in the German Democratic Republic.

title: Concepts and Working Methods in Open Pits (I).
authors: Huidu E.; Jeseu I.
abstract: Up to now, the technical literature has not clarified the problems regarding the classification and the origin of the technological concepts related to the open pit mining. The authors review the following methods: conventional, European, American, combined, and hydraulic mining as well as special open pit mining methods. Examples are also given.

title: Mining of Oil Sands in Alberta, Canada.
authors: Golosinski T.
abstract: The article describes the mining of oil sands in Alberta, Canada. Open pit mining is described. The article reviews the geology of the mine and the excavating machinery which is used.

title: EUROPEAN BROWNCOAL MINING TO-DATE AND FUTURE TRENDS.
source: Gluckauf Die Fachzeitschrift Fur Rohstoff Bergbau Und Energie
authors: Hagelueken M.
abstract: This survey deals with browncoal mining in all European countries except for the Soviet Union. For several of these - GDR, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Bulgaria and Yugoslavia - browncoal is the major primary energy form. The survey indicates that major developments are in open pit mining. The mining costs are lower and safety is better in open pit operations than in underground mining. Refs.

title: Comparison of geostatistical calculations with the results of open pit mining at the Iharkut bauxite district, Hungary: A case study
source: Journal of the International Association for Mathematical Geology
authors: Bárdossy A.; Bárdossy G.
keywords: bauxite prospecting | geostatistics | open-pit mining | reserve evaluation
abstract: Geostatistical calculations were carried out on two completely exhausted open-pit bauxite mines in the Iharkut bauxite district, Hungary. Fictitious regular drilling grids were laid on the maps, and horizontal variograms were calculated for drilling grids evaluating the bauxite surface, footwall surface, and bauxite thickness. Point kriging was carried out for all three parameters. Bauxite reserves were calculated using block kriging for bauxite thickness. The total estimation variance of the reserves has been established. Results were compared with real reserves obtained from the mine maps. © 1984 Plenum Publishing Corporation.

title: BLUE RIDGE MINING TACKLES MAJOR PROJECT.
authors: Herod B.
abstract: A major realignment of mining and quarrying operations has been undertaken during the past year at the Luttrell, Tenn. , property of Penn-Virginia Limestone Corp. For many years, the high-quality limestone strata exposed here have been extracted to supply a lime kiln and grinding plant processing uncalcined chemical grade stone. Since the end of 1983, a program has been well underway that concentrated on developing open pit operations to the point where, in 6 months, most stone would be extracted from full time quarrying. The goal was met early in 1984, well ahead of schedule, and underground workings no longer are the primary source of raw material. The open pit mining operations are described in detail.

title: Conversion from Trucks to Conveyor Belts in Open Pit Mining.
source: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Streck W.
