title: Effect of the Methods of Transportation of Large-Sized Open Pit Mine Equipment Assemblies on Time-Limits and Cost of Its Manufacture.
authors: Chernegov Y.; Daskovskii V.; Alekseev V.
abstract: An analysis is presented of the constraints on the manufacture of large-sized equipment units imposed by the limitations of road, railroad and air transportation capabilities. It is suggested that a fleet of airships be built in the USSR to transport large-sized mining equipment components.

title: AMERICAN CONGRESS ON SURVEYING AND MAPPING, FALL CONVENTION, PROCEEDINGS, 1975.
source: Proc Am Congr Surv Mapp Fall Conv
authors: Anon
abstract: Thirty-two papers, eight abstracts, and fourteen titles by various authors are presented. The topics discussed are: Terrestrial cameras, layout machines, electronic distance measuring, boundary disputes, cadastral standards, dendrology, computer mapping, reproduction techniques, aerial photography, trilateration, defense mapping, three dimensional deadload deflection, topographic information bank, surveying education, cognitive maps comparison methodology, cartographic raster scanners, ultra-precise control nets, open pit mine surveys, Doppler satellite point positioning, planned unit developments, satellite imagery, national mapping requirements, technical obsolescence, automated map compilation, cartographic data bases, slope maps, new Colorado maps, multi-dimensional analysis processing system, digital mapping, Skylab imagery, space photography, aerotriangulation, and Skylab cartography. Selected papers are indexed separately.

title: SACATON - ASARCO'S NEW COPPER MINE IN ARIZONA.
authors: Anon
abstract: American Smelting and Refining Company (Asarco) has put into operation its newest major producing copper mine, the Sacaton unit, near Case Grande in Arizona. The open pit mine and concentrator was developed by Asarco at a cost of some 40 million. Currently the mine is building up to its full planned production rate of 21,000 ton/year copper in concentrates from a mill throughput of some 9,000 ton/day. The new mine area encompasses two separate orebodies. The shallower orebody is the one now being mined, and it is planned to phase in underground operations at a later date in the deeper lying orebody. The shallow west orebody varies in thickness up to 700 ft and contains about 33. 9 million tons of porphyry-type ore averaging 0. 76% copper taking a 0. 3% cut off grade. The smaller and deeper east deposit is about 300 ft thick and contains about 14 million tons of ore grading 1. 37% copper.

title: EXPANSION PROGRAMME AT PALABORA.
authors: Anon
abstract: This article descrives a major expansion program undertaken by the Palabora mine, South Africa's most important copper producer, which will increase refined copper output to 125,000 metric tons/yr. The program is designed to enable Palabora to retain its place as one of the world's cheapest copper producers. At the new mining rate, the open pit mine will have a life of about 20 years. Plans for an underground mine to replace pit production in the 1990's are also discussed.

title: OPEN PIT MINE SURVEYS.
source: Proc Am Congr Surv Mapp Fall Conv
authors: Noice G.V.
abstract: Overview of methods used for modern open pit mine surveying in control, daily routines, slope stability, drill locations, computations, land surveying and construction is given. Control is established by resection, triangulation, or traverse based on a tight control network on the surface. A unique slope stability monitoring program is operated using an HP3805 and a Lietz TM1A. Data are shown in graphical form.

title: Justification of the Construction of a Mathematical Model of the State of Operations at an Open Pit Mine.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Cheremkhin Y.P.; Mamontova S.A.
abstract: A mathematical model of an open pit mine, relying on the method of vertical cross-sections, is developed. It permits one to obtain data on the state of the mining operations more easily, to arrange for automatic data transmission through the system until its complete destruction, to improve the precision of the determination of the volumetric indices of mining operations.

title: Experience of Designing a Skip Hoist for the Sibayskiy Open Pit Mine.
authors: Simakov P.; Dolinin K.; Khokhryakov V.; Sorokin L.; Moor A.
abstract: In 1971, the West German firm ″Siemag″ delivered a strip hoist for the Libayskiy open pit mine in Kazakhstan. The design depth of the mine is 490 m. The first stage of the hoist trench, to the depth of 180 m, is 286 m long, 14. 5 m wide, has an inclination of 39 degree , and is provided with two rail tracks, each 3070 mm wide. The hoist is equipped with two 40-ton skips. Construction problems and solutions are briefly related.

title: PINTO VALLEY, NEWEST ARIZONA COPPER PORPHYRY; MINE 40,000 DAILY TONS ORE.
authors: Anon
abstract: Pinto Valley copper mining complex has completed its start-up phase, and is now in continuous operation with the ability to exceed design throughput of 40,000 tons of ore per day. One of the larger copper mines in Arizona, Pinto valley is expected to produce 62,500 tons of copper per year, plus some molybdenum. The ore body will provide a 24-year ore reserve, based on an initial production target of 40,000 tons per day ore and 60,000 tons per day of waste. The estimated 100,000,000 project, the largest single construction project ever undertaken by Cities Service Company, includes the Pinto Valley open pit mine, a 40,000 ton per day concentrator, and a 10-mile slurry pipeline that transports a 28 percent copper concentrate slurry to a new filter plant located in Miami.

title: BLACK SEA COPPER - GEOLOGY, DRILLING DATA, PIPELINE DESIGN.
authors: Ethem M.
abstract: The Black Sea Copper Works Corporation operates several open pit and underground copper mines, flotation mills, a 50-mile long concentrate pipeline, and a 40,000 annual metric ton blister copper flash smelter along Turkey's Black Sea coast. This article has been prepared with the intention of giving more detailed information on specificc aspects of the project such as: Geology of the Murgul area (Cakmakkaya and Damar open pit mines) and Kure area (Asikoy open pit mine and Bakibaba underground mine) and vertical development chart of the Bakibaba underground mine.

title: Geology of the Biwabik Iron Formation, Dunka River area, Minnesota
authors: Bonnichsen B.
abstract: Applied geology at the Nickel Mountain nickel-silicate mine, the only producing nickel mine in the United States, in its broader aspects is little different from that where mining geology is used extensively in mining metallic mineral deposits. Important differences arise, however, because of the nature of the ore deposit, its general geology, mineralogy, structure, rock alteration, chemistry, and origin, all of which are unique in North America. The Riddle ore bodies are nickel-silicate or nickel-bearing saprolite deposits that probably represent the erosional remnants of original nickel-laterites that formed on old erosion surfaces by weathering and supergene enrichment. Much of the initial, deep, residual products of weathering now have been removed by erosion, leaving a complex blanket of decomposed, leached, and enriched saprolite that grades laterally and downward into fresh peridotite and dunite. The ore mineralization extends downward along a rather definite fracture and fault system forming nickel silicate-chalcedony (or boxwork) veins in depth. Applied geology consists of (1) the collection of geologic facts by open pit mine mapping, drilling and laboratory work, and (2) the use of geologic data in ore reserve computations, mine planning, grade control and study of special problems relating to mining, beneficiation, and smelter operation. Each of these pursuits has important and interesting ramifications owing to the characteristics of the ore deposits and the reliance that must be placedo n the geological work for successful mine operation. Grade control, which includes not only the control of nickel grade but also the selection of ores to be blended for optimum smelter performance, is perhaps the single most important aspect of applied geology and essential to the successful operation of the mine.

title: Container Pneumatic Transport at Mining Enterprises.
authors: Vasil'ev M.; Yakovenko B.; Bulgakov A.
abstract: Special characteristics and prospects of application of container pneumatic transport at open pit mines are considered. Several existing and planned systems of this kind in the USSR are described. It is concluded that pneumatic pipeline transportation with the use of containers can be advantageous in some cases in shallow open pit mines (up to 80 - 100 m deep) with the capacity of up to 10 million t p. a. to deliver a mineral to a separation factory situated at a distance of 3 - 5 km or more, with preliminary crushing at the open pit mine to a coarseness not exceeding 280 - 300 mm.

title: Procedure of Selecting and Changing Open Pit Stripping Schedules (Using Motor Transportation).
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Istomin V.; Belozerov V.
abstract: Planning of open pit mine stripping schedules is carried out with consideration of their possible restructuring in accordance with the dynamics of the mining work. Laboriousness of the multi-variable selection of schedules is reduced, thanks to an aggregate determination of the indices of operation of the motor transport and the use of the dynamic programming method.

title: DEFINITION OF DESIGN JOINTS FOR TWO-DIMENSIONAL ROCK-SLOPE ANALYSES.
authors: Steffen O.K.H.; Jennings J.E.
abstract: Analysis of the stability of rock slopes can be performed using a three-dimensional or a two-dimensional analysis. The relative importance of various factors incorporated in a two-dimensional analysis are examined and a method proposed for determining reliable average values for dip angle, dip direction and joint spacing of the joints belonging to a joint set. Observational errors in recording of dip direction and dip angles are analyzed for a joint survey carried out in an open pit mine. Results obtained from a two- and three-dimensional analysis are compared for an open pit mine slope.

title: DEVICE FOR CHARGING WET BLASTHOLES.
authors: Anon
abstract: A new Swedish invention known as the Wangu has been designed specifically for charging blastholes with Anfo and slurries. The primary purposes of the Wangu IIB unit is to protect Anfo against water in blastholes. Wangu consists of three main parts: the nose cap, the container and the thin plastic bag. The plastic bag, which can be as long as the borehole is deep, is folded and protected before use in the container. The nose cap protects the insulation of the electric wires and prevents water getting backwards in the container through the evacuation channels. These parts are intended to be used once and thereafter thrown away. The procedure for charging a borehole is exactly the same with or without Wangu. The loader is filled with explosives and charged with compressed air. From the carton of Wangu one of the correct dimensions is selected. The primer and perhaps a dynamite chargeis put in the nose cap and the Wangu attached to the filling hose. Charging can now take place normally. Results of testing the Wangu technique at the Boliden open pit mine are given.

title: Investigation of Prospective Contours of Open Pit Mines.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Sakantsev G.; Dzusova V.
abstract: A method is proposed for the determination of promising outlines of open pit mines. It is based on the method of statistical tests. The depth of an open pit mine is regarded as a random value depending on the errors of the initial data. Distribution of the random depth of open pit mines is investigated and the probable interval of excess of the real value of the depth over the calculated value is determined. Based on the investigations, recommendations are given for the determination of the promising depth and contours of an open pit mine on the surface.

title: DESIGNING THE SACATON CONCENTRATOR.
authors: Mortensen D.K.
abstract: Asarco's Sacaton unit was brought into ore production in February, 1974, at an estimated capital cost of 40 million. The open pit mine and concentrator, located 45 mi southeast of Phoenix, Ariz. , is expected to recover concentrates containing 21,000 tpy Cu. Ore reserves are currently estimated close to 48 million t at 0. 95% Cu. Sacaton's production schedule calls for the mining of about 41,000 tpd waste and 9000 tpd ore. The Sacaton mineralization contains both sulfide and oxide ores. Primary mineral constituents are chalcocite, azurite, malachite, chrysocolla, and minor amounts of silver and occasional gold. Sulfides are distinguished from oxides when more than half the total copper content is in the form of a sulfide copper mineral. While non-sulfide copper minerals are considerably less prevalent throughout the orebody, they tend to occur quite intimately with the sulfide minerals, particularly in the upper zones of the mineralization. For this reason the decision was made to treat all the ore in a flotation circuit using existing sulfidizing methods. Flowsheet of the concentrator is shown and described.

title: Determination of the Optimal Variant of Development of Mining Work with Blending Operations, Using Mathematical Modeling for Design.
authors: Shugaev I.; Zuenkova M.
abstract: A method is presented for matehamtical modeling of a deposit and geometric elements of an open pit mine. Calculation of stage-by-stage volumes of mining work and of qualitative indices by means of a computer, and in different variants, is carried out. A mathematical model of the process of ore mining is presented. Based on it, an optimal variant of the development of the mining work with blending operations is selected for project design.

title: HOW TO PLAN OPEN PIT WORKSHOP AND SERVICE FACILITIES.
authors: Rau R.
abstract: Development of an open pit mine is very expensive; therefore, planning must be thorough. The main criterion is always the highest possible machine availability. In the implementation of the above criterion, paper discusses: planning of workshops and service bays; design of a fuel and lubricants tank farm; wash bays; as well as service of light vehicle and trucks.

title: Methods of Combating Deformations of Clayey Soils at Open Pit Mines in Subcarpathian Area.
authors: Pevzner M.; Androsova O.; Belen'kii P.; Valer'yanova L.; Ostashkova I.; Reutskii V.
abstract: Methods of strengthening of open pit mine edges and slopes of dumps consisting of clayey soils, developed at the yavorov sulfur mining combine, are described. The method consists of the creation of zones of increased hardness with the so-called ″soil piles″ . These are cylindrical soil piles hardened by means of a constant electric field or a composition binder material.

title: Thorium Veins in the United States
authors: Staatz M.
abstract: 50 Thorium-bearing veins present the largest known potential resource of thorium in the United States in deposits that can be easily exploitable in the near future. Veins of this type are principally of quartz, feldspar, and iron oxides and are known from at least 13 widely scattered areas: extending from Montana to California and New Mexico. Veins in these areas range in length from a few feet to at least 5,000 feet and in thickness from thin seams to 50 feet. Many are 200 to 600 feet long and 0. 5 to 3. 0 feet thick. Thorite is by far the most abundant thorium mineral. Monazite is also commonly present and in a few veins there is brockite and allanite. The thorium content of samples from various veins ranges from 0. 001 to 21. 0 percent ThO//2. The rare-earth content of the veins is substantial and, depending on demand, may be economically as important as the thorium. Although rare earths commonly are present in the same minerals as thorium, there may be little correlation between thorium and rare-earth content in a sample.

title: Experimental with High-Pressure, Down-Hole Rock Drill at the ″Erzberg″ Iron Mine in Austria.
source: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Klobassa O.
abstract: Paper describes the development of the large diameter drilling of blastholes at the iron open pit mine ″Erzberg″ in Austria, with particular emphasis on the introduction of the high-pressure, down-hole percussive drills. The technique is successful wherever the tectonic conditions and hardness of rock do not permit an economical rotary drilling. The anticipated increase of drilling rate and of bit life have been achieved. Investigation of abatement of dust by addition of water to compressed air is being carried on.

title: TRUCK SERVICING AND MAINTENANCE PROGRAM AT KAISER'S EAGLE MOUNTAIN MINE.
authors: Olson E.
abstract: Open pit mine is located about 80 mi east of Palm Springs, Cal. in an arid area with summer temperatures commonly exceeding 120 F. It produces hematite ore at a rate of between 35 and 60-million tpy with a stripping ratio of 4:1. There are about 75-100 plus capacity haulage trucks for ore and waste employed. Haulage distances vary between 4 and 6 mi for ore and are about 1 mi for waste. Paper describes the truck, service and maintenance program that contributed to a significant increase of : overall truck productivity; average life of diesel engines, transmissions and tires.

title: All-Purpose Ventilation Jet Unit for Deep Open Pit Mines.
authors: Bukhman Y.; Simakov P.; Gal'tsev V.
abstract: An all-purpose ventilation jet unit based on the latest model of the turbojet engine RD-3M-500 motor truck, is described. It is marked by increased output, flexibility of control of the jet trajectory, universality and self-contained operation. The flow of air in the jet is 298 kg/s at the initial speed of 455 m/s. The capacity of the unit is 40,000 h. p. and its size is 9 multiplied by 4 multiplied by 4 m. The unit is suitable for an open pit mine 200 m deep, 1000 m in diameter.

title: Effect of Open Pit Geometry on the Parameters of a Free Stream.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Ushakov K.; Silaev V.; Starostin I.
abstract: It is found that parameters of an air stream carrying out natural ventilation of an open pit mine depend on the geometry of the excavated space. On the basis of experimental and natural investigations, relations are proposed that permit determination of the quantity of air taking part in the ventilation of the open pit. Its depth and the slope angle of the leeward side are taken into account. The formulas derived make it possible to calculate more precisely natural ventilation in an open pit mine, taking into account its geometry and the specific features of the development of a free stream in the pit.

title: Environmental impact study. A tool for sound mineral development
authors: Ackerman D.H.
abstract: As a result of some 8 years of exploratory work the American Metal Climax Co. has ascertained that copper-molybdenum deposit located in northwest Wyoming, near an old mining camp of Kiroin has sufficient Cu-Mo mineralization to warrant its consideration as an open pit mined. Paper discusses the scope of an environmental impact study which will have to be completed with cooperation of local authorities before a final decision is taken. Some more significant elements of the study are: reclamation of the vegetation at the altitude of open pit from 8,000 to 11,000 ft; waste and tailings disposal in a high, narrow valley; water pollution by mine drainage and ore treatment plant; housing etc.

title: Influence of Climate on the Organization and Planning of Mining Works at an Open Pit Mine.
authors: Shpanskii O.; Kiseleva E.; Ovodenko B.; Maslov V.
abstract: A method of calendar planning of monthly productivity of open-pit equipment and of the monthly volumes of drilling and blasting and excavation work, taking into account changes in the climatic conditions in the course of a year, is described. This method is appropriate for severe arctic conditions.

title: Overvoltages with Single-Phase Grounding in 6-10 kV Networks with an Insulated Neutral Wire.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenij I Energeticheskikh Ob Edinenij Sng Energetika
authors: Volotkovskii S.; Kur'yan A.; Gorbunov Y.
abstract: The problem of the influence of inter-phase capacitance on overvoltage values in conditions of single-phase grounding in networks with an insulated neutral wire is considered. Methods are presented for determining the magnitude of inter-phase capacitance for the limitation of overvoltages in conditions of single-phase grounding. The influence of the limitation of overvoltages on the operation of protections against single-phase groundings is analyzed. Application in open pit mine electric networks is mentioned.

title: Calculation Basis for a New Method of Recording the Indices of the Transportation Systems of Open Pit Mines Using Automobile Transport.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Selyanin V.; Fabrovskii E.
abstract: A new method of recording the productivity of open pit mine dump trucks is considered. It is based on interrelation between the pressure in the hydraulic system of the tilting arrangement and the weight of the transported rock. The main design principles of the method are presented and the devices worked out on the basis of the stated principle are described.

title: Determination of a Rational Direction of Deepening an Open-Pit Mine by Graphs of Isolines of Specific Return.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Zagoruiko G.
abstract: A method is set forth for determining a rational direction of deepening an open pit mine by using the example of a deposit of silicate nickel ores in the Urals, characterized by a variety of forms and condition of bedding of ore bodies. The problem is solved by the method of variants in two stages. Plane problems are solved by means of geometric mine graphs of isolines of specific return. The spatial problem is solved by means of a longitudinal section of the pit on which the lines of the transverse sections are imposed, indicating the gain at the level of the calculated horizons when lowering the mining operations in accordance with the rational direction found for the plane problem. The variants of the pit deepening are evaluated by the summary reduced gain, taking into account the factor of time and the capital investment efficiency coefficient.

title: Automatic Stabilization of the Vibration Level of the Drilling Machines.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Marasanov Y.; Borovkov V.; Shtrombasser R.; Kovin V.
abstract: A new principle of designing a systen of automatic control of the rasp drilling process is explained. The permissible (according to industrial hygiene norms) level of vibrations of the drilling machines is adopted as control criterion. In a particular case, the system can be adjusted to any capacity of the machine. The system realizes the most effective method of removing a machine from the vibration zone. Industrial tests of the system, carried out at the main open pit mine of the Kachkanarskig ore dressing combine, and maintenance experience have proved its efficiency and reliability.

title: Synthesis of Optimal Technological Schemes of Open-Pit Mine Workings.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Lepilkin N.; Pinchuk A.; Trid I.
abstract: An attempt is made to formulate and to outline the ways of solving the problem of synthesis of optimal technological schemes of open pit mine workings using continuous action technology. On the basis of an analysis of the features of some of the main such technological schemes, a series of structural parameters are established, defining the class of the discussed technological schemes in an identical way. Introduction of structural parameters enables the synthesis problem to be reduced to that of nonlinear integer-value programming. A method is proposed for the determination of the optimum values of the parameters, based on the principle of self-instruction.

title: Field of Application of the Promising Types of Transportation in Deep Open Pit Mines.
source: Izvestiya Vysshikh Uchebnykh Zavedenii Gornyi Zhurnal
authors: Novozhilov M.; Bondar S.; Drizhenko A.
abstract: Dependence of the parameters of the working zone of an open pit mine, its productive capacity and the main technical and economic indices of the handling and transport equipment on the depth of the working zone and the plane size of the pit are considered. It is established that the dimensions of the pit and its working zone exert essential influence on the productive capacity and volume of technological shipments. For open pits of different length and form, the fields of application and parameters of promising types of transportation are determined.

title: BOUGAINVILLE.
authors: Anon
abstract: Open pit mine and concentrator built by Conzinc Riotinto of Australia and New Broken Hill Cons. at a total cost of 426-million (see Ei 1970 p 719 Abs. #09484 and 12923) scheduled to mill 90,000 tpd of ore containing 0. 65% Cu and 0. 02 oz Au/ton started operation 6 mo. ahead of schedule. Issue contains monographic description of the mining and milling operations, inclusive of listing the equipment employed. Detailed flow sheets of the concentrator are shown. Concentrate is pumped through a 6 in. od pipeline over a distance of 17 mi to a filter and drying plant at the sea shore.

title: FUNCTIONAL OPTIMIZATION OF OPEN PIT MINE DESIGN UTILIZING GEOLOGIC CROSS-SECTION DATA.
authors: Luke K.
abstract: A computer programming system has been devised to assist in open pit mine design planning. This system operates upon data generated for cross sections in the mine plan, and parallels present manual methods used in mine design, resulting in a minimal communications barrier between the mine planner and the computer. Input data for each cross section includes geologic interpretation and mine design parameters such as wall angles, bench heights, berm widths, and ramping system. The program will optimize the design of each cross section to give minimum stripping at any desired ore reserve level.

title: GRADIENT CONTROL AT AN OPEN-CAST MINE
source: J Inst Mine Survey S Afr
authors: MOBSBY CM
abstract: Article examines methods used for gradient control in an open pit mine with particular reference to an adjustable gradient indicator.

title: MARQUESADO, SPAIN'S PREMIER IRON ORE MINE FORGES AHEAD
authors: ANON
abstract: This large, producing 2 million tons/yr of hematite ore, open pit mine, located in southeastern part of Spain presents an interest in that it had switched from shovel excavator, rail transportation system to trackless method employing rubber tired front-end- leaxers and dumpers. Proved reserves are estimated to amount to 50 million tons of ore, assaying between 53 and 57% Fe. The shipping port at Almeria is 60 mi distant from the mine.

title: AITIK. WORLD'S FIRST THIRD GENERATION OPEN PIT COPPER MINE IN LAPLAN
authors: WYLLIE RJM
abstract: In Swedish Lapland about 30 mi north of Arctic Circle, the Boliden Company is producing 2,000,000 t/yr of copper ore, assaying 0. 5%Cu, from its Aitik open pit mine under harsh climatic condition. The sub-outcrop of the ore body, covered by glacial moraine overburden 6 to 40 ft thick, is about 6500 ft long and from 165 to 600 ft wide dipping about 25//0. Highly mechanised and automated mining and milling operations produce an overall productivity per employee of 20,000 t/yr thus assuring a profitable operation. Measures taken to allay cold weather problems are discussed.

title: PHELPS DODGE UNVEILS TYRONE. NEWEST SOUTHWEST COPPER MINE
authors: ARGALL G.
abstract: Located in Grant County, NMex, open pit mine is designed for 25,000 tpd of ore, assaying about 0. 80% Cu, thus adding 55,000 tons/yr of copper and solidifying Phelps Dodge Corp position as second largest copper producer in the United States. The primarily sulfidic orebody is located in a broken or faulted block in quartz monzonite stock, intruded into Precambrian granite. Mine is unusual in that, during its life, re will be hauled downhill to the mill. Mining is done with six electric shovels with 10 cu yd bucket. Ore and waste are hauled by fleet of 27 LectraHaul 85-ton trucks.

title: Metamorphic aspects of the magnetite-hematite deposit at Benson Mines, New York
authors: Hagni R.; Masiello R.; Tumialan P.
abstract: The relationships between the iron oxide, sulfide, and silicate minerals were deter-mined in more than 500 polished sections and about 200 thin sections of Benson magnetite-hematite ore and host gneiss. The universal stage was utilized to determine the orienta-tion of those opaque ore minerals that have a unique physical direction and the determined ore abric was compared with that of biotite and sillimanite in the host gneiss. Rims of garnet, sillimanite, and plagioclase about the iron oxide and some sulfide grains, together with poikiloblastically enclosed iron oxide and sulfide grains in garnet and sillimanite, indicate that some of the opaque minerals were present at the time of formation of those silicate minerals. Similar microtextures show that part of the sulfide minerals, pyrite, pyrrhotite, and chalcopyrite, were present at the time of iron oxide crystallization. Other grains of those sulfide minerals form later veinlets that transgress the silicate, oxide, and earlier sulfide grains. ?etrofabric diagrams for the basal cleavage of biotite grains in thin sections of oriented specimens collected from the Benson open pit mine exhibit well the foliation that may be observed in the mine; the c-axes of sillimanite crystals commonly are aligned in a direction of lineation within the biotite foliation plane. ?etrofabric diagrams for the long axes of ovate ore grains exhibit more scatter than those of biotite and sillimanite, but the axes of such grains exhibit a tendency to lie within the biotite foliation plane and to be relatively concentrated in the direction of sillimanite lineation. This tendency is greatest in the more strongly foliated and lineated specimens. The writers interpret the ore microscopic, petrographic, and petrofabric results to indicate that metamorphism has played an important role in the development of the present nature of the Benson ores. © 1969 Society of Economic Geologists, Inc.

title: DESIGN OF OPEN PIT MINE SLOPES
authors: RANA MH; BULLOCK WD
abstract: Surface mines operating in Canada's Sub-Arctic have developed slope design adapted to geological and climatic conditions of region; geology of Labrador Trough is discussed; samples of Ruth Slate and Quartzite, these being the two rock types which had been most in evidence in past failures, have been subjected to triaxial compression tests; developed in Soviet Union in 1966, L. F. Savkov's equation for determining slope stability has been applied to delineate potential failure planes for different slope angles with given slope height; practical conclusions are drawn.

title: Applied geology at the Nickel Mountain Mine, Riddle, Oregon
authors: CHACE FM; CUMBERLIDGE JT; CAMERON WL; VAN NORT SD
abstract: Nature of nickelsilicate ore deposit, its general geology, mineralogy, structure, rock alteration, chemistry, and origin, are all unique in North America. Applied geology activity consists of collection of geologic facts by open pit mine mapping, drilling and laboratory work, and use of geologic data in ore reserve computations, mine planning, grade control and study of special problems relating to mining, beneficiation, and smelter operation. Of these, nickel grade control is perhaps most important single aspect.

title: Research on a novel dust control method for open-pit mine truck transportation based on airflow regulation
authors: Qiao Y.; Liu J.; Gu D.; Lin M.; Jueraiti M.; Yu J.; Lin C.; Jin L.
keywords: Airflow field | Airflow regulation | Dust control | Open-pit mine | Road dust
abstract: Dust emissions from truck haul roads are the primary source of particulate pollution in open-pit mines. Current dust suppression methods mainly rely on water spraying and chemical suppressants, which generally suffer from high water consumption, high operating costs, and poor environmental adaptability. To address this issue, this study analyzed the airflow field characteristics around trucks on haul roads and their relationship with dust concentration distribution using numerical simulation. The results reveal that the wake vortex airflow and local negative pressure behind the truck are key factors driving the generation and dispersion of road dust. Based on this finding, a dust control method using airflow regulation was proposed, and its mechanism and effectiveness were systematically analyzed. The results show that the airflow regulation method effectively reorganizes the turbulent airflow behind the truck, creating an ordered flow pattern that tends to align with the ambient wind direction. This significantly reduces both the intensity and size of the wake vortex, and decreases the maximum extent of the recirculation zone from 14 m (without regulation) to 4 m behind the truck, thereby effectively mitigating the unfavorable flow conditions that promote dust generation and dispersion. Consequently, the airflow regulation method significantly reduces the dispersion of high-concentration dust during truck operation. It confines over 90% of dust particles below the pedestrian breathing zone height and reduces the peak dust concentrations in the driver's and pedestrian's breathing zones from 12.60 mg/m<sup>3</sup> and 11.02 mg/m<sup>3</sup> to 0.18 mg/m<sup>3</sup> and 3.74 mg/m<sup>3</sup>, respectively, achieving effective control of road dust from truck haulage in open-pit mines. The proposed airflow-regulated dust control method offers a new technical approach for efficiently controlling dust emissions from truck haul roads in open-pit mines.

title: Spatially partitioned identification of geological features on open-pit slopes via morphological cross-image reconstruction and quantitative feature analysis: rock veins as a case study
source: Measurement Journal of the International Measurement Confederation
authors: Hao-bin X.; Yong Z.; Wen-jing N.; Guang-liang F.; Guo-shao S.; Zhen-hua Q.
keywords: Cross-image reconstruction | Machine vision | Open-pit slope | Rock vein | Trace-length quantification
abstract: This study presents an integrated workflow for reconstructing and quantitatively characterizing rock veins in large-scale, high-resolution images of open-pit slopes, where block-based recognition may cause topological discontinuities. The main contribution is an endpoint-circle-based reconstruction strategy integrated with established morphological preprocessing to reconnect fractured rock vein segments across and within sub-images. Morphological closing and connected-component filtering are first applied to remove noise, fill small defects, and smooth the recognized masks, enabling extraction of continuous rock vein skeletons. Endpoint-circle-based connection criteria, together with a local circular search and multi-endpoint collaborative matching mechanism, are then used to resolve many-to-many correspondence in endpoint-dense regions and reconstruct fractured rock veins across and within sub-images. Rock vein trace lengths are subsequently quantified using a field-calibrated pixel-to-dimension relationship. Field verification at an open-pit mine in southern China showed a reconstruction accuracy of 86.7%, representing an improvement of 46.7%–60.1% over conventional ant colony optimization and Dijkstra algorithms, while computational efficiency increased by approximately threefold. The intraclass correlation coefficient between extracted and field-measured trace lengths reached 0.988, with an average relative error of 11.2%. The proposed method provides an efficient approach for extracting two-dimensional rock vein geometry from open-pit slope images, supplying basic geometric information for subsequent slope-structure analysis.

title: With one foot in the future – Situating autonomous systems in mining through communities of practice
authors: Lund E.; Nygren M.
keywords: Autonomous systems | Communities of practice | Organisational change | Technology implementation
abstract: Purpose – This article explores how autonomous systems are socially situated in the mining industry through the lens of Communities of Practice. It examines how learning, coordination and shared meaning-making unfold when new technology is introduced, and how implementation extends beyond technical deployment to include social and organisational processes. Design/methodology/approach – The study draws on a qualitative case study of a Swedish open-pit mine where an autonomous haulage system was implemented. Wenger's (2008) Communities of Practice framework was used as a sensitising concept to analyse empirical material, focusing on mutual engagement, joint enterprise and shared repertoire in everyday work practices. Findings – The analysis shows how community members co-constructed new work practices, formed collective interpretations of the technology, and engaged in relational work to legitimise the system within the wider organisation. Successful implementation was found to depend not only on technical performance but also on social processes of meaning-making, identity formation, and the negotiation of organisational change. Practical implications – By foregrounding the social dimensions of technological change, the study suggests that organisations introducing autonomous systems should support collaborative learning and provide spaces for shared meaning-making, thereby increasing the likelihood of successful implementation. Originality/value – The paper contributes to research on technology, work, and organisation by highlighting the situated and practice-based nature of technological implementation. It underscores the value of attending to communities of practice when investigating how new technology gains traction and relevance in complex organisational settings.

title: A point cloud segmentation method for open-pit mines considering multi-scale local features
authors: Li X.; Dai H.; Li F.; Hao C.
keywords: Downsampling | Improved PointNet++ | Open-pit mine | Point cloud data | Semantic segmentation
abstract: Semantic segmentation of point clouds is essential for intelligent monitoring, terrain understanding, and autonomous driving in open-pit mines. However, large-scale coverage, complex topography, non-uniform point distribution, class imbalance, and noise pose great challenges to effective feature learning, leading to insufficient segmentation accuracy in existing methods. To tackle these problems, this paper proposes a multi-scale local feature enhanced point cloud segmentation method for open-pit mines. In preprocessing, a collaborative strategy combining global coarse sampling, structure extraction, block-wise sampling, and merging optimization is proposed using Voxel Grid Sampling (VGS) and Farthest Point Sampling (FPS) to efficiently simplify point clouds. Based on PointNet++, a Multi-Scale Local Feature Enhancement (MS-LFE) module is constructed by introducing Boundary-aware Local Twin-attention (BLT) and Boundary-aware Gating Unit (BGU), which improves the Set Abstraction (SA) module and strengthens the perception of geometric details and boundaries. Weighted cross-entropy is adopted to stabilize training and alleviate class imbalance. Experiments are conducted on two open-pit mine datasets. On Mine 1, the proposed method achieves 93.88% OA and 85.17% mIoU, with IoUs of 94.40%, 86.20%, and 74.91% for bench, slope, and benchline. On the more complex Mine 2, mIoU is improved by 6.28% over PointNet++. Compared with PointNet, KPConv, and RandLA-Net, mIoU is increased by 13.49%, 3.67%, and 1.71%, respectively, especially for the boundary class. Ablation studies and visualization verify the effectiveness of each component. The method generates continuous boundaries and reduces misclassification, showing strong capability in complex mine scenes.

title: Landslide Risk Early Warning in Open-Pit Mines: An Integrated Framework Combining Fuzzy Comprehensive Evaluation and Intelligent Prediction
authors: Bai J.; Mehmood M.; Zhang Z.; Nie W.; Qin Z.; Yao Y.
keywords: Complete ensemble empirical mode decomposition with adaptive noise (CEEMDAN) | EXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) residual compensation | Fuzzy mathematics | Landslide monitoring and early warning | Open-pit mine | Particle-whale optimization algorithm (PWOA)
abstract: Landslide hazards in open-pit mines pose a critical threat to personnel safety and sustainable resource exploitation, underscoring the necessity for accurate and proactive early-warning systems. Accordingly, this study constructs an integrated analytical framework that couples multi-level fuzzy comprehensive evaluation with intelligent prediction, explicitly designed to capture the nonlinear interdependencies among heterogeneous risk factors. The evaluation model is structured across three criterion layers-deformation monitoring, external influencing factors, and management practices, supported by nine subordinate indicators whose weights are rigorously determined, thereby facilitating effective fusion of multi-source hazard information and fuzzy discrimination of risk levels. Within this hierarchy, slope displacement emerges as the principal indicator, and its accurate forecasting is essential for enhancing early-warning reliability. Therefore, a hybrid prediction architecture integrating Complete Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition with Adaptive Noise (CEEMDAN), Sample Entropy (SE), a hybrid Particle-Whale Optimization Algorithm (PWOA), Convolutional Long Short-Term Memory (ConvLSTM), and eXtreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) is developed to predict slope displacement with high precision. This integration forms the CEEMDAN-SE-PWOA-ConvLSTM-XGBoost hybrid model. Predicted displacement data, when embedded alongside real-time monitoring inputs into the evaluation framework, yield an integrated early-warning strategy of “intelligent prediction-multi-parameter evaluation.” This system enables continuous updates of monitoring data, dynamic threshold adjustment, and adaptive optimization, ultimately establishing a self-evolving monitoring and early-warning mechanism. The proposed approach provides a robust scientific and technical foundation for stability assessment and risk prevention in complex open-pit mine environments.

title: Ground Vibration and Air Overpressure Prediction Caused by Blasting Operations in a Gneiss Quarry Using a Gene Expression Programming Approach
source: Journal of Vibration Engineering and Technologies
authors: da Cunha Meireles A.; Barbieri N.; Fiorentin L.D.; de Lima K.F.
keywords: AOp | Gene expression programming | Multiple linear regression | PPV | Rock blasting | Shock waves
abstract: Introduction: Rock blasting is a fundamental operation in mining and civil engineering, but it generates ground vibrations and air overpressure that can affect nearby structures and communities. Among these effects, peak particle velocity (PPV) and air overpressure (AOp) are commonly used indicators for environmental control and regulatory compliance. Traditional empirical predictors, such as scaled-distance relationships, have been widely used for their simplicity and ease of interpretation. However, these approaches often rely on strong assumptions about the functional form of the relationship between blasting parameters and vibration response, which may not adequately capture complex site-specific conditions. In recent years, data-driven techniques have been increasingly explored to improve predictive performance. Linear statistical models, such as Multiple Linear Regression (MLR), offer interpretability but may suffer from multicollinearity and limited flexibility for modeling nonlinear interactions. Alternatively, evolutionary algorithms such as Gene Expression Programming (GEP) can generate explicit nonlinear equations without requiring predefined model structures, potentially capturing more complex relationships. Despite these advances, comparative studies of interpretable linear models and symbolic regression approaches remain limited, particularly when both PPV and AOp are considered simultaneously using field data from real blasting operations. This study aims to compare the performance of MLR and GEP in predicting PPV and AOp using a limited dataset of 31 detonations at a gneiss open-pit mine in southern Brazil. The objective is not to develop generalized predictive models but to evaluate how different modeling paradigms perform under data-constrained conditions and to assess their respective advantages and limitations in practical applications. The dataset showed notable dispersion in the response variables, as indicated by statistical measures such as standard deviation and the observed spread of the data distribution. Materials and Methods: A methodology was proposed to predict the physical parameters associated with PPV and AOp. An engineering seismograph monitored shockwaves over a three-year period. The seismograph reports obtained were evaluated using SPSS Statistics IBM and Microsoft Excel to develop MLR models, and via GeneXproTools 5.0 to construct a shock wave prediction model using GEP. The MLR approach initially included multiple predictors but required variable reduction because of multicollinearity, resulting in simplified models primarily based on scaled distance relationships. In contrast, GEP was used to derive explicit nonlinear equations without prior assumptions about the functional form. Results: Model performance was evaluated using the coefficient of determination (R²) and error metrics. For PPV prediction, the MLR and GEP models achieved R² values of 0.795 and 0.903, respectively. For AOp, the corresponding R² values were 0.557 and 0.824. The results indicate that GEP provided improved fitting capability for the available dataset, particularly for AOp. Conclusions: GEP produced nonlinear explicit equations that achieved a higher goodness-of-fit than MLR, particularly for AOp prediction. Although GEP demonstrated improved performance, the results must be interpreted cautiously. The limited number of observations, the absence of external validation, and the site-specific nature of the data limit the robustness and transferability of the proposed models. Therefore, the main contribution of this study is an exploratory comparison of linear and symbolic regression approaches under constrained data conditions. Future work should focus on larger datasets, independent validation, and incorporating additional physically meaningful variables to improve model reliability and generalization.

title: Evaluating 2D and 3D slope stability in a complex open-pit mine: a CAD-based numerical study
authors: Hamzaban M.T.; Kanoundoust S.; Geraili Mikola R.
keywords: 2D versus 3D slope analysis comparison | 3D slope stability analysis | CAD-based geotechnical modeling | FLAC3D numerical modeling | Open-pit mine geomechanics
abstract: Accurate slope stability assessment is essential for the safe and economical operation of deep open-pit mines, especially in areas with complex geological and hydrological conditions. While two-dimensional (2D) analyses are still widely used in engineering practice, they struggle to accurately reflect true failure mechanisms in three-dimensional (3D) environments. This study offers a comprehensive comparison between 2D and 3D slope stability analyses specifically for the Sungun open-pit copper mine in Iran. A detailed 3D base model was developed using Rhinoceros and Griddle to accurately represent the pit geometry, geotechnical domains, and groundwater surface. This model facilitated the generation of a hexahedral mesh for FLAC<sup>3D</sup> simulations and allowed for the extraction of multiple 2D cross-sections for FLAC analyses in various directions. The 3D model predicted a rotational failure mechanism, yielding a global safety factor (FS<sup>3D</sup>) of 1.285, which was validated against field observations of tension cracks and active slope deformation. In contrast, the comparative 2D analyses produced varying results based on the orientation and location of the sections, with FS<sup>2D</sup> values ranging from 1.04 to 4.11. While some 2D sections approximated FS<sup>3D</sup> values reasonably, none accurately captured both the geometry and extent of the failure surface. Notably, sections aligned with the primary direction of displacement (North-South) yielded the most representative results. These findings underscore the limitations of relying solely on 2D analyses for pit slope design in geologically complex settings. The integration of 3D numerical modeling with CAD-based geometry management is crucial for achieving reliable slope stability assessments and for minimizing design uncertainties in large-scale mining projects.

title: Constraints from C-O-Sr isotopes on the origin of carbonate minerals in coal-bearing sequences from the Dong Open-pit Mine, Ningwu coal field, Shanxi, China
authors: Di S.; Dai S.; Spiro B.; Delgado A.; French D.; Graham I.; Liu J.; Zhang S.
keywords: C isotope | Coal-hosted carbonates | Fluid sources | O isotope | Sr isotope
abstract: Carbonate minerals are ubiquitous in coal and can serve as long-term records of peat depositional environments, compositions of sediment-source rocks, paleo-climates, and alteration during coalification and subsequent epigenetic processes, as well as water–rock interactions associated with fluid movements. Given that the origins of carbonate minerals in coal remain poorly understood, this paper examined the isotopes of C-O-Sr in carbonate minerals from the No. 4 coal of the Dong Open-pit Mine, Ningwu coal field, Shanxi Province, China. The results show that carbonate (calcite and/or ankerite) mineralization within the coal is dominantly epigenetic. The C–O–Sr isotope data are consistent with a mixed-source model, in which carbonate precipitation involved isotopically light carbon derived from organic matter decarboxylation, meteoric groundwater–rock interaction, and a possible contribution from underlying Ordovician limestones. In contrast, carbonate mineralization in the overlying roof, underlying floor and interbedded parting layers reflects a combination of syngenetic and epigenetic processes. The low δ<sup>18</sup>O values indicate precipitation from <sup>18</sup>O-depleted meteoric waters, whereas the <sup>87</sup>Sr/<sup>86</sup>Sr signatures indicate interaction with carbonate-bearing strata, potentially including the underlying Ordovician limestones. However, the current dataset does not uniquely resolve the relative proportions of these possible sources, and additional contributions from dolomite, groundwater-mediated leaching, and adjacent strata cannot be excluded. These observations constrain the fluid sources of carbonate minerals in the coal-bearing succession, while indicating that the involvement of the underlying Ordovician limestones should be regarded as plausible rather than definitive.

title: Detection-guided stereo ranging framework for 2.5-D obstacle measurement on mining haul trucks
authors: Guo H.; Yin J.; Feng Z.
keywords: Detection-guided stereo matching | Haul-truck obstacle ranging | Measurement uncertainty | Open-pit mining | Semi-global block matching
abstract: Accurate obstacle ranging is essential for haul-truck safety in open-pit mines, where dust, illumination changes, weak textures, and large target-scale variation degrade detection and stereo matching. This study presents an in-domain offline detection-guided stereo framework for 2.5-D obstacle localization. It couples Detection-Informed Stereo YOLO (DIS-YOLO), a lightweight YOLOv11n-based detector, with a customized Semi-Global Block Matching (SGBM) variant that uses detections to restrict regions of interest, adapt disparity-search parameters, fuse Census/color/gradient costs, and refine valid disparities at object measurement points. Experiments were mainly conducted using recorded stereo data from one primary open-pit mine, with an additional small external-mine subset used for limited transfer validation. DIS-YOLO achieved 92.1% mAP@0.5. Across 20 test distances from 5 to 100 m, the proposed pipeline reduced mean absolute error (MAE) from 1.943 to 1.006 m relative to original SGBM. On 240 paired valid-output real-scene measurements, MAE decreased from 1.47 to 0.80 m, a 45.8% relative reduction with a bootstrap 95% confidence interval of 41.9%–49.6%. The distance-wise uncertainty budget yielded standard uncertainties of 0.04–1.31 m and expanded uncertainties of 0.07–2.63 m (k = 2). The results support in-domain offline validation and preliminary external-mine transfer evidence; broader cross-site, cross-camera, underground, and closed-loop deployment still require larger multi-site validation.

title: Dust dispersion and prevention in deep concave open-pit coal mines
authors: Long Y.; Song Z.; Wu L.; Wen Y.
keywords: Dust control measures | Dust dispersion pattern | Dust generation mechanism | Numerical simulation | Open-pit coal mine
abstract: To address dust diffusion in deep concave open-pit coal mines, this study examined Fushun East open-pit coal mine in Liaoning Province, a deep concave open-pit coal mine. Employing theoretical analyses, field testing, numerical simulation, and experimental validation, we comprehensively investigated the mechanisms of dust generation, migration, and effective control strategies, revealing the mine dust migration patterns and providing practical foundations for dust control systems. Based on field measurements, road transportation was identified as the primary source of dust emissions. Atmospheric flow within the deep concave open-pit mine follows a complex recirculation pattern. Using COMSOL numerical simulation software, a fluid-solid coupling dust dispersion model was established based on the scale conditions of deep concave open-pit mines, revealing the formation mechanism of negative pressure dust accumulation zones induced by the inclination angle of the pit’s lateral slopes, while the pit’s shape illustrated dust migration trajectories. The air flow inside the pit was vortex-induced, primarily concentrated near the intake air areas of the pit. The study simulated air flow and dust particle trajectories in the flow field around mining vehicles, determining that the air disturbance range during vehicle movement extends to 1.5 times the vehicle’s volume. It is found that under low-speed driving conditions, dust dispersion behavior is mainly controlled by external wind speed and direction, with relative speed playing a dominant role in affecting the dust dispersion rate around mining vehicles. This in-depth study of dust sources, generation mechanisms, dispersion patterns, and precise control measures in deep concave open-pit coal mines has significant implications for achieving coordinated development between economic benefits and environmental protection.

title: Blasting fragmentation recognition technology for intelligent mining: A synergistic application of deep learning and binocular vision
source: International Journal of Coal Science and Technology
authors: Xu Y.; Tao M.; Liu Y.; Huang L.; Xiang G.; Li X.
keywords: Binocular vision | Blasting fragmentation | Deep learning | Dynamic region of interest (DROI) | Fully automatic recognition
abstract: Against the backdrop of intelligent mining development, precise control of blasting fragmentation has become a critical factor in improving production efficiency and achieving energy conservation. However, existing fragmentation recognition methods rely largely on cumbersome manual operations, making it difficult to efficiently and accurately evaluate blasting performance. This study proposes an intelligent recognition method for blasting fragmentation to address limitations such as limited fragment samples, complex operational procedures, and low segmentation quality. A binocular camera is fixedly deployed to automatically capture images of rock fragments transported by passing trucks, and a You Only Look Once version 8 (YOLOv8) instance segmentation model is constructed to identify the fragments loaded on the trucks. The accuracy of fragment recognition and size estimation under dynamic conditions is validated through laboratory dynamic scanning experiments and field tests conducted in an open-pit mine. Experimental results demonstrate that the YOLOv8 segmentation model achieved a rock fragment recognition accuracy of 94.4%, with 94.12% of fragment size estimations exhibiting an accuracy exceeding 90%. To address the challenges posed by shadows and environmental disturbances under field conditions, a dynamic region of interest (DROI) method is proposed to accurately localize fragmented rocks within the truck bed. Comparative analysis against conventional image processing software reveals that the proposed method exhibits higher accuracy in fragment recognition, along with strong adaptability.

title: Analysis of a rock slope instability mechanism combining wedge and circular failure in a soft rock mass
source: International Journal of Coal Science and Technology
authors: Yuan S.; Ding B.; Guan K.; Pérez-Rey I.; Li T.; Alejano L.R.
keywords: Combined failure mechanisms | Slope stability | Soft rock | Wedge-circular failure
abstract: One of the most common failure mechanisms in rock slope stability analysis is wedge failure, where sliding of an element of a rock mass occurs along two pre-existing discontinuities, whose intersection daylights on the slope face. The kinematic analysis of this mechanism prescribes that failure can only take place when the intersection of both discontinuities at stake dips less than the slope face. However, when the intersection line of a wedge dips slightly more than the slope face, a modified version of this mechanism can occur. In this paper, the authors describe in detail an actual case study of this type of failure mechanism that occurred in a 25-m high, 38°-dipping bench of an abandoned open-pit mine in Spain. To illustrate how this phenomenon indeed takes place, a timeline description of events, intact rock and rock mass characterization and a detailed slope failure analysis are included. Moreover, indicative limit equilibrium and more accurate numerical modelling approaches are presented guiding how to estimate factors of safety against this complex type of instability mechanisms. Furthermore, some situations associated with soft rock where these and similar slope failure mechanisms could take place are discussed. These approaches can be of help for the purpose of back analyzing similar case studies and for designing slopes when potential failures of this type are prone to occur.

title: Dynamic splitting mechanical properties and strength prediction model of freeze–thawed water-saturated sandstone
source: Geomechanics and Geophysics for Geo Energy and Geo Resources
authors: Xu Y.; Xie H.; Zheng Q.; Li C.; Yang G.
keywords: Cyclic freeze–thaw | Dynamic splitting tensile behavior | Energy analysis | Scaling law model | Water-saturated sandstone
abstract: To evaluate the effects of freeze–thaw (F–T) cycling on the tensile performance and energy evolution of water-saturated sandstone, this study utilized slope rock specimens collected from a high-altitude open-pit mine in western China. Dynamic Brazilian disc tests were conducted using a split Hopkinson pressure bar (SHPB) system under four distinct strain rate conditions. The specimens were pretreated with varying numbers of F–T cycles before testing. Experimental analysis revealed that under constant F–T conditions, both the tensile strength and energy dissipation ability under impact loading increased with increasing strain rate. In contrast, when the strain rate remained steady, a greater number of F–T cycles led to decreases in the splitting strength and energy dissipation capacity. Moreover, the dynamic increase factor (DIF) increased progressively with increasing strain rate and F–T cycle number. The deterioration in dynamic performance is attributed to internal degradation mechanisms, including the dissolution of cementing materials and the development of microcracks and pores, which reduce the overall integrity of the rock and promote more fragmented macroscopic failure modes. F–T-induced damage is identified as the primary factor responsible for the decrease in impact resistance and increase in the fragmentation of the specimens. Moreover, a scaling law model grounded in weakest-link theory was established to estimate the tensile capacity of F–T-degraded water-saturated sandstone.

title: Optimization of ecological and efficient restoration technology for green mines based on hesitant fuzzy TOPSIS
authors: Wang B.; Guo D.; Sun J.; Guo J.; Gao S.; Lu W.
keywords: 3D laser scanning | Digital terrain model (DTM) | Ecological restoration | Green mine | Hesitant fuzzy TOPSIS | Rock mass quality
abstract: The geological conditions of mines are complex and diverse, and existing restoration methods may not be sufficient to meet the requirements for all types of mine rehabilitation. A study on the optimization of ecological restoration technologies for green mines based on hesitant fuzzy TOPSIS has been proposed, offering a novel approach for selecting ecological restoration solutions for rock slopes in green mines. First, a remote 3D laser scanner is used to construct a digital terrain model (DTM) for the target mine. Then, based on characteristics such as geological lithology, slope aspect, and slope angle, the open-pit mine slopes are divided into zones. Finally, the rock mass quality of each slope zone is evaluated using eight indicators, including uniaxial saturated compressive strength, rock quality designation (RQD), structural plane condition, joint spacing, and integrity coefficient. The evaluation process specifically includes: constructing a hesitant fuzzy decision matrix based on the eight key indicators for each slope zone; objectively determining the weights of the indicators using the maximum deviation method to minimize subjectivity; calculating the weighted distance between each slope zone scheme and the defined hesitant fuzzy positive/negative ideal solutions; determining the relative closeness coefficient for each zone to classify the rock mass quality grade. Based on the grading results, the most suitable ecological restoration techniques are matched to each slope zone to achieve differentiated ecological restoration. Experimental results show that the mining slope is divided into seven zones using this approach. After ecological restoration, near-ground dust is effectively controlled. The vegetation restoration rate reaches up to 25%, whereas the rates of comparative methods are all below 15%. This indicates that the proposed method can help improve restoration efficiency and quality, promote sustainable development, better meet the requirements for efficient ecological restoration in mines, and possesses practical applicability.

title: A Q-learning approach to waste rock reduction in open-pit mine design based on cleaner production principles
authors: Badakhshan N.; Bakhtavar E.; Shahriar K.; Khosravi H.; Afraei S.; Maremi A.
keywords: Optimization | Reinforcement learning | Sustainable mining | Ultimate pit limit | Waste rock
abstract: Large-scale metal mining operations extract vast quantities of ore and waste rock annually, generating both economic benefits and significant environmental challenges. While mining supports industrial growth, technological advancement, and job creation, it also imposes substantial social and ecological costs, particularly from the disposal of waste rock. These mine wastes increase the burden of handling, dumping, reclamation, and long-term monitoring, often undermining sustainability objectives. Reducing waste generation within ultimate pit limit design is therefore essential to align mining with sustainable development policies. This study develops a novel framework that integrates mathematical modeling with Q-learning, a reinforcement learning algorithm, to optimize ultimate pit limit by maximizing ore recovery and profitability while minimizing waste rock extraction. A key innovation of the model is the explicit inclusion of environmental costs, covering prevention, mitigation, and compensation of impacts, as a fundamental component of block economic value. The approach is validated using a large scale copper ore deposit, and compared against the widely used Lerchs–Grossmann algorithm. Results show that the Q-learning framework reduces waste rock extraction by 2.7 million tons, with about 0.5 million tons less ore recovered, while also lowering computational time from 7.2 to 5.8 h. Although Lerchs–Grossmann yields slightly higher profit, it ignores environmental costs, leading to less sustainable outcomes. Overall, the framework prioritizes realistic pit design over superior economic gains. By embedding environmental factors into mine planning, it enhances resource efficiency, minimizes ecological impacts, and promotes cleaner production, thereby advancing sustainability in mining through reinforcement learning-based optimization.

title: Research on multi-scale feature detection of open-pit mine road cracks
authors: Wang L.; Zhao M.; Yu Z.; Yang G.; Wang Q.; Liu G.; Lei J.
keywords: Crack detection | Feature fusion | Open-pit mine road | Road safety | U-Net
abstract: Road crack detection in open-pit mines is of great significance for ensuring the safety and efficiency of mining production. Traditional detection methods and existing deep learning-based approaches have numerous limitations. This paper proposes an open-pit mine road crack detection method based on feature fusion, which introduces an Adaptive Feature Fusion Module (AF2M) and a Channel-Spatial Attention Module (CASP) into the original U-Net network, and optimizes the model using the Layer-Adaptive Magnitude Pruning (LAMP) algorithm.The AF2M module first unifies the scale of four-level multi-scale feature maps from the decoder through upsampling, concatenates them along the channel dimension, then exploits channel dependencies via the ECA (Efficient Channel Attention) module and fuses global-local contextual information using the GC (Global Context) module. It dynamically weights features from different dimensions to enhance key crack features and reduce background interference, whose multi-scale fusion capability surpasses the inherent processing capacity of the U-Net’s native encoder-decoder structure.The CASP module innovatively applies the multi-head self-attention mechanism to channel-wise interaction: it reconstructs channel attention through dimension transformation and QTK (Query-Key-Value) matrix operations, then fuses pooled spatial information to impose spatial attention. Compared with traditional attention mechanisms such as SE (Squeeze-and-Excitation) and CBAM (Convolutional Block Attention Module), it achieves deep synergy of channel-spatial information and improves crack localization accuracy.The LAMP algorithm rescales and sorts the weights of each layer through a unique scoring mechanism, adaptively assigns sparsity at the layer level, and prunes redundant weights within a pruning rate range of 0-0.3 (non-uniformly applied to all layers), ensuring that key feature extraction remains unaffected.Experiments were conducted on a dataset consisting of 2,847 high-resolution images collected from an open-pit coal mine in Inner Mongolia. The results show that the improved model achieves a mean Intersection over Union (mIoU) of 0.83, precision of 0.89, and F1-score of 0.82, representing improvements of 7%, 7%, and 9% respectively compared to the original U-Net. Additionally, the model parameters are reduced to 4.73 M (a 24.1% decrease), the Floating-Point Operations (FLOPs) are 4.25G (a 28.7% decrease), and the inference time per image is 0.30s (a 33.3% speedup).This method exhibits significant advantages in detection accuracy and model complexity, and can effectively meet the requirements of open-pit mine road crack detection, providing a reliable basis for mine road maintenance. Combined with technologies such as UAVs (Unmanned Aerial Vehicles) and GIS (Geographic Information Systems), it is expected to promote the intelligent development of open-pit mine road maintenance.

title: Delineating homogeneous zones for rock joint wall mechanical properties in open-pit mine slope based on a multi-indicator stacked generalization model
authors: Yu X.; Zheng A.; Ye J.; Qin J.; An P.; Wang R.
keywords: Homogeneous zones | Joint wall | Rock joints | Slope stability | Stacked generalization
abstract: Rock joints significantly influence slope stability, making it essential to delineate homogeneous zones. Traditional empirical methods are often subjective and ineffective when the mechanical properties of the joint walls are similar. To address this limitation, this study introduces a data-driven Stacked Generalization (SG) model that captures relationships between data points. Based on this model, a method for homogeneous zones division is proposed, incorporating five key indicators representing the mechanical properties of joint walls as feature parameters: joint wall compressive strength, disintegration resistance, wave velocity ratio, weathering coefficient, and linear density of the rock joints. These parameters can be quantified through field measurements and laboratory testing of rock joints that govern slope stability. The preprocessing stage integrates quadratic polynomial feature expansion and mutual information analysis to identify and select significant nonlinear relationships among these indicators. A case study demonstrates that the SG model achieves 94% balanced accuracy, outperforming traditional classifiers. The classification results of the model output are mapped onto an engineering geological plan of the study area, dividing it into four homogeneous zones. This approach provides an effective framework for delineating homogeneous zones of joint wall mechanical properties in open-pit mines and assessing slope stability under complex geological conditions.

title: Research on the extraction of landslide features, identification of early warning signals, and prediction of instability time based on synthetic aperture radar monitoring: A critical slowing down theory perspective
authors: Zhong J.; Yu Z.; Zhang Y.; Ren Y.; Ma H.
keywords: Critical slow down theory | Early warning signs of landslides | Instability time prediction | Inverse power law of variance | K-means clustering | S-SAR radar monitoring
abstract: Accurately identifying early warning signs of landslides and predicting the time of instability are crucial for disaster prevention and control, as well as for workplace safety in open-cast mines. Based on S-SAR monitoring data from slopes, this paper establishes a comprehensive analytical framework that integrates feature extraction, early warning signal identification, and instability time prediction. A large-scale open-pit mine landslide is selected as the study case to analyze the displacement time-series data of more than one hundred monitoring points within the landslide area. The results indicate that K-means clustering reveals the spatial partition characteristics of the landslide mass, with the optimal number of clusters determined to be three. Cluster 3, comprising 207 monitoring points, corresponds to the main deformation zone and the area of most active deformation. Through sliding-window Pearson correlation analysis, monitoring points No. 148 and No. 201 are identified as representative points characterizing the overall deformation trend of the landslide. By further integrating the theory of critical slowing down (CSD), the evolutionary characteristics of variance and autocorrelation coefficients are extracted. The system's instability warning points are determined by tracing back from the segment where variance continues to increase to the local minimum of the autocorrelation coefficient. The results show that the mean variance of the monitoring point group reaches its peak between August 24 and 26, 2024, and the high-value zones expand along the main sliding direction from the slope crest toward the middle and lower sections of the slope. Taking the identified early warning time as the starting point, a power-law model based on the inverse of the variance was established to predict the time of landslide instability, achieving a high level of predictive accuracy. Consistent results were obtained when applying this method to multiple mining landslide cases, validating its effectiveness and engineering feasibility in dynamic monitoring and real-time early warning of complex landslide bodies. This approach provides technical support for slope safety monitoring and disaster early warning in open-pit mines.

title: InterMine: A foundation model-based multi-task interaction network for remote sensing interpretation of open-pit coal mining activity
source: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
authors: Xing J.; Li J.; Zhang C.; Zhang J.; Du S.; Wang Y.; Yang F.; Cheng Y.; Gao Y.
keywords: Extent extraction | Fine-grained change detection | Foundation model | Interpretation of mining activity | Multi-task learning | Open-pit coal mine
abstract: The interpretation of open-pit coal mining activity is critical for resource management and ecological protection. It comprises two key tasks: extent extraction and fine-grained change detection. However, existing methods usually suffer from task separation, and their outputs cannot fully meet the requirements of interpretation. Therefore, this study proposes a foundation model-based multi-task interaction network (InterMine) to jointly perform open-pit mine extent extraction and fine-grained change detection. First, InterMine employs a Siamese foundation model as the encoder to enhance feature representation from images of complex open-pit coal mines and incorporates a channel-spatial feature reconstruction module to adapt the encoded features to meet the semantic and spatial requirements of the decoder. Second, a multi-task interaction mechanism is proposed to facilitate complementary information exchange between tasks. Finally, a consistency loss function based on hard-sample reweighting is designed to mitigate inconsistencies among multi-task outputs. InterMine is trained and evaluated on a self-constructed multi-temporal open-pit coal mining activity interpretation dataset (OMSet). Experimental results demonstrate that InterMine outperforms the compared methods. In particular, InterMine achieves F1-scores of 87.57 %, 83.68 %, and 79.43 % for open-pit mine extent extraction, excavation change detection, and reclamation change detection, respectively, outperforming the comparison methods by 1.89 ∼ 5.29, 3.04 ∼ 7.83, and 2.79 ∼ 7.42 percentage points, respectively. This work provides both technical and data support for open-pit coal mine monitoring. OMSet and the code of InterMine have been made publicly available at https://figshare.com/s/03c029d8e4846faef69f.

title: A Total Displacement Catastrophe Criterion for Assessing Open-Pit Slope Stability Under Rainfall Conditions
source: International Journal for Numerical and Analytical Methods in Geomechanics
authors: He L.; Ren J.; Shang Y.; Song G.; Kong D.; Wu D.
keywords: cusp catastrophe theory | instability criterion | slope stability | strength reduction method | total displacement catastrophe criterion
abstract: The aim of the present study is to address the challenge of accurately assessing the stability of open-pit mine slopes under rainfall infiltration. This study innovatively combines total displacement theory with the cusp catastrophe model. A slope instability criterion based on total displacement mutation is proposed. The MATLAB platform was used for model validation and comparative analysis. Firstly, a quartic polynomial model was developed to characterize the relationship between the total displacement and the reduction coefficient based on the strength reduction method and total displacement theory. The equilibrium and discriminant equations for the cusp catastrophe model were then derived. Secondly, a typical mine slope in Guizhou Province, China, was selected as a case study to assess the applicability and accuracy of three instability criteria: the plastic zone penetration criterion, the key point displacement catastrophe criterion, and the total displacement catastrophe criterion (TDCC). The results indicate that the slope safety factor calculated by the TDCC is 1.201. This criterion is objective and independent of the monitoring point location, significantly reducing human errors. The criterion's accuracy was further verified by varying the cohesion and the internal friction angle. The results obtained from the TDCC were stable and central, aligning with the variation trends of the other two criteria, thereby confirming its reliability and accuracy. This work provides a quantitative, operational method for identifying instability in slope rainfall-infiltration stability analysis. It is of theoretical and engineering guidance significance for the prevention and control of slope disasters in open-pit mines.

title: Bi-objective chance-constrained evolutionary optimization for large-scale open-pit mine scheduling under geological uncertainty
authors: Hewa Pathiranage I.; Neumann A.
keywords: Bi-objective optimization | Chance constraints | Grade uncertainty | Multi-objective evolutionary algorithms | Open-pit mine scheduling
abstract: The open-pit mine scheduling problem (OPMSP) is a complex optimization problem in long-term mine planning that involves numerous operational and geological constraints. Traditional deterministic approaches often ignore geological uncertainty, leading to suboptimal or unreliable production schedules. Chance constraints provide a framework for handling uncertainty by ensuring that probabilistic constraints are satisfied with a predefined confidence level. In this paper, we consider the OPMSP under geological grade uncertainty and propose a bi-objective chance-constrained formulation that simultaneously maximizes the expected discounted net present value and minimizes scheduling risk. Unlike traditional chance-constrained approaches, the proposed formulation does not require a predefined confidence level during optimization. Instead, it generates a set of Pareto-optimal solutions representing different trade-offs between profitability and risk within a single optimization run. To solve the resulting large-scale stochastic optimization problem, we employ multi-objective evolutionary algorithms and compare their performance against a single-objective chance-constrained evolutionary approach and a deterministic MILP benchmark. We further evaluate the contribution of the problem-specific initialization and mutation components through an ablation study.
