Experimental results on MineLib benchmark instances containing up to (Formula presented) blocks demonstrate that the proposed formulation effectively captures the trade-off between profitability and risk under geological uncertainty while providing greater flexibility than confidence-level-dependent approaches.

title: TCR-LM: Terrain confidence region-guided LiDAR mapping for open-pit mine loading operations
authors: Zhao Z.; Hong X.; Wang Z.; Bi L.
keywords: cloth simulation filtering | keyframe maintenance | LiDAR mapping | open-pit mine | shoveling and loading scenario
abstract: Robust LiDAR mapping in open-pit mine shoveling and loading scenarios is challenging because point-cloud registration is affected by dynamic equipment occlusion, dust-induced returns, platform vibration, and continuously changing terrain. This study proposes TCR-LM, a terrain-confidence-region-guided LiDAR mapping method that improves the reliability of scan-to-map constraints in disturbed shoveling and loading scenarios. TCR-LM uses relatively stable terrain observations as the primary constraints for pose estimation, rather than directly matching raw point clouds contaminated by non-terrain objects. Terrain confidence regions are constructed through continuous terrain-envelope extraction and neighborhood-based confidence refinement to reduce the influence from trucks, buckets, mechanical structures, and dust-contaminated regions. Spatially balanced feature selection and unstable-feature removal near occlusion boundaries are then used to improve the spatial coverage and geometric reliability of the matching constraints. To handle time-varying terrain, local elevation changes are detected from temporal layers in the keyframe map, and outdated terrain points are progressively down-weighted through point-level state updating. Controlled simulation and single-site field experiments show that, under the evaluated conditions, TCR-LM achieves lower trajectory errors in simulation and better relative trajectory consistency in the field than the compared methods. Deployment on a field edge-computing platform indicates its feasibility for quasi-real-time, low-frequency operating-area map updating and candidate terrain-change perception.

title: Multi-point prediction and interpretable analysis of dust concentration in open-pit coal mine during the cold season using a stacking learning framework
authors: Lu X.; Wang Z.; Zhou W.; Lei S.; Luo H.
keywords: Cold season | Multi-point monitoring | Open-pit coal mine | Stacking learning | TSP
abstract: Dust pollution in open-pit coal mines varies strongly across space and time, particularly during the cold season when weak atmospheric diffusion can intensify dust accumulation. However, prediction based on a single monitoring point may not adequately represent the spatially heterogeneous dust variation across an open-pit mine monitoring network. This study developed a multi-point stacking learning framework to predict TSP concentration 5 min ahead using current noise, temperature, humidity, wind speed, atmospheric pressure, and TSP concentration. Both an integrated seven-point dataset and point-specific datasets were constructed to evaluate overall and local prediction performance. The integrated seven-point model was designed to capture the general dust variation pattern of the mining area while retaining the ability to compare local prediction behavior among individual monitoring points. The integrated model achieved good accuracy on the testing set, with R<sup>2</sup> = 0.891, MAE = 13.71 μg/m<sup>3</sup>, and RMSE = 25.95 μg/m<sup>3</sup>. Most point-specific models also performed well, although point 7#, located closer to the active working area, showed weaker generalization. Interpretation results showed that current TSP was the dominant predictor, indicating strong short-term persistence. Meteorological factors had nonlinear and site-dependent effects, while two-factor interactions revealed their synergistic influence on TSP suspension, transport, and deposition. These findings demonstrate that multi-point monitoring improves dust prediction and provides practical support for mining-area-level early warning and targeted dust-control strategies in open-pit coal mines.

title: Biopolymer-modified soil–rock mixtures for open-pit mine waste-dump slopes: investigation of mechanical behavior and microscopic mechanisms
source: Bulletin of Engineering Geology and the Environment
authors: Li R.; Qi X.; Lu Y.; Lu X.; Guo Y.; Tu L.; Tian Y.; Wang Z.
keywords: Bio-polymers | Mechanical behavior | Microscopic mechanism | Soil–rock mixture
abstract: The reshaping of soil–rock mixtures (S-RM) on slopes within the secondary stripping zones of open-pit mines constrains both resource recovery and production safety. In this study, calcium lignosulfonate (CLS) and xanthan gum (XG) were used to enhance the mechanical performance of S-RM. The effects of varying dosages were evaluated through Atterberg limits, standard Proctor compaction, and consolidated undrained triaxial tests, while scanning electron microscopy (SEM) and X-ray diffraction (XRD) analyses were employed to elucidate the underlying modification mechanisms. Results show that at CLS and XG contents of 3% and 1. 5%, respectively, inflection points appear in the liquid limit and plasticity index curves. At the corresponding optimum moisture contents, cohesion increased by 42. 8% for CLS-modified specimens and by 70. 5% for XG-modified specimens compared to the unmodified state, while the internal friction angle increased by 63. 02% and 49%, respectively. Microstructural observations reveal that CLS primarily reinforces the mixture through consolidation, pore optimization, and ionic flocculation, whereas XG relies on networked consolidation, surface adsorption, and ionic bridging to improve strength. However, excessive addition leads to binder agglomeration, overfilling of voids, and insufficient structural support, ultimately reducing stability. This work provides a theoretical basis for the environmentally friendly application of bio-polymers in modifying reconstituted S-RM slopes in open-pit mines.

title: A Multimodal Benchmark for Open-Pit Mine Remote Sensing Change Detection With Vision-Language Guidance
authors: Chen W.; Li C.; Feng Y.; Tang H.; Wang H.; Yang J.; Xu Y.; Fang Q.
keywords: Multimodal | open pit mining | remote sensing | vision–language model (VLM)
abstract: Remote sensing change detection (CD) is a core capability for Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled monitoring of large-scale, open-pit mines, where reliable perception and interpretable analytics are required for environmental compliance, safety governance, and operational optimization. However, existing benchmarks remain largely limited to pixel-level annotations and unimodal visual inputs, hindering semantic understanding and decision support in practical industrial IoT workflows. We introduce MinBench, a comprehensive multimodal benchmark for open-pit mine CD that systematically integrates vision–language supervision into traditional CD pipelines. MinBench is built upon the MineNetCD database and further incorporates grounded semantic change descriptions, enabling the evaluation of vision–language models (VLMs), multimodal fusion strategies, and captioning mechanisms under a unified protocol. To facilitate principled multimodal benchmarking, we include the RL-ACR (reinforcement learning (RL)-based agentic caption refinement) framework as a reference captioning pipeline that produces semantically rich change descriptions with grounded object coordinates via iterative self-correction, and supports multiple fusion paradigms such as cross-attention, feature-wise linear modulation (FiLM), and feature concatenation. We benchmark a wide range of state-of-the-art CD models and VLMs on over 70 000 bitemporal image pairs from 100 mining sites, with pixel-level annotations and expert-verified grounded captions. Our benchmark reveals consistent gains from vision–language guidance over unimodal baselines and highlights substantial performance variation across fusion strategies and captioning models, providing a systematic analysis of multimodal design choices for industrial IoT-oriented remote sensing monitoring.

title: Machine Learning-Based Prediction of Radon Emissions from Underground Coal Fires Based on Atmospheric Changes
authors: Zhang H.; Zhang Z.; Vo Thanh H.; Jia S.; Dai Z.; Zhang Y.; Wang Y.
keywords: Environmental risk | Gradient boosting | Machine learning | Radon | Underground coal fires
abstract: Underground coal fires can cause environmental damage and resource wastage. Accurately predicting the combustion state is critical for assessing their hazard levels and implementing control measures. Underground coal fires produce radon gas, which serves as an effective indicator for predicting the coal fire. However, traditional radon measurement is time-consuming and costly. This study proposes a machine learning (ML)-based prediction method that correlates surface radon concentration with atmospheric environmental factors. Four ML models—ridge regression, random forest, gradient boosting, and extra trees—were applied to predict surface radon concentration anomalies caused by underground coal fires. In total, 216 samples were collected from the Haizhou open-pit mine fire area, including four key variables: ambient temperature, ambient pressure, relative humidity (RH), and wind velocity. The results demonstrated that the gradient boosting model exhibited exceptional fit and robust generalizability, achieving R<sup>2</sup> of 0.981, RMSE of 170.29, and MAE of 124.69 on the testing dataset. Sensitivity analysis revealed that RH was the most influential factors. The gradient boosting model proved to exhibit high stability and accuracy in predicting radon concentrations over different time durations. The application of this model in radon concentration prediction provides significant support for forecasting underground coal fires and expands new directions for the application of ML in environmental fields.

title: Source-Unbiased Subsurface Monitoring With Seismic Noise
authors: Sánchez-Pastor P.; Schimmel M.; Jorde S.; Seivane H.; Díaz J.; Balaguera A.; Rodríguez S.; Torné M.
keywords: anthropogenic sources | seismic noise interferometry | subsurface monitoring | tailings dam
abstract: This study addresses a key limitation of seismic noise interferometry for subsurface monitoring: the impact of non-stationary sources on seismic velocity change estimates. Conventional methods rely on time-period references, which can inherit source-related effects when source conditions vary, biasing the estimated velocity changes. This is particularly relevant in urban and industrial environments, where quasi-monochromatic sources are often present. We show that frequency variations in such signals can produce apparent seismic velocity changes of equivalent magnitude through analytical and numerical analyses. To address this issue, we introduce REFTION, a spatial-reference approach based on synchronous comparison of correlation functions across seismic stations. We demonstrate its performance in an active open-pit mine, successfully monitoring a tailings dam under complex noise conditions. By reducing sensitivity to source variability, REFTION enables reliable subsurface monitoring in challenging environments, where anthropogenic noise can be transformed into a valuable monitoring tool.

title: Knowledge-driven MOEA/D for optimizing the road network of open-pit mines
authors: Huang Y.; Guo Y.; Zhang S.; Lu L.; Ai Y.; Ge S.
keywords: Haul road network | MOEA/D | Multi-objective optimization | Open-pit mining | Q-learning
abstract: The haul road network is a critical infrastructure in open-pit mines, serving as the backbone that connects mining faces, dumping area and auxiliary facilities. Its geometric configuration directly influences transportation efficiency and operational costs. Although extensive research has focused on route planning and truck dispatching, the optimization of road network remains underexplored. To bridge this gap, the haul road network optimization problem is formulated as a constrained multi-objective optimization model, aiming to minimize earthwork volume and maximize transportation efficiency while satisfying the constraints on longitudinal slope, bend radius and forbidden area. After simplifying a road to its alignment, a knowledge-driven MOEA/D (KD-MOEA/D) is proposed to find the optimal road layouts. A hybrid initialization strategy is introduced to generate high-quality initial road alignments along straight line or terrain in terms of their types. Then, seven knowledge-guidance evolutionary operators tailored to specific characteristics of haul roads are designed. During the evolution, the most appropriate one is adaptively selected by Q-learning in terms of the evolution state. Experimental results on four real-world instances from an open-pit mine in Inner Mongolia demonstrate that the proposed KD-MOEA/D significantly outperforms several state-of-the-art multi-objective optimization algorithms on both convergence and diversity.

title: Dynamic tensile cracking behaviours of frozen fractured rock with an ice-filled flaw
authors: Wang T.; Zhu W.; Liu K.; Niu L.; Jiang Z.; Luo K.
keywords: Dynamic tensile properties | Failure mode | Frozen fractured rock | Ice-filled flaw | Tensile stress wave
abstract: Tensile cracking induced by dynamic events (e.g. rock blasting, seismic, earthquakes) is a critical factor governing the instability and potential catastrophic failure of frozen fractured rock masses filled with ice in cold region mining or construction engineering. This study investigates the dynamic response and splitting failure mechanisms of frozen fractured rock under impact loading using a Split Hopkinson Pressure Bar (SHPB) apparatus with pendulum impact loading. The initiation and propagation of micro-cracks during dynamic loading are captured in real time using a high-speed digital image correlation (HS-DIC) technique, and a pixel-based virtual extensometer method is developed to quantify crack evolution with high spatial resolution, offering a reliable alternative to conventional contact-based strain gauges in low-temperature environments. The effects of impact velocity and ice-filled flaw angle on tensile strength and cracking mode of frozen fractured rock are discussed. The results reveal that dynamic tensile strength of frozen fractured rock exhibits a non-monotonic trend with increasing the ice-filled flaw angle, initially decreasing and then increasing, consistent with the trend observed under static tensile conditions. Compared to intact specimens, the strength of specimens with an ice-filled flaw decreases by 35.65% to 42.81%, depending on the variation in angles, with energy dissipation following a similar trend. In contrast, specimens containing ice-filled flaws exhibit higher dynamic tensile strength than those with unfilled flaws, as ice-rock interface provides additional resistance during crack propagation. During dynamic impact splitting, cracks initiate at the ice-filled flaw tips and propagate toward both ends until failure. These findings provide insights for optimizing open-pit mine blasting design and improving the safety of engineering operations in cold regions.

title: An Adaptive Bounded Hybrid A* Planner for Autonomous Mining Trucks in Confined Unstructured Mining Environments
authors: Meng Z.; Zhang R.
keywords: adaptive expansion | autonomous mining trucks | bounded continued search | Hybrid A*
abstract: Automated valet-parking trajectory planning has been widely studied in structured environments, whereas its counterpart in unstructured environments remains insufficiently explored. The working face of an open-pit mine is a typical unstructured production environment, where autonomous mining trucks (AMTs) must perform collision-free and kinematically feasible maneuvers under irregular boundaries, locally confined passages, large vehicle footprints, and strict terminal pose requirements. To address this problem, we introduce an adaptive bounded Hybrid A* planner for AMT maneuver planning at mining working faces. The proposed planner integrates local-geometry-aware top-K motion primitive scheduling, adaptive rollout-length assignment, progress-reward-based dual-cost correction, and bounded continuation after the first feasible Reeds–Shepp closure. By ranking and filtering motion primitives according to obstacle clearance, maneuver margin, goal distance, and heading alignment, the planner reduces ineffective successor generation during search. By adapting rollout lengths to local spatial constraints and primitive curvature, it improves the consistency between expansion scale and environmental structure. By retaining the first feasible Reeds–Shepp connection as an initial upper bound and continuing bounded refinement, it improves the final returned path beyond the first feasible solution. Comparative studies demonstrate that, relative to the conventional Hybrid A* baseline, the proposed planner reduces the average final planning time, generated nodes, and final path cost by 54.73%, 74.10%, and 12.76%, respectively, in the abstract mine-like scenarios. In the real-map-derived mining working-face scenarios, the corresponding reductions are 25.12%, 37.98%, and 7.15%, respectively. These results indicate that the proposed method reduces search redundancy while improving the efficiency–quality trade-off in confined and geometrically irregular working-face environments.

title: A LiDAR-Based Multimodal 3D Object Detection Algorithm for Intelligent Driving in Open-Pit Mines
authors: Wang S.; Zhang X.
keywords: 3D object detection | intelligent driving in open-pit mines | multimodal fusion | sparse point cloud perception | Voxel R-CNN
abstract: This study addresses the challenges of sparse long-range point clouds, complex background interference, and inconsistent localization quality in 3D object detection for intelligent driving in open-pit mines. A camera–LiDAR multimodal detection method based on Voxel R-CNN is proposed. We introduce a Multimodal Focal Sparse Voxel Enhancement module that combines Focal Sparse Convolution with shallow visual features to guide voxel importance prediction and selective sparse propagation. An Intersection over Union (IoU)-Aware Quality and Geometry Refinement Head is further designed to improve the localization accuracy and ranking reliability of 3D proposals. Experimental results show that the proposed method achieves BEV mAP@0.40 and 3D mAP@0.40 values of 63.43% and 61.23%, respectively, outperforming the strongest comparison method, MambaFusion, by 5.37 and 7.61 percentage points. In the 60–80 m range, the average translation error is reduced to 0.41 m, while the inference speed reaches 27 FPS. These results demonstrate that the proposed method improves the detection and localization of distant sparse objects in complex open-pit mine environments while maintaining real-time inference capability.

title: Influence Mechanism of Underground Goafs on Open-Pit Slope Stability and Overburden Movement Characteristics in an Open-Pit Coal Mine
authors: Jia M.; Wang D.; Tang Y.
keywords: 3DEC | limit equilibrium theory | slope stability | slope with goaf | three zones
abstract: Scientific evaluation of open-pit slope stability under the disturbance of underground goaf is critical to the safe production of open-pit coal mines. Taking an open-pit coal mine in Inner Mongolia as the engineering background, this study investigates the influence mechanism of underground goaf on slope stability. With discrete element numerical simulation, the movement law of overlying strata above the goaf is revealed, and the heights of the “three zones” and boundary movement angles are determined. Furthermore, limit-equilibrium theory is adopted to analyze slope stability affected by goafs from three perspectives: goaf span, occurrence position and inter-goaf spacing. The results indicate that under partial extraction conditions, goaf span is positively correlated with the height of the caving zone and negatively correlated with the boundary movement angle. As the goaf width increases, the mining-induced deformation field expands progressively, and a distinct bending-subsidence zone develops in the 50 m wide single-goaf case, resulting in a complete caving–fractured–bending-subsidence zonation. For adjacent goafs, smaller inter-goaf spacing promotes overlap of the mining-induced deformation fields and generally enhances overburden disturbance. As the spacing increases, the interaction between adjacent goafs tends to weaken, although the degree of reduction depends on goaf width and the deformation parameter considered. Therefore, the spacing of approximately 50 m observed in the present simulations is interpreted as a site-specific transition range rather than a universal critical threshold. Two landslide modes are identified in the Baozhixil open-pit mine: circular arc sliding and composite sliding controlled by the weak interlayer of No. 1 coal seam. Slope stability is negatively correlated with goaf span and positively correlated with the horizontal distance between the goaf and the slope face. For the analysis of inter-goaf spacing, slope stability shows a positive correlation with the proportion of non-collapse deformation area within the sliding mass.

title: Assessment of Predicted and Measured Rock Fragmentation Using the Kuz–Ram Model and Wip-Frag
authors: Tabet A.; Zerzour O.; Dinar H.; Kefi K.; Benyoucef A.A.; Batouche T.
keywords: blasting | Kuz-Ram | mining | oversized blocks | Wip-Frag
abstract: The Ouenza open-pit mine is one of Algeria’s major iron ore producers, where efficient blasting and fragmentation control are essential to maintaining stable, productive mining operations. The primary objective of this study is to quantitatively assess the agreement between predicted and measured rock fragmentation at the Ouenza open-pit mine. The research methodology includes a comprehensive analysis of blasting parameters. Field experiments used four blasts, all executed with the same blasting plans on the same working face to ensure comparability. The rock fragmentation was precisely measured and analyzed using the advanced image-processing software Wip-Frag to determine the particle-size distribution. The Kuz–Ram model predicted the fragment size distribution using the same blasting design implemented in the field, and the predicted fragmentation was quantitatively evaluated against Wip-Frag measurements using the coefficient of determination (R<sup>2</sup>), root mean square error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). The statistical evaluation yielded an R<sup>2</sup> of 0.9095, an RMSE of 9.71%, and an MAE of 6.54%, indicating good overall agreement between the predicted and measured fragmentation, despite noticeable deviations in the coarse-fragment size range. The observed discrepancies were mainly associated with potential inaccuracies in the field implementation of the designed blast pattern, limited compliance with blasting procedures, and the natural heterogeneity of the rock mass. The results show that comparing Wip-Frag measurements with Kuz–Ram predictions is an effective way to identify discrepancies between predicted and actual fragmentation and to determine the field factors driving these differences. These findings provide practical insights into blast implementation and fragmentation control under actual mining conditions.

title: Optimization of Land Pattern in Mining Area Based on the Improvement of Ecosystem Service Function—A Case Study of Fushun Mining Area
authors: Rong L.; An C.
keywords: driving factors | ecosystem service | land pattern | mining reclamation | surface mining
abstract: Mining activities are prevalent worldwide and pose significant threats to the supply of ecosystem services (ESs) for humanity. Many mining areas face challenges related to recovery and reclamation following resource depletion. A key challenge for the sustainable development of these areas is how to achieve collaborative optimization of land pattern and enhancing ESs during the restoration process. To address the above challenges, we have innovatively analyzed land suitability through machine learning, and combined with ESs assessment (InVEST) and driving factor analysis (Geographic detector, Structural equation model) to explore the optimal land pattern for future Fushun mining area restoration. The findings are as follows: (1) From 1990 to 2020, water yield (WY), soil conservation (SC), and food production (FP) exhibited an increasing trend (8%, 3%, 22%), while habitat quality (HQ) and carbon sequestration (CS) showed a decreasing trend (12%, 4%). Plus model predicts that ESs will decrease 4%–60% in the future from 2030 to 2050. (2) Surface mining significantly impacts SC by indirectly altering terrain, which subsequently affects ESs that are coordinated with SC; normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) is the main factor to improve ESs (0.2–0.6). (3) Machine learning analysis revealed that high forestland reclamation suitability is primarily concentrated in the open-pit mine and factory boundaries, whereas mine pits are more suitable for water reclamation. The peripheral areas of the mining site are more suited for farmland and construction land reclamation. (4) Based on the results of land suitability and ecosystem services, the optimal land pattern under ESs enhancement scenarios was proposed. In the future, the land pattern of “pit water storage—in field farming—peripheral afforestation” should be formed to rationally restore land and comprehensively enhance ESs. This study proposes a new method for optimizing the land pattern of mining areas for the improvement of ecosystem services, which provides an important reference for the sustainable development of other mining areas in the world.

title: Surface Subsidence Analysis and Prediction in an Open-Pit Mine Using Time-Series InSAR and a CL-TSF Hybrid Model
authors: Liu G.; Zhao P.; Wang J.; Fan H.; Zhao S.
keywords: deep learning–based prediction | hybrid convolutional neural network–long short-term memory model | mining-induced deformation | surface subsidence | time-series interferometric synthetic aperture radar
abstract: Surface subsidence in mining areas is a widespread, long-term, and slow-onset geological hazard that can induce cascading failures, including slope instability and ground collapse, thereby threatening infrastructure and human safety. Accurate characterization of its spatiotemporal evolution and reliable prediction of future trends are therefore essential for effective mine safety management and hazard assessment. This study investigates an open-pit mine by integrating time-series Interferometric Synthetic Aperture Radar (InSAR) monitoring with a deep learning–based prediction framework. A total of 70 Sentinel-1A synthetic aperture radar (SAR) images acquired between January 2023 and May 2025 were processed to quantify surface deformation. The results reveal a large-scale subsidence funnel, with a maximum subsidence rate of 143.00 mm/yr and a cumulative displacement of −337.89 mm. The observed deformation is controlled by combined effects of rainfall, seismic activity, and local geological conditions. To predict the temporal evolution of subsidence, a hybrid convolutional neural network–long short-term memory (CNN–LSTM) time-series forecasting model (CL-TSF) is proposed. By integrating convolutional feature extraction with long short-term memory–based sequence modeling, the model effectively captures spatial patterns and long-term temporal dependencies. Compared with conventional CNN and LSTM models, the proposed approach achieves superior performance, with a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 2.24% and a Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of 5.260. Its robustness is validated through accurate multi-step prediction of the final five deformation periods. These findings provide insights into mining-induced subsidence mechanisms and demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework for dynamic early warning and risk assessment in mining areas.

title: Water-Induced Shear-Strength Degradation of Coal-Measure Rocks and Its Engineering Implications: A Case Study of the Fushun West Open-Pit Mine, China
authors: Wu J.; Zhang F.; Li X.; Ma T.; Zhao Y.
keywords: coal-measure strata | condition-dependent Mohr–Coulomb strength | Fushun Coalfield | shear strength degradation | slope stability | staged warning | water–rock interaction
abstract: Slopes excavated in coal-measure strata are prone to rainfall-induced landslides because water-induced disturbances progressively degrade rock-mass shear strength. This study investigated six coal-measure lithologies from the unloading zone of the Fushun West Open-Pit Mine using triaxial compression tests after separate wetting–drying and continuous-immersion treatments. Condition-dependent cohesion, c, and internal friction angle, φ, were fitted with exponential functions and incorporated into the Mohr–Coulomb criterion. For scenario analysis, the retention ratios measured in the two separate treatment series were applied sequentially in a separable empirical parameterization. This no-interaction approximation was used to update coal-measure strength inputs in representative slope models. Cohesion and φ decreased exponentially within the tested ranges, with in-sample R<sup>2</sup> values greater than 0.85, and cohesion was generally more sensitive. Continuous immersion produced rapid early softening, whereas wetting–drying cycles produced cumulative deterioration. Limit-equilibrium and finite-element calculations showed lower safety factors and more concentrated deformation under more severe parameter-reduction scenarios. Model-specific cumulative-displacement reference values of 52.36–213.82 mm were paired with Fs levels of approximately 1.15, 1.05, and 1.00 and compared qualitatively with historical monitoring curves. The findings provide a reference for rainy-season slope-stability prediction and staged warning in open-pit coal mines.

title: Physical Similarity Simulation of Overburden-Slope Deformation and Fracture Evolution Under Sequential Highwall-Mining Excavation at Different Chamber Heights
authors: Dai L.; Zhang J.; Li X.; Wang H.; Zhou N.; Chen Q.
keywords: highwall mining | overburden-slope deformation | physical similarity simulation | sequential excavation
abstract: To reveal the evolution of overburden movement, slope deformation, and fracture damage during highwall mining, a physical similarity model was established based on the geological conditions of the Heishan Open-Pit Mine, Xinjiang. The excavation extended through the model thickness and was idealized as a continuous slot. Different chamber heights were considered to simulate the extraction of Coal Seam 13-2 and the subsequent mining of the overlying Coal Seam 9. Overburden and slope displacements, fracture-area ratio, and fractal dimension were analyzed using the MatchID-2D digital image correlation method, displacement monitoring, and fracture image processing. The results show that deformation initially concentrates in the chamber roof and lower overburden and subsequently propagates toward the slope toe and surface, exhibiting distinct stage-dependent and spatially differentiated characteristics. As the chamber height increases, overburden subsidence, slope-toe displacement, fracture-area ratio, and fractal dimension all increase. During the extraction of Coal Seam 9, displacement continues to accumulate within the previously formed deformation zones, accompanied by further propagation and coalescence of existing fractures. The results characterize progressive local damage and spatially coordinated deformation within the model. These findings improve understanding of overburden-slope deformation and fracture evolution under the investigated conditions.

title: Assessing Long-term ecological environment quality dynamics and anthropogenic disturbance in the lower Jinsha River basin (LJRB): Integrating MRSEI with Hurst-based persistence analysis
authors: Sodango T.H.; Ma J.; Deng Y.; Liu L.; He S.; Wang J.
keywords: Cascade hydropower impacts | Ecological stability | Mining disturbance | MRSEI | Watershed sustainability assessment
abstract: The Lower Jinsha River Basin (LJRB) has experienced decades of concurrent cascade hydropower construction, mineral exploitation and large-scale Grain for Green (GFG) restoration. Comprehensive long-term multi-dimensional assessments linking these overlapping human activities to basin ecological sustainability remain limited in existing research. This study develops an integrated evaluation framework built on a 35-year (1991–2025) Modified Remote Sensing Ecological Index (MRSEI) dataset, Hurst exponent persistence analysis, a composite Ecological Stability Index (ESI) developed for this study, and Convergent Cross Mapping (CCM) causal attribution to quantify long-term ecological trajectories and identify the ecological regime shift. Results show sustained basin-wide ecological improvement with the mean MRSEI rising from 0.201 to 0.386, with Sen's slope = 0.0055 yr<sup>−1</sup> and Kendall's τ = 0.476 ( p < 0.01). Three phases of uninterrupted MRSEI growth are distinguished throughout the study timeline: slow baseline improvement from 1991 to 2000, moderate steady gains between 2001 and 2012, and notably accelerated ecological recovery after 2012 coinciding with reservoir impoundments where EVI and WET increased markedly after reservoir impoundment, by 0.456 and 0.567, respectively. While 93.08% of the basin presents positive MRSEI trends, only 42.51% corresponds to stable long-term recovery; 45.21% displays anti-persistent trajectories (Hurst <0.5), a latent vulnerability that single-indicator trend analysis may not identify. Mining disturbance follows a clear distance-decay gradient (R<sup>2</sup> = 0.63), with functional ecosystem recovery observable 8–10 km from open-pit mine sites. CCM analysis confirms reservoir impoundment as the primary trigger of post-2012 ecological improvement (ρ = 0.617), with cross-map skill 39.3% stronger than GFG revegetation (ρ = 0.443) and 22.7% greater than the reverse feedback pathway (ρ = 0.503). Geodetector modelling shows the interaction between land cover and evapotranspiration delivers the highest explanatory power (q = 0.534), exceeding all single independent variables and reflecting coupled land-water-climate feedbacks shaping regional ecological conditions. The integrated MRSEI–ESI workflow supports delineation of spatial management zones, including stable conservation areas, mining degradation corridors, and empirical 2 km disturbance buffers around reservoirs and mine sites. This analytical framework may be adapted to assess ecological sustainability in other mountain river basins undergoing rapid anthropogenic transformation.

title: Intelligent blasting fragmentation assessment in open-pit mines: An automated system based on YOLOv8-seg and binocular vision
source: Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering
authors: Liu Y.; Tao M.; Huang L.; Xiang G.; Xu Y.; He J.
keywords: Blasting rock fragmentation | Computer vision | Intelligent analysis | Open-pit mine
abstract: An essential parameter for assessing the blasting effect in mining, tunnelling and mineral processing industries is the fragment size distribution of the rock mass subjected to blasting. Traditional methods for measuring rock pile size data typically rely on reference objects, which are affected by low manual efficiency and subjective operation. In this study, an image recognition method for post-blast rock fragmentation integrating binocular depth vision and the YOLOv8-seg model was proposed and implemented in an open-pit mine. Accurate measurement of rock fragmentation size without a reference object was achieved by combining binocular camera depth calculation with a deep learning-based segmentation algorithm. Firstly, a diverse dataset covering actual open-pit mine post-blast rock fragmentation, open-source rock images, and engineering site truckload scenes is constructed. Subsequently, a semi-automatic annotation technology was applied to improve data labeling efficiency. Moreover, an intelligent analysis system for rapid and automatic recognition of blasting fragmentation was developed. This system comprises a set of hardware components and a web-based visual operation platform. Eventually, the intelligent fragmentation recognition system was successfully applied to on-site production at the Husab uranium mine following laboratory and field optimization tests. The laboratory and field test results indicate that the recognition accuracy exceeds 90%, with an on-site error rate below 5%. This study verifies the engineering applicability of a deep learning algorithm based on binocular vision in mining and blasting scenarios, providing a valuable technical reference for the intelligent upgrading of mines.

title: A Learning-Guided MPC Control Framework for Autonomous Mining Trucks
authors: Wang C.; Zhu D.; Ke X.; Yang K.; Ge S.
keywords: Autonomous mining trucks | differentiable model predictive control (MPC) | model-free reinforcement learning (MF-RL) | obstacle avoidance | trajectory tracking
abstract: With the increasing adoption of Internet of Things (IoT)-enabled sensing and connectivity in open-pit autonomous haulage, autonomous mining trucks are required to operate more safely and efficiently in complex and changing environments. These vehicles operate in highly dynamic and unstructured conditions, which impose stringent requirements on trajectory tracking accuracy and dynamic obstacle avoidance. Conventional model predictive control (MPC) exhibits limited adaptability in such settings and struggles to adapt control strategies online, while reinforcement learning (RL) methods often suffer from low training efficiency and poor closed-loop stability. In this article, we propose an integrated multitask control framework that combines differentiable MPC with model-free RL (MF-RL) for autonomous mining trucks. The framework leverages precomputed global trajectories for high-level guidance, employs MPC for local trajectory optimization, and uses an MF-RL policy to dynamically tune task-level cost weights online for tracking accuracy, control smoothness, obstacle avoidance, and payload adaptation, thereby improving performance across different payload levels. A MATLAB-CARLA co-simulation environment is constructed using real open-pit mine road geometry and vehicle parameters to enable evaluation under representative operating scenarios. Extensive comparisons in complex obstacle-interaction scenarios show that the proposed MF-RL+MPC approach achieves effective tracking and obstacle avoidance with smoother control inputs and consistently higher success rates under varying payloads, demonstrating robust payload-aware control performance while respecting system constraints in open-pit mine scenarios.

title: A new unstable block identification method using deterministic discrete fracture networks for rockfall hazard assessment in open-pit mines
authors: Zhang Z.; Guo J.; Yang T.; Cheng B.; Zhang P.; Liu L.
keywords: 3D point cloud | Deterministic discrete fracture network | Open-pit mine | Rockfall hazard assessment | Unstable rock block identification
abstract: Rock blocks are the core structural units of rock masses bounded by multiple sets of discontinuities, and their stability directly affects the safety of geotechnical engineering. In particular, potential unstable rock blocks on open-pit mine slopes may pose a severe threat to the safety of on-site personnel and infrastructure once sliding occurs. Traditional rock block identification methods rely on manual measurement, which is inefficient and involves safety risks; the discrete fracture network (DFN) approach struggles to accurately characterize the spatial distribution of fractures due to its stochastic nature; and outcrop-based sectioning methods lack systematic analysis of the spatial assembly and mechanical interaction of rock blocks. To address these shortcomings, this paper proposes an unstable rock block identification method based on the deterministic discrete fracture network (DDFN). Firstly, field-measured discontinuity parameters (occurrence, spacing and joint length) are integrated with a high-precision three-dimensional slope model, and discontinuity length constraints are introduced to construct a deterministic block system consistent with the actual slope morphology. Subsequently, a quantitative calculation model for the block safety factor is established through coupled analysis of slope failure modes and mechanical interactions between rock blocks, enabling targeted identification of potentially unstable blocks. The proposed method is validated using real open-pit mines slope engineering project. The results demonstrate that the method effectively overcomes the deficiencies of existing approaches in the accuracy of fracture characterization and block system analysis. It provides a reliable theoretical basis and technical support for disaster prevention and mitigation in rock mass engineering such as open-pit mine slopes, and exhibits favorable engineering practical value.

title: Integrating morphological texture classification with MCDA for early-stage trade-off analysis in open-pit mine design
source: Mining Technology Transactions of the Institutions of Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Luna S.I.J.; Shimada H.; Sasaoka T.; Hamanaka A.; Gabo-Ratio J.A.S.
keywords: decision-support framework | MCDA | mine feasibility assessment | Morphological texture classification | rock mass characterisation | slope stability
abstract: At the early stage of mine feasibility assessment, decision-making is constrained by high geological uncertainty despite the need for rapid evaluation of economic viability. This study proposes a morphological texture-based classification framework as a screening tool for early-stage mine design. Distinct textural variants within a single ore deposit are classified using field and laboratory data and evaluated across slope stability, excavation energy, and ore grade. A multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA) approach is applied to quantify trade-offs among these factors. Results show that weakly banded ores, such as deposition type 1 (DT), are easier to excavate but less stable, whereas competent units, such as DT6 and DT4, allow steeper, more stable slopes. The intermediate unit, as in DT5, exhibits higher grades but moderate constraints. MCDA ranking identifies DT6 as the most balanced unit. The framework demonstrates that morphological texture can effectively link geology with engineering and economic considerations, providing early-stage guidance for slope design and prioritisation under uncertainty.

title: Displacement prediction model for rainfall-induced landslides based on PDL-VMD-SVR: A case study of the southern slope landslide at Fushun West Open-pit Mine, China
authors: Zhang M.; Cai S.; Jin L.; Shen S.; Xu Y.
keywords: Fushun West Open-pit Mine | Lag effect | PDL-VMD-SVR hybrid model | Rainfall-induced landslide
abstract: Accurate rainfall-triggered landslide displacement prediction is vital for early warning systems. Rainfall-induced landslides typically exhibit significant hysteresis and abrupt changes in displacement. However, current models often oversimplify the relationship between landslide displacement and rainfall as static connections, making it challenging to capture the dynamic evolution of landslide displacements over time. We propose an AI-statistical hybrid model for rainfall-based displacement forecasting. This model incorporates Polynomial Distributed Lag (PDL), Support Vector Regression (SVR), and Variational Mode Decomposition (VMD) to address the complexities of rainfall-induced landslides. This study takes the southern slope landslide of the Fushun West Open-Pit Mine in China as a case study. Utilizing an improved version of the PDL model rooted in the Almonte method, the research aims to quantify the delayed effects of rainfall on landslides and establish a dynamic relationship between rainfall and landslide displacement. The results demonstrate that the PDL prediction model effectively identifies the hysteresis-like relationships between rainfall and landslide displacement. VMD-SVR refinement significantly improves accuracy, especially for lag-sensitive deformation. This integrated approach provides an efficient and innovative solution for predicting rainfall-induced landslide movements, offering valuable insights for disaster prevention and mitigation efforts.

title: Back-analysis of the rock landslide at the northeastern part of Kef Essenoun open-pit mine (NE Algeria): Post-disaster observations and numerical assessment
source: Journal of King Saud University Science
authors: Djabri M.; Bekkar H.; Boufarh R.; Gasri A.
keywords: Kef Essenoun | Landslide | Numerical analysis | Open-pit mine stability | Phosphate deposits | Post-disaster
abstract: In the early morning hours of September 8, 2007, a massive landslide occurred at the northeastern part of the Kef Essenoun (KEs) open-pit phosphate mine in Djebel Onk, northeast Algeria. Although no human casualties or direct material damage were recorded, the disaster had significant economic consequences, including the prolonged cessation of mining operations in the affected area and the abandonment of substantial phosphate reserves, which considerably reduced overall production. Therefore, this research aims to analyze the failure mechanism and stability of the KEs open-cast mine following a major landslide that brought mining operations to a halt. The stability analysis adopts two approaches, post-landslide observation and numerical analysis, intended to identify the probable cause of the disaster and delineate the unstable zone. Numerical simulation was carried out through the limit equilibrium method (LEM) and finite element method (FEM), where the failure surface and the factor of safety (FoS) were chosen as indicators to evaluate the stability of the KEs open-cast mine. Post-disaster geological and geotechnical investigation indicates that the low-strength phosphate-marl layer governs the instability, where the planar failure mode crosses this zone. The numerical simulation shows that the FoS values are significantly less than unity; both the LEM and FEM analyses yield close results, confirming that the studied quarry was unstable. In addition, the FEM (FoS=0.83) is more conservative than LEM (FoS=0.944) and produces a planar sliding that faithfully reflects the realistic failure mechanism. The study demonstrates the importance of integrated back-analysis in understanding open-pit landslide mechanisms and highlights the need to combine multiple analytical approaches to ensure reliable stability assessments.

title: Study on the Intelligent Recognition Algorithm for Open-Pit Mine Slope Fissures: Crack-YOLO with Texture and Semantic Enhancement
authors: Zhao H.; Wei H.; Liu W.; Jia H.; He C.
keywords: deep learning | fissure identification | open-pit mine | rock slope
abstract: Rock fissure parameters, such as length, width, and density, are essential for analyzing the progressive instability of open-pit mine slopes. Under the combined effects of engineering disturbance, geological conditions, and environmental factors, slope fissures continuously propagate and evolve. However, large variations in fissure scale, complex rock-surface textures, blurred boundaries, and weak micro-fissure features increase the difficulty of intelligent fissure segmentation, identification, and parameter extraction. Consequently, many mining enterprises still rely on manual interpretation, which is time-consuming and susceptible to subjective errors. To address these challenges, this study develops Crack-YOLO, a task-oriented fissure detection and instance-segmentation model based on YOLOv8-Seg. A total of 500 original UAV images were collected from multiple open-pit mines and processed to construct a dataset containing 3600 fissure image patches, including 3240 images for training and 360 images for testing. In Crack-YOLO, selected C2f modules are replaced with contextual semantic enhancement modules (CoT Blocks), and a texture information enhancement module (SM Block) is incorporated to strengthen contextual semantic representation and fine-grained texture-feature extraction. The model achieved segmentation precision, recall, mAP50, and mAP50:95 values of 0.896, 0.787, 0.854, and 0.392, respectively. For object detection, the corresponding values were 0.968, 0.862, 0.959, and 0.773, respectively. The segmentation results were further processed using K3M skeleton extraction and physical-scale calibration to quantitatively extract geometric parameters, including fissure length, equivalent average width, and azimuth. Validation using an image containing seven representative fissures yielded mean absolute errors of 0.016 m, 0.010 m, and 0.90° for fissure length, equivalent average width, and azimuth, respectively, indicating the feasibility of the proposed parameter-quantification workflow. In an application test conducted in a typical open-pit mine scene, the proposed workflow identified 196 fissures within approximately 22 s and quantitatively analyzed their geometric parameters and distribution characteristics. The results indicate that the proposed method has potential for fissure identification and geometric-parameter quantification in open-pit mine slopes and may provide quantitative data support for slope-fissure monitoring and stability analysis.

title: Fusion positioning method of “RTK+INS+Odometer” in unmanned mining trucks in open-pit mines
source: Meitan Kexue Jishu Coal Science and Technology Peking
authors: Mao Q.; Ren Z.; Qin S.; Ma H.; Xue X.
keywords: adaptive extended Kalman filter | INS and odometer integration | precise positioning | RTK | unmanned mining truck in open-pit mine | variational Bayesian optimization
abstract: To address the positioning inaccuracies of Real-Time Kinematic (RTK) technology caused by GPS signal attenuation, multipath, and communication interruptions in deep open-pit mines for unmanned mining trucks, as well as the errors in integrated inertial navigation system (INS) and odometer positioning resulting from tire slippage and the accumulation of INS pose detection deviations over time, proposes a "RTK+INS+Odometer" fusion positioning method based on Variational Bayesian-optimized Sage-Husa Adaptive Extended Kalman Filter (VB-AEKF). For precise position detection, a fusion positioning scheme combining RTK global positioning with INS+odometer local positioning is introduced, where the VB-AEKF algorithm estimates and optimizes process and measurement noise covariances in real time to mitigate the impact of system model uncertainties and time-varying noise characteristics on positioning. By integrating INS and odometer data to correct RTK instability, the stability and accuracy of position detection are significantly enhanced. To counteract tire slippage on rugged, vibrating terrain and the accumulation of INS attitude angle errors, a method constructing pseudo attitude angle constraints from displacement information is proposed, effectively suppressing attitude angle drift. A multi-sensor fusion positioning platform for unmanned mining trucks was established, and simulated open-pit mine environment experiments demonstrated that when the RTK signal is obstructed, the maximum positioning errors in the East, North, and Up directions are 0.5707m, 0.5543m, and 0.3647m, respectively, representing reductions of 0.2221m, 0.1465m, and 0.2162m compared to standalone RTK, with decrease rates of 28.01, 20.90, and 37.22. During unblocked turning, the maximum positioning errors in the East, North, and Up directions are 0.0081m, 0.0097m, and 0.0186m, reduced by 0.0021m, 0.0048m, and 0.0067m relative to standalone RTK, corresponding to decrease rates of 8.3, 20.69, and 19.14. On rugged turning sections, the maximum attitude angle error of the MEMS-based INS is 0.3121°, which is reduced by approximately 20 compared to the error of 0.4253° without constraints, significantly improving the system's positioning accuracy and stability in complex dynamic environments.

title: Deep-Profile Soil Water Replenishment for Sustainable Water-Saving Restoration of Open-Pit Mine Dumps in Arid and Semi-Arid Regions
authors: Lu X.; Chen S.; Wang L.; Zhu W.; Ji D.
keywords: arid and semi-arid regions | deep-profile soil water replenishment | non-productive evaporation | reconstructed mine-dump soil | sustainable mine restoration | vegetation establishment | water-use efficiency
abstract: Water scarcity, high non-productive soil evaporation, and poor vegetation establishment are major constraints on the sustainable ecological restoration of reconstructed open-pit mine dumps in arid and semi-arid regions. Conventional surface-applied water replenishment can result in rapid evaporative loss, thereby reducing the ecological benefits obtained from limited water resources. However, whether redistributing water into deeper reconstructed soil layers can simultaneously reduce non-productive evaporation, stabilize the root-zone hydrothermal environment, and improve vegetation growth remains insufficiently verified. In this study, a deep-profile soil water replenishment (DPSWR) device was tested in reconstructed mine-dump soil columns planted with locally adapted Stipa. Surface-applied water replenishment (CK) and DPSWR were compared using a single-run simulated rainfall comparison, soil water-retention and water-loss measurements, continuous temperature and moisture monitoring at 10 and 40 cm depths, and plant growth indicators. In the rainfall-simulation comparison, DPSWR showed lower cumulative water loss across the tested rainfall intensities and improved water-retention stability; the evaporation rate under CK was approximately 1.3 times that under DPSWR, whereas final soil water-holding capacity under DPSWR was approximately 2.4 times that under CK. Root fresh weight, plant fresh weight, and seedling number were significantly higher under DPSWR than under CK (p < 0.01), and maximum plant height and root length also increased significantly (p < 0.05). Under equal water-input conditions, DPSWR reduced non-productive water loss, prolonged soil water retention, and supported vegetation establishment. These findings suggest that DPSWR may provide a more water-efficient approach to the sustainable restoration of reconstructed mine dumps in water-limited regions.

title: Experimental Investigation and Numerical Simulation on the Strength and Deformation Characteristics of Granular Materials at Various Elevations of Dump Slope
authors: Meng J.; Liu J.; Li K.; Zhou T.; Zhou H.
keywords: discrete element simulation | dump slope | granular materials | large-scale triaxial tests | slope stability
abstract: Determining the shear strength parameters of granular materials in high waste rock dump slopes is essential for reliable slope stability analysis. In this study, dump materials were sampled from six benches (elevations 2800–2950 m) of an open-pit mine dump slope, and in situ density tests, gradation analyses, and large-scale consolidated drained (CD) triaxial tests were performed. Two PFC2D slope models—one with uniform (spatially averaged) parameters and one with elevation-dependent (layered) parameters—were then established to quantify how spatial heterogeneity affects stability predictions. The results show pronounced vertical heterogeneity: density, porosity, gradation, and shear strength parameters vary systematically among benches, reflecting the combined effects of compaction history and particle segregation during dumping. All specimens exhibited strain hardening and continuous shear contraction, and specimens with a denser, better-graded structure showed higher strength and lower compressibility. The layered model yields a higher factor of safety and shallower, bench-scale slip surfaces, whereas the uniform model underestimates stability and misplaces the critical slip zones. These findings demonstrate that elevation-dependent parameter assignment better represents the heterogeneous failure mechanism of high dump slopes and should be preferred over uniform parameterization in stability analyses of similar waste rock dumps.

title: Integrated Geophysical Characterization of Internal Structure and Preferential Seepage in Open-Pit Mine Waste Dump
authors: Li K.; Qiu H.; Li H.; Lu K.; Lian Y.; Jia R.; Li W.; Wang Y.
keywords: electrical resistivity tomography | open-pit mine waste dump | preferential seepage | spontaneous potential | surface nuclear magnetic resonance
abstract: The Mao open-pit coal mine waste dump in Hequ, Shanxi, is a loose, anthropogenic mass accumulated over the original topography. Following a recent sliding and significant settlement event, this dump became the subject of intense stability concerns. Due to the high moisture sensitivity of its interlayered soil and coal gangue structure, rainfall infiltration can reduce internal effective stress, triggering slope instability. Although conventional geological surveys have mapped surface fractures, implementing precise, targeted drainage control requires characterizing the internal geometric structure and preferred seepage directions. To address this, this study integrates electrical resistivity tomography (ERT), surface nuclear magnetic resonance (SNMR), and spontaneous potential (SP) methods. Multiple ERT profiles (270–600 m long) were deployed across several benches at varying elevations, supplemented by fixed-point SNMR sounding over typical low-resistivity anomalies and dense SP grid scanning. The integrated results successfully delineate the internal architecture and seepage characteristics of the dump. Specifically, ERT imaging resolves the primary geoelectrical interface (tentatively inferred as the potential sliding surface) separating the overlying loose mass from the stable underlying strata while mapping the spatial extent of the inferred water accumulation zone (IWAZ). SNMR sounding quantitatively reveals a two-layer water-bearing structure at the specific sounding site, with a deep primary water-bearing zone at 45–80 m depth. Furthermore, SP inversions illuminate the seepage process, demonstrating that meteoric water deflects along the geoelectrical interface to converge laterally toward the central axis at approximately 42°, before transitioning into a high-angle vertical deep infiltration zone (61.7°) within the axial region. These findings suggest a potential engineering direction for remediating surficial fractures and designing subsurface drainage along this 1040 m bench axis, which would mitigate future landslide risks by reducing internal pore water pressure.

title: Dual-Module Bench-Line Extraction and Surface-Object Segmentation from UAV LiDAR Point Clouds in Open-Pit Mines Using Neighborhood Geometric Analysis and an Enhanced PointNet++ Network
authors: Ge S.; Qian N.; Gao J.; Liu X.; Zhang W.; Feng Y.; Yang D.
keywords: 3D point-cloud processing | digital mine mapping | inverted residual learning | local self-attention | neighborhood geometry | semantic segmentation | structural discontinuity detection
abstract: Featured Application: The dual-module workflow provides complementary bench-line and surface-object information from UAV LiDAR point clouds. The geometry-based output can assist visual interpretation of bench morphology, while the semantic labels can support mine-map updating, haul-road mapping, and surface-object inventory. The case study demonstrates the feasibility of obtaining structural and semantic information from a common point-cloud dataset. Further reference-based evaluation and cross-mine testing will extend the applicability of the workflow to broader operational environments. Open-pit mines contain rapidly changing terrain, discontinuous bench structures, and mixed artificial–natural objects, which complicate automated three-dimensional mapping. This study presents a dual-module workflow for UAV LiDAR point clouds. Module A characterizes local geometry using normal and curvature descriptors, constructs local plane support through RANSAC fitting, and detects candidate bench-line points using an angular-gap criterion, followed by regional grouping and Kalman-filter refinement. Qualitative overlay with the orthophoto showed coherent correspondence with principal platform–slope transitions. Module B segments buildings, roads, and vegetation using a PointNet++ network enhanced by local Transformer self-attention and inverted residual feature transformation. Under a fixed spatial hold-out setting, the network achieved an overall accuracy of 97.6% and a mean intersection over union of 96.4%. It obtained the highest overall accuracy, mean intersection over union, and class-wise intersection over union among the selected baselines, whereas Point Transformer achieved a slightly higher mean class accuracy. The two independently operated modules provide complementary structural and semantic information for open-pit mine mapping. Broader applicability requires reference-based bench-line assessment and evaluation across additional mines and survey periods.

title: Determining the optimal power rating of a diesel generator and onboard energy storage system for a hybrid locomotive power plant used in haulage operations on quarry railways
authors: Riabov I.S.; Yeritsyan B.K.; Demydov O.V.; Tykhonov A.S.; Usychenko O.Y.
keywords: energy efficiency | energy storage | fuel and energy resources | hybrid power plant | locomotive | rolling stock
abstract: The paper examines the application of a hybrid power plant to locomotives performing shunting and hauling operations on quarry railways. The implementation of hybrid traction systems contributes to a reduction in diesel fuel consumption, thereby lowering CO<inf>2</inf> emissions and decreasing overall fuel and energy costs. The study focuses on a quarry railway line used to transport iron ore from an open-pit mine to a processing plant. A mathematical model was developed to determine the operating parameters under various locomotive operating modes. The simulation studies were carried out for train movements with both empty and loaded dump cars. The results show that the use of a hybrid power plant reduces fuel consumption during the loaded half-trip by 20.6%–30.8%, depending on the power rating of the diesel generator and the onboard energy storage system. During the empty half-trip, fuel consumption can be reduced by more than 50%. It was determined that the optimal power rating of the diesel generator is 800 kW. The minimum required power rating of the onboard energy storage system is also 800 kW. Although increasing the power rating of the energy storage system provides additional reductions in diesel fuel consumption, it results in its increased weight, larger overall dimensions, and higher cost.

title: Validation of UAV-Derived Discontinuity Data Against Field-Based Measurements for Kinematic Analysis in an Open-Pit Mine
authors: Kalhan M.K.E.; Kincal C.
keywords: Geographic Information Systems | Kinematic Analysis | Photogrammetry | Point Cloud | Rock Slope
abstract: This study conducted a kinematic analysis of rock slopes in an open-pit feldspar mine in Çine (Aydın, Turkiye) € and explicitly focused on the validation of uncrewed aerial vehicle (UAV)–based photogrammetry with structural data obtained from traditional field surveys. Input parameters (dip direction and dip angles) were collected using a traditional geological compass at 119 observation points and extracted from a UAV-generated dense point cloud using the CloudCompare Compass plugin. A direct reliability assessment between the two methods revealed that the UAV-derived orientations matched the traditional field measurements with high precision, specifically within a 2° to 3° margin of error. Furthermore, the UAV approach effectively facilitated data collection in inaccessible or hazardous zones, such as high bench faces and block debris areas, safely increasing spatial data coverage and saving time. Using these validated parameters, kinematic analyses identified 65 wedge, 40 planar, and 87 toppling failures, predominantly concentrated on northwest-facing slopes. Spatial evaluations using geographic information system (GIS) mapping techniques highlighted the finding that stable wedges are restricted to paleo-stream channels, whereas unstable cases are located in weathered zones affected by water infiltration. Ultimately, the study demonstrates that integration of UAV photogrammetry with conventional surveys provides a highly reliable, safe, and efficient framework for kinematic assessments in open-pit mines.

title: Real-Time Monitoring of Mine Dumps Using UAV-Based Remote Sensing Technology and Robotic Total Station: A Review-Based Methodological Framework
authors: Chand K.; Koner R.; Xu T.; Mitra R.
keywords: Failure prediction | OB dump | Real-time displacement monitoring | Slope displacement classification | Susceptible zone identification | UAV technology
abstract: Large open-pit coal mining operations traditionally rely on conventional survey techniques for overburden (OB) dump monitoring and management. However, as the open-pit mine expands, the stripping ratio also increases, resulting in the generation of a massive volume of OB material. Moreover, the height of the OB dump is increasing to over a hundred meters. Unplanned OB continuous deposition, high-intensity precipitation, and seismic loading trigger the OB dump slope failure. It is a serious concern for the mining industry because it interrupts production and, due to failure, leads to fatalities and loss of equipment, buried and stuck in massive OB debris flow. Therefore, real-time monitoring of zones susceptible to dump instability is essential for maintaining safety and promoting sustainable operations. In the era of Mining 4.0, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) technology has emerged as a relatively low-cost and reliable alternative for dump monitoring with high precision. The change detection technique is effective in identifying potential hazards in large dumps. Real-time monitoring of the susceptible zone will be conducted using a robotic total station (RTS). This review presents an integrated, innovative, and robust dump slope monitoring approach aimed at enhancing the mining industry’s understanding of real field conditions. By enabling real-time monitoring, this approach allows continuous observation of OB dump displacements providing critical insights into their behavior over time. This integrated monitoring framework supports the development of data-driven strategies effective for the dump planning, design, and safety management.

title: Blasting vibration analyses of open-pit mine slope
source: Journal of Rock Mechanics and Geotechnical Engineering
authors: Wang Z.; Hu B.; Ma Y.; Yuan L.; Li J.; Zhong Z.; Kong Z.
keywords: Blasting vibration | Energy characteristic | Safety criteria | Slope
abstract: Blasting vibration is a primary factor influencing the stability of mining slopes. Therefore, it is essential to investigate the vibration characteristics and establish safety criteria for open-pit mine slopes subjected to blasting activities. In this study, the high slope of a representative limestone mine was selected as the research object, and vibration wave data of the slope rock were obtained through blasting vibration monitoring. The study reveals the failure mechanism of mine slopes under blasting-induced vibrations and introduces a new criterion for blasting vibration safety. The analysis results show that the primary frequency range for the limestone mine slope is 10–45 Hz. As the distance from the blasting center increases, the peak particle velocity (PPV) of the blasting vibration wave gradually decreases and stabilizes at approximately 0.5 cm/s. When employing adaptive optimal kernel time-frequency analysis technology, the energy parameter of the Gaussian kernel function should be set to 2.4 to achieve superior suppression of cross-term interference and enhance resolution. The energy of the blasting vibration waves responsible for slope rock mass damage is concentrated within the frequency range of 0–78.125 Hz. Moreover, the influence of blasting vibration on the stepped does not produce a significant "whiplash effect". Comparative analysis between numerical simulations and safety criterion calculations confirms the reliability of the proposed safety criteria, as demonstrated by the consistent predictive accuracy under geomechanical conditions. The findings of this research provide critical insights for developing future technical standards and guidelines for blast vibration monitoring.

title: Prediction Model and Engineering Application of Slope Subsidence under the Influence of Goaf
authors: Sun S.; Wang X.; Zeng Y.; Li J.; Ma Y.
keywords: Goaf | Prediction | Slope | Subsidence
abstract: Under the transition from open-pit to underground mining, slopes above underground goafs commonly exhibit asymmetric subsidence and downslope deformation, posing increasing challenges for engineering assessment. To address the lack of simplified analytical methods for such conditions, this study develops a slope-subsidence prediction framework by extending classical flat-ground settlement-trough theory to slope environments. The proposed method comprises three coupled steps: construction of an equivalent horizontal settlement trough, introduction of a terrain-induced biased-loading correction, and geometric mapping of the corrected response back onto the actual slope surface. A Python-based computational model was developed to investigate the effects of internal friction angle, Poisson’s ratio, unit weight, elastic modulus, slope angle, and burial depth on the magnitude and morphology of slope subsidence, and gray relational analysis was employed to identify the dominant controlling factors. The Fushun West Open-Pit Mine was selected as the primary engineering case, whereas the Pusa and Jianshanying slopes were used as supplementary cases to assess the transferability of the proposed framework under more complex geological and topographic conditions. The results indicate that, within the stated simplifying assumptions, the proposed model can reasonably capture the first-order geometry of the subsidence basin, including its asymmetry, peak position, and attenuation trend, with reasonable engineering consistency. Internal friction angle and elastic modulus are identified as the dominant internal controlling factors, whereas slope angle primarily governs basin asymmetry. Overall, the proposed framework provides a simplified yet physically interpretable tool for the preliminary assessment and design screening of slope subsidence under open-pit to underground transition conditions.

title: Evaluation and Optimization of In-Pit Crushing and Conveying (IPCC) Systems in Open-pit Metal Mining: a Systematic Literature Review
authors: Wang X.; Li B.; Wang F.; Zhang Y.; Bi L.; Dai B.; Sun G.; Shi P.
keywords: In-Pit Crushing and Conveying Systems | Open-Pit Metal Mine | Sustainability in Mining | Transportation Systems Optimization | Truck-Shovel Systems
abstract: The optimization of open-pit metal mining transportation systems is pivotal for enhancing economic viability, operational efficiency, and environmental stewardship. While the traditional Truck-Shovel (TS) system remains prevalent, the In-Pit Crushing and Conveying (IPCC) system presents a transformative alternative with significant potential. This paper provides a comprehensive and systematic review of the advancements in both TS and IPCC systems, critically evaluating their performance across economic, safety, social, and environmental dimensions. Given the promise of IPCC technology, the review dedicates particular focus to its core optimization challenges: (i) determining the Ultimate Pit Limit (UPL) integrated with conveyor layout, (ii) optimizing the transition depth and crusher location, and (iii) synchronizing production scheduling with crusher relocation strategies. We synthesize a wide body of literature to analyze the strengths and limitations of prevalent optimization methodologies, from classical algorithms to modern stochastic and integrated frameworks. Furthermore, the paper identifies and discusses persistent challenges in transportation process evaluation and system-wide IPCC optimization. Finally, we propose a forward-looking research agenda aimed at developing intelligent, sustainable, and integrated transportation systems for the deep open-pit mines of the future. This work aims to serve as a foundational reference for mine planners considering IPCC implementation and to chart a course for future academic inquiry in open-pit mine transportation optimization.

title: A novel thermo-hydro-mechanical coupled model for soil-rock mixtures incorporating preferential flow: A case study of Hesigewula mine dump
authors: Cao J.; Zhou Z.; Zhang L.; Chen Z.; Wang Z.; Zeng X.; Han P.
keywords: Freeze-thaw-seepage | Preferential flow | Soil-rock mixture | Thermo-hydro-mechanical model | Waste dump slope
abstract: Landslides in soil-rock mixture dumps within cold-region open-pit mines involve intricate thermo-hydro-mechanical (THM) coupling processes. However, conventional multi-field coupling models often fail to capture the impacts of multiscale pore structures on slope responses. This study addresses this knowledge gap by conceptualizing the soil-rock mixture as a dual-porosity medium comprising matrix and fracture domains. Based on this framework, a novel thermo-hydro-mechanical model incorporating preferential flow (PF-THM) was developed to quantify the fracture-matrix water exchange during freezing-thawing processes. Taking the Hesigewula South open-pit mine dump as a case study, numerical simulations were performed to analyze the THM evolution under freeze-thaw and precipitation conditions. Results indicated that during the freezing process, the average water content increment in the frozen region of the fracture domain is approximately twice that of the matrix domain, with inter-domain exchange contributing about 1.0% of this increase. During precipitation, snowmelt infiltration is primarily dictated by the matrix domain (75.8%), leading to localized settlement due to the combined effects of snowmelt and dumped frozen materials. In contrast, rainfall infiltration occurs predominantly through the fracture domain (88.2%), triggering cutting-bedding-shear expansion failure along weak basal planes. Field validation demonstrates that the proposed PF-THM model achieves a superior fit compared to the conventional single-permeability model (SPM). Particularly for the hydraulic field, the root mean square error (RMSE) of water content during snowmelt is significantly reduced from 1.63% to 0.19%, and the rainfall-induced preferential flow is accurately reproduced. This study elucidates the cascading failure mechanism in cold-region dumps, providing a theoretical basis for disaster prevention and mitigation.

title: Monitoring the evolution of an open-pit mine-induced landslide using SBAS-InSAR: The Himmetoğlu case, Bolu, Türkiye
authors: Poyraz B.
keywords: InSAR | Landslide | LOS | SBAS | Time series
abstract: On December 12, 2017, a mass movement occurred at an open-pit mine site located approximately 18 km south of the Göynük district in Bolu province. As a result, deep cracks formed in the upper step, which had been left for safety purposes, and seven residences in the residential area near the operating boundary were damaged. In this study, the landslide area in question was analysed using the InSAR method using SAR data divided into consecutive periods with 75% temporal overlap. The detectability of deformation signals from the pre-landslide period was investigated. Deformation rates for each period were analysed as a percentage based on the DS points identified in the deformation area, and the time-dependent deformation behaviour of these points was examined in detail. Furthermore, a ten-month time series covering the pre-landslide period was created to evaluate the temporal evolution of the mass movement. The findings showed that approximately 10 months before the landslide, the DS points located in the landslide crown area were subjected to horizontal deformation toward the west; the vertical components accompanying this deformation varied in the form of uplift and subsidence. This provides important clues about surface tension accumulation, soil weaknesses, and the initial mechanics of movement. The study demonstrates that periodic monitoring of InSAR data can be an effective method for early detection of slowly developing landslides.

title: Enhanced-classification collaborative network: Rock recognitio n in low-light and blurry open-pit mines
authors: Sun D.; Yang R.; Zuo J.
keywords: Borehole image analysis | Deep learning | Enhancement-classification collaboration | Intelligent rock recognition | Low-light image restoration
abstract: In open-pit mine borehole imaging, insufficient ambient lighting and probe vibration often result in low-light and motion-blurred images, significantly compromising lithological identification accuracy and consequently constraining the precision of cast blasting parameter design. Existing approaches predominantly treat image restoration and rock classification as separate tasks, relying on physical priors that entail complex workflows and limited practicality. To address this, we propose an Enhancement-Classification Collaborative Network (ECC-Net) that enables simultaneous processing of low-quality image restoration and rock recognition. The image restoration module (BPLD-Net) incorporates multi-branch attention-based residual down sampling and a spatial-frequency joint enhancement module to preserve critical details and improve deblurring performance. The classification network (MSRC-Net), through its designed Basic Block and contextual feature extraction module, collaboratively captures local details and global structures, thereby enhancing feature dependencies and model generalization. Experimental results demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance in both restoration and classification tasks. Notably, in the challenging task of rock classification under low-light and motion-blurred conditions, the accuracy, precision, recall, and F1-score of ECC-Net are improved by 0.11, 0.04, 0.08, and 0.07, respectively, compared to the ResNet50 baseline. This consistent improvement, achieved while maintaining parameter efficiency, highlights the practical value of our collaborative framework in demanding real-world scenarios.

title: Enhancing the safety assessment of open-pit mine slopes with interpretable, data-driven stacking learning and three-dimensional stability analysis
authors: Tian Y.; Yang Y.; Ma L.; Qi X.; Lu X.
keywords: Artificial intelligence application | Data driven | Shapley additive explanations | Slope stability prediction | Stacking learning | Three-dimensional
abstract: Slopes, as complex geological structures, predominantly exist in three-dimensional (3D) forms, a characteristic particularly evident in human-engineered open-pit mines, and their stability directly influences overall reliability of mining system.
