The remaining species are attributed to four genera, Kanakyella, Pidaconomus, Caledoconcha, and Leiorhagium, which are all introduced in this paper. The radiation as a whole is characterized by the formation of the digestive gland, the stomach with an additional, ciliated proximal chamber, and the subdivision of the pallial oviduct. Whether or not a denticle situated behind the outer lip is a synapomorphy of the whole group cannot be stated with certainty. The genera are distinguished mainly by features of the genital system. For the cladistic analysis, which resulted in 419 equally parsimonious trees, only five characters could be used, and even those were not free of homoplasy. The genera Hemistomia and Pidaconomus are paraphyletic according to this analysis. In contrast to the widely accepted principles of phylogenetic systematics we retain these paraphyletic genera, because otherwise the diversification, i.e. the evolution, which has taken place within the clade could not be expressed in the classification. The majority of the species occur in very restricted areas. Twenty-six (48%) species were found in a single locality and only six species (11%) in ten or more places. The hydrobiid diversity of west coast drainages is much higher than that of river systems draining to the east. This is, at least partly, explained by the differing precipitation regimes and geological conditions of the regions considered. The west coast receives much less rainfall so that in continuous periods of drought the area of a species would be fragmented by drying up of springs and consequently gene flow between the remaining populations reduced, enhancing speciation. In addition, the west is geologically more heterogenous. Unfavourable, insular ultramafic mountains represent barriers for the dispersal along the west coast. Many of the taxa are highly threatened to become extinct in the closer future as a consequence of human activities, such as deforestation, agriculture, surface mining, or uncontrolled fires. The conservation of the unique New Caledonian radiation of crenobiontic gastropods requires a transformation of land management practices on privately-owned sites, and a more global reappraisal of the impact of fire and deforestation on water resources. © 1998 Kluwer Academic Publishers.

title: Progressive plant invasion and colonization of an area adjacent to ancient woodland at Edford Wood, Somerset, England
source: Botanical Journal of the Linnean Society
authors: Davie J.; Akeroyd J.; Thompson D.
keywords: Bulbous perennials | Conservation | Native status | Succession | Woodland management
abstract: Edford Wood, near Holcombe in Somerset, England has a rich and varied flora. Topography and species composition indicate that much of the woodland is of ancient origin. The history of the site is complex, with the woodland long subjected to considerable human disturbance from surface mining of coal, drainage and the felling of larger trees. Documentary and other evidence has revealed that part of the wood has developed from grassland during the present century. This area of secondary woodland illustrates processes of succession as woodland plants invade.

title: Growth of cottonwood and sycamore in relation to age, soils and topography on pre-1972 Ohio strip mine law sites
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Brown J.H.; Greenberg C.J.
abstract: Growth of two tree species planted at several different times on surface-mined sites in the unglaciated Allegheny Plateau of Ohio prior to passage of the 1972 Ohio Surface Mining Reclamation Law was studied. The <2 mm fraction of the minesoils on the sites are predominantly fine textured with over 20 percent coarse fragments. Peaks of spoil piles had typically been graded off, creating level to moderately sloping upland plateaus or ridges which dropped off abruptly to steep side slopes. Multiple regression analyses were used to study height growth of trees in relation to various combinations of topographic, soil physical and soil chemical conditions. Growth of cottonwood (Populus deltoides) varied from approximately 0.7 to 1.4 m per year. Multiple regression equations accounted for up to 78.6 percent of the variation in tree heights, with 45.1 percent attributable to tree age and the remaining 33.5 percent to other factors. Best growth occurred on level to gently sloping, northwest facing sites and minesoils having relatively high amounts of sand and low stone content. Height growth of sycamore (Platanus occidentalis) showed little variation in relation to varying topographic and soil conditions, with average growth of 0.8 m per year. In equations, age accounted for 83 percent of the variation in heights and up to an additional 5 percent was accounted for by other factors. Cottonwood appeared to reach an early pathological rotation age on study sites, with trees over 20 years of age showing top breakage and signs of decay, while older sycamore appeared to have high vigor, with little evidence of decay or/breakage.

title: Mine subsidence remediation using multiple grouting techniques
authors: Weber M.W.; Popper G.H.P.
abstract: A technically complex and multi-phased project to stabilize two homes threatened by mine subsidence was undertaken by the U.S. Department of Interior, Office of Surface Mining (OSM). The project was performed under OSM's Abandoned Mine Land emergency program. Two residents in the small community of Slickport, Pennsylvania filed a complaint with OSM claiming their properties had experienced damage due to subsidence in an abandoned underground coal mine. The damage to the homes included foundation settlement, deflection of support columns, infiltration of groundwater into the basements, cracking of walls, and wedging of doors and windows. A geotechnical subsurface investigation was performed to determine if mine subsidence was responsible for the damage.

title: An integrated approach to the design and management of surface mine haul roads in South Africa
authors: Thompson R.; Visser A.
abstract: The surface mining and quarrying industry make extensive use of haul roads for bulk handling and transport of both ore and waste. Most of these haul road designs are based on local experience, and researchers at the University of Pretoria Departments of Civil and Mining Engineering recognised scope for improvement in design, construction and maintenance management guidelines for mine haul roads. Following four years of research, the application of these new and comprehensive guidelines has enabled mine operators in the Republic of South Africa to reduce total haulage costs significantly whilst providing optimally safe transport operating conditions. The worldwide expansion of surface mining has led to the development of very large off-highway trucks currently capable of hauling payloads in excess of 160 t. Typical axle loads ranging from 110 t to 170 t are applied to haul roads that have been, at best, empirically designed on the premise of "satisfactory" or "failed", both in terms of structure and function of the road. The use of these empirical pavement design techniques will prove inadequate when high axle loads are encountered. Not only will the maintenance costs of existing haul roads of inadequate thickness increase, but vehicle operating and maintenance costs will also increase prohibitively. Under these conditions there is thus a clearly defined need for improved technologies encompassing the construction and management techniques of flexible mine haul roads, appropriate for the wheel loads of vehicles now in use. The aim of this paper is to present the improved haul road design and management techniques which have been developed specifically for bulk material transport operations on South African surface mines. The paper illustrates how these developments are combined into an integrated design strategy combining mine layout, construction techniques, available material and road maintenance equipment with hauler choice to realise a reduction in haulage and road maintenance costs. In conclusion, it was found that the proposed mechanistic structural design methodology can significantly reduce road construction costs and improve the structural strength of the pavement. The improved functionality of a pavement was achieved through the specification of performance related wearing course material selection parameters, based on road-user acceptability criteria. Finally, the maintenance management design was centred on the development of a maintenance scheduling model from which it was seen that considerable financial benefit could accrue from applying a maintenance management system to mine haul roads.

title: Impacts of surface mining and the planning process for their restoration
source: Engineering Geology and the Environment Proc Symposium Athens 1997 Vol 3
authors: Hatzistathis A.; Gkanatsas P.; Ispikoudis I.
abstract: Mining industry, as almost any human activity, has a profound influence on environmental values and provides an inevitable conflict between landscape and environmental preservation and economic wealth in Greece. This paper, tries to analyze the above influences and the factors related to the proper planning of both, exploitation and restoration of mining sites, in such a way, that their impact on landscape and natural environment will be as less as possible.

title: Blast vibrations in oil shale surface mining
authors: Toomik A.; Tomberg T.
abstract: The blast vibrations were studied in the soil of quaternary sediments and in Ordovician limestone in mining area. The measurements were performed by seismograph DS-277 Blast-Mate Series II of Instantel Inc. and seismograph UVS-1500 of ABEM Instruments AB. The analysis of measured data pointed at a good correlation between vibration velocity and scaled distance from charges. The formulas for prediction of vibration velocity and for maximum charge weights were elaborated for both vibration media - soil and limestone. © 1997 Institute of Chemistry Estonian Academy of Sciences.

title: Controlled blasting operations and high wall stability in surface mining in Australia
authors: Pilcher B.
abstract: This paper will present the controlled blasting methods used in surface operations in Australia and mentions some of the design guidelines used in maintaining pit wall stability. The methods will include cushion blasting, presplitting, postsplitting and the use of these methods with production blasts.

title: Advantageous use of long-distance exploration in surface mining as exemplified by the Lusatian brown coal mining industry
authors: Drebenstedt C.; Knorr F.; Marek K.
abstract: Brown coal mining encroaches on the immediate environment like no other process of human activity. It is characteristic of the mining process in particular that it has an effect on nature over a large area and also over a long period of time. In order to lessen and compensate the effects of this encroachment by the mining industry, measures are adopted already during the mining process which aim, above all, to reduce the effects resulting from changed ground-water conditions and to ensure the creation of local abiotic features on the dumps and tips so that stable natural conditions can be established again after the cessation of mining operations. Long-distance exploration is a valuable aid for determining and recording the manifold and complicated relationships between mining and the environment. In this way the geometry and characteristic features of the objects in question can be determined. From sequential photographs showing changes in nature conclusions can be drawn, for instance, as to whether such changes have been caused by mining, as to the extent to which safety and preservation measures are effective, and whether recultivation can be carried out systematically. Together with other data on the area in question, long-distance exploration data can be stored in geo-information systems and can be evaluated and used very effectively for planning and monitoring purposes.

title: Developments in the analysis of footwall slopes in surface coal mining
authors: Stead D.; Eberhardt E.
keywords: Analysis of footwall slopes | Mountainous topography | Surface coal mining | Two-dimensional limit equilibrium technique
abstract: Surface mining of coal, particularly in areas of mountainous topography, often involves the formation of extensive footwall slopes parallel to the strata dip. Due to structural deformation steep dips on the limbs of folds may be encountered in association with thrust faults, jointing and residual shear strength conditions. Such an environment necessitates a rigorous assessment of footwall stability in order to ensure safe and economic exploitation of the coal. This paper provides a detailed review of the factors influencing footwall slope instability in surface coal mining and the major instability mechanisms which have been recognized within the published literature. The analysis of footwalls in the design stage and the back analysis of footwall slope failures has in general been undertaken using predominantly two-dimensional limit equilibrium techniques often incorporating a simplistic elastic column analysis. The application of numerical modelling techniques to surface coal mine footwalls has received little attention. In this paper the authors attempt to illustrate the potential for investigating footwall failure mechanisms and stability using principally the distinct element method. © 1997 Elsevier Science B.V.

title: Retreat of halophytes in the Czech Republic: Agricultural, mining, and urbanization effects: [The Case of Dentated Melilot - Melilotus dentata (Fabaceae)]
source: Journal of Agricultural and Environmental Ethics
authors: Nováková J.
keywords: Biodiversity | Halophytes | Land use | Melilotus dentata | Salt marshes
abstract: As a result of expanding human pressures, the heterogeneity of a formerly diverse landscape has been reduced and the richness of animal and plant species has decreased. Some particular stand types and their species are especially connected with impoverishment caused by man's activities. Halophyte Dentated Melilot (Melilotus dentata, Fabaceae) is one of such species, which is vanishing apparently as a result of intensive agriculture, surface mining, and urbanization. The data on its distribution were compiled from herbarium specimens, literature, and the author's own field observations. The distribution was mapped separately for four periods: up to 1900, 1901-1945, 1946-1975, and after 1975. The trend in reduction of localities was documented. At the same time, their environmental quality was changing as well. Basically, the salt marshes in their original areal extent and their former species richness have disappeared. Current localities of M. dentata include poor fragments of the salt marshes mentioned above and secondary stands, e.g. ruderal places inside villages, strips along drainage ditches, paths, railway lines, fields, etc.

title: Getting maximum yield from surface mining land by reclaiming pits with municipal waste
authors: Lee Aston R.; Hedges P.D.
abstract: Surface mines, particularly those of construction minerals, are prime sites for solid waste depositories. Annual surface mining amply creates sufficient void space to accommodate annual volumes of waste generated. Open pits should be used as landfills to accomplish complete reclamation of a majority of mined voids, restoring the land to beneficial surface re-use, thereby conserving land. Present day technology can make almost any pit safe from landfill leachate contaminating groundwaters. Successful examples are given in three Anglo nations. The combining of two earth-disturbing industries, surface mining and landfilling, is advocated. Landfilling problems and pit preparation are discussed. Voluntary reclamation by landfilling and regulatory dual purpose permitting for mining and landfilling is proposed. The public's urgent need for waste disposal space is simultaneously resolved. Fully restored mined lands create increased land values by highly profitable landfilling. Industry and environmentalists should rejoice.

title: Different types of belt conveyors and their applications in surface mines
authors: Kesimal A.
abstract: Due to its nature, open-cast mining requires a variety of conveying systems able to offer: high capacity to suit the mine's throughput, flexibility by means of extensible or shiftable machines, to accommodate a continuously moving quarry-face, uphill conveying at steep angles in order to adapt to the mine grades, downhill conveying, accommodation of a variety of material sizes, and suitability for long hauls over difficult terrain. Most of the transportation studies related to surface mining will evaluate the economics of the belt conveying technology versus truck hauling. Sometimes, depending on specific local conditions, railway based transport will be considered. As conveyor technology advances and the operators increasingly take a long-term approach, flexible and reliable belt conveying systems become the method of choice in such operations. In this paper, presently and commonly used belt conveyors in surface mining have been reviewed.

title: An overview of diesel particulate exposures and control technology in the u.S. mining industry
authors: Haney R.A.; Saseen G.P.; Waytulonis R.W.
abstract: Studies of diesel particulate exposures in the U.S. mining industry indicate that diesel particulate exposures in surface mining operations are generally less than 0.2 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground coal mines using diesel-powered equipment ranged from 0.1 to 2.1 mg/m3. Average diesel particulate exposures in underground metal and nonmetal mines ranged from 0.3 to 1.6 mg/m<sup>3</sup>. The purpose of this article is to provide an overview on worker exposure to diesel particulate matter (DPM) and to discuss the effect of control technology on that exposure. Worker exposure has been assessed from in-mine diesel particulate measurements. The effect of control technology has been evaluated by a systems approach, which includes engine emission rate, mine ventilation system, and the effectiveness of engine after treatment devices. Studies conducted by the Mine Safety and Health Administration and the Bureau of Mines show that the primary means currently employed by the mining industry to control worker exposure to DPM include mine design, ventilation, engine maintenance, and the use of low sulfur fuel. Additional reductions in exposure can be obtained through the use of electronic engine technology. Commercially available after treatment devices are capable of reducing DPM by 25 to 95 percent. Reductions in exposure to DPM are dependent on the application of available engine emission control technology and modifications to mine ventilation systems. © 1997, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Impact of coal surface mining on three Ohio watersheds - Surface-water hydrology
source: Journal of the American Water Resources Association
authors: Bonta J.; Amerman C.; Harlukowicz T.; Dick W.
keywords: Curve number | Flow duration | Hydrology | Peak flow | Strip mine | Surface mine
abstract: A study was conducted to determine the effects of mining and reclaiming originally undisturbed watersheds on surface-water hydrology in three small experimental watersheds in Ohio. Approximately six years of data were collected at each site, with differing lengths of premining (Phase 1), mining and reclamation (Phase 2), and post-reclamation (Phase 3) periods. Mining and reclamation activities showed no consistent pattern in base-flow, and caused slightly more frequent higher daily flow volumes. Phase 2 activities can cause reductions in seasonal variation in double mass curves compared with Phase 1. Restoration of seasonal variations was noticeably apparent at one site during Phase 3. The responses of the watersheds to rainfall intensities causing larger peak flow rates generally decreased due to mining and reclamation, but tended to exceed responses observed in Phase I during Phase 3. Natural Resources Conservation Service (NRCS) curve numbers increased due to mining and reclamation (Phase 2), ranging from 83 to 91. During Phase 3, curve numbers remained approximately constant from Phase 2, ranging from 87 to 91.

title: An introduction to the integrated design of surface mine haul roads
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Thompson R.; Visser A.
abstract: The world-wide expansion of surface mining has led to the development of very large off-highway trucks currently capable of hauling payloads in excess of 160t. Typical axle loads ranging from 110t to 170t are applied to haul roads that have been, at best, empirically designed on the premise of "satisfactory" or "failed", both in terms of structure and function of the road. The use of these empirical pavement design techniques will prove inadequate when high axle loads are encountered. Not only will the maintenance costs of existing haul roads of inadequate thickness increase, but vehicle operating and maintenance costs will also increase prohibitively. Under these conditions there is thus a clearly defined need for improved construction and management techniques for flexible mine haul roads, appropriate for the wheel loads of vehicles now in use. The aim of this paper is to introduce developments in haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management which overcome the limitations associated with the previously empirical design techniques and to show how these developments are combined into an integrated design strategy combining construction techniques, available material and road maintenance equipment with hauler choice to realise a reduction in haulage and road maintenance costs. Future contributions will enumerate on the fundamental haul road structural, functional and maintenance design and management research from which these developments originated.

title: Surface mining equipment cost analysis with a developed linear break even model
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Cebesoy T.
abstract: As the international surface mining industry proceeds into twenty first century, surface operation throughout the world will increasingly encounter many problems in terms of economic viability and in such situations, true cost analysis techniques taking into account time value of money approach have gained more important than ever before. Linear break even model as a true cost analysis model contributes an important role in surface mining equipment cost analysis. As an illustration, this paper introduces a linear break even model developed for equipment replacement analysis and in so doing, also the adaptation of two linear models which will be used in estimating equipment operating cost over time are examined in detail. Hence the paper is concluded with a given numerical example.

title: Achieving effective telerobotic control of industrial equipment
authors: Hunter D.; Wells D.; Chrystall K.; Feighan P.
keywords: Automation | Surface mining | Telerobotic control | Telerobotic equipment
abstract: Equipment which may be remotely operated, has some degree of on-board intelligence, and which for periods of time may operate autonomously, is referred to as telerobotic. Recent advances in electronics, computers and hydraulic equipment have dramatically reduced the cost and simplified the process of converting standard industrial equipment to telerobotic control. The benefits of telerobotic equipment include improved safety by removing the operator from dangerous situations, reduced maintenance costs and increased productivity. This technology has been proven in various military, nuclear, and police applications. The surface mining industry has expressed an interest in automation and is characterized by a willingness to use remotely operated equipment, however, the majority of telerobotic equipment currently in use is experimental or prototypical. Potential applications of telerobotic equipment for surface mining include remote operation of equipment near dangerous highwalls and other unsafe areas, utilization of robotic trucks for routine hauling operations, and control of jointed equipment In addition, component technologies of telerobotic systems are relevant to various forms of condition monitoring, operator feedback systems, and vehicle positioning. Attention must now be directed toward resolving more complex problems associated with enhancing feedback to the operator, improving the man/machine interface, and ultimately, improving efficiency. Removal of the human operator from the work site introduces significant complications in replacing the sensory inputs that an operator normally uses to efficiently run his machinery. These can be difficult to define and even more difficult to replicate remotely and may include restrictions pertaining to vision, hearing, and touch. In cooperation with Defence Research Establishment Suffield and the Alberta Research Council, Robotech Industries Ltd. is pursuing the development of additional technologies to further enhance an operator's ability to control remote telerobotic equipment. These developments include a head-mounted display, additional control station displays and improvements to coordinated motion control software. Prototypes of these developments are expected to be completed and tested by the fourth quarter of 1997.

title: Materials for controlling wear in surface mining
authors: Llewellyn R.
keywords: Abrasion | Elastomers | Erosion | Friction | Surface mining | Wear
abstract: It has been estimated conservatively that the costs of wear damage and friction in the Canadian mining and mineral processing industry amount to over one billion dollars per year. These are mainly incurred through the repair or replacement of worn parts and production losses from related equipment downtime. The selection and application of the most appropriate wear protection components and systems, can thus have a very significant influence on productivity, profitability and global competitiveness. Details are presented of the wide diversity of materials used to counteract the varied and often complex wear attack mechanisms that occur in surface mining. The majority are various forms of steels and irons with generally very high hardness. However, they also include relatively soft elastomers and polymeric products. The main characteristics and applications of the different classes are reviewed. Case studies record significant performance improvements achieved through more judicious selections. Finally, some new developments which reduce maintenance charges by substantially increasing wear component life, are described.

title: Mining process optimization and quality control by computer-aided development planning in surface mining
authors: Emons A.; Schwarzkopp F.
abstract: This paper briefly describes how to use specialized mining software in order to optimize the mining process and quality output. Before simulating future mining operations, two models have to be set up. One model which describes the actual mining situation by using survey data, whilst the second model represents the deposit, using borehole data and other available geological information such as existing cross-sections. By using geostatistical modules, a block model can be built up which acts as a spatial data base and allows all necessary data for the mine scheduling processes to be calculated and visualized.

title: The primacy quandry
authors: Sprouls M.
abstract: Mistrust often fuels the debate when federal and state surface mining law enforcement agencies collide.

title: Appearance of wear in brown coal surface mining - reduction of wear by application of modern materials technology
authors: van den Heuvel B.
abstract: A number of modern materials technology researches have been carried out to improve wear behavior in excavators. The existence of different wear types and wear parameters complicates the wear problem and presents great difficulties in material selection. St 37, a structural steel with a high hardness number, was proven effective for buckets and their wearing parts, while deposition welding with plasma powder demonstrated longer service life and reduced costs for bucket replacement. However, the application of these developments are limited and unsuccessful for other wear parameters.

title: New surface mining developments in India
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Mozumdar B.

title: Supervisory control systems and the intelligent mine - A new tool for productivity improvement in surface mining
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Olivieri F.
abstract: In the late 70's Modular implemented its first mine management system, called DISPATCH, for haulage optimization in open pit mines. Since that time, this system has been placed in over 75 mines worldwide. Initially just used for dispatching haul trucks, the system has evolved to provide complete, real-time and historical production data and maintenance data. It also allows connection to onboard PLCs (programmable logic controllers) supplied by major equipment manufacturers for monitoring machine data and global positioning systems (GPS). The DISPATCH mine management system has developed into the cornerstone of these operations. Every ton dug and every second worked is counted. Each equipment work assignment is optimized. Global positioning systems and on-board monitoring computers are laying the groundwork for video arcade age mines. The advances in equipment electronics technology over the pasl five years has been tremendous. Who knows how our mines will look after the next five years. How about a glimpse into the future? First a little background history.

title: Surface mining collaborative research initiatives: a progress report
authors: Muirhead I.
abstract: Over the past year or so, a number of mining companies have been meeting to examine the role of research in surface mining and, in particular, how to establish a collaborative research effort for the surface mining industry. A review has been completed which has identified the topics that are of interest to the surface mining companies for undertaking collaborative research. This has identified key subject areas such as Operations & Equipment; Maintenance; Environment & Reclamation; and Stability. Specific research projects for the initial research effort have been selected which include Wireless Data Communications, Analysis and Management; Application of GPS in Mining; and Tires for Heavy Haulers. In addition, attention has also been focussed on finding a suitable low cost, but effective, organization to coordinate and manage the collaborative research. The recently formed CONRAD Organization (Canadian Oilsands Network for Research and Development) appears to be a suitable candidate and discussions are ongoing with that group. This paper provides a summary of the review of surface mining research needs and of the status of the establishment of a collaborative research body for surface mining.

title: Results of in-situ measurement of breaking characteristics of rocks in lignite surface mines
source: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
authors: Jurman J.; Vrbický J.
abstract: The breaking characteristics of rock is expressed for individual excavation technologies, and, with regard to differences of individual processes, there is no universal criterion of such breaking evaluation. A demand for information quality and quantity increase in a sense of the breaking characteristics with surface mining, led to the consideration of using drilling process monitoring results that could be applied easily on given terms. However, it means the expression of a correlation between when drilling = drillability, and between breaking when drilling with a rotary excavator = digging resistance. On the basis of operational measurements, the problem analysis was performed and possibilities of the solution were outlined.

title: Development of surface mining technology and operation management in the Rhineland lignite basin
source: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
authors: Oster A.
abstract: The largest German lignite deposit is found to the west of the city of Cologne, Rhineland. The lignite is mined in four opencast mines with a total capacity of 110 - 120 Mt/a. The gradual deterioration of mining conditions has been encountered by concentrating lignite recovery in very four mines, implementing new concepts in the mine design and operation and realizing numerous technical and organizational innovations. All this contributed to a notable increase in productivity of the mines, which allows competition on the energy market. Since the seventies, bucket wheel excavators, stackers and belt conveyors with a capacity of 240.000 m<sup>3</sup>+t/d have been in use which since then have proven their versatility even in difficult conditions. For the effective operation of this equipment, each mine is run via a modern electronic monitoring and communication center.

title: Definition and asessment of harmful wasts deposited in mine dumping grounds
source: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
authors: Piatkowiak N.; Golczyk W.
abstract: Surface mining of brown coal deposits leaves dumping grounds that need to be returned to the natural environment. They often contain materials that are harmful or potentially harmful to the environment. The location of such materials is usually not known. An attempt has been made to define and classify those harmful and potentially harmful wastes. The need for a unified classification and assessment model has. Such a model should be applied, in a legislative form, all over Germany. Geotechnical parameters should be included as a significant part of the model.

title: Natural environment quality assessment as a basis for prediction of changes in ecosystems within lignite surface mining areas
source: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
authors: Dyrduła J.; Jȩdrzejczak M.
abstract: The paper includes remarks relating to the value of environmental quality recognition as an important initial basis for performing and realizing procedure Environmental Impact Assessment (EIA) for the existing and designed mining plants. The attention is called to the possibilites for the use of spatial information sytems, particularly Geographical Information Systems (GIS), as an aid in gathering, processing and making available information on the environment within lignite surface areas.

title: Pushing the envelope
authors: Whiteway P.
abstract: Since 1978, Syncrude Canada has acquired a wealth of operating experience in Alberta's tough oil sands environment. Today, the company's owners are excited about investing in expansion, and Syncrude is utilizing technology that should enable the company to mine sands further removed than ever before from its processing complex. The success of the project will allow even more of the huge Athabasca oil sand deposit to be mined using surface mining methods and owners will realize their target of a 12% return on capital invested.

title: Influence of stratification of reclaimed slopes of dumps on water regime
authors: Kuráž V.; Čermák P.; Gurtz J.
keywords: Hydraulic characteristics | Moisture measurements | Numerical simulation | Reclamation of dumps | Water regime
abstract: Reclamation of surface dumps, where the waste earth from surface mining is collected, seems to be very important technical problem. At the present time, the following variants of reclamation of the dump surface are used: surface covered by 10 to 20 cm of different organic matter and mixture of organic matter and the basic earth of the dump. The influence of stratification of soil profile in the case, when hydraulic functions of layers are significantly different have been tested in laboratory conditions. The results were compared with those of numerical simulation using model BOWAM and with results of field measurements. It was proved, that the covering of the surface of the dump using organic matter negatively influences water regime. Total amount of rainfall is consumed by the organic matter and due to stratification of soil profile and significantly lower hydraulic conductivity of basic material water is not able to penetrate to deeper parts of the profile.

title: The development of highwall mining systems
authors: Seear P.
abstract: Highwall mining has existed in many forms for several decades. This paper analyses the recent advance in highwall mining with the development of the Addcar mining system. The paper provides an historical perspective of various systems over the last 30 years.

title: Hard rock overburden - a basalt 'quarry' in a clay pit
authors: Ladnorg U.
abstract: When winning raw ceramic materials in a surface mining operation, overburden layers to be cleared are currently up to 30 m thick. To some extent, these overlying layers are composed of hard rock in the form of basalt. The movement of a such overburden represents a distinctive problem, since typical overburden technology is oriented to the clearing of loose rock such as, gravel, sand, clay and tuff, which account to a great extent for the predominant share of the overlying layers. Clearing of compact basalt requires the utilisation of methods taken from hard rock quarrying operations.

title: A review of comparative study of transportation systems for surface mining operations
authors: Kesimal A.

title: Development of welded structures for mining equipment
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation
authors: Powers B.
abstract: The trend in equipment selection for the surface mining industry is the use of larger but fewer machines. This puts increased demands on the reliability of these machines since a single breakdown can significantly reduce a mines output. To meet these higher availability requirements, the Harnischfeger Corporation utilizes contemporary design methods coupled with innovative manufacturing processes to develop the large, welded structures which are used in today's surface mining equipment.

title: An evaluation of habitat rehabilitation on coastal dune forests in Northern KwaZulu-Natal, South Africa
authors: Van Aarde R.J.; Ferreira S.M.; Kritzinger J.J.; Van Dyk P.J.; Vogt M.; Wassenaar T.D.
abstract: The rehabilitation program conducted by Richards Bay Minerals (RBM) of areas exposed to opencast surface mining of sand dunes north of Richards Bay (28°43′S, 32°12′E) on the coast of northern KwaZulu-Natal Province commenced 16 years before this study and has resulted in the development of a series of known-aged stands of vegetation. By assuming that these spatially separated stands develop along a similar pathway over time, instantaneous sampling should reveal successional or other changes usually associated with aging and should provide an opportunity to evaluate the success of rehabilitation. We compare relative densities of pioneer and secondary species, species richness, and a similarity index of the herbaceous layer, tree, beetle, millipede, bird, and small-mammal communities of rehabilitating areas of known age with those of 30-year-old unmined forests and unmined forests of unknown age adjacent to the rehabilitating area. Species richness for all but the mammalian taxa increased with increasing age of rehabilitating stands. For all taxa but the mammals and herbaceous layer, the unmined stands harbored more species than the mined rehabilitating stands. The relative densities of pioneer species of all the taxa decreased with an increase in the age of rehabilitating stands, whereas those of the secondary species increased with an increase in habitat age. Similarity between unmined stands and rehabilitating stands of different ages increased with increasing regeneration age of rehabilitating stands, suggesting that rehabilitating communities, in terms of species composition and relative densities, are developing towards the status of unmined communities. Rehabilitation based on RBM's management program of limited interference is occurring and may result in the reestablishment of a coastal dune forest ecosystem. But rehabilitation resulting from succession depends on the availability of species sources from which colonization can take place. In the Richards Bay mining operation the present mining path is laid out so that such refuges are present.

title: Preserving natural environments on coal lands at minimum cost
authors: Watson W.
abstract: In the U.S., about 67 billion tons of coal (27% of the nation's surface minable coal) have been placed off-limits to surface mining by the Federal Land Policy Management Act and other restrictions in order to protect the environment. By the year 2005, it is projected that this reduction in coal reserves will add about $500 million per year to the nation's energy costs. As set-aside costs grow and the locked-up coal is perceived as progressively more valuable over time, it is likely that pressure will be brought on the U.S. Department of the Interior to revise its resource management plans. As a general rule, a rational management objective is to achieve a given amount of environmental preservation at the lowest cost. This paper provides an analytic framework, namely constrained cost minimization, for implementing that objective. Examples are given for protecting sage grouse and eagle habitat.

title: Surface mining equipment developments worldwide
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Atkinson T.; El-Alfy S.; Terezopoulos N.

title: Potential applications of EDP in surface mining
authors: Stoll R.; Tudeshki H.; Zuehlsdorff R.
abstract: The Department of Mining Engineering III of the Technical University, Aachen, increasingly combines commercially available and self-developed software systems in the planning of complex quarry operations. The use of such computer programs permits the simulation of deposits, systems of working, also the deployment of different equipment types for loading, transporting and crushing. Within short times the active operations of a quarry or the use of specific equipment can be simulated, including cost calculations. Alternatives can be developed and compared in order to select the best solution or to optimize operations. This paper presents the potential of such computer programs by the way of extracts from a recent planning project for a quarry in Germany.

title: Development in exploration, evaluation and exploitation of cement raw materials
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Kumar V.; Raju U.; Rao Y.
abstract: Computers are playing an increasingly important role in geological exploration, evaluation and mine planning. Their capability to significantly increase the interpretative skills, efficiency and productivity of both explorationists and mine planners has bean proved beyond doubt. This paper focuses on the computer capabilities and its application in formulating exploration strategies and assessing mineral deposits, etc. apart from highlighting the salient features of available commercial softwares. An overview of technological advancements in surface mining methods and haulage systems, particularly from environmental angle is also presented.

title: Sulfide oxidation in brown coal overburden and chemical modeling of reactions in aquifers influenced by sulfide oxidation
authors: van Berk W.; Wisotzky F.
keywords: Brown coal mining | Chemical modeling | Ground water chemistry | Hydrochemistry | Pyrite oxidation | Soil gas | Sulfide oxidation
abstract: Surface mining of brown coal in the Rhineland brown coal mining area (Germany) causes acidification of pyritic sandy overburden sediments. Convective transport of air, indicated by an enrichment of nitrogen gas in oxidized overburden, is, in addition to diffusion of oxygen, the driving mechanism for sulfide oxidation. Products of sulfide oxidation (2SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup> + 2H<sup>+</sup> + Fe<sup>2+</sup>) stored in acidic material in the overburden dump are leached by groundwater filling the dump and react with the carbonate phases of nonacidic material. The resulting hydrochemical composition (up to 6000 mg l<sup>-1</sup> SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup>, 3000 mg l<sup>-1</sup> Fe<sup>2+</sup>, pH 4.5) in groundwaters is controlled by simultaneous solubility equilibria with CaSO<inf>4</inf>·2H<inf>2</inf>O<inf>(s)</inf>, Fe(OH)<inf>3(s)</inf>, Fe<inf>0.9</inf>Ca<inf>0.1</inf>CO<inf>3(s)</inf> and CO<inf>2(g)</inf>. Calculated equilibrium concentrations of major components and pH in groundwater, partial pressure of CO<inf>2(g)</inf> in soil gas, and coupled mass transfer match observed conditions. © 1995 Springer-Verlag.

title: Servicing Olympic Dam
authors: Chadwick J.
abstract: Product support/service agreements are becoming more common around in the mining industry. Led by surface mining, the underground sector is also now beginning to develop such relationship between supplier and mining company. A good example of this agreement is between Tamrock and Olympic Dam. Both parties benefit greatly from the agreement. Olympic Dam report that it saves money in equipment maintenance and parts and benefited from increased machine availability and reliability. Tamrock safeguards its parts sales from 'pirates' and generates more business with the Olympic Dam, while both parties able to benefit from product development in a very high productivity underground operation.

title: Formal versus Substantive Justice: The Legislative History of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977
authors: Unnever J.D.; Higgins P.

title: Optimizing mine life and design capacity
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Hajdasinski M.
abstract: In his recent paper, “A theoretical approach to determination of mine life and design capacity,” (International Journal of Surface Mining, vol.3, 1989, pp. 49-50), Z. Li maintains that, under the reinvestment assumption, the objective functions of models for the optimization of mine life and design capacity should be based on the Net Future Value rather than on the Net Present Value concept. The current contribution proves that, in fact, the opposite is true, and that the Net Future Value would make models with unconstrained time variable, like Li's model, undefined. It is also demonstrated that Li's sensitivity analysis is misleading, as are his optimization results, since meaningful optimal solutions cannot be obtained from his optimization model. © 1995, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Lung cancer in former bismuth workers (1992)
authors: Bruske-Hohlfeld I.; Kreienbrock L.; Heinrich J.; Kreuzer M.; Scherb H.; Baudrexl A.; Weber J.; Wiesner B.; Wichmann H.E.
abstract: As part of a case-control study on lung cancer risk and exposure to indoor radon, 93 patients with lung cancer were detected who had been employed in a uranium mining company in the former German Democratic Republic. The youngest patient was 51 and the oldest 78 years old. Employment was started in nearly every case before 1955. 81 of the 93 patients had had occupational exposure to radon and its progeny. 78 worked as miners or craftsmen underground and 3 were employed in surface mining or uranium processing. 12 men had exclusively worked above ground in jobs that involved no exposure to radon. The mean cumulative exposure was 606 WLM (Range: 2 WLM - 1791 WLM). Using the mean risk coefficient of the International Commission on Radiological Protection of 1.3%/WLM as a basis, the patients' mean lung cancer risk was increased by a factor of 9. Nearly 10% of the patients lived in the study region of West Germany. Therefore lung cancer patients should always be asked about former employment in uranium mining.

title: Rock anchor support systems at Smoky River Coal Limited, Grande Cache, Alberta
authors: Dawson R.; Bagnall A.; Barron K.
abstract: At Smoky River Coal Limited (SRCL), economic occurrences of structurally thickened coal deposits form attractive surface mining targets. These steeply dipping, structurally complex deposits require that special attention be given to pit wall design and operational practices. Where feasible, there is potential for reducing footwall waste requirements and/or increasing coal recovery. This paper outlines design considerations and performance of rock anchor support systems at SRCL. Three case histories are included that illustrate the design process for supporting steeply dipping footwall slopes using rock anchors. -from Authors

title: State-of-the-art in mountaintop removal and contour mining
authors: White M.; Barata F.
abstract: Contour mining results in low mining ratios, but also lengthy outcrop disturbances (highwalls) and numerous environmental problems. Initially, the mining ratio in a contour mine operation was less than 7 to 1. Under present regulations and coal prices, contour mining has been reduced in the US. However, it is efficient in mountaintop removal operations. Contour mining incorporated into a mountaintop removal operation helps control drainage, minimize downslope placements (overshots) and balance the mining ratios. While mountaintop removal optimizes the coal reserve, the nature of this method results in coal being produced with higher mining ratios. This is due to the topography of the mining area. However, another contributor to these ratio increases include previous mining operations in the area. The mountaintop removal method of surface mining on this reserve began during the 1970s. The top of the mountain is removed to uncover the most economically minable coal seams. The overburden and interburden removed are placed in valley fills and backstacked on previously mined areas as required to produce the coal. Under ideal conditions, it is possible to extract nearly 100% of the minable coal, except for the outcrop barriers. -from Authors

title: Wildlife Management, Surface Mining, and Regional Planning
authors: NIEMAN T.; MERKIN Z.
abstract: ABSTRACT Wildlife management, surface mining, and regional planning historically have had conflicting missions. The cooperative public/private venture which created the Robinson Forest and Cyprus‐Amax Wildlife Management Areas is presented as an example of how a regional perspective encourages a symbiotic relationship among these Functions. Wildlife management areas, as either an interim or final land use. are shown to incorporate development concepts which benefit the general public, the coal industry, and the environment. Examining the regional pattern or wildlife management areas and refuges confirms the appropriateness of the subject site for this use. It is suggested that the pattern of mined lands can be studied to identify other sites with potential to provide linkages between wildlife habitat areas and encourage reclamation of such sites to the “fish and wildlife” postmining land use. Such reclamation strategies should be pursued within a long‐term planning framework. More research is needed to recreate specific habitat types on drastically disturbed land and planning is needed to assure that sensitive habitats or species arc located away from zones likely to undergo future development. Use of geographic information systems to integrate existing environmental information could make such studies more effective. Copyright © 1995, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Characterizing rare plant habitat for restoration in the San Bernardino National Forest
source: General Technical Report US Department of Agriculture Forest Service
authors: Gonella M.P.; Neel M.C.
abstract: Surface mining of limestone in the San Bernardino Mountains has caused loss of native vegetation and of habitat for four carbonate-endemic plant taxa. This paper characterizes features of carbonate substrates and of habitat occupied by two of these species: cushenbury milkvetch (Astragalus albens) and Cushenbury buckwheat (Eriogonum ovalifolium var. Vineum) to assist in developing revegetation success criteria for mined lands. Carbonate substrates in the San Bernardino Mountains were vegetationally and floristically distinct from non-carbonate substrates. Habitats occupied by Cushenbury milkvetch and Cushenbury buckwheat were distinguished from general carbonate substrate by higher % soil calcium, different slope angles, surface soil characteristics, and floristic composition. -from Authors

title: Environmental issues of the Appalachian coal region
authors: Kleinmann R.L.P.; Allwes R.A.; Jeran P.W.; Jones P.M.; Matetic R.J.; Statnick R.
abstract: Mining has been a significant component of the Appalachian economy for about 200 yr. The region continues to be adversely affected by the environmental degradation associated with these past activities. In addition, companies today are being denied permits at sites where acid generation appears likely. And air emission limitations at power plants now threaten the economic health of many moderate- to high-sulfur coal mines. Thus, when considering the environmental impacts of mining coal in Appalachia, it is important to consider abandoned and active mine issues. For example, abandoned mines generate acidic, iron-rich waters that adversely affect more than 6400 km (4000 miles) of rivers and streams in Appalachia. In contrast, operations that were active after the enactment of the 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (SMCRA) cause little water pollution. Subsidence in the region results from the degradation of abandoned, shallow room-and-pillar mines and from high-extraction deep mining. Several field studies revealed that the maximum vertical displacement can be as much as 60% of the extracted thickness. About 1.5 m (5 ft) of coal extracted can produce as much as 0.9 m (3 ft) of vertical movement. This maximum movement occurs over the center of the extracted area and vertical movement decreases laterally outwards. Above the edges of the extracted area, subsidence is generally less than 13 mm (6 in.) and decreases to zero within several hundred feet. Air quality is perhaps the only environmental issue that is associated almost exclusively with active operations. -from Authors

title: Depicting California's critical environmental zones
source: Yearbook Association of Pacific Coast Geographers
authors: Pryde P.; Rogers C.; Chaddock L.
abstract: A set of critical environmental area maps for the state of California has been prepared. These maps show regions of the state where the natural environment has been adversely affected by the consequences of economic activities, in some cases exacerbated by natural conditions. Environmental topics mapped include air pollution, pollution of inland and coastal waters, hazardous wastes, surface mining, and deterioration of forests and sensitive habitats. Initially, for clarity, mapping was done on three separate sheets, under the topic headings of water problems, habitat problems, and air and toxic pollutants. Subsequently, all of the data were combined onto a single comprehensive map. This resultant map illustrates by means of overlapping areal and point symbols the generalized locales and regions of concentrations of contemporary environmental problems in California.

title: Ethics, surface mining and the environment
authors: Cragg W.; Pearson D.; Cooney J.
abstract: This paper describes what is involved in building an ethical component into mine planning, development, operations, closure and site rehabilitation. How best corporate practice measures up to ethical criteria is examined. Finally, reasons for adopting an ethical stance in mining are set out and evaluated. © 1996.

title: An evaluation of fluidized bed combustor ash as a source of alkalinity to treat toxic rock materials
authors: Renton J.; Brown H.
abstract: The coal mining industry is in need of effective, locally available, low-cost ameliorants that can be used to treat the toxic materials generated by surface mining and coal cleaning plants. Ashes generated by fluidized bed combustors may locally fit these criteria. Samples of fly ash and bottom ash were acquired from facilities in West Virginia, Texas, and California and evaluated for their ability to generate alkalinity. The results show that FBC ash has the potential to produce solutions of high alkalinity depending on the CaO and CaCO<inf>3</inf> contents. The relative content of CaO, and to a lesser extent Ca(OH)<inf>2</inf>, determines the rate at which alkalinity will be produced. The neutralization potential is the best parameter to evaluate the potential of an FBC ash to produce alkalinity. Because the composition of ashes from a facility vary over time and because no single parameter will accurately evaluate the rate at which alkalinity will be produced, the rate of alkaline production must be evaluated by controlled leach experiments. © 1996.

title: Nitrogen loss from a soil restored after surface mining
authors: Davies R.; Hodgkinson R.; Younger A.; Chapman R.
abstract: Anaerobic conditions develop below about 1-m depth in soil stock-piles and this can lead to an accumulation of ammonium (NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>) and transformations of a normally relatively inert organic-N pool within the soil. After reinstatement of the soil from the stockpile, the NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup> may rapidly be transformed to nitrate (NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup>) and lost from the soil with the labile organic-N. These losses may lead to a pollution risk in addition to the loss of a resource. The magnitude of N losses were measured from a soil that had been reinstated for agricultural use after being stored in a stockpile for 12 yr. Nitrogen movement in the soil profile and losses into the water-course were monitored for 2 yr beginning immediately after reinstatement. Relatively large movements of N were detected within the soil profile and large losses to the atmosphere and/or water-courses were estimated. Over the 2-yr monitoring period, 2449 kg ha<sup>-1</sup> of N was lost from the soil profile; 90% of this was not accounted for either in the soil or in the runoff or drainage water as mineral-N and was presumed to have entered either the atmosphere or aquatic environment as organic-N. To aid remedial measures, the proportion entering the atmosphere as nitrogen and nitrous oxides or the aquatic environment as organic-N, needs further investigation.

title: Geogenically Acidified Mining Lakes — Living Conditions and Possibilities of Restoration
source: Internationale Revue Der Gesamten Hydrobiologie Und Hydrographie
authors: Klapper H.; Schultze M.
keywords: acidification | desulfurication | living conditions | mining lakes | restoration
abstract: Pyrite and marcasite oxidation in the consequence of lignite surface mining creates lakes with pH as low as 2 to 3, buffered by high contents of iron and aluminium. Living conditions in this extreme habitat for plants and animals are described as well as the characteristics of the pioneer settlement. The utilization of these fish‐free lakes is very limited. As possibilities for a water quality improvement special recultivation methods of overburden, chemical neutralization and biological ecotechnologies are recommended. Copyright © 1995 WILEY‐VCH Verlag GmbH & Co. KGaA, Weinheim

title: Estimation of mercury content in tailings of the gold mine area of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil
authors: von Tümpling W.; Zeilhofer P.; Ammer U.; Einax J.; Wilken R.D.
keywords: contamination through gold mining operations | Gold mine | Landsat satellite data | mercury content in tailings
abstract: As in many other parts of the world, gold is produced in the surface mining region of Poconé, Mato Grosso, Brazil, using mercury. The goal of this investigation was to estimate the amount of mercury in certain tailings and to determine the area of the land that has been contaminated by the gold mining operations. Mercury concentrations from 2 to 495 ng/g (dw) were determined in the tailing materials. It was observed that only isolated sites were acting as central points of contamination. Using digital Landsat satellite data (The-matic Mapper) and aerial photos, the sites degraded by the mining were classified, and their total area was estimated to be 12.3 km<sup>2</sup> in the region of Poconé. It was estimated, that 4.9 km<sup>2</sup> were occupied by the contaminated tailings. The mean height of the pile slags was determined to be 4.5 m. From the experimentally calculated average density of the material in the tailings, 2.01 g/cm<sup>3</sup>, the total mercury content in the piles of tailings was estimated to be 1600 ± 350 kg. © 1995, Ecomed Publishers. All rights reserved.

title: Effects of surface mining on aquatic resources in north america
authors: Starnes L.B.

title: Tree survival and growth on land reclaimed in accord with Public Law 95- 87
authors: Chaney W.R.; Pope P.E.; Byrnes W.R.
abstract: The objective of this study was to determine survival and growth of black walnut (Juglans nigra L.) and northern red oak (Quercus alba L.) 12 yr after planting on a surface-mined site in southern Indiana reclaimed according to specifications of Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. A stocking level adequate to meet the requirements for forest land use (1112 trees/ha, or 450 trees/acre) was attained only for black walnut and only if competing ground cover vegetation was controlled in the tree rows. Height of both tree species was significantly grater when ground cover vegetation was controlled during the first 2 yr, but the growth rate, approximately 10 cm/yr, was very slow.

title: Monitoring airborne dust from quarrying and surface mining operations
source: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
authors: Merefield J.R.; Stone I.; Roberts J.; Dean A.; Jones J.
abstract: This note introduces the concept of "finger-printing' airborne dust samples on the basis of mineralogy by providing information on ambient dust levels before opencast mining and quarrying operations and a dynamic record during them. The intention is to provide site operators and regulators with the means to eliminate dust nuisance from disputes over planning and licence applications before it becomes a serious hazard. -Authors

title: Mining equipment into the 21st century
authors: Wiebmer J.
abstract: Several industry trends are putting new demands on surface mining equipment. This is true both on the 'hard' side of the equipment business - the research and product development programs, and on the 'soft' side - the business processes, human resources and competitive strategies. This article describes seven key industry trends and the impact each is having on surface mining equipment suppliers. These trends are, respectively, globalization, consolidation, improved asset management and utilization, a scarcity of skilled labor, environmental issues, cost competition, and information management.

title: Automating surface mines
authors: White J.W.; Zoschke L.T.
abstract: This is a truly exciting time in surface mining technology. A revolution is coming -- a revolution made possible by complete mine management systems working in concert with many devices currently available or in the prototype stage. By the turn of the century, the face of surface mining will indeed be different. Many 'futuristic' applications of advanced data processing to surface mining systems and individual mining functions are already available. Acceptance of such technology is beginning to take hold and will accelerate, despite some resistance in what is an essentially conservative industry. Examples of this new technology include drill monitoring, load weighing, equipment tracking systems, production reporting systems, and robotic haul trucks.

title: Possible use of wetlands in ecological restoration of surface mined lands
authors: Atkinson R.; Cairns J.
keywords: accidental wetlands | colonization | hydrophytes | restoration ecology | surface mining
abstract: Surface mining for coal has dramatically altered millions of hectares throughout the Appalachian region of eastern North America. Flat benches and vertical high walls have replaced well-drained slopes, and wetlands have developed 'accidentally' on abandoned benches. Surface mining is continuing in this region, but new regulations do not include specifications for wetland construction in the reclamation process. Recent research has suggested that many ecosystem services appropriate for the Appalachian landscape could be performed by constructed wetlands. Inclusion of wetland construction in a reclamation plan could lead to a net increase in wetland acreage locally, as well as offset the loss of natural and/or accidental wetlands. By studying accidentally-formed wetlands, we hope to determine what species can be established in wetlands that are constructed to enhance nontreatment goals in reclamation. Study sites included 14 emergent wetlands in Wise County, Virginia. Sampling in June and August detected a total of 94 species in 36 vascular plant families. Obligate wetlands species, species that occur in wetlands over 99 percent of the time, were found in all 14 sites and included 26 species. The presence of so many wetland species without intentional management efforts suggests that wetland establishment could become a common component of mine reclamation. © 1994 Kluwer Academic Publishers.

title: Evaluation of procedures to estimate biomass on surface coal mine lands reclaimed under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977
authors: Brenner F.J.; Brenner E.K.; Brenner P.E.; Steiner R.P.
keywords: Biomass | Estimate | Evaluation | Procedures | Surface coal mines
abstract: Current surface mine regulations as ascribed under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 require that mine lands be returned to the approximate original contours (AOC) with an area coverage of at least 70% and to biological productivity equal to or greater than that which existed prior to mining. Six different procedures were evaluated on nine mine sites in northwestern Pennsylvania as to their suitability to estimate aboveground biomass on mines reclaimed as hayland and pastures. Biomass estimates determined by different procedures were compared to those obtained by random clip plots and with landowner estimates of the annual yield from each site. Biomass estimates determined from a disk meter and landowner interviews varied approximately ±10% from those obtained from random clip plots compared to a variation of ±8%-37% for the other procedures. The number of samples required to obtain reliable estimates within ±10% of the mean at 95% confidence intervals varied among the different sampling procedures according to the variance in biomass on the site. Although all procedures may be used either singly or in combination to estimate above ground biomass on reclaimed mine lands, the combination of the disk meter, profile board, and vegetation height is recommended because of their ease of measurement compared to the other procedures. © 1994 Springer-Verlag New York Inc.

title: Particle size distribution of an aerosol and its sub-fractions
authors: Verma D.K.; Sebestyen A.; Julian J.A.; Muir D.C.F.; Shaw D.S.; Macdougall R.
abstract: Particle size distribution of an aerosol and its sub-fractions was carried out as part of an epidemiological study by using a Retsch Precision High Volume Cascade Impactor.The impactor was used in the underground and surface mining operations as they are currently practised. It was also used in experimental stopes in gold, uranium and nickel mines where conditions of dry drilling were simulated. The impactor fractionates airborne dust into seven ranges of particle size from submicron to 32 μm aerodynamic diameter, when operating at 40 l. min<sup>-1</sup> Since the impactor operated at high flow rate, sufficient dust was collected to permit further analysis of the sub- fractions, such as free crystalline silica or metal (iron).A unique system was designed by using a venturi and compressed air for its use in an underground environment. For some tasks the particle size distribution of the sub-fraction was found to be similar to that of the total dust but different for other tasks. © 1994 British Occupational Hygiene Society.

title: Regulating in Space and Time: The Case of Regulatory Federalism
authors: Hedge D.M.; Scicchitano M.
abstract: We outline and test an empirical model of federal regulatory behavior that reflects the spatial (i.e., interstate) and temporal dimensions of regulation within a federal system. A pooled time-series design is used to examine the interplay of national and subnational influences on the oversight decisions of officials at the U.S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM, Department of the Interior) during the period 1985–1989. The analysis indicates that the regulatory decisions of federal authorities at OSM reflect shifts in the nation's political climate, the freelancing efforts of individual members of Congress, and the states' political climates. Taken together, the findings suggest that national policymakers are able to direct the oversight activities of bureaucratic subordinates but are constrained in that regard by “botrrm iin”. © 1994, Southern Political Science Association. All rights reserved.

title: Automated downtime recording and processing for continuous surface mining systems
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Agioutantis Z.
abstract: A number of open pit mines, employing mainly continuous mining methods, are currently in operation at the lignite basin of Ptolemais-Amydeon in northern Greece. This study presents the design characteristics and implementation of a software system developed for a network environment, using a popular database framework, in order to facilitate recording and processing of downtime as well as generation of various equipment status and statistical reports for any period within a calendar year for chained production systems involving BWEs, conveyors and stackers. © 1994, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Continous surface mining equipment: how to achieve success
authors: Delilla E.
abstract: Continuous mining systems (bucketwheel excavators or continuous mining machines by Wirtgen, Voest-Alpine, etc.) must be matched to specific operating conditions. There are no "off-the-shelf' machines, and there are usually no simple modifications that will make a machine perform differently in response to changing mining conditions. In some cases, it has taken years for a mismatched machine to be made to perform effectively. There have been numerous cases where the machines were just not compatible with the conditions and never performed to expectations. Continuous mining systems can work. They offer an opportunity for high productivity at low operating costs for mining operations. However, everyone involved must be aware of the many tasks that must be successfully completed to apply these systems in their mines. -Author

title: Surface mining
authors: Dunn A.; Hoddinott P.
abstract: This report gives an overview of worldwide surface mining operations during 1993. It emphasises the importance of regulations and adverse public opinion that severely restrict mining activity and gives examples of rehabilitation schemes. Coverage includes developments in and examples of highwall mining, drilling, fragmentation, crushing and breaking, continuous extraction and information technology. Developments and projection of future trends in machinery are covered. These include specific reference to hydraulic excavators, front-end loaders, rope excavators, dump trucks and continuous transport systems. -S.E.Long

title: Surface mining of Canadian coal
authors: Singhal R.; Collins J.; Fytas K.
abstract: Canada's coal production is approximately 65.4 million tonnes of which 95% is produced by surface mining methods, mostly from the three Western provinces. The mines are highly mechanised; productivity gains during the past few years have ranged from 60-80%. This paper provides an overview of the Canadian coal mining industry vis-a-vis surface mining. -from Authors

title: Morphological characteristics of reconstructed prime farmland soils in western Pennsylvania
authors: Bell J.C.; Cunningham R.L.; Anthony C.T.
abstract: The major soil horizons of prime farmlands disturbed by surface mining in the USA must be reconstructed during reclamation in accordance with current federal legislation. Consequently, the topsoil (Ap horizon) and subsoil (B and C horizons) are removed and stockpiled separately during overburden removal activities and are replaced over spoil during reclamation in an attempt to reconstruct the original soil profile and to help maintain soil productivity. This study was conducted to investigate the morphological, physical, and chemical properties of reconstructed mine soils and to identify characteristics of these soils that could limit crop growth. We described and sampled a total of 72, 1- to 2-year-old, reconstructed soil profiles at eight reclaimed surface mines throughout western Pennsylvania. Soil depth over spoil was generally >75 cm with an observed range of 5 cm to >2 m. Well- expressed Ap horizons were observed in nearly all profiles. The structure of the reconstructed subsoils was drastically altered by mining to a structureless and massive condition. Excessively compacted shallow soil layers restricted downward penetration of plant roots within 47% of the soil profiles described. Reconstructed soil horizons that are likely to restrict plant growth included horizons composed of spoil, horizons with >50% rock fragments and excessively compacted soil layers. These restrictive soil horizons were found within 1 m of the surface for 57 of the 72 soil profiles described and within 50 cm for 51% of the soil profiles. Morphological investigations of reconstructed soils could be useful for evaluating reclamation success and soil productivity potential.

title: Environmental planning in regulation and management of instream gravel mining in California
authors: Mathias Kondolf G.
keywords: Aggregate extraction | Gravel mining | River management | Wetlands
abstract: In California, the mining of sand and gravel from rivers and streams is presently regulated under the state's Surface Mining and Reclamation Act of 1975 (SMARA), with 113 different countries and cities designated as lead agencies for approving reclamation plans and issuing special use permits. These agencies rarely have the technical expertise or resouces to assess cumulative impacts of instream mining or to monitor the sometimes subtle and frequently delayed off-site environmental impacts. Moreover, the concept of 'reclamation' is unsuitable for instream mining whose effects propagate upstream and downstream during mining and cannot be reversed by subsequent on-site reclamation. Instream operators also fall under the jurisdiction of other agencies, such as the US Army Corps of Engineers and the California Department of Fish and Game, but these agencies lack resources and a consistent approach to evaluate and mitigate the environmental effects of instream mining. Instream gravel mining can be properly addressed only by comprehensive environmental planning that evaluates all potential aggregate sources, including upland deposits, and the environmental impacts of their extraction. Aggregate extraction from rivers must be managed on the scale of river basins, while the demand for aggregate and the various sources of its supply must be managed on the scale of production-consumption regions. © 1994.

title: Radiation exposure at the high background area at Manavalakurichi - The changing trends
authors: Paul A.; Velayudhan T.; Pillai P.; Maniyan C.; Pillai K.
abstract: Large-scale surface mining and refilling of the mined areas with monazite-free tailings have reduced the external radiation fields by an order of magnitude, at some locations at the natural high background areas situated in the coastal regions of peninsular India. Significant reduction by a factor of 3 has been observed in the airborne activity due to lower emanation of thoron (220Rn) at the refilled areas. The thathched huts in the area are giving way to brick and concrete structures, thus radically altering the indoor exposures. The exposure due to gamma radiation from the external surroundings was reduced by a factor of 4 due to the shielding by the construction materials. 220 Rn levels as high as 420 Bq m<sup>-3</sup> have been observed in some of the mud houses. Significant levels of 232 Th and 228 Ra were found in the urine samples collected from the adult residing in a village, situated in the high background area. © 1994.

title: A review of computer-based truck dispatching strategies for surface mining operations
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Munirathinarn M.; Yingling J.C.
abstract: Computer-based truck dispatching systems are becoming a widely used means for improving equipment utilization and productivity at surface mining operations and for helping to insure that extraction operations at these mines meet additional performance requirements such as maintenance of stripping ratios and ore grade standards. This paper classifies existing truck dispatching strategies and examines their underlying mathematical formulations in detail. Strengths and weaknesses of the alternative approaches are identified and information on their expected performance in the field is summarized. © 1994, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Arch of Illinois - look to the future
authors: Bierei G.
abstract: The application of a more appropriate technology puts Arch of Illinois at the region's most profitable position as the mining complex undergoes a gradual shift from surface mining to underground mining. In response to dwindling low ratio reserves and increasing land acquisition and environmental costs, the mining complex shifted its attention to underground reserves. This entailed a corresponding change from truck haulage to beltline haulage. The underground operations brought about an increase in the amount of coal fines and this involved the construction of a fine coal circuit that would recover particles down to -150 μm (-100 mesh). Meanwhile, to maintain the profitability of remaining surface reserves, Arch of Illinois uses modified continuous miners and a battery haulage.

title: System development woes
authors: Neumann P.
abstract: Complex computer systems are rarely developed on time, within budget, and up to spec. In the paper are just a few examples from the RISKS archives. Among the case study presented are: Virginia system for distributing child support checks, Bank of America computerized trust accounting and reporting system, Allstate Insurance computerized automation system, Blue Cross and Blue Shield of Wisconsin with an Electronic Data System (EDS) that did not worked. Other systems discussed are the one used for the U.S. Office of surface Mining to prevent violators of strip-mine laws from getting new permits, and the Airborne Self-Protection Jammer (ASJP), an electronic air-defense system installed in over 2,00 Navy fighters and attack planes.

title: Speedy backfilling for old mines
authors: Dyni R.; Burnett M.
