The substantial opportunities for geotechnical engineering to contribute to both safe and economical operations in the extractive industries are emphasized. -Authors

title: Mining and landscape modification on the Sydney coalfield
source: Geographical Perspectives on the Maritime Provinces
authors: Millward H.
abstract: Cape Breton's Sydney coalfield has been worked continuously since 1720. This paper describes the cumulative impact of underground and surface mining as evidenced in today's land use pattern and visual landscape. Particular attention is paid to the effects of recent environmental improvement policies. -Author

title: Continuous haulage and in-pit crushing in surface mining
authors: Terezopoulos N.G.
abstract: The paper discusses the use of high speed, side-slewable belt conveyors in large-scale surface mining, in conjunction with in-pit crushing. The reasons for the use of such a transport system are discussed and compared to other systems. Bucket Chain Excavators (BCE), or Bucket Wheel Excavators (BWE) used in surface mining can only be fully utilised with a continuous transport system, such as a conveyor belt. Loading of the belts is carried out by the excavators in the pit and the spoil is taken around the pit to the spoil bank. In cases where the overburden is thick and competent, pre-stripping and crushing are required, to enable the use of belt conveyors for transport. The application criteria and the method of use of such systems are described, and economical factors are considered. © 1988 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V.

title: AGGREGATE RESOURCES - CALIFORNIA'S EFFORT UNDER SMARA TO ENSURE THEIR CONTINUED AVAILABILITY.
authors: Beeby D.
abstract: California's Surface Mining and Reclamation Act (SMARA) was passed in 1975 to identify and protect mineral resources in areas of high land use conflict and ensure reclamation of mined lands. Under SMARA, aggregate resource availability is quantified and compared to forecast demand in specific market regions. Fifteen regions studied thus far cover 51,800 km**2 (20,000 sq miles) and contain 45 Gt (50 billion st) of high-quality aggregate resources that have been legally designated as regionally significant, providing a measure of protection previously unavailable. SMARA reports and state testimony at local hearings have supplied objective information and helped reduce conflict in mine permitting decisions.

title: LAND SHAPING AND SOIL CONSTRUCTION.
authors: Jansen I.; Melsted S.
abstract: Reclamation after surface mining or other drastic land disturbance involves shaping the land surface and constructing a soil. One must begin by selecting a land use objective. Considerations are local needs and potential for constructing the needed supporting land resource. Use objectives determine land resource needs, but available materials and material handling equipment limit the kind of soil resource that can be constructed and hence the land use options that can be considered. A reasonable reclamation objective would be to construct a land resource of maximum feasible utility and versatility for future generations. Utility implies concern that it not only have some productive use, but that it complement other land resource that is capable of multiple uses, to keep options open for future generations. Cost is one consideration under feasibility, at least to the extent that a significant increase in the utility or versatility of the finished product should result from any reclamation practice of significant cost.

title: PYRITIC MATERIALS: ACID DRAINAGE, SOIL ACIDITY, AND LIMING.
authors: Caruccio F.; Hossner L.; Geidel G.
abstract: Sulfide minerals, when exposed to the atmosphere, can form acid sulfate soils and acidic-, ferrous-, and sulfate-enriched drainage water. These conditions generally arise from the oxidation of iron disulfides exposed by surface mining. Rock analyses can provide a first approximation of the anticipated acidity characteristics of the overburden and anticipated drainage quality. Pyrite oxidation products are readily soluble in water and hydrolyze to produce acidic waters which severely impact drainage systems. Acid sulfate weathering as a result of pyrite oxidation can produce acid sulfate soils. Recognition of the potential for formation of acid sulfate soils, measurement of the forms of soil acidity, and deep burial or neutralization of that acidity are essential if establishment and sustained growth of plants are to be achieved. The above data illustrate several points regarding the liming of acid sulfate soils. First, using the appropriate analytical methods, total lime requirements can be calculated. Second, application of adequate amounts of lime to neutralize the active acidity as well as the potential acidity is feasible in these systems, particularly if CaCO//3 is the lime source.

title: RELATION OF PUBLIC POLICY TO RECLAMATION GOALS AND RESPONSIBILITIES.
authors: Doll E.
abstract: The enactment of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 or SMCRA (PL 95-87) set federal standards for the reclamation of lands disturbed by surface mining for coal. This act provides guidelines and regulatory procedures under which the industry is responsible for the reclamation of surface-mines lands; costs of reclamation are passed on to the consumer. Compliance with these provisions has required major changes in mining practices and reclamation techniques. The coal industry has accepted this responsibility, and surface-mined lands have generally been successfully reclaimed. Reclamation planning cannot become static; it must be flexible and responsive to changes in public needs and policy and to the development of more efficient and cost-effective reclamation techniques. In the discussion, the author attempts to evaluate the reclamation goals and practices in this context. A brief review of the changing attitude toward public responsibilities for reclamtion of surface-mined land, which led to the enactment of federal legislation, is given to place the discussion in proper context.

title: CORRECTION OF PHYSICAL LIMITATIONS TO RECLAMATION.
authors: Barnhisel R.
abstract: The physical properties of disturbed soils are changed as the result of surface mining. These changes may be beneficial to future land use when the surface-mine operator uses proper techniques and takes advantage of selecting more desirable materials for the restored soil than existed in the natural soil. Perhaps more frequently, the physical properties of the restored soils are degraded during mining. The degradation may result from mixing undesirable soil horizons together, as well as excessive soil compaction which often occurs in the removal and reconstruction process. These physical limitations often result in poorer root penetration into the replace soil, thereby reducing plant growth. The possible effects on plant growth of such changes in the physical properties during surface mining are presented. Methods of reducing such occurrences, ways of recognizing them, and possible methods for correcting them are discussed.

title: LESS CONVENTIONAL METHODS FOR MINING UNDERGROUND COAL.
authors: Muirhead I.; Kolada R.
abstract: In recent years, mining considerations and economics have encouraged a transition from underground mining to surface mining. However, a change in market conditions or the development of superior underground mining methods may reverse this trend. This paper reports on a CANMET-funded examination of less conventional underground coal mining methods. These methods are documented and those that show the most promise for application to western Canadian conditions are discussed in detail.

title: RESOURCES RECOVERABLE BY SURFACE MINING.
authors: Doolittle J.J.; Hossner L.R.
abstract: The methods used to mine mineral resources can be separated into two broad categories: surface and underground. Both of these mining methods cause a 'disturbance' at the earth's surface; however, in surface mining all of the soil and strata overlying a mineral deposit are removed to expose the deposit. This procedure disturbs more surface acreage than in underground mining where the mineral deposit is removed from beneath intact surface layers. Of the major mineral resources in the U. S. , 11 are totally or partially removed by surface mining: bauxite, coal, clay, copper, gypsum, iron, limestone/dolomite, molybdenum, phosphate rock, sand/gravel, and uranium. Oil shale will also be recovered by surface mining when it becomes economically feasible to extract oil products from it. These minerals are discussed in more detail in this paper. Most of the information within this paper adheres to the system of classification of mineral deposits jointly developed by the U. S. Bureau of Mines and U. S. Geological Survey.

title: Discrimination of factors influencing biota of a stream receiving multiple-source perturbations
authors: Van Hassel J.H.; Cherry D.S.; Hendricks J.C.; Specht W.L.
abstract: Blaine Creek is a fifth-order stream located in eastern Kentucky that has been subject to contamination by oil brines, surface mining, and a coal fly ash settling pond discharge. Toxicity tests, effluent and receiving water chemical monitoring, and Blaine Creek benthic sampling were used to evaluate the effect of the ash pond effluent on the creek. Reproductive impairment of Ceriodaphnia was demonstrated at effluent concentrations ranging from 30 to 100%, but no instream impact on benthic invertebrates could be found at effluent flows that provided up to 65% of the creek's discharge. Correlation and regression analysis of physicochemical versus benthic monitoring data indicated that upstream oil brine contamination and scouring of the creek's predominately shifting sand substrate during rainfall events were the primary factors affecting the benthic fauna, and appeared to override potential effects from other sources. These results demonstrated the value of integrated field/laboratory investigations for effluent impact assessments. © 1988.

title: DEM-determination in lignite surface mining - test for digital image correlation
authors: Boochs F.; Woytowicz D.
abstract: The automatic DEM-determination by digital image correlation is tested in the case of a stereo-model of lignite surface mining. The special reason for this test is given by the characteristic vertical structure of the object connected with small contrast. As expected the success rate for the point determination has been first under the average. By means of a better approximation of the object geometry and a repetition of the correlation the success rate could have been substantially improved. The accuracy of the determination which has been achieved is near to the level of manual measurements. -English summary

title: CURRENT SURFACE MINING TECHNIQUES.
authors: Bullivant D.
abstract: The paper looks at the present position regarding the status of surface mining operations throughout the world compared with underground mining and examines the various continuous conveying techniques available to overcome the problems encountered in developing various types of geological deposits. A case is put for the employment of a skilled engineering supplier/contractor to effectively integrate the various elements into an efficient system of material transportation.

title: Intersection graphic method - a method for calculating quantity of coal and rock by using a computer for selection of surface mining schemes
source: Meitan Xuebao Journal of the China Coal Society
authors: Tian H.
abstract: This paper proposes a method based on the exhaustion method for calculating the quantity of coal and rock by using a computer for selecting an optimal surface mining scheme provides a mathematical model for the calculations. The system adopts the template technique for producing frustum files. This system has improved the accuracy of calculation by separating different zone so that a variable slope can be varied at different azimuths and depths within the boundary of a surface mine.

title: NEW TECHNOLOGY FOR LARGE SURFACE MINES.
authors: Singhal R.
abstract: High-volume surface mining operations such as the Canadian oil sands mines depend on high-capacity equipment for excavation and transportation of overburden and ore. Dragline and bucket wheel excavator/conveyor systems have been developed to high levels of productivity, and numerous improvements have been made in all phases of mining practice. However, mines throughout the world continue to devote considerable effort to developing innovative new technologies, operating techniques, and procedures for improving productivity. Operators of such mines should periodically prepare an awareness report, evaluating outside technology for in-house use. This type of intelligence and technology transfer is vital to maintenance of competitive and cost effective operations. This article briefly reviews some technology and operating practices that have recently become available to large-scale surface mines.

title: AMAX TAKES ITS DELTA SURFACE MINE UNDERGROUND.
authors: Trewhitt J.
abstract: Amax Coal Co. has brought longer life to a former section of its Delta surface mine near Harrisburg, Ill. , by punching entries into the highwall to form a 500,000-tpy underground mine. Delta's mined-out Harco section has been transformed into the company's first highwall mine. If the mine succeeds, the company might create other underground mines when surface operations reach their economic limits. At Harco, surface mining stopped when the overburden to coal ratio reached 24. 27:1.

title: COMPUTER-AIDED BLAST DESIGNS SUCCEED IN SURFACE MINING.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Blasting simulation programs have been developed that can permit almost any blasting procedure in the field to be tried first as a simulated event in the computer. One of the programs is Du Pont's Computer Simulated Blasting (CSB) program. Based on the Blaspa method, the program has been used in more than 50 mines and quarries to simulate blasting conditions. The CSB program is based on a mathematical model that takes into account site-specific conditions such as type of explosive, rock type, blast geometry and drilling patterns. The program predicts the results of the blast and lets the blaster alter the input variables one at a time.

title: A case study in surface mining simulation with special reference to the problem of model evaluation
source: International Journal of Mining and Geological Engineering
authors: Ogbonlowo D.B.; Wang Y.J.
keywords: coal mining | materials handling | mine simulation | Surface mining
abstract: This paper discusses the framework for modelling and analysing the materials handling aspects of a conventional contour mine as related to the smaller to medium-size coal mining companies. Special emphasis is placed on model evaluation. The methodology employed consists of: (a) using the surface geometry of the area to be stripped for developing the equations that are used for analysing the critical factors affecting pit layout, (b) effecting engineering and graphical layout of the mine, (c) collecting - through time studies - and analysing equipment characteristic data, (d) constructing the model, and (e) evaluating the model. The results show that the graphical approach for model construction and evaluation is fast, accurate, and reliable. © 1987 Chapman and Hall Ltd.

title: MOWING OF ANNUAL COLONIZERS TO ENHANCE REVEGETATION AFTER SURFACE MINING.
authors: Iverson L.; Wali M.
abstract: Mowing of first-year erect, annual, colonizing vegetation (especially Kochia scoparia and Salsola collina) was beneficial in the growth and establishment of wheatgrasses (Agropyron caninum, A. smithii and A. elongatum) on restored mined land in western North Dakota. Sample plots containing primarily Kochia, Salsola and Agropyron spp. It was found that Kochia, densities were reduced to about 2% and biomass to one-third that of the control when the area was mowed in mid-August. Agropyron spp. , however, showed an increase of 860% in biomass production over the control due to mowing in mid-August.

title: MICROPROCESSOR-AIDED EQUIPMENT PROVES PRODUCTIVE AND RELIABLE.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Teamed with miniature sensors and advanced electronic gadgetry, microprocessors are improving the performance of earthmoving equipment and haulers for surface mining operations. The microprocessor may be only about 1 one-half in. wide by 2 in. long, a flat component with a series of I-O's (input-output) prongs on both sides to read sensors feeding into it information on speeds, pressures, temperatures and other machine functions while it sends signals to control a range of components from LED lights to engines. Such microprocessors are being designed into excavators, shovels, scrapers and trucks. The article gives examples.

title: Environmental impact assessment procedure for surface mining projects in India - a status review
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Banerjee S.; Mehta R.
abstract: In India, the present system of granting environmental clearance to mining projects has been introduced from early 1982. The Ministry of Environment and Forests has constituted four Environmental Appraisal Committees (EACs) to comment on the environmental impact of large development projects. The mining EAC has representatives from various Government Departments. The Committee has an advisory status only, and makes its recommendations to the Department of Environment, Forests and Wildlife. In fact the requirement of getting an environmental clearance is based on administrative instructions of the Public Investment Board to which the public sector organizations have to apply for getting sanction of fund for new large projects or extension of projects. Another route through which projects get referred to the mining EAC is from the Forestry Wing of the Department of Environment, Forests and Wildlife when request for release of forest land for mining purposes is received by that wing.

title: Blasting in overburden with site mixed slurry - a techno-economic assessment
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Sinha A.K.; Arora O.P.; Pradhan G.K.
abstract: The future years of Indian coal mining will see a significant increase in the production of coal from large mechanized opencast mines and huge quantities of overburden removal by deploying large capacity dragline and other heavy earth moving machinery. To attain overall economics, the very initial operating such as blasting, has to be very much cost efective as well as low manpower intensive. This can be achieved only by bulk handling of explosives and more R&D efforts to generate direct cost reduction in addition to the highest degree of safety. This article highlights investment, annual production capacity, average stripping ratio and the total excavation of overburden of some of the major ongoing surface mining projects in the coal sector of India. Various technical and economical benefits associated with mechanized bulk handling of site-mixed explosive slurries are reviewed.

title: Failure study of dumper tyres in surface mining project
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: De A.; Chandra M.
abstract: In the present work, an investigation has been undertaken to study the failure of tires. Two opencast projects were considered for the study. Tires were inspected five times and samples were taken on a random basis. Defective tires were inspected visually. The article presents the results of this study. Analysis has been based on statistical methods and failure mode.

title: DEVELOPMENTS IN OPEN-PIT MACHINERY.
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: Rao K.
abstract: Trends in the development of mining equipment used in surface mining for excavation, loading and transport and their applications are discussed. Equipment and methods aimed at reducing energy costs with continuous conveying and trolley-assist trucks are discussed in detail.

title: KRIEL COLLIERY MINES COAL FROM ABOVE AND BELOW.
authors: Anon
abstract: The Witbank-Highveld coalfield is one of the most important in South Africa and covers a large portion of the southeastern Transvaal. Colliery was originally planned as an underground mine only. Production began in 1975, but as planning progressed the possibilities of surface mining were investigated. Three of the power station's six boilers were subsequently modified to accommodate the lower quality surface-mined coal. There is no preparation plant. All coal is crushed to 25 mm and transported direct to the power station silos. Underground, the No. 4 Seam is mined by room-and-pillar methods. The seam is horizontal and very consistent, and there are no water problems. A typical underground section will advance on 15 headings at a time. Fresh air enters the central roadways of the section and spreads out both ways along the face.

title: MODERN EQUIPMENT FOR KENNECOTT'S BINGHAM CANYON COPPER MINE.
authors: Kaerst D.
abstract: In order to maintain and/or increase in the economic viability of their companies, mining operators are therefore being forced to adopt rationalization programs, particularly in high-wage-level countries. In the surface mining industry, particularly as far as hard rock mining is concerned, such ratonalization measures generally signify a transition from purely discontinuously functioning extraction and conveying equipment to continuously operating equipment or to a combination of these two modes. An up-to-date project is illustrated in this article. A large contract was recently awarded to PHB Weserhuette AG, Bad Oeynhausen Works, Federal Republic of Germany by Kennecott Corporation, Salt Lake City, Utah which is presently being implemented. The contract concerns the conversion of ore transport to the preparation plant from a railway to a conveyor belt operation at the Bingham Canyon Copper Mine.

title: SURFACE COAL MINING OPERATION.
authors: Kelly D.
abstract: Previous articles in this series concentrated upon the geological aspects of surface mining in Great Britain and upon site planning and authorization procedures. This article concentrates upon the actual working of the site. Overburden removal, blasting, equipment used, environmental problems and the like are briefly discussed.

title: FUTURE CONCEPTS IN SURFACE MINING OPERATIONS.
authors: Atkinson T.; Waller M.D.; Denby B.
abstract: Many surface mines have depleted reserves of near-surface, high-grade ore in a simple geological setting. This will require mining companies to consider deeper deposits in more complex geological settings with more critical groundwater conditions, increased geotechnical problems and greater stripping ratios and waste volumes, and which are also further from the markets. The article reviews developments in equipment and techniques. Included are continuous equipment, in-pit crushing, conveyors, trolley-assisted trade haulage, blasthole drilling, explosives, electric power systems, electronics, image analysis, ultrasonics, lasers, radio waves, computers and artificial intelligence.

title: SURFACE MINING OF OIL SANDS IN CANADA: DEVELOPMENTS IN PRODUCTIVITY IMPROVEMENT.
authors: Singhal R.K.; Kolada R.
abstract: A variety of equipment is used to surface mine oil sands, including bucket wheel excavators/conveyors, draglines, hydraulic shovels, and off-highway trucks. This paper examines the existing mining schemes and equipment used. Several proposals to improve mine productivity are presented.

title: PROPOSED CRITERIA FOR ASSESSING SUBSIDENCE DAMAGE TO RENEWABLE RESOURCE LANDS.
authors: Singh M.; Bhattacharya S.
abstract: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (SMCRA) requires underground coal mine operations to prevent 'material damage' to renewable resource lands caused by subsidence. However, what constitutes material damage is not defined. This paper discusses the applicable criteria for agricultural lands, forests and grazing lands, surface water bodies, and ground water aquifers. Although data on the subject are limited, an attempt is made to present quantitative guidelines to distinguish between the moderate and severe damage due to subsidence.

title: RELIABILITY ASSESSMENT OF HYDRAULIC EXCAVATOR.
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mechanical Engineering Division
authors: De A.
abstract: The paper discusses the reliability assessment technique of a hydraulic excavator, a very important machine of surface mining project. The work was performed with data from an open cast project, so that real life situations could be taken into consideration. The results were analyzed and conclusions drawn.

title: BUREAU SEEKS INNOVATIONS IN PRODUCTIVITY AND SAFETY.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Even with the growth of surface mining in recent years, two thirds of U. S. reserves can be reached economically only with underground mining methods. The geological conditions and the stricter regulations on subsidence favor room-and-pillar methods for the foreseeable future. In particular, the coal regions east of the Mississippi contain substantial deep coal reserves that cannot be mined by longwall methods because they would cause surface subsidence. The focus of research by the U. S. Bureau of Mines is on improving the productivity and health and safety of room-and-pillar mining.

title: MODELS FOR ALLOCATING AND DISPATCHING TRUCKS IN SURFACE MINING OPERATIONS.
authors: Topuz E.; Luo Z.
abstract: In surface mining operations, truck haulage is the largest item in the operating costs, consituting 50 to 60% of the total. In order to reduce this cost, it is necessary to allocate and dispatch the trucks efficiently. This paper describes different shovel-truck operation models and optimization approaches for the allocation and dispatching of trucks under various operating conditions.

title: Explosive source location by relative arrival times of atmospherically and seismically propagating disturbances
source: Journal of the Acoustical Society of America
authors: Dowding C.H.; Hryciw R.D.; Garretta J.M.
abstract: Detonation of explosives during rock excavation in surface mining produces both atmospherically and seismically propagating disturbances. By manipulating the difference in arrival times of the air blast and ground motion, shot-to-recorder distance can be determined with only one recording station. This shot-to-recorder distance is needed for automatic development of ground motion attenuation curves with automatic recording devices and is generally helpful in mine activity detection. With two recording stations, the location of the blast may be determined even if the stations are not time synchronized. Data from production blasting at a coal mine were evaluated to verify the method proposed herein. The blast location as determined by the difference in arrival times of the atmospherically and seismically propagating disturbances showed excellent agreement with the location of blasts as provided by field personnel. The method may be employed to detect any explosive activity that produces both types of disturbances. PACS numbers: 43.40.Ph, 43.28.Tc. © 1987, Acoustical Society of America. All rights reserved.

title: Basic considerations in selection of bucketwheel excavators
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Golosinski T.S.; Singhal R.K.
abstract: The bucketwheel excavators offers a number of advantages as compared to the standard surface mining equipment. However, to realize these advantages and make a bucketwheel excavator operation efficient, the excavator design must reflect the site specific conditions, the efficient operating procedures must be developed, and sufficient digging force must be available at the digging wheel. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Research into the stability of restored opencast coal mine sites in the north east of England
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Singh R.; Reed S.; Hughes D.
abstract: The paper presents an analysis of backfill settlement observations conducted at a number of opencast mine sites in the North-East of England. The work is aimed at developing a better understanding of the stability of the restored mine backfills from the point of view of structural development. The project is specifically concerned with the effect on fill movements of the re-establishment of groundwater regime on the completion of surface mining, in particular the occurrence of collapse settlements associated with groundwater recovery within the backfill mass. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Optimum curvature in pit slope design
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Dhar B.; Shrivastva B.; Raj G.
abstract: In surface mining the curvature of the pit slope is an important parameter in its safe and economic design. Research has shown that concave slope faces are more stable than planar or convex ones. The object of this paper is to demomstrate the effect of concavity on the optimum curvature, for the two slope angles commonly practiced in surface mines, 60° and 65°. The Finite Element Method (FEM) was used to simulate the variable mining conditions and the changing material properties. The analysis has been limited to stress analysis and the corresponding factor of safety to arrfve at on optimum slope curvature. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Status and trends of freshwater wetlands in the coal-mining region of Pennsylvania, USA
authors: Brooks R.; Hill J.
keywords: Coal mining | Pennsylvania | Surface mining | Wetlands
abstract: The impact of surface mining for coal on the nature and extent of freshwater wetlands was assessed on 73,200 ha in western Pennsylvania. The influence of mining on wetlands was not uniform across physiographic regions, varying with regional differences in hydrology and soils. Overall, mined lands supported 18% more palustrine wetlands than unmined lands, primarily because of a 270% gain in permanent, open-water wetlands on mined lands in the glaciated region. Open-water wetlands declined on mined lands in unglaciated regions owing to unfavorable hydrologic conditions. The number and size of emergent wetlands declined as a result of mining. Mined lands supported 81% fewer riverine wetlands than unmined lands. This was caused primarily by avoidance of lands containing streams, and secondarily by a 10% reduction in replacement of riverine wetlands during reclamation. Land managers need to develop land use policies that maximize the ecological and social benefits that can be derived from developing diverse wetland communities on mined lands. © 1987 Springer-Verlag New York Inc.

title: Simulation models for surface mines
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Sturgul J.R.; Harrison J.F.
abstract: ; The ease and speed of constructing computer simulation models using the GPSS programming language is discussed. GPSS is a computer programming language and so each problem requires a separate program to be written. However, this is not a problem since the programs can be written in a matter of hours or days. This is the case for even the most complicated mining situations. The examples presented here represent three different mining situations from actual mines in Australia. It is shown that the GPSS language provides a rapid, inexpensive and very accurate method of simulating a variety of surface mining operations. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Surface mining of coal: Efficiency of US interior mines
authors: Byrnes P.; Fare R.
abstract: In this paper the relative efficiency in surface mining of US interior coal is investigated. A non-parametric, non-stochastic method is applied to 186 observations and each firm's efficiency is calculated relative to the piecewise linear frontier technology. In addition, three sources of inefficiency are identified, namely: scale, congestion and purely technical inefficiency. The outcome of the study shows among other things that on the average, captive mines are more efficient than non-captive mines, and that unionized mines are more efficient than non-unionized mines. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: The effect of surface mining on the infectivity of vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi
authors: Jasper D.; Robson A.; Abbott L.
abstract: We tested the hypothesis that soil disturbance associated with mining will reduce the infectivity of propagules of vesicular-arbuscular (VA) mycorrhizal fungi to different extents, depending on the mining operation and the environment. At each of four mine sites, the infectivity of VA mycorrhizal fungi was estimated in soil from native vegetation, disturbed topsoil and revegetated soil. Infectivity was measured using subterranean clover and Acacia species as bioassay plants. In a second experiment the effects of soil disturbance and soil storage on infectivity of VA mycorrhizal fungi were measured separately. Topsoil disturbance decreased the number of spores or the number of spore types that could be isolated from the soil, and reduced or delayed formation of VA mycorrhizas. Glasshouse treatments indicated that both disturbance and a period of storage without plant growth contributed to the loss in infectivity of propagules of VA mycorrhizal fungi. After 4-5 years of revegetation, the number of infective propagules appears to be restored to a level equivalent to that of undisturbed soils. The possibility of improving revegetation by increasing the inoculum potential of disturbed soils needs to be investigated. © 1987, CSIRO. All rights reserved.

title: A case-control study to investigate the association between indices of dust exposure and the development of radiologic pneumoconiosis
authors: Moore E.; Martin J.R.; Edwards A.C.; Muir D.C.F.
abstract: A case-control study on employees at an iron ore surface mining plant was undertaken to determine which indices of occupational dust exposure related most closely to radiologic categories for pneumoconiosis. Forty cases, with radiographs compatible with the ILO Categories (1980) for simple pneumoconiosis, were matched for age, smoking habit, and date of entry into the workforce with 80 control subjects whose radiographs were read as normal. The six indices of dust exposure were cumulative and “peak” respirable dust, quartz, and iron oxide. Both iron oxide indices were not significant at the 5% level for either ILO Category 1 or Categories 2,3. The association between dust composition and ILO radiologic category for simple pneumoconiosis was consistent, with respirable quartz being the best differentiating index between the case and control groups. © 1987 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: PENETROMETER RESISTANCE AND BULK DENSITY AS PARAMETERS FOR PREDICTING ROOT SYSTEM PERFORMANCE IN MINE SOILS.
source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
authors: Thompson P.; Jansen I.; Hooks C.
abstract: Material handling methods used in the construction of soils after surface mining often result in a soil with physical and structural characteristics that restrict root development. A method to quickly and easily predict root system performance and compare mine soils on the basis of their suitability for root growth is needed. This study was conducted to determine the effectiveness of penetrometer resistance (as measured by a constant rate cone penetrometer) and bulk density as parameters for predicting root system performance. Both penetrometer resistance and bulk density data fit well into a multiple linear regression model that could be used to predict root length density.

title: Computer-aided planning and management of surface coal mines
authors: Chugh Y.P.; Caudle R.D.
abstract: Mini-, micro- and main-frame computers and their associated software are being utilized to (1) analyze geologic and hydrologic data obtained during exploration, (2) select and replace equipment, (3) develop alternate mining and reclamation plans, (4) establish technical and economic feasibility of various mining alternatives, (5) evaluate hydrologic impacts of mining, (6) develop management information systems for effective and efficient control of surface mining equipment and operations, and (7) train mine personnel. This paper briefly describes a variety of applications of computers in surface mining operations. Specific examples are given of five research projects involving development and use of new computer-based planning and management techniques. © 1987 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V.

title: Determinants of chronic bronchitis and lung dysfunction in Western Australian gold miners
authors: Holman C.D.J.; Psaila-Savona P.; Roberts M.; McNulty J.C.
abstract: The relation of chronic bronchitis and respiratory dysfunction to age, tobacco smoking, and occupational exposure to surface and underground mining operations were examined in a cross sectional survey of 1363 men employed in the Kalgoorlie mining industry in 1985. Overall, the prevalence of chronic bronchitis was 14%. Eleven per cent of the workers had obstructive lung disorder (FEV<inf>1</inf>/FVC < 0.70) and 9% had restrictive lung disorder (FVC < 0.80 of predicted for height and age). There was little change in the prevalence of chronic bronchitis from that observed in a survey of the same industry in 1961-2. Only 1% of the workers in 1985 had radiographic signs of silicosis compared with 22% in 1961-2. Age, smoking, and underground mining experience all exerted strong effects on the development of chronic bronchitis with or without associated respiratory function abnormalities. After control of confounding by age and smoking, it was estimated that compared with a lifetime non-miner, the odds ratio (OR) of chronic bronchitis was 1.8 (95% confidence interval, 1.0-3.3) for one to nine years underground mining gold, 2.5 (1.2-5.2) for 10-19 years, and 5.1 (2.4-10.9) for 20 or more years. Underground mining of minerals other than gold was also associated with chronic bronchitis (OR = 5.1; 95% CI, 1.1-25.0) whereas exclusive surface mining had only a small empirical effect (OR = 1.3; 95% CI, 0.6-2.5). It is estimated that the proportion of cases of chronic bronchitis in working underground miners due to occupational factors is 50%. The results support the existence of an industrial cause of chronic bronchitis, although caution must be exercised in generalising the results to miners with progressive and severe respiratory impairment.

title: Statistical analysis of surface-water-quality data in and near the coal-mining region of southwestern Indiana, 1957-80
source: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
authors: Martin J.; Crawford C.
abstract: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act requires that applications for coal-mining permits contain information about the water quality of local streams. To meet this need for information, streamflow, specific conductance, pH, and concentrations of total alkalinity, sulfate, dissolved solids, suspended solids, total iron, and total manganese at 37 stations were analyzed to determine the spatial and seasonal variations in water quality and to develop equations for predicting water quality. -from Authors

title: Comparison of some soil properties on natural and reclaimed hillslopes
authors: Toy T.J.; Shay D.
abstract: Handling of soil materials during surface mining may substantially modify their physical and chemical properties. In this report, a comparison is presented among: (1) bulk density, (2) particle-size distribution, (3) soil reaction, and (4) organic matter content of soils on natural and reclaimed hillslopes at the Dave Johnston Mine, Glenrock, Wyoming. At this site, no significant difference occurred in bulk density between the soils of natural and reclaimed hillslopes. No significant difference occurred in gravel content, but sand content was significantly higher on the soils of natural sites than on those of reclaimed sites. There were no significant difference in average pH between the soils of the natural and reclaimed hillslopes for the first decimeter of depth; however, the average pH of soils on the reclaimed hillslopes was significantly lower than those on the reclaimed hillslopes for the second, third, and fourth decimeters. Finally, no significant difference occurred in organic matter values between the soils of natural and reclaimed hillslopes for the first decimeter, but the difference was significant in the second decimeter. © 1987 The Williams & Wilkins Co.

title: Water prevention of the planned Vadna I open coal mine.
source: Acta Geodaetica Geophysica Et Montanistica Hungarica
authors: Jeney Jambrik R.
abstract: Out of the characteristic five coal seams the lowest, developed in the Vadna brown coal territory belongs to the East-Borsod brown coal basin. This coal bed being near to the surface is planned to be mined with stripping in two parts. The hydrogeological and hydrological conditions of the territory are discussed in the paper, and a proposal is given for the protection of part 1 of the surface mining against surface and underground water.-from Author

title: LOW-FREQUENCY VIBRATIONS PRODUCED BY SURFACE MINE BLASTING OVER ABANDONED UNDERGROUND MINES.
source: Report of Investigations United States Bureau of Mines
authors: Siskind D.; Stachura V.; Nutting M.
abstract: Bureau of Mines researchers assisted the U. S. Office of Surface Mining (OSM) by studying complaint-producing blasting vibrations resulting from an active surface mine operating over abandoned mine workings beneath the surface mine and the nearby town of Blanford, IN. Ground vibrations were of high amplitude and dominated by unusual and more structure response-producing low frequencies (4-8 Hz) than previous studies at other sites. These conditions resulted primarily from the geologic structure as the vibration propagating medium. Blast designs were partly responsible, with high level casting and complex multidelayed blasts producing wave interaction and constructive reinforcement. The traditional 8-ms criteria for separating charge weights per delay appears insufficient for this low-frequency site.

title: AUTOMATION, SIMPLIFICATION OF OPERATION AND INCREASE IN PERFORMANCE OF SELF-PROPELLED CONSTRUCTION AND SURFACE MINING MACHINES BY USE OF ELECTRONICS.
source: Transactions of the Iron and Steel Institute of Japan
authors: Leidinger G.
abstract: The complexities of surface mining and construction machines have reached a degree at which operators are no longer in a position to operate them continuously in the most efficient way and guarantee full utilization of the available performance. It is necessary, therefore, to ease the operation, either by supplying the operator with information on the overall status of his machine or by giving him direct operating instructions. This information must be presented to the operator in such a manner that it requires only a small amount of attention. By the introduction of closed control circuits the operator can be partly - or in some cases entirely - relieved from the direction of certain functions of the machine. Increased efficiency by reductions in fuel consumption and maintenance is also made possible by improved machine monitoring techniques. These rely on the application of microelectronics in connection with variable hydraulic systems. The main emphasis of automation today is on these means of optimizing the performance of the machine.

title: Efficient Extraction of Brown Coal and other Raw Materials using Advanced Surface Mining Technology and Equipment under Different Conditions.
authors: Gerlach P.; Melzer A.; Trogisch R.; Seifert W.
abstract: The GDR covers 72% of its primary energy needs with brown coal. In 1985 it mined 312 Mt of lignite, i. e. 27% of world output. In view of the increasingly worsening conditions of brown coal quality and bedding, more complicated open-cast techniques and equipment is required. The article describes some of the open-cast mining operation under difficult geological conditions.

title: MINE-BUILT PONDS ECONOMICALLY CLEAR ACID MINE WATERS.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: One of the by-products of surface mining is acid mine drainage. Studies show that properly designed and constructed wetlands outfitted with cattails and other marsh plants can efficiently and inexpensively treat discharges of acid mine water. Wetland plants remove metals from acid water by adsorption (especially ion exchange); consumption (plant uptake); and simple filtration.

title: Reclamation planning for coal strip-mined lands in Montana
authors: Hall D.L.
abstract: Strip mining for coal is causing serious environmental problems in the coal-rich lands of Eastern Montana (U.S.A.). A comparison of surface-mine reclamation planning in the state of Montana and planning in other regions shows that local planning authority is relatively absent in Montana. Reclamation planning efforts in the United States have generally improved since passage of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 and since enactment of state reclamation laws. However, of the vast amounts of drastically disturbed land in Montana, only a small fraction has been successfully reclaimed. Local site-specific comprehensive plans may be essential for ensuring that the negative ecological and cultural impacts of strip mining are temporary. © 1987.

title: Subsea mineral resources.
authors: McKelvey V.
abstract: About 20 nonpetroliferous minerals are produced from the continental margins. Sand and gravel, lime from shells and aragonite mud, precious coral, and placer minerals, such as rutile, ilmenite, leucoxene, cassiterite, zircon, monazite, magnetite, gold, platinum, and diamonds are recovered by surface mining. Sulfur and salt are recovered by solution mining through drill holes. Barite is recovered by subsea quarrying. Coal and iron ore are mined underground from entry on adjacent land or from artificial islands. Potash is likely to be produced from subsea salt basins, and offshore production of phosphate is being considered in several areas. The resources of the deep-ocean floor are yet to be developed. Those drawing the most interest are manganese nodules and encrustations, metallic sulfide deposits, and red clays.-from Author

title: Optimization of overburden drill dust control systems on surface coal mines
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Zimmer R.A.; Lueck S.R.; Page S.J.
abstract: A significant problem at U.S. surface mining operations is complying with more stringent dust standards resulting from high respirable free silica concentrations. In areas where potentially harmful concentrations of silica-bearing dust exist, more stringent dust standards are applied to limit the amount of respirable free silica to which the workers are exposed. According to U.S. Mine Safety and Health Administration (MSHA) data, overburden drilling occupations have the greatest exposure to silica. Worker exposure may be reduced by reducing the amount of dust produced by the drill. This can be accomplished with either dry collection or wet suppression systems. Both of these systems were evaluated in the field, results of this testing are the subject of this paper. This work was performed under a U.S. Bureau of Mines contract by PEI Associates, Inc. A special study of dry and wet systems was conducted to determine the proper operating parameters for each type of system. Shroud height was evaluated for dry systems and water flow rate was evaluated for wet systems. In the case of dry systems, it was found that a nearly inverse relationship exists between shroud height and control efficiency. The dry system performed most efficiently when the shroud was positioned 0.23 m or less from the ground. In the case of wet systems, the control efficiency versus water flow rate curve showed a steep increase in efficiency in the range of 0.09 to 0.14 m3/hr. The highest control efficiency (96%) was at a water flow rate of 0.27 m3/hr. Flow rates this high however, can cause operational problems, such as plugging of the drill bit. In general, the results of the study demonstrated the efficacy of control equipment available in the U.S. for overburden drills. Used in combination, dust control equipment, pressurized cabs, and personal protective equipment should allow U.S. surface mine operators to comply with more stringent dust standards at surface coal mines. © 1987, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: DISCUSSION ON A METHOD FOR DETERMINING THE CUTTING DRAG INDICES OF COAL AND ROCK.
source: Meitan Xuebao Journal of the China Coal Society
authors: Liu Jinghui; Xu Chaozuo
abstract: This paper discusses the cutting drag indices, which represent the cutting characteristics of coal and rock in China, and several methods for determining these indices by taking into consideration the measured cuting drag of in-situ coal and rock in mines and the mining technology of surface mining, rock properties, rock cutting drag and design calculation of selected excavators, etc. After deduction and analysis, the paper introduces four indices, namely the average cutting drag, K//c//l, peak value average cutting drag, K//F//c//l; quadratic equivalent cuting drag, K//2; peak value maximum cutting drag, K//m//a//x, for representing the cutting characteristics of coal and rock. A first attempt is made of using this method for predicting the cutting drag of brown coal in Zhaotong in Yunnan Province.

title: Environmental benefits of surface mining
authors: Grimshaw P.N.
abstract: Most forms of economic activity affect the environment in ways which can be claimed to be detrimental. Some of the worst results were produced in the past by mining. However, handled correctly, surface mining can have beneficial effects and the author discusses this, taking examples from coal mining activities in Great Britain.

title: EVALUATION OF SELECTED PIT CONFIGURATIONS FOR SURFACE MINING A MODERATELY PITCHING COAL SEAM.
source: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
authors: Chugh Y.; Ehie I.
abstract: The objective of this study was to conduct a technical and economic evaluation of selected pit orientations in mining a single seam dipping at 8. 53 degree (15%) to a maximum depth of 46 m (150 ft). Such mining conditions are prevalent in the Hanna Coal Basin in Wyoming. The evaluation emphasized the effect of pit orientation on overburden stripping operations since it constitutes the major portion of the mining cost. The study utilized physical models of the mining systems with different pit orientations, a dragline simulation model developed by Fluor Mining and Metals (1981), the Open Pit Material Handling Simulation Model (OPMHS), and a surface mine cost model (COSTMOD) developed by Manula et al. (1976).

title: ANALYSIS OF COAL SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT IN ILLINOIS.
source: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
authors: Bhagwat S.
abstract: Equipment capacities of sample of Illinois surface coal mines representing about 60% of surface production in the state were studied. Available equipment capacity was compared with the required capacity as indicated by coal production and stripping ratios reported. Most mines sampled showed surplus equipment capacity, which if avoided, would result in cost savings. The surplus capacity results mostly from market fluctuations that result in underutilization of equipment. Study findings underline the importance of market assessment at the time of mine planning.

title: PROBLEMS IN RECLAIMING STRIPPED MINED TUNDRA LANDS ON THE NORTH SLOPE, ALASKA.
source: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
authors: Bandopadhyay S.; Maneval D.
abstract: The coal resources of the North Slope can be expected to attract interest because the nearly flat-lying coal beds are especially amenable to surface mining. Mining on a scale large enough to justify coal development in this area could have severe environmental effects. The mitigation would be uncertain because large-scale coal mining and reclamation operations have not been carried out in the arctic. The objective of this paper is to establish the interrelationship between the problems due to permafrost and factors in reclamation of post-mining land in order to suggest reclamation approaches that may be appropriate in this region.

title: SELECTION OF EXPLOSIVES FOR SURFACE MINING INDUSTRY - A CRITIQUE.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Ghose A.
abstract: This paper seeks to address the methodology of explosive selection based on an appraisal of the current state-of-the-art of the theory and practice of explosive usage in surface mining industry. Limited results from studies carried out in India are also presented to underscore the feasibility of the approaches. Additionally, the need for a purposive rock mass classification, based on field data of explosive utilization, is outlined.

title: REDUCTION OF QUARRYING COST THROUGH USE OF CRUSHER/BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEMS.
authors: Mueller G.
abstract: In the 1950s the German cement industry was the first to develop crusher/belt conveyor systems. Handling rates of 250 tph and sizes of less than 50 mm did not present any problem for rubber belt conveyors. By 1975 conveyor installations capable of handling 1000 tph and by 1980 of 2000 tph were available. While the impetus to these development efforts emanated from the cement industry where limestone is the raw material, crusher/conveyor systems made their appearance in 1975 in the surface mining of bauxite and phosphate and, in 1980, copper ore. In 1986, Krupp Industrietechnik GmbH will supply the first 6000 tph mining system for iron ore. It will be commissioned in Australia. This article discusses mobile crushing plant markets, costs, and other aspects of the subject.

title: Use of hold-gro erosion control fabric in the establishment of plant species on coal mine soil
authors: Day A.D.; Ludeke K.L.
abstract: Experiments were conducted on the Black Mesa Coal Mine, Kayenta, Arizona in 1977 and 1978 to study the effectiveness of Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric (a product from the Gulf States Paper Corporation, Tuscaloosa, Alabama) in the establishment of plants on coal mine soil following the surface mining of coal. Four plant species were planted: (1) spring barley (Horduem vulgare L.), an annual grass (2) crested wheatgrass (Agropyron cristatum L.), a perennial grass (3) alfalfa (lucerne) (Medicago sativa L.), a perennial legume and (4) fourwing saltbush (Atriplex canescens Pursh.), a perennial shrub. Seeds of each plant species were planted in reclaimed coal mine soil in the spring of the year by both broadcast seeding (conventional culture) and the incorporation of seeds in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric. Average numbers of seedlings established and percent ground cover for all species studied were higher in areas where conventional culture was used than they were in areas where seeds were incorporated in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric. The incorporation of seeds in Hold-Gro Erosion Control Fabric in the establishment of plant species on coal mine soil was not an effective cultural practice in the southwestern United States. © 1986 Science and Technology Letters.

title: GROUNDWATER RECOVERY PROBLEMS ASSOCIATED WITH OPENCAST MINE BACKFILLS IN THE UNITED KINGDOM.
authors: Reed S.M.; Singh R.N.
abstract: The paper presents the main findings of the research work conducted over the past three years into the environmental effects associated with surface mining. Especial considerations have been given to the re-establishment of the natural groundwater regime, as a consequence of opencast site restoration. A summary of the results of the research is presented and two specific topics, namely, the stability of backfilled masses and the pollution of groundwater, are detailed. The project was based on field and laboratory investigations, and details of this work along with some general conclusions are given.

title: IMPROVED BLAST DESIGNS CAN REDUCE ROCKFALL HAZARDS.
authors: Anon
abstract: The most serious hazard in surface mining is falling rock from high-walls. Looking for ways to improve high-wall stability, the Bureau of Mines evaluated blasting practices at several surface coal mines. In most cases, blasting practices contributed to highwall instability. Improved blast designs reduced highwall overbreak through simple changes in the timing blasts that changed the direction and time of burden movement.

title: SHIFTABLE BELT CONVEYORS IN SURFACE MINING.
authors: Anon
abstract: Increasing demand for bulk materials such as ore, coal, lignite, oilsand, oilshale and bauxite has led to more opencast operations, where huge amounts of overburden and partings must be transported by conveyors, trucks or trains. Shiftable belt conveyors have proved to be versatile and economical in many such applications.

title: SURFACE MINING OF COAL . . . GROWTH THROUGH EVOLUTION.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Starting with primitive steam shovels and converted dredges and fostered by ability of American manufacturers to build larger, powerful stripping machines, surface mining of coal advanced from modest beginnings 75 years ago to reach its dominant role today. But although the age of big strippers is still here, smaller, more versatile equipment is coming on the scene.

title: WESTERN SURFACE MINING: OUTSTANDING TECHNICAL ISSUES.
authors: Anon
abstract: Research could resolve most of the uncertainties about Western surface mine reclamation, and could increase the probability of reclamation success with fewer design problems and lower costs. However, cutbacks in Federal funding have significantly reduced reclamation research. The Office of Surface Mining's inflexible application of some reclamation standards also has inhibited the adoption of innovative reclamation methods. This article discusses some of the outstanding technical issues involved, including acid potential in Western mine spoils, sediment control, revegetation, and others.

title: HOW TO TAKE ADVANTAGE OF THE NEW OSM BLASTING REGULATIONS.
authors: Ayat M.; Schneider L.
abstract: The frequencies of blastwaves can at times disturb the more distant structures more than the nearer ones. To address such conditions, the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) recently completed new regulations designed to be more effective in preventing damage to structures in the vicinity of surface coal mines. Many operators are not taking advantage of the methods that OSM and the associated state regulatory authorities are now allowing; these methods are discussed.

title: MITSUBISHI CONSTRUCTION MACHINERY FOR COAL SURFACE MINING.
authors: Anon
abstract: Mitsubishi Heavy Industries, Ltd. have been offering almost all types of construction machinery. This paper particularly highlights typical machines used in coal surface mining. Moreover, the company is presently developing a superlarge hydraulic excavator based on the latest technology.

title: Geotechnical stability in surface mining. Proceedings of the international symposium, Calgary, 6-7 November 1986.
source: Geotechnical Stability in Surface Mining Proceedings of the International Symposium Calgary 6 7 November 1986
authors: Singhal R.K.
abstract: The over 50 papers are concerned with on-going research and developments concerning the geotechnical stability of natural and man-made geo-structures implicated in surface mining. The main session themes are: surface mine design; design of pit wall slopes; drilling and blasting; slope excavation; artificial support; geotechnical stability-case histories; liquid storage and tailings pond; geotechnical properties; design of waste dumps; slope stability monitoring. Most of the papers are abstracted separately. -M.A.Bass

title: Use of computers in the coal industry. Proceedings of the third conference, Morgantown, WV, 28-30 July 1986.
source: Use of Computers in the Coal Industry Proceedings of the Third Conference Morgantown Wv 28 30 July 1986
authors: Wang Y.J.; Grayson R.L.; Sanford R.L.
abstract: The 34 papers present computer applications covering many aspects of the industry. They are grouped into thematic sections: mine management and economics; surface mining; geology and exploration; mine safety and ventilation; information systems; blasting; coal preparation; ground control and rock mechanics; mining machinery and equipment; geotechnical applications; exploration and reserve analysis. About a third are abstracted separately for publication; details of the others are entered on the Geo Abstracts data base.-M.A.Bass

title: Rilling of hillslopes reclaimed before 1977 surface mining law, Dave Johnston Mine, Wyoming
authors: Soulliere E.; Toy T.
keywords: Hillslopes | Rill erosion | Surface‐mine reclamation
abstract: The erosion of hillslopes reclaimed following the surface‐mining of coal is an important geomorphologic concern. However, progress in the design of post‐mining topography and its hydrologic response has been hampered by the paucity of research focusing on the propensity of rill formation on these disturbed surfaces. This investigation is intended to partially rectify this situation through the development of regression equations for the prediction of rill frequency and magnitude based upon site characteristics. Rill width can be estimated using soil bulk density, hillslope age, and hillslope length with a standard error of 0.152 log<inf>10</inf> units at this location. Rill depth can be estimated using soil shear strength, hillslope length, and hillslope age with a standard error of 0.114 log<inf>10</inf> units. Rill length can be estimated using hillslope length, percent silt in the soil, hillslope age, Bouyoucos Clay Ratio, and soil bulk density with a standard error of 3.515 m. Rill frequency can be estimated using soil bulk density, Bouyoucos Clay Ratio, soil compaction, soil reaction (pH), and hillslope age with a standard error of 0.241 rills/m. The cross‐product of rill width times depth can be estimated using soil shear strength, hillslope length, hillslope age, and soil bulk density with a standard error of 0.260 log<inf>10</inf> units. These results must be tested further under various environmental conditions. Nevertheless, prediction of rill formation seems to be a problem capable of solution. Copyright © 1986 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

title: Problems associated with rock material properties in surface mining equipment selection.
source: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
authors: Atkinson T.; Denby B.; Cassapi V.
abstract: Continuous mining systems may be split into 2 major sub-systems - excavation and haulage - in which characteristic problems occur. The main materials-related problems that affect both continuous and non-continuous surface mining operations are summarized. The factors that influence materials excavation and handling problems are discussed and index tests are presented that may be used to identify abrasive mineralogy and the physical properties of materials. The importance of materials testing both prior to equipment selection and during excavation is stressed and consideration is given to the integration of data on material properties into long- and short- term planning. -from Authors

title: Coal resources of the Tongue River member, Fort Union formation (Paleocene), Powder River Basin, Wyoming and Montana.
source: Report of Investigations Geological Survey of Wyoming
authors: Ayres W.
abstract: The Tongue River member contains >1.16 X 10<sup>9</sup> short tons of low-sulphur subbituminous coal to a depth of 3000 ft in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana. Coal occurs in thick (commonly >60 ft), laterally extensive beds that have been correlated >50 miles along strike. In a regional subsurface study, data from 1790 geophysical well logs were used to map Tongue River coal beds and calculate resources for an area of 9651 sq ft at places in the centre of the basin. Much of the Powder River Basin's coal resources are contained in two thick strike-parallel coal beds. The first (commonly called the Wyodak coal bed) crops out along the E margin of the basin where it is exploited by surface mining; the second seam (identified as Seam 14 in this study) lies basinward (W) of the first at depths of 1000-2000 ft.-G.B.G.

title: Aspects of geotechnical reliability in surface mining.
source: Geotechnical Stability in Surface Mining Proc Symposium Calgary 1986
authors: Chowdhury R.
abstract: Attention is focussed on a) choice of approach and method of analysis b) increasing the reliability where calculated risk is unacceptable and c) integrating reliability studies within an observational approach. -from Author

title: Coal-mining technology in China
authors: Shen S.
abstract: Although China is the second largest coal-producing country in the world, the geological conditions of the country's coal seams are not always favorable. The coal seams in most of the existing coal-mining areas are to deep for surface mining. Therefore, about 96% of China's total coal production is from underground mines. Since the early 1950s great efforts have been made to improve coal-mining technology in China. The longwall retreating mining method has been popularized, and production from longwall faces account for about 92% of the total. About 40% of the total production is from thick coal seams using the slicing system. During the last 10 years the priority has been to improve the mechanization of longwall face operations. In the near future research will emphasize the development of new coal technologies for mining thin seams, extra thick seams, and steeply dipping seams. © 1986.

title: Chemical quality of suspended sediment from watersheds subjected to surface coal mining
authors: Dick W.; Bonta J.; Haghiri F.
abstract: The chemical quality of suspended sediment in surface water runoff, which is changed as a result of surface coal activities, may influence water quality and have effects where the sediment is deposited downstream from the mine site. Suspended sediment samples were collected from three small watersheds in east-central Ohio prior to, during and after surface mining and reclamation. The chemical quality of the suspended sediment was determined by measuring Ca, Mg, Fe, Al, Mn, Ni, Pb, Cd, Cu, Zn, Sr, P (following pretreatment of the sample with 30% H<inf>2</inf>O<inf>2</inf> and extraction with 0.3 M HCl), acetate-soluble SO<inf>4</inf><sup>2-</sup>, pH, organic C, and Hg. Differences in concentrations of parameters were observed among the three watersheds and were related to the composition of the overburden material. At Watersheds C06 and M09, the concentrations of the chemical parameters in suspended sediment samples, collected after reclamation had been completed, were not significantly (P = 0.05) different than concentrations measured prior to surface mining. An exception was the concentration of organic C, which was lower during the postreclamation period. The concentrations of Mg, Fe, and Al were significantly greater at Watershed J11 during the postreclamation period compared to the premine period while P, organic C, Mn, and Pb concentrations were significantly lower. Concentrations of parameters in suspended sediment samples collected concurrently at the inlet and outlet of the sediment ponds at Watersheds C06 and M09 were not significantly (P = 0.05) different. However, due to settling of the larger and heavier sediment particles, a trend toward increased concentration of parameters in sediment samples collected at the pond outlet compared to the pond inlet occurred at both Watersheds C06 and M09.

title: BASIN WATER MONITORING: HYDROLOGIC IMPACT OR LEGAL COMPLIANCE
source: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
authors: Duckson D.
keywords: basin water monitoring | Maryland | modeling | OSM regulations
abstract: ABSTRACT: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (PL 95–87) requires data collection prior to mining which will allow a determination to be made of the probable hydrologic consequences. Modeling strategies exist which allow for such determination, but selection of a specific model form will dictate the length of data record needed. The absence of a sound management strategy by the regulatory authority in‘Maryland does not result in valid data collection and suggests that the agency is concerned more with legal compliance than with integrated resource management. Copyright © 1986, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Nickel, cadmium, and selenium levels in native soil, overburden, and spoil materials
authors: Pitt J.; Hossner L.; Melton J.
abstract: Nickel (Ni), cadmium (Cd), and selenium (Se) analyses showed that there was no significant difference in the concentration of these elements when compared over the three sample types examined (native soil, overburden, and spoil materials obtained from four surface mining operations in Texas). The soils belong to the Paleustalf, Paleudult, Hapludalf, and Paleudalf Great Groups. Ranges in total concentrations of the individual elements were 4.01 to 71.4 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Ni, 0.00 to 2.46 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Cd, and 0.04 to 10.7 mg kg<sup>-1</sup> Se for the native soil, overburden, and spoil samples. At each site, the geological environments of deposition had significantly different levels of Ni, Cd, and Se. Depositional environments containing higher concentrations of fine materials (Backswamp, flood basin, etc.) had the highest concentrations of Ni and Cd. Selenium was highest in the lignite and deposits closely associated with the lignite. Results of this study indicate that no significant elevation of total Ni, Cd, and Se would be expected from the complete mixing of overburden following the surface mining operation.

title: SURFACE MINING: EQUIPMENT SELECTION AND USE ARE THE KEYS TO PROFITS.
authors: Singhal R.K.
auto_equipment_tags: pala_excavadora; cargador_lhd; camion_extraccion; dragalina; chancador_correa; scraper_compactador
abstract: A wide variety of equipment is used for material excavation in surface mining including scrapers, electric cable shovels, front-end loaders, hydraulic shovels, draglines, and bucketwheels. Various types of haulage trucks, conveyors, scrapers, trains, and pipelines are used for transporting the excavated material. The article examines selection factors.

title: Towards reducing the physical environmental impact of North American surface coal mines; a review of potential selective overburden handling techniques
authors: George H.; Meech J.; Workman L.
abstract: In North America, coal and lignite are presently extracted from natural materials by a variety of surface mining techniques that are largely dictated by factors such as coal thickness and attitude, overburden characteristics, and geological complexity of the deposit. Although a large variety of techniques are used, they are often similar within certain geographic regions, each being associated with a typical method of overburden handling and one or more major type(s) of physical environmental impact (topographic, stratigraphic and/or geohydrologic). While it is technically feasible to modify current routine overburden handling practice, or to introduce effective novel selective handling techniques in order to reduce subsequent environmental damage within each geographic region, economic factors do not always favour selective methods. Because of the possibility of increased stripping costs, the implementation of any selective overburden placement scheme requires site-specific appraisal of the profitability of the operation. In some situations, however, the use of selective techniques in place of conventional methods can actually be economically superior. The appropriate selective overburden placement schemes that can be applied in the different geographic regions are assessed in this review. © 1986 Elesevier Science Publishers B.V.

title: EVALUATING WHEEL LOADERS AND FRONT SHOVELS.
authors: Anon
abstract: The availability of hydraulic front shovels in the 10- to 12-yd**3 class increases the number of large loading machines for surface mining. Although both the wheel loader and front shovel have distinct advantages, and each can often handle the work of the other, the economics are different. Manufacturers of front shovels often claim their machines are a better choice in tough digging applications because of high breakout forces and faster cycle times. Although the hydraulic shovel cycled faster, the wheel loader had a significant advantage in the amount of overburden moved per bucket load. The result, the wheel loader uncovered 2700 st more coal per eight-hour shift - a 30% production advantage. Even when comparing a 13-yd**3 front shovel to a 13. 5-yd**3 wheel loader, which Caterpillar did in a more recent study, the advantage still goes to the wheel loader.

title: COMMERCIALIZATION OF EASTERN US OIL SHALES - A REVIEW.
source: Transactions of the American Institute of Mining Metallurgical and Petroleum Engineers Society
authors: Rajaram V.
abstract: The oil shales located in the Appalachian Basin cover an eight-state area of the eastern US and are referred to as Devonian (black) shales. These shales have been exploited for their gas potential for several years. The Institute of Gas Technology (IGT) has conducted research since 1972 on the production of shale oil from the Devonian shales. This resulted in the development of the HYTORT process. This process demonstrated that the yield from the Eastern oil shales can be greater than the value indicated by the Fischer assay method. IGT estimates that 67 Gm**3 (423 billion bbl) of oil could be recovered by HYTORT processing of surface minable eastern US shales. Recently, American Syncrude Corp. and Southern Pacific Petroleum NL have proposed oil shale projects in Kentucky. This paper will describe the surface mining and retorting techniques that have been studied for exploitation of the Devonian shales, and enumerate the problems that have to be overcome before commercial production can be realized.

title: RELATION BETWEEN GROUND-WATER QUALITY AND MINERALOGY IN THE COAL-PRODUCING NORTON FORMATION OF BUCHANAN COUNTY, VIRGINIA.
source: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
authors: Powell J.; Larson J.
abstract: Core material from the Norton Formation of the Pennsylvania Period is composed of slightly more than one-half sandstone; siltstone and minor amounts of shale, clay, and coal account for the majority of the remainder. Petrographic analyses and x-ray diffraction studies indicate that the sandstone is about 75 percent quartz, 15 percent plagioclase feldspar, 2 percent potassium feldspar, 2 percent plagioclase feldspar, 2 percent potassium feldspar, 2 percent muscovite, 4 percent chlorite, and 1 percent siderite. No limestone strata were identified. Three reaction models are used to account for the observed water chemistry. The models derive sulfate from pyrite, iron from pyrite and siderite, calcium from plagioclase and calcite, sodium from plagioclase and cation exchange, magnesium from chlorite, and carbon from carbon dioxide, calcite, and siderite. Kaolinite, chalcedony, and goethite are formed authigenically. Carbon-13 data define the relative contributions of carbon sources to models. Comparison of adjacent unmined and mined basins indicates that surface mining significantly increases the weathering reaction of pyrite in contrast to weathering reactions of other minerals. Refs.

title: Marsh community development in a central Florida phosphate surface-mined reclaimed wetland
authors: Erwin K.L.; Ronnie Best G.
abstract: As the nation's acreage of productive freshwater marsh/wetlands continues to decrease the need for sucessful marsh restoration/reclamation increases. A variety of land uses including surface mining, residential development and agriculture create direct impacts on wetlands often resulting in a net loss of habitat if appropriate restoration or reclamation of the ecosystem is not obtained within a reasonable period of time. The 30 hectare freshwater marsh reclaimed from a phosphate mined area is part of a 148 hectare upland, 61 hectare wetland ecosystem (Agrico Swamp) reclaimed in 1981/82. Topsoil additions have been a successful means of establishing a marsh system within the site. This technique shows distinct advantages over natural revegetation of overburden. At the end of two full growing seasons the topsoiled area has higher species richness and cover values than the overburden areas. During this period a slight decline in the species richness in the topsoiled area was evident due in part to the aggressive nature of Pontederiacordata. Conversely, the species richness of the overburden areas increased significantly. Topsoiling appears to encourage the accelerated establisment of late successional plants in sufficient quantities to compete with aggressive weedy species such as Typhalatifolia. © 1985 Society of Wetland Scientists.

title: BUCKAU WOLF SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT IN NEYVELI LIGNITE MINES IN INDIA.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Raybarman P.
abstract: Buckau Wolf India manufactures a range of bulk material handling machinery and cement machinery. Their German partner is M/s. Buckau Wolf of Germany (Krupp Industrietechnik). The lignite field at Neyveli is spread over approximately 100 sq miles with an estimated range of 2000 million tonnes. Continuous mining technology as used in German mines has been adopted.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF BUCKET WHEEL EXCAVATOR.
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: De A.
abstract: Bucket wheel excavator is an important equipment for surface mining projects, which are used in lignite mines throughout the world. The concept and its application are more than 100 years old. The machine has been modified on several occasions to suit project conditions. Important changes are the modifications of buckets, cell chutes, bucket driving units, travel mechanisms, luffing arrangements, and counter weight structures. This paper presents these and the latest techniques that have been incorporated in a systematic way.

title: SEDIMENT YIELD AND WATER QUALITY FROM A STEEP-SLOPE SURFACE MINE SPOIL.
source: Transactions of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers
authors: Dickens P.S.; Tschantz B.A.; Minear R.A.
abstract: Sediment yield and storm runoff water quality from a steep-slope, back-to-contour, coal surface mining spoil in the New River Basin of Tennessee were monitored for a period of three years. Sediment and mineral constituent concentrations observed in storm runoff from the spoil increased to a maximum 1. 1 to 1. 3 years following the completion of mining, then declined. This increase was associated with the loss of mulch provided at reclamation and the onset of rill and gully erosion. Maximum sediment yield also occurred within this period. By the end of the third year following mining, a dense and uniform vegetative cover had become established on the spoil.

title: PRODUCTIVITY FROM BUCKET WHEEL EXCAVATORS.
authors: Golosinski T.; Singhal R.
