In addition, a historical review of rules and regulations governing subsidence-related problems is given, leading to Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, and finally, the new regulations being developed under the regulatory reform program are discussed. © 1982 Science and technology letters.

title: Engineering's role in surface mining
source: Journal of the Energy Division Proceedings of the ASCE
authors: Schivley W.W.
abstract: As a result of Public Law 95-87, the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, many new consulting opportunities are being developed by engineering firms. Many of these opportunities are in the form of established services given a new perspective to meet regulatory compliance and/or reclamation data base requirements. Some of these engineering and environmental services are discussed and, utilizing actual case study experience, a scenario is presented of the engineering firm's new role in this most controversial legislation. Given the environmental ethics established in the 1970's, it seems unlikely that our nation's environmental protection will be rescinded. With this future course of action the engineering firm should continue to play a major role in the environmental aspects of surface mining.

title: Changes in the groundwater due to surface mining
authors: Libicki J.
abstract: Open-cast mining operations conducted below groundwater table often affect the drawdown of the water table over large areas which as a consequence changes the natural regional hydrological balance. Remedial measures may include construction of new water intakes, and changes in the land usage may be necessary. Tipping of wastes (most often coal wastes and ashes) affects ground water pollution. Instead of removal of effects, preventive methods are recommended. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

title: Control of groundwater in surface mining
authors: Brawner C.O.
abstract: The presence of groundwater in surface mining operations often creates serious problems. The most important is generally a reduction in stability of the pit slopes. This is caused by pore water pressures and hydrodynamic shock due to blasting which reduce the shear strength and seepage pressures, water in tension cracks and increased unit weight which increase the shear stress. Groundwater and seepage also increase the cost of pit drainage, shipping, drilling and blasting, tyre wear and equipment maintenance. Surface erosion may also be increased and, in northern climates, ice flows on the slopes may occur. Procedures have been developed in the field of soil mechanics and engineering of dams to obtain quantitative data on pore water pressures and rock permeability, to evaluate the influence of pore water and seepage pressures on stability and to estimate the magnitude of ground-water flow. Based on field investigations, a design can be prepared for the control of groundwater in the slope and in the pit. Methods of control include the use of horizontal drains, blasted toe drains, construction of adits or drainage tunnels and pumping from wells in or outside of the pit. Recent research indicates that subsurface drainage can be augmented by applying a vacuum or by selective blasting. Instrumentation should be installed to monitor the groundwater changes created by drainage. Typical case histories are described that indicate the approach used to evaluate groundwater conditions. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

title: Groundwater problems in surface coal mining in Scotland
authors: Norton P.J.
abstract: The paper reviews the problems encountered with groundwater in surface mining in Scotland. The problems which occur at various stages of the mining process from initial exploration to mine planning and final restoration are referred to. Special consideration is given to mine drainage and pumping methods. © 1982 Springer-Verlag.

title: Sediment control for the surface mining industry.
authors: Lagasse P.F.; Li R.M.; Simons D.B.
abstract: The paper presents a discussion of the physical processes of erosion and sedimentation in relation to the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency and Office of Surface Mining regulations for sediment control in effluent from surface coal mines. The processes of erosion and sedimentation were studied extensively, and although quite complex, they may be characterized by modern simulation techniques to predict sediment loads from disturbed and undisturbed lands. Therefore, it is possible to design systems to control sediment from coal mining activities using such techniques as are discussed in the paper. The authors, however, contend that one cannot treat sediment uniformly as a pollutant and, at the same time, minimize disturbances to the hydrologic balance. (from authors' abstract)

title: Sedimentation in the East Branch Mahoning Creek basin, Clearfield and Jefferson Counties, Pennsylvania, June 1979 to June 1980.
authors: Wetzel K.
abstract: Parts of the basin, a forested area of 29.6 square miles in west-central Pennsylvania, are disturbed by farming, surface mining, unpaved haul roads, eroding reclaimed areas, and logging. Streamflow was measured and water samples collected at a site upstream from the mouth during base flow and storm periods to evaluate sediment discharges. An additional site on a tributary draining mostly farmland was also sampled. Samples were analyzed for suspended sediment, turbidity, and specific conductance. Daily mean suspended-sediment concentrations and discharges were computed. From June 1979 to June 1980, 3570 tons of suspended sediment was transported from the basin. This was an average yield of 121 tons mi<sup>2</sup>/yr.-from US Govt Reports Announcements, 19, 1982

title: Proceedings of the conference on water and energy: technical and policy issues.
authors: Kilpatrick F.; Matchett D.
abstract: Industrial, political, legal, hydrological, and environmental issues surrounding development of energy and associated water resources are examined. Water use and requirements, and wastewater treatment are examined in respect to the synthetic fuel industry, coal slurry pipelines, surface mining, hydropower, and oil shale production. Water conservation and reuse, trends in energy/water legislation, policy and public management, and citizen participation in energy/water resource problems are reviewed. Attention is given to new energy resources and impacts, and to water related research needs for energy development.-from ASCE Publications Abstracts

title: PROCEEDINGS - SYMPOSIUM ON SURFACE MINING HYDROLOGY, SEDIMENTOLOGY, AND RECLAMATION, 1981.
source: University of Kentucky Office of Engineering Services Bulletin Uky Bu
abstract: Proceedings include 81 papers that deal with management of mines and mining, mine land reclamation, mine hydrology and disposal of mine wastes, protection of water quality, sewage sludge application, mine sedimentation, and application of mine wastes to wildlife and recreation of surface mines. Technical and professional papers from this conference are indexed with the conference code no. 00813 in the Ei Engineering Meetings (TM) database produced by Engineering Information, Inc.

title: The allocative impacts of mineral severance: implications for the regulation of surface mining.
authors: Huffman J.L.
abstract: Examines the respective rights of surface and subsurface owners when surface mining is contemplated, and in particular the regulations designed to protect the rights of third parties. -T.O'Riordan

title: Instability of contoured surface- mined landscapes in the northern Great Plains: causes and implications.
authors: Groenewold G.; Rehm B.
abstract: Reclamation of surface-mined landscapes is commonly defined only in terms of biological productivity. Other critical concerns associated with surface mining include the long-term quality of groundwater and the stability of the post-mining landscape. Types of instability include area-wide settling, localized collapse and piping.-from Authors

title: Seismicity induced by surface mining: the Belchatow, Poland, earthquake of 29 November 1980.
authors: Gibowicz S.; Guterch B.; Lewandowska-Marciniak H.; Wysokinski L.
abstract: On 29 November 1980 a magnitude 4.6 earthquake occurred in the brown coal mining area of Belchatow in central Poland. The tremor is characterized by a seismic moment M<inf>o</inf> = 2.5 X 10<sup>22</sup> dyne-cm, source radius r = 810m and stress drop DELTA sigma = 21 bar. The fault plane solution, found from P-wave first motion at 28 stations, is unfortunately not univocal and it implies either strike-slip fault motion with a left lateral transcurrent faulting or dip-slip motion with considerable strike-component on a reversed fault. The tremor was felt on large area and a maximum intensity was 7 of the MSK-64 scale. From the isoseismal map the depth was estimated to be approx 2km.-AuthorsInst of Geophys, Polish Acad of Sci, 00-973 Warsaw, PO Box 155, Pasteura 4, Poland.

title: Reproductive success of grassland sparrows on a reclaimed surface mine in West Virginia.
authors: Wray T.; Strait K.A.; Whitmore R.C.
abstract: Examines the reproductive success of grasshopper sparrows Ammodramus savannarum, savannah sparrows Passerculus sandwichensis, vesper sparrows Pooecetes gramineus and field sparrows Spizella pusilla. Only vesper sparrows showed significant annual differences in clutch size. Predation was the major cause of egg and nestling losses. The study site, surrounded by woodlots and pastureland, concentrated predators. Northern black racers Coluber constrictor constrictor and common crows Corvus brachyrhynchos were the major predators. Variable nesting success reflects differential predation pressure. Adults are not replacing themselves and immigration is necessary to maintain a stable population. Environmental cues are sufficient to elicit a settling response, but, due to predation, reproductive success is low. Although surface mining is providing new nesting habitat, inadequate reproductive success suggests that these man-made grasslands may not be of benefit to the sparrow populations. -from Authors

title: (The Belchatow earthquakes induced by surface mining, Central Poland)).
source: Polish Academy of Sciences Publications Inst Geophysics Series M
authors: Gibowicz S.; Droste Z.; Guterch B.; Hordejuk J.
abstract: Five seismic events which occurred between August 1979 and May 1980 in the Belchatow trench area in Central Poland, where large brown coal deposits are situated and where surface mining works have been carried out since 1976, are described. The three largest shocks are characterized by the local magnitude M<inf>L</inf> = 3.5, seismic moment M<inf>o</inf> = 7.5X10<sup>13</sup> N.m and source radius r = 350 m, approximately. The tremors were felt with maximum intensity between 5 and 6, and from the magnitude-intensity-depth relation the focus depth was tentatively estimated to be between 1 and 5 km. The Belchatow tremors are the manifestation of an unusual type of induced seismicity - seismicity connected with surface mining. The removal of the overburden and drainage of coal deposits by extensive ground water withdrawal seem to be direct factors responsible for stress concentration, though the preexisting tectonic stress might well be the most important indirect factor responsible for the origin of these events.-English summary

title: Hodel v. Virginia Surface Mining and Reclamation Association and Hodel v. Indiana.
authors: Conner T.
abstract: Examines two recent Supreme Court rulings under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. The issue relates primarily to the degree of federal versus state control over mining operations.-T.O'Riordan

title: Some chemical characteristics of mine drainage in Illinois.
source: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
authors: Toler L.
abstract: Surface mining for coal in Illinois has affected runoff from the mined areas and altered water quality in the streams. Average annual sulfate loads in streams are 3000-4000 tons per square mile of mined land in the Big Muddy and Saline River basins in S Illinois. Relatively high concentrations of dissolved aluminum, arsenic, chromium, copper, iron, manganese, and zinc are commonly associated with concentrations of sulfate greater than about 2000 milligrams per liter.-Author

title: Remote sensing applications to the Pennsylvania abandoned mine reclamation program.
source: Proc National Conference on Energy Resource Management Baltimore 1982 Vol 2
authors: Clemens E.; Warnick L.
abstract: Pennsylvania Abandoned Mine Land Inventory demonstrated the effective use of remote sensing techniques within the context of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977. The inventory combined data from field work, a literature search, and photointerpretation. A primary project objective was to identify accurately and map all surface features and disturbances from abandoned surface and underground mining. Black-and-white aerial photographs were used to record pits, contour benches, highwalls, spoil material, graded and recontoured areas, impounded water, and serious erosion and slide prone areas. In addition, vegetation cover estimates and surrounding land uses were noted. -from STAR, 21(15) , 1983

title: Reclamation planning in California - a cooperative approach ( mining).
authors: Mankoski Z.; Cole K.
abstract: An overview of the way in which the issue of mining land reclamation has been handled in the US since the early 1970s. Mining is seen increasingly as an interim land use, reflected in planning applications and the Surface Mining and Reclamation Act (SMARA) of 1975. Increasing public awareness of the importance of resource management is a goal of the CDMG Reclamation Program.-after Author

title: Nematode densities on reclaimed sites on a cold desert shrub- steppe.
authors: Stanton N.; Krementz D.
abstract: Nematode populations were sampled under shrubs (Atriplex confertifolia), grasses and an introduced annual (Halogeton glomeratus) in a cold desert native shrub-steppe and on 3 neighboring sites disturbed by topsoil removal or surface mining. Of these 4 treatments, the native vegetation consistently supported the highest densities of all trophic groups of nematodes. On all sites, the native shrub, A. confertifolia, supported the highest densities while the introduced annual, H. glomeratus, supported the lowest.-from Authors

title: Ohio's abandoned mine lands reclamation program: a study of data collection and evaluation techniques.
source: Proc National Conference on Energy Resource Management Baltimore 1982 Vol 2 Applications
authors: Sperry S.
abstract: The planning process for a statewide reclamation plan of Ohio abandoned minelands in response to the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 included: 1) the development of a screening and ranking methodology; 2) the establishment of a statewide review of major watersheds affected by mining; 3) the development of an immediate action process; and 4) a prototypical study of a priority watershed demonstrating the data collection, analysis, display and evaluation to be used for the remaining state watersheds.-from STAR, 21(15), 1983

title: UNIQUE METHOD TO ENRICH MINE SPOILS.
authors: Younos T.; Teo B.; Smolen M.
abstract: The paper reviews studies which show that rice cultivation on sludge-amended mine spoils offers sound practice to retain runoff water and build up fertility during reclamation phase of surface mining.

title: Watersheds in muskeg terrain. 2. Evaluations based on water chemistry
authors: Schwartz F.W.; Milne-Home W.A.
abstract: This paper discusses the application of data on stream water chemistry to regional groundwater evaluation, hydrograph separation, and evaluation of the effects of basin disturbance. We have selected for analysis the Firebag, Steepbank and Muskeg River basins, and Hartley and Thickwood Creek basins in northern Alberta, Canada. They cover slightly more than 9000 km<sup>2</sup> within a region containing vast quantities of surface mineable, oil sand deposits. All basins are drift covered and underlain by bedrock that can range in age from Precambrian to Cretaceous. Comparison of chemical data for stream water from all basins with that for groundwater from Hartley Creek basin confirms that groundwater is a major source of streamflow in winter. Indications are that this groundwater inflow is almost entirely from glacial drift. Hydrograph separations based on chemical parameters indicate that during the spring and summer the proportion of groundwater in the streamflow is less than winter values with the largest contribution by far coming from the drainage of muskeg. Muskeg thus exerts important control on stream discharge and chemistry. If surface mining in these basins causes the removal of muskeg and replacement by mineral soil, stream discharge from affected areas will be less during summer and more during spring runoff and stormflow periods. As well, major-ion concentrations should be generally higher in the summer and fall months. However, the impact of local disturbances in a larger basin will be diminished downstream as waters from affected areas are mixed with other waters. © 1982.

title: IMPACT OF PUBLIC POLICY ON SURFACE MINE PLANNING AND DESIGN IN THE UNITED STATES.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Sweigard R.; Ramani R.
abstract: The major effects that public policy has had on the planning design, and organization of surface mines in the United States are summarized in this paper. The public policy impacts are grouped into three separate categories: mine planning, mine design, and mine organization. A clear distinction is made between the Federal, state, and local governmental responsibilities in formulating public policy with regard to surface mining operations.

title: STATUS OF TECHNOLOGY IN SURFACE MINING IN INDIA.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Mozumdar B.
abstract: In this article, the status of Indian surface mining activity in different mineral sectors are first reviewed followed by some observations of general interest. It is shown that surface mining is destined to play a pivotal role in meeting the mineral and fuel need of the country. The expertise available within the country as well as the expanding machine manufacturing capability will help in sustaining its pace of rapid development. Adequate mandatory steps will be necessary in ensuring environmental protection.

title: ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT OF SURFACE COAL MINING IN THE UNITED STATES.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Chugh Y.; Kharkar R.
abstract: Surface coal mining contributes over 60% of the U. S. coal production. Environmental constraints on surface coal mining have been increasing for the past two decades and have resulted in a substantial decline in productivity. This paper briefly describes the different acts and agencies regulating surface mining, primary mining and reclamation techniques, overall environmental assessment, regional environment concerns and their abatement.

title: SURFACE MINING TECHNIQUES - A GLOBAL REVIEW.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Rickus J.; Bailey J.
abstract: Surface mining methods in use world-wide for the extraction of stratified and metalliferous minerals are briefly examined, together with the equipment for excavation, loading and transportation. Trends in the development of mining equipment, their application, and mine planning techniques are discussed. Some of the important mine developments throughout the world are reviewed.

authors: Anon

authors: Anon
abstract: Proceedings includes 12 papers that are divided into three sessions dealing with surface mining, mine power systems, and power system analysis. Emphasis is on the protection of personnel and electric equipment in coal, metal, and nonmetal mines. Topics considered include: overcurrent and relay protection, accident prevention, hazards, negligence, energy saving by use of highly efficient electric motors, electromechanical vs solid-state relays, shielded cables, and computer-aided analysis of electric power and industrial distribution systems. Technical and professional papers from this conference are indexed with the conference code no. 00669 in the Ei Engineering Meetings (TM) database produced by Engineering Information, Inc.

title: Hydrological problems of surface mining.
authors: Wood P.
abstract: Recent literature concerned with the physical problems arising from the interrelationships between hydrology ad the surface mining of coal is reviewed. Both surface water and ground water are considered at all stages of the mining operation: planning, extraction and restoration. Aspects covered include the collection and handling of hydrological data, the construction of river diversions, the control of runoff, erosion and sediment, the problems of ground water and dewatering, and spoil bank hydrology. It is concluded that the interrelationships are complex and far reaching, and should be considered to ensure the efficient running of a surface mining operation while adequately protecting the environment.

title: Second Eastern regional remote sensing applications conference, Danvers, MA, 9-11 March 1981.
authors: Imhoff M.L.; Witt R.G.; Kugelmann D.
abstract: Participants from state and local governments share experiences in remote sensing applications with one another and with users in the Federal government, universities, and the private sector during technical sessions and forums covering agriculture and forestry; land cover analysis and planning; surface mining and energy; data processing; water quality and the coastal zone; geographic information systems; and user development programs. Items are abstracted separately. -NASA abstract E83-10189

authors: Kun J.
abstract: Concisely surveys the state and development of surface mining of lignite in the world and particularly in Yugoslavia, from its first beginnings until the present day. A description is given of the mining technique itself, and especially of extraction, transportation, disposal, and of the dependence of the technology of surface mining on the conditions of the deposits. In addition to geological, geophysical, and prospect drillings, an interpretation of prospecting results is given, together with an estimation of the mass of surface excavation. -Bull. Sci. Sect. abstract: Two editorials draw attention to a number of the broad public policy isues that relate agriculture and energy. Important questions are raised concerning the massive expenditures for imported oil and the attempt to balance these foreign payments through the export of agricultural products the high levels of soil erosion associated with current agricultural production and the possibility that available agricultural land would be impaired by strip mining for coal. abstract: The enormous cost of replacing worn parts in mining machinery is a continual challenge to the metallurgist. Parts designed for sacrificial wear must possess adequate abrasion resistance and frequently they must also have the ability to withstand impact. There are many cases of materials being hard and abrasion resistant but so brittle as to be unusable for many applications. ESCO's attempt to solve the toughness-wear resistant problem in two different operations is discussed. (A)

title: Surface mining and reclamation: initial changes in soil character.
authors: Indorante S.; Jansen I.; Boast C.
abstract: Five different, newly reconstructed soil units on surface-mined land and three undisturbed (cultivated, but not mined) soil units were defined and characterized. Selected properties of the reclaimed soils were compared with those of nearby undisturbed soils to determine what changes took place during the mining and reclamation operations. Compared with the undisturbed soils, the constructed soils had higher bulk densities and lacked structure. In general, the pH, exchangeable calcium levels, and exchangeable sodium levels were higher and the exchangeable magnesium levels were equal or higher in the constructed soils than in the natural soils. The properties of the constructed soils reflect premining overburden character and method of soil construction, suggesting that considerable control over postmine soil characteristics can be managed by careful selection of materials and material-handling methods.-from Authors

title: The belchatow, Poland, earthquakes of 1979 and 1980 induced by surface mining
authors: Gibowicz S.; Droste Z.; Guterch B.; Hordejuk J.
abstract: Five seismic events occurred between August 1979 and May 1980 in the Belchatow trench area in central Poland, where large brown-coal deposits have been surface-mined since 1976. The three largest shocks had a local magnitude M<inf>L</inf> = 3.5, seismic moment M<inf>o</inf> = 1.5 · 10<sup>14</sup> N-m and source radius r = 350 m, approximately. The tremors had maximum intensity between 5 and 6, and from the magnitude-intensity-depth relation, the focal depth was estimated to be between 1 and 5 km. The Belchatow tremors are the manifestation of an unusual type of induced seismicity, i.e., seismicity connected with surface mining. The removal of overburden and extensive ground-water withdrawal by the mining operations seem to be direct factors responsible for stress concentration, although preexisting tectonic stress might be the most important indirect factor responsible for the origin of these events. © 1981.

title: Depositional setting and groundwater quality in coal-bearing sediments and spoils in western North Dakota ( USA).
source: Recent and Ancient Nonmarine Depositional Environments Models for Exploration
authors: Groenewold G.; Rehm B.; Cherry J.
abstract: Studies of several active and proposed surface coal-mining sites in western N Dakota have resulted in the development of a hydrogeochemical framework which accounts for the chemical characteristics of groundwater in coal-bearing strata. There is much regional similarity in the hydrogeochemical characteristics of shallow aquifers. SO<inf>4</inf> <sup>=</sup> and HCO<inf>3</inf> <sup>-</sup> are commonly dominant anions. Na and Ca are generally the dominant cations. The pH of the groundwater normally ranges from 7 to 9. Critical hydrogeochemical processes include pyrite oxidation, carbonate mineral dissolution, and sulfate reduction. During surface mining operations unweathered materials are commonly emplaced in the zone of active weathering. Hydrochemical data from postmining landscapes suggest that severe degradation of groundwater quality is possible in some settings. The degree of weathering, dissolution, and ion exchange is largely dependent upon mineralogical variables in the overburden sediments. Degradation of groundwater quality in postmining landscapes can be minimized if these factors are integrated within the framework of mine design. -from Author

title: The Use of Geologic, Hydrologic, and Geochemical Mapping Techniques in Environmental Assessment
authors: Coe C.J.
abstract: A method of researching data at a mine to determine the environmental and economic impact to the operator has been developed. This method consists of developing geologic, hydrologic, and geochemical maps that can be used to provide a three‐dimensional view of the subsurface environment before, during, and after mining. The following maps were developed: a standard topographic base map, structure contour maps, static water level maps, and several iso‐concentration maps for pH, iron, manganese, sulfate, and specific conductance. Where possible geologic‐hydrologic cross sections were drawn to aid in the environmental interpretations. It is possible to use the data to develop the best possible mining plan for a geologic region which considers geographic, technical, economic, and environmental parameters. The iso‐concentration maps for a proposed surface mine site can be used to define the extent of concentration fields, point source locations, and concentration gradients. To demonstrate the use and interpretations of the data provided by this method, the results of two mine site case studies are presented that will discuss: (1) Dewatering problems; (2) Mining recharge areas; (3) Mining coal overlain by an acid overburden; and (4) The impact of prior surface mining. title: Coal.
source: American Association of Petroleum Geologists Bulletin
authors: Groat C.
abstract: Coal production for 1980 was up 6.9% from 1979 levels. Surface mines produced 60%: costs are lower, resource recovery is greater, and there are fewer health and safety problems. 70% of all the coal produced originated E of Mississippi. Western mines will account for a larger share of production in future because of increased demand for low-sulfur coal. Additionally many of the western deposits are suitable for surface mining, which is more attractive. Only 45% of presently estimated reserves of coal lie west of the Mississippi, and it is estimated that only 33% of all recoverable reserves could be recovered by surface mining. The largest consumer during 1980 continued to be electric utilities. Exports were up 39% over 1979. Domestic prices increased in 1980 and will continue to rise. Transport costs will be a major factor in raising prices. State severance taxes, especially in Montana and Wyoming, will add significantly to costs unless the federal government sets a maximum rate. There was no major legislation concerning the environmental aspects of coal production during 1980. Leasing of federal coal lands increased and shifts in lease ownership led to a greater variety of industries that hold federal coal leases. Electric utilities hold the largest percent of all leaseholds. The interest in synthetic fuels from coal continues. -from Author

title: DYNAMIC PROPERTIES OF RESIDENTIAL STRUCTURES SUBJECTED TO BLASTING VIBRATIONS
authors: Dowding C.; Murray P.; Atmatzidis D.
abstract: The responses of 23 single family residences to motions from surface mining blasts were analyzed with Fourier power spectral density and transfer functions to determine their dynamic response properties. The fundamental frequency of the structural frames, which had an average value of 7. 0 Hz, decreased with increasing height of the structure. The damping of these structures was observed to increase with increasing induced absolute motions. Walls vibrating in flexure had fundamental frequencies higher than those of the structural frames (12 Hz - 21 Hz). These results apply directly to the study of the response of structures subject to ground motions from mining activities, and are also useful for the study of response to earthquakes.

title: EFFECT OF SURFACE MINING ON STORM FLOW AND PEAK FLOW FROM SIX SMALL BASINS IN EASTERN KENTUCKY
source: Jawra Journal of the American Water Resources Association
authors: Bryan B.; Hewlett J.
keywords: peak flow | R‐index | storm flow | surface mining
abstract: ABSTRACT: Hydrologic records from six small Eastern Kentucky watersheds were analyzed to determine the effect of surface mining on storm flows and peak flows. Average storm flow volumes were not changed by surface mining, whereas average peak flows were increased 36 percent. Peak flow increases were only in the summer. Smaller peak flows are doubled; moderate ones are increased by about a third; peak flows around 100 csm seem to be largely unaffected; and the larger peak flows may have been reduced by surface mining. The maximum annual storm flows, usually in winter or spring, appeared slightly reduced. No time trend in either storm flows or peak flows could be detected in five years of postmining record. Surface mining is not a serious floodwater discharge problem. Copyright © 1981, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: LABORATORY INVESTIGATION OF HYDRAULIC FRACTURING IN OIL SANDS.
authors: Raisbeck J.; Currie J.
abstract: The design of hydraulic fracturing operations in conjunction with in-situ heavy oil recovery relies on a detailed knowledge of the engineering geology. Although some geotechnical data are available for oil sand deposits in the surface mining area of Athabasca, Alberta (Canada), virtually no information has been published for deeper deposits. The paper reviews the significant physical properties and reports the results from laboratory measurements conducted on oil sands. Data suggest that oil sand may exhibit time-dependent properties under in-situ recovery conditions. The authors also describe exploratory experimentation designed to study conditions under which an open path of fluid injection may be created in oil-sand aggregates.

title: Impact of road building, urbanisation and general infrastructural development on the Nigerian rainforest ecosystem
authors: Ofomata G.
abstract: Man has increasingly affected the succession of the rainforest ecosystem in Nigeria through various activities connected with his settlement on land. Consequently, little of the Nigerian rainforest ecosystem has remained undisturbed, and extensive areas of original climax vegetation no longer exist in the country. The paper reviews some of the major areas of man's impact on this forest ecosystem. Specifically, it examines me issues of pollution, surface mining, road building, industrialisation and urbanisation. Brief attention is paid to cultural eutrophication, which has been attributed largely to the increase of nitrates and phosphorus added to the water from many sources; this is particularly noticeable in the aquatic sectors of the Nigerian forest ecosystem. Surface mining in Nigeria (which is essentially area strip-mining) causes dereliction of the land, and to combat its undesirable effects, it is suggested that extensive reclamation regulations should be formulated and enforced to cover such issues as slope reduction, back-filling, levelling, revegetation and burying of toxic materials. Industrialisation and urbanisation involve total forest removal, the consequences of which include flooding and soil erosion. Similar consequences arise from road building in the country, and the paper stresses the need to make these operations more rational, not by discontinuing the work but by modifying it so as to save the Nigerian rainforests from total destruction. Accordingly, careful management of the forests is required, whilst continuing the attempt to improve the status of the population. To achieve this desired objective, the paper emphasises the need for a comprehensive national land-use policy, including careful management of the forests. Such an approach would ensure that Nigeria does not indulge in the costly option of improving the circumstances of one generation at the expense of the next. © 1981.

title: Small watershed modeling using DTM.
source: In Water Forum 81 Proc Specialty Conf San Francisco U S A Aug 10 14 1981
authors: Eli R.
abstract: Modelling stream flow from small ungauged watersheds is difficult at best, and the difficulties are compounded if watershed characteristics are highly modified by surface mining. In the Eastern United States, the Appalachian coal fields are located in rough terrain and the topography is of major influence. Under these conditions, traditional runoff models using synthesized unit hydrographs are inadequate to determine the hydrologic impacts. Digital terrain modelling (DTM) technology using the ADAPT system is combined with the Hewlett concept of variable source areas of runoff in a proposed concept of continuous or storm event modelling involving the prediction of runoff and sediment yield. title: Soil-algal relationships from surface mined soils
authors: Shubert L.E.; Starks T.L.
abstract: Intensive energy development is taking place in the western United States, because of the large coal reserves that are readily available by surface mining. This study provided baseline data on the physical, chemical and biological properties of spoil and topsoil collected from surface mined sites in three states (Arizona, New Mexico and North Dakota). Integration of analytical data on the physical-chemical properties of the soils with the algae present revealed distinct relationships by the cluster analysis and multiple linear regression methods. High sodium and low nitrogen levels may have accounted for predominance of blue-green algae at the Arizona and New Mexico sites. Other nutrients, such as calcium, chloride and certain trace elements may have been important to the soil algal community. The importance of algae in succession and soil genesis is stressed. © Taylor & Francis Group LLC.

title: Effects of topsoil storage during surface mining on the viability of VA mycorrhiza
authors: Rives C.S.; Bajwa M.I.; Liberta A.E.; Miller R.M.
abstract: Storing topsoil for 3 years was shown to reduce substantially the levels of viable inocula relative to levels in adjacent, undisturbed prairie soils. The detrimental effect of storage on VA mycorrhiza is associated with the loss of viability of mycorrhizal fragments occurring in the stored soil. Data are also presented supporting an interaction between infected root segments and roots of uninfected plants as a major means of spreading mycorrhiza in these soils. © 1980 The Williams & Wilkins Co.

title: AMERICAN NATIONAL STANDARD FOR WIRE ROPE FOR MINES.
authors: Anon
abstract: This standard is intended to establish practical and adequate design features for, and safety recommendations for, the proper care and use of wire rope that is used in underground mining, surface mining (opencast), and related work areas where metals, nonmetals, coal, sand and gravel, stones, and minerals are mined.

title: Implementation of US Surface Mine and Reclamation Act
authors: Sani E.
abstract: The US Congress is currently studying various ways through which legislation similar to that of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977— which is concerned mainly with coal, can be applied to all minerals other than coal. This study analyses three US mineral industries—copper, iron ore, and phosphate rock - and identifies a number of areas which Congress and other decision makers ought to consider in arriving at such legislation. The author concludes that reclamation costs may affect the economic and financial performance of each of these industries in a different manner; furthermore, their economic behaviour is significantly different from that of coal. The author's main recommendation is that if surface mining regulations are to be legislated, they should be industry- and commodity-specific rather than umbrella legislation for all non-coal minerals. © 1980, All rights reserved.

title: ( Recultivation of areas devastated by mining of calcium phosphate).
authors: Karlowitsch S.; Tjulina O.; Arbusowa S.
abstract: On an area where surface mining of calcium phosphate had been carried out, red clover, white clover, timothy, cocksfoot, maize, oats and potatoes were grown on 1) the topsoil or 2) the underlying glacuonite sand, which contained more P, K and trace elements and had a higher pH. Without fertilizer, red clover and white clover yielded more on 2) than on 1). Potato yields were similar on both substrates. Grass and cereal yields were low and less on 2) than on 1). Yield responses of grasses and cereals to NPK were greater on 2) than on 1). Oat yields were increased 5.9 and 2.1 times and maize yields 10.9 and 2.3 times on 2) and 1), respectively. The clovers showed smaller responses to NPK. N had most influence on yield, especially on 2) where P and K had scarcely any effect.-from Field Crop Abstracts

title: An inventory of particulate emissions from open sources
source: Journal of the Air Pollution Control Association
authors: Evans J.S.; Cooper D.W.
abstract: Open sources are those stationary sources of air pollution too great in extent to be controlled through enclosure or ducting. Open sources of atmospheric particles include: wind erosion, tilling, and prescribed burning of agricultural cropland; surface mining and wind erosion of tailings piles; vehicular travel on both paved and unpaved roads; construction site activity; and forest fires. It is estimated that in 1976 the total open source emissions of particles in the U.S. amounted to over 580 × 10<sup>6</sup> ton. These estimates indicate that emissions from the two largest open source classes, travel on unpaved roads and agricultural wind erosion, accounted for 86% of this total. The open source emissions in ten states (AZ, CA, KS, MN, MT, NM, ND, OH, SD, TX) contributed 6 2% of the national emissions for 1976. © 1980 Air & Waste Management Association.

title: Energy law and the environment.
abstract: 8 articles and a concluding perspective. The topics are grouped into 3 categories relating to coal, nuclear power and institutional mechanisms for developing energy resources. The titles are: The Energy Mobilization Board - Ross Cheil; New source performance standards for coal-fired electric power plants - David W. Hercher; Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977, regulatory controversies and constitutional challenges Steve Wadsworth; Coal conversion and the Powerplant and Industrial Fuel Use Act of 1978 - Erik Dryburgh; The development of synthetic fuels - Ann Sherman; Nuclear waste management - David R. Frankel; The Uranium Mill Tailings Radiation Control Act of 1978 - John Magoe; The Kemeny Report on the accident of Three Mile Island - Jon F. Elliot; and energy and environmental law in transition, a practitioner's perspective - Ginger Lew & Leon Silverstrom.-J.Clayton

title: Detection of changes in a coal surface mining area by ratioing multidate Landsat digital data.
source: Proc 6th Canadian Symposium on Remote Sensing May 1980 Halifax Nova Scotia
authors: Ohlen D.
abstract: Compares 2 procedures for determining change in a coal surface mining area in S Montana, using ratioed multidate (1976 and 1977) Landsat data. Neither procedure provided adequate results. -after Author

title: The regulation of surface mining on American Indian lands: some key policy issues.
authors: Richardson D.
abstract: Discusses the research undertaken by the Indian Lands Study and the key geographical and natural resource regulatory policy issues which it raised.-from Author

title: The land restoration provisions of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act: constitutional considerations ( coal mining, USA).
authors: Eichbaum W.M.; Buente D.T.
abstract: Examines the 2 constitutional challenges to SMCRA: the standard may substantially burden or entirely prohibit coal mining, in violation of the 5th Amendment; the standard violates the 10th Amendment because it regulates land use.-from Author

title: Coal problems and prospects.
source: University of Texas Bureau of Economic Geology Mineral Resources Circular
authors: Van Rensburg W.C.J.; Cooper H.B.H.; Kaiser W.R.; Spurr S.H.
abstract: Outlines the National Energy Plan as it pertains to coal as a potential major energy source and describes how production constraints may make the NEP's 1985 goal of l,265 million tons of coal unobtainable. The authors review constraints such as regulations on mining, health and safety and air quality control solid waste disposal problems, and needs regarding labor, transportation, and capital. They also point up the need for new conversion processes and for continued research and development in pollution control, gasification, liquefaction, and deep surface mining. Also reviews the impact of President Carter's latest energy program and the benefits to coal production from his proposed excess profits tax on the oil industry. Tabular material covers the additional mines, equipment, and transportation needed to reach the NEP goal, estimated coal consumption in Texas and the nation, capital required for such consumption, and capital and operating costs of environmental controls on new coal-fired power plants. Make's specific recommendations for realizing the potential of coal as a major energy source, recommending the formulation of a consistent environmental policy, immediate construction of gasification and liquefaction plants, and a thorough review of all regulations that impede the development of coal mines and utilization plants. -Authors

title: Surface mining regulation in the Federal Republic of Germany, Great Britain, Australia, and the United States: a comparative study ( coal).
authors: Galloway L.T.; McAteer J.D.
abstract: Discusses the growing importance of surface mining in coal production and the adverse environmental impacts historically associated with such mining. The attempts of several important coal producing nations to regulate the impact of surface mining on the environment are examined.-from Authors

title: Surface- mining legislation and regulation.
source: Journal of the Environmental Engineering Division ASCE
authors: Harper J.
abstract: This paper highlights the relevant provisions of The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 and provides an overview of the surface mining reclamation and enforcement provisions issued by the Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement. Topics addressed include: topsoiling, hydrologic balance, use of explosives, diposal of excess spoil and coal processing wastes, backfilling and grading, road, mountaintop removal, and steep- slope operations. -from ASCE Publications Abstracts

title: Regulations complicate land reclamation in the west.
authors: Selz-Petrash A.
abstract: The 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act provides necessary protection to land during and after strip mining. However, according to the coal industry, some of the regulations are misguided. The article is an overview of some of the problems industry thinks are most severe. Sidebar on the basics of land reclamation after surface mining in the West.-from ASCE Publications Abstracts

title: Southern Illinois mine waste control plan: a summary ( United States).
source: Journal of the Environmental Engineering Division ASCE
authors: Pisano W.; Aronson G.
abstract: Summarizes the results of a two-year study aimed at assessing the 300-sq mile acid mine drainage impacted area within Southern Illinois, funded by Section 208 of PL 92-500. The 208 Plan focused on upgrading existing water quality through reclamation on mine-related pollution sources, especially those pertaining to past mining activities, utilizing monies generated under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 (PL-95-87). -from ASCE Publications Abstracts

title: FUEL COSTS ARE CAUSING CHANGES IN SURFACE MINING METHODS.
authors: Loy M.D.; Wise J.H.
abstract: The article illustrates several instances where rising fuel costs are causing changes. Machinery can in many instances be switched from diesel to electric-powered. Additionally, new mining techniques are being developed that substitute electrically-based technologies for more traditional diesel based technologies. As fuel costs escalate at a rate far exceeding that of electricity costs, the balance will swing to increased utilization of electricity.

title: RECORD HYDRAULIC EXCAVATOR TESTED.
authors: Savage P.
abstract: With a breakout force of 500,000 lb, the world's largest hydraulic excavator moves 50-ton bites of coal and clay at a 500,000-tpy. British surface mining contractor, Northern Strip Mines, Ltd.

title: Aerial survey techniques for locating abandoned strip mine land
authors: Dattavio L.; Mroczynski R.; Weismiller R.
abstract: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act required that states develop regulatory programs and reclamation plans for surface mining activities. Prior to passage of this law, the Indiana legislature required Indiana Department of Natural Resources (IDNR) to survey abandoned mine lands not under the control of state reclamation laws. IDNR then contracted the Laboratory for Applications of Remote Sensing (LARS) at Purdue University to conduct a preliminary survey of these lands. Photointerpretation techniques of medium scale color infrared photography enabled the LARS staff to identify partially reclaimed and nonreclaimed sites within a 20-county area in southwestern Indiana. Over 4,700 ha of abandoned lands were located and classified on the aerial photography. This information is currently being used by IDNR to develop reclamation plants to revegetate the abandoned lands. The results of this survey clearly indicate that photointerpretation is an effective technique to complete initial inventories of nonreclaimed mine lands.

title: PEABODY FOCUSES ON SURFACE MINING.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The application of industrial engineering techniques, combined with the development of computer-based systems analysis, is becoming a key management tool by which Peabody hopes to maximize its production output, improve control of its operations, and reduce its operating costs.

title: COAL MINING TECHNOLOGY IN THE WESTERN UNITED STATES.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Ramani R.V.; Kenzy G.W.; Bise C.J.
abstract: This paper gives a brief overview of the current status of underground and surface coal mining in the Western United States. Mining methods practised at six mines are reviewed to illustrate the technology of surface and underground methods. The advancing longwall at the Dutch Creek mine is the only one currently being practised in the country. Room and pillar operations will continue to be the most important underground mining method in the near future. Surface mining methods reviewed here are fairly standard for thick and multiple seams that are near surface. The greatest impact on surface mining industry is due to the current legislative, administrative, and public attitudes which make it necessary for a greater government-industry interaction on various planning, operation and reclamation aspects.

title: CHALLENGE OF FINANCING CANADIAN OIL SANDS DEVELOPMENT.
authors: McMillian J.
abstract: The author discusses the economic viability and methods available for financing major oil sands projects in Canada. The focus of the paper is directed at analyzing the estimated capital costs, operating costs and potential financing methods for the proposed Alsands surface mining project and the Cold Lake in situ project. The effect of royalties, taxes, capital availability and future oil prices are assessed in relation to these projects.

title: CAPTAIN MINE: A NATIONAL SHOWCASE FOR SURFACE MINING & RECLAMATION.
authors: Blakely W.
abstract: By using bucketwheel excavators, shovels, spreaders and a round-the-pit conveyor system, Southwestern Illinois Coal's Captain Mine has become a major producer while reclaiming its land.

title: SURFACE MINING PROBLEMS RUN DEEP.
authors: Anon
abstract: Steeply pitching multiple seams are hard to mine. Western producers use computerized engineering and a variety of equipment combinations to deal with them.

title: STATUS REPORT ON CANADIAN COAL MINING.
authors: Jamieson E.
abstract: How well is the Canadian coal industry able to expand in the tough competition with other fuels in Canada and with other suppliers in the international, metallurgical and thermal coal trade? Coal production as a whole decreased between 1950 and 1960 and, although there has been a tripling of production since then, underground production continued to decrease until 1975. This trend has been reversed to a certain extent as a result of the modernization of mines in Cape Breton, but in 1978 over 85% of coal production came from surface mining. Against this background, the paper reviews current Canadian mining operations. Conclusions are then drawn regarding some of the longer-term mining applications in relation to the latest coal demand forecast.

title: FRONT-END LOADERS: VERSATILE AND PRODUCTIVE MACHINES.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Front-end wheel loaders are becoming an increasingly important tool to surface mining throughout the coal regions of the United States. Their extraordinary versatility is evidenced by the wide range of jobs that they are assigned to. The larger loaders efficiently strip overburden and dig and load coal. Smaller units maintain haul roads, build ditches and dikes, and excavate settling ponds. A survey is presented of different types and sizes of front-end loaders used in U. S. coal mines.

title: FORDING RIVER MINE - AN OVERVIEW.
authors: Urso P.
abstract: This paper discusses the mining problems encountered at the Fording River coal mine, B. C. , Canada, to date, and how they have been solved. All of the production now comes from surface mining, but underground hydraulic mining is planned and briefly described. Other facets of the operation, including markets, equipment and personnel, are covered.

title: COSMAR OVERVIEW.
authors: Cook C.
abstract: The Committee on Surface Mining and Reclamation (COSMAR) submitted its report to the Council on Environmental Quality and the Congress in 1979. The report, ″The Surface Mining of Noncoal Minerals,″ is briefly summarized.

title: MARTIN COUNTY'S MINING PRACTICES.
authors: Mason R.
abstract: Martin County Coal's mining practices are described, showing how the company achieves production goals by applying surface and underground extraction methods that are especially adapted to eastern Kentucky conditions. The 2 1/2-million-tpy producer mines four seams with two underground mines, four surface mines and three mine contractors. Mining by both methods helps assure that reserves will be recovered to the maximum. Surface mining accounts for 55% of total output, and underground contributes 45%.

title: 1980: ANOTHER YEAR OF (STUNTED) GROWTH.
authors: Guccione E.
abstract: A brief forecast is given for the U. S. coal industry's performance in 1980. Long-term US coal production is most likely to reach the 1-billion-tpy level in 1985. However, the short-term picture throughout 1980 is not expected to be appreciably better than it was in 1979. Although this year's U. S. coal production and consumption figures should surpass 1979's levels, excess capacity will continue in the eastern and western U. S. coal fields. Further, the coal industry is likely to get some relief from amendments to the Surface Mining and the Clean Air Acts. Salient figures for U. S. bituminous coal and lignite are given in accompanying tables.

title: Soil nitrogen relationships in spoil material generated by the surface mining of lignite coal
authors: Hons F.M.; Hossner L.R.
abstract: Three acid, surface-mined soils and an adjacent undisturbed soil were evaluated for nitrification potentials and nonexchangeable NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N retention to better understand N mechanisms and improve the reclamation efficiency of these soils. The mined soils nitrified a maximum of only 7% of an added 100 ppm NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N, although the undisturbed soil nitrified 93% of the applied N. Total N digestion showed one mined soil to have a nonexchangeable NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N retention capacity of 6.2 meq/100g. Organically retained NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N accounted for 73% of the total retention. Another procedure utilizing differences in exchangeable NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N between moist and dried samples as estimates of nonexchangeable NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N retention, showed retentive capacities of the mined soils ranging from 4.1 to 7.8 meq NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N/100g. Lignite exhibited a retentive capacity of 46.0 meq NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N/100g. Nonexchangeable retention was significantly correlated with the residual lignite content of the soil. Low nitrification potentials and large nonexchangeable NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N retention capacities suggested that applied NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>-N fertilizers might be inefficient in the mined soils. © 1980 The Williams & Wilkins Co.

title: UI'S TRAPPER MINES THE HIGH COUNTRY.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: A brief account is given of how Utah International (UI) is successfully solving some surface mining problems at its Trapper coal mine near Craig, Colo. Some of these involve surface mining at minus 45 degree F at an altitude of 6,800 ft, deep snow and difficult mountainous terrain, four coal seams that pitch at 16%, as well as scheduling mining activities at three different pits. The company uses three 30-cu-yd draglines in up-dip/down-dip cycles to remove overburden and interburden in the three pits, each containing two seams.

title: SUB-BITUMINOUS COAL RESOURCES IN THE WESTERN USA - THEIR EXPLOITATION AND UTILIZATION.
authors: Dunham R.K.
abstract: Recent increases in the price of oil have given significant impetus in the western U. S. to the exploitation and conversion of low rank sub-bituminous coals into either gaseous or liquid fuels. At the present time, emphasis is on surface mining but, in the longer term, the majority of this coal can be recovered only by underground methods. This article presents a review of the surface mining techniques in use and reviews the coal conversion techniques being investigated, including surface and underground gasification and a variety of liquefaction processes.

title: KEMMERER SURFACE-MINES 12 SEAMS.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: This article highlights the successful coal mining operations of Kemmerer Coal Co. , a not-so-large but fast-growing western U. S. coal operator based in Wyoming. Using three surface mining methods - truck-shovel, dragline and scraper-dozer, the company mines a dozen seams with an aggregate thickness of 300 ft. Although the various pits works at different overburden-to-coal ratios, the overall mining operation is designed for an average 4:1 ratio. Kemmerer Coal's coal preparation and coal handling facilities are also described.

title: OPENCAST COAL IN BURGUNDY.
authors: Anon
abstract: Extraction of coal by surface mining in France, while not extensive, is nevertheless of growing interest. Environmental considerations are of prime importance, particularly when operations are conducted close to towns and other industry. Rehabilitation may be required to improve the site for the benefit of the local community. This article surveys equipment and techniques used in opencast mining of coal at Montceau-les-Mines, Burgundy, France.

title: Research on the hydrology and water quality of watersheds subjected to surface mining. Phase 1: premining hydrologic and water quality conditions. Summary report 22 Jan 1976 - 22 Jan 1978.
authors: McIntosh G.; Harmon W.
abstract: Five watersheds, ranging in size from 29 to 52 acres, were selected in east-central Ohio for the purpose of investigating the hydrologic and water quality conditions occurring before, during, and after surface mining. The average concentrations of the water quality parameters for all watersheds were as low or lower than the Environmental Protection Agency recommended maximum allowable concentrations in drinking water except for suspended solids.-from STAR, 18(18), 1980

title: Characterization of vegetation and drainage in strip mined land utilizing remote sensing techniques. Final report.
authors: Johannsen C.J.; Barney T.W.; Coble A.D.; Carrel J.E.; McFarland W.
abstract: Research conducted during this project has utilized remote sensing images and data to study surface vegetation identification, vegetation biomass and drainage patterns of coal strip mined land. Study sites were located in Boone, Randolph and Macon counties in central Missouri. This report presents the results of surface vegetation and drainage analyses of those sites and methodologies used for accurate, timely and useful applications of remotely gathered data for monitoring coal surface mining reclamation activities. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 2, 1980

title: Environmental assessment of surface mining methods: head-of- hollow fill and mountaintop removal. Interim report Nov 75 - January 77
authors: Robins J.; Hutchins J.
abstract: The study explores the environmental impact of the mining and reclamation techniques employed in West Virginia and Kentucky mountaintop removal and head-of-hollow fill sites. The project is divided into four major phases, the first three of which are discussed in this Interim Report: I. State-of-the-Art Review, II. General Environmental Assessment of West Virginia and Kentucky Mines Sites, III. Intensive Mine Site Monitoring and Environmental Assessment in Both States, and IV. Evaluation and Update of Construction Guidelines. -from US Govt Reports Announcement, 26, 1979

title: Coal surface mining reclamation.
source: Vance Bibliographies Public Administration Series Bibliography
authors: Rowe J.E.
abstract: The degree of environmental degradation caused by coal surface mining can be controlled by the enforcement of strict standards. This bibliography examines the many environmental, legal and economic factors affecting reclamation, but it omits the large number of studies concerning soil conditions, tree/vegetation species, wildlife habitat, and other biological/ecological factors associated with surface mining reclamation. About 350 references, mainly to periodical and report literature, arranged alphabetically by author, are given.-after Author

title: SURFACE MINING TECHNOLOGY, PRACTICES, AND PLANS AND GULF COAST LIGNITE.
source: Industrial and Engineering Chemistry Product Research and Development
authors: Russell J.E.
abstract: Lignite resources of 20 billion tons are estimated for the Gulf Coast Region. Geology of deposits and analyses of the lignites are given. Exploration techniques and leasing practices are reviewed. Necessary mining permits and regulatory agencies are listed for the five Gulf Coast states. In addition, several Federal, state, county and local agencies require permits of notification. These agencies are summarized for Texas. Feasibility studies, mine development, and mining operations are discussed. In 1979, the only operating surface mines were in Texas, with 84 pct of total production used in electrical power generation by one utility. Over 20 million tons were mined in 1978, and projections indicate production of 65 million tons in 1985. Reclamation of mined land is satisfactory. Impact of extensive development on water, air, and socieconomic factors are reviewed.

title: IMPLICATIONS OF RCRA, SMCRA, AND TSCA ON UNDERGROUND COAL GASIFICATION.
source: American Society of Mechanical Engineers Applied Mechanics Division AMD
authors: Hagen A.A.; Meyer L.L.; Tipton L.M.
abstract: This paper presents an assessment of the implications of current legislative and regulatory actions associated with the Resource Conservation and Recovery Act (RCRA), Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (SMCRA), and Toxic Substances Control Act (TSCA) on underground coal gasification. RCRA and TSCA regulations are not final; however, under the regulations as currently proposed, liquids and tars condensed from UCG product gas stream will be classified hazardous wastes, requiring application of prescribed waste disposal techniques. Options will include use of incinerators meeting specific design and performance criteria, or storage and disposal that must be documented through s manifest system for up to 20 years. TSCA premanufacture notice of chemical substances may apply. SMCRA regulations are final, and coal in situ processing is to be regulated under underground mining provisions.

title: USDA teamwork in reclamation.
authors: Unger D.
abstract: Introductory remarks to a symposium on surface mining and reclamation. The new voluntary programme is called RAMP (Rural Abandoned Mine Program). The role of USDA is outlined. -Jennifer Clayton

title: The protection of hydrologic and land preservation values under the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977: a welcome reform ( West Virginia).
authors: Woley D.
abstract: The 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (Act) is evaluated in the context of West Virginia's 1971 Surface Mining and Reclamation Act. Several land use considerations are discussed in relation to the federal Act. The public participation aspects of the Act are outlined in a typical scenario.-from Selected Water Resources Abstracts Strip mining strip mine wastes surface runoff soil conservation water pollution control land fills public rights sediment control land use government finance governmental interrelations hydrology.

title: The effects of surface mining of coal on water quality near Grande Cache, Alberta.
authors: Hackbarth D.
abstract: The effects of mining activity on water quality vary in intensity but follow a consistent pattern. The relative proportion of the various cations does not change; however, their concentrations may rise to four times background values. The concentration of anions also increases and there is a shift in the relative proportions from bicarbonate to sulfate and, at the more strongly affected sites, to nitrate. The distribution of pH values is not significantly different from unaffected sites. -from Author

title: Toxic substances from coal energy: An overview
authors: Shy C.M.
abstract: Environmental concerns over increased coal consumption are fully justified by the past history of coal use. Although improved technology has provided some safeguards, increased utilization will require mining practices, emission control technologies, and waste disposal procedures that are not yet fully integrated into the routine use of the coal energy system. The Committee on Health and Environmental Effects of Increased Coal Utilization identified six critical environmental issues which are of concern: coal mine worker health and safety, reclamation of arid lands from surface mining, the health effects of coal combustion products, toxic trace elements in coal combustion wastes, acid fallout, and global effects of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere. This presentation addresses the first four of these issues.

title: Planning erosion control for coal mining and reclamaton ( Iowa, USA).
authors: Anderson C.; Briggs J.
abstract: The special problems relating to surface mining and erosion are briefly described and methods of control on active and reclaimed mines are noted. Describes the Iowa Coal Project mine experiment in which a series of bench terraces, parallel to the original contour were used to fit the post-mining land use and to minimise likely erosion. Measures taken to ensure adequate drainage and to preserve the overburden during the slip mining operation are described.-R.H.Johnson

title: The hydrogeology of the Athabasca Oil Sands area, Alberta.
authors: Hackbarth D.; Nastasa N.
abstract: West of a major fault 3 hydrostratigraphic units are defined. Two hydrostratigraphic units merge E of the fault. Groundwater flows W towards the fault, with total dissolved solids concentrations seldom exceeding 50 000mg/L. On a regional basis, the oil sands have a finite hydraulic conductivity commonly of 10<sup>-6</sup> to 10<sup>-4</sup>cm/sec. Surface mining ventures will generally require that the oil sands and underlying aquifers be depressurized. Structural conditions are suitable for injection of waste liquids into the D- 2 hydrostratigraphic unit only west of the limits of evaporite solution. -after Authors

title: Surface mining reclamation in Appalachia: impact of the 1977 Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act ( USA).
authors: Sweeney L.
abstract: Reclamation procedures used in Appalachian hill areas have often created level bench or plateau landforms and soils which are of greater value than were the original hillslopes and soils. In West Virginia considerable success in reclamation of mined areas has been achieved by the use of a coal tax, but the rest of the U.S.A. so far has not employed this means of financing redevelopment measures.-R.H.Johnson

title: Lignite Mining in the Rhine Basin.
authors: Bastidon J.
abstract: In 1977, West German lignite production rose to 123 million tons, of which 88% came from the Rhine Basin. This article describes the mining methods employed in the basin, and then analyzes mining and other costs of the Rhine lignite. Surface mining and land reclamation are also discussed.

title: KEEP YOUR BLASTING UNDER CONTROL.
authors: Dick R.; Siskind D.
abstract: To protect various structures from the adverse effect of overburden blasting, the Office of Surface Mining (OSM) gives the mine operator three possible alternatives. This article discusses the three options, and explains how to choose among them in order to comply with the new regulations. Control of blast vibrations is also discussed.

title: DRAGLINES CAN REDUCE SURFACE MINING COSTS.
authors: Morey P.
abstract: Draglines are often the most effective way to surface mine coal. This article briefly explains how to develop dragline stripping mine designs that use the dragline in the most efficient and economic way. Dragline production simulation is also considered.

title: RIP INSTEAD OF DRILLING AND BLASTING.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: As tractor size, weight and horsepower have steadily increased, the use of rippers has expanded dramatically in surface mining, both in their capabilities and applications. Harder materials can be ripped to greater depths at higher production rates than ever before, offering economic advantages over drilling and blasting. One company, CRC Kelley, now offers a 179-in. -long ripper shank to match the strength of the new super dozers, a major leap in ripper capability. Units are now in operation in North Dakota and Colorado. Advantages of this tractor ripper are discussed, and its operating performance is evaluated.

title: SURFACE MINING AND THE HYDROLOGIC BALANCE.
authors: Curtis W.
abstract: A properly reclaimed mined watershed may have higher retention storage capacity than before mining. With proper surface treatment and vegetative cover, infiltration rates can be as high as or higher than before mining. Surface storage can be built in during the mining and reclamation phases. Surface impoundments can be strategically placed to control runoff and water movement. However, water quality may suffer after surface mining. More geologic materials are exposed to weathering, which can result in mineral or acid pollution in the streams. Care in moving and placing the overburden can minimize chemical release.

title: NEW LAND USES CREATED BY SURFACE MINING.
authors: Christy P.; Smith W.; Filer E.
abstract: Mined lands in Illinois are being restored to near their original use capabilities and in some cases to a more productive level than existed prior to mining. A brief description of the major types of surface mining equipment utilized and an elementary explanation of their fundamental operation aid in reviewing the tables and data are presented.

title: U. K. OPENCAST COAL MINING.
authors: Anon
abstract: Although underground mining continues to account for most of the coal produced in the United Kingdom (during 1977 104. 5 million tonnes were produced from 231 collieries), the Opencast Executive of the U. K. National Coal Board (NCB) continues to expand its production capacity. In the U. K. , these surface mining operations are carried out on large opencast sites worked by contractors. This brief article looks at some of the sites operated by George Wimpey & Co. and considers the type of equipment used by this contractor.

title: CHALLENGES OF REVEGETATION.
authors: Alder G.M.
abstract: Proposed draft regulations from the Office of Surface Mining will require mine operators to revegetate surface mined lands to provide a plant cover that is ″diverse, effective, and permanent″ . The article defines the biological processes that underlie the terms.

title: Multiple objectives under uncertainty: An illustrative application of protrade
authors: Goicoechea A.; Duckstein L.; Fogel M.
abstract: A decision making method labeled Protrade has been developed to account for both multiple objectives and uncertainty aspects. This method is applied to the case study of the Black Mesa Region in Northern Arizona which is being strip mined for coal. One important concern in large‐scale surface mining is the reclamation of mine spoils to bring about beneficial land uses while observing economic, social, environmental, and legal constraints. Protrade considers a set of linear objective functions with random parameters, subject to a set of physical constraints; the preferences of the decision maker are articulated in a progressive manner, and alternative solutions are generated. Nonlinear deterministic equivalents are introduced to account for uncertainty in some of the parameters involved. While no final policy recommendations are made, this illustration of Protrade is carried out to investigate the potential of the method for trading off multiple objectives and measures of uncertainty in water and other natural resource system design problems. Copyright 1979 by the American Geophysical Union.

title: SIMULATION OF THE EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING ON GROUNDWATER IN THE POWDER RIVER BASIN.
authors: McIntosh G.
abstract: This paper discusses a US Bureau of Mines projects designed to assess and predict the impacts which surface project mining will have on the regional shallow groundwater systems in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana. The primary objective will be met through the accomplishment of the following: (1) The design and establishment of a regional network for monitoring shallow groundwater systems in the basin; (2) monitoring the direction and rate of flow, water quality, and aquifer characteristics of the shallow groundwater systems; and (3) development of a regional groundwater simulation model, with appurtenant subroutines to determine local effects.

title: MINING SHOVELS AND DRAGLINES REVIEWED.
authors: Anon
abstract: The major share of the market for machines to load or shift overburden and mineral at surface mining operations is held by rope operated shovels and draglines. This article outlines some of the trends in operational methods and reviews the ranges of equipment offered by the major manufacturers. Recently introduced machines are especially highlighted. The trend to modular designs to facilitate transportation, erection and maintenance is noted. The differing attributes of crawler and walking draglines are considered.

title: GET THE BIG PICTURE - TO COMPLY WITH RECLAMATION LAWS.
authors: Brumbaugh F.
abstract: The Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 has created a need for better reclamation technology and management. These needs can be met with remote sensing and normal field reconnaissance. By combining these methods, opeators can measure reclamation effectiveness and obtain reliable data for planning. The author emphasizes that remote sensing should be an integral part of a reclamation program. A complete reclamation management program should consist of conventional field reconnaissance; high and low altitude aerial photography; and selected satellite imagery.

title: SURFACE MINING REGULATIONS AND LITIGATION FOR 1978.
authors: Todd D.
abstract: This article covers the regulatory and litigation activities during 1978 regarding the Surface Mine Control and Reclamation Act and the regulations issued thereunder.

title: Ground‐Water Quality Standards — Irrelevant
authors: Rayner F.
abstract: Proposals to establish national ground‐water quality standards appear to be premature, and redundant because of the geohydrologic and geochemical factors governing the occurrence and development of ground water. Although it can be reasoned that there is no “good time” to establish additional governmental standards (and the resultant additional governmental regulations), it can also be strongly argued that now is a “bad time” to consider establishment of the proposed standards. First, a present mood of the general public is away from more governmental involvement in the business and private sectors, and a rebellion against the increasing cost of government. Second, the applicability and workability of present Federal (and some State) laws that could be used to adequately protect ground‐water quality, have yet to be implemented or otherwise sufficiently tested. The full force and effect of the Water Pollution Control Act (PL 92‐500 with amendments) has yet to be implemented, and Congress is still considering its “oversights” in their drafting of same. The Safe Drinking Water Act (PL 93‐523), particularly those sections designed or usable to protect ground‐water quality, have yet to be tested by the EPA. Like PL 92‐500, the deadline for implementation of parts of PL 93‐523 has long since passed. And the far‐reaching effects on ground‐water quality protection that three other federal laws‐the Resource Conservation Recovery Act (PL 94‐580); the Toxic Substances Control Act (PL 94‐469); and Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act (PL 95‐87)—are totally unknown, since the procedures for full implementation of these acts have yet to be developed. Therefore, it appears that establishing a new ground‐water quality control act prior to testing existing law and thereby learning from their flaws or shortcomings, could result in unnecessary proliferation of law without its reasonable testing. This appears to be good time to interrupt the geometric progression that tends to spawn additional laws when laws are developed ahead of their established need. Equitable and workable ground‐water quality protection could be fostered through the enactment of the long overdue requirements for the integration of surface‐and ground‐water development and management structures. This integration would decrease inefficiency of use of these water resources—which are actually inseparable in identity to their users, the American taxpayers. Copyright © 1979, Wiley Blackwell. title: Impact of human influences on the vegetation of the Western Himalaya
authors: Gupta R.
keywords: Anthropogenic disturbance | Fire | Forest | Grassland | Himalaya | Overgrazing | Run-off | Soil moisture
abstract: Effects of human influences on the vegetation of the Western Himalaya have been reviewed. Impacts of forest management practices, over-grazing, surface mining, defence and development operations, and road building activities, are severe in the region. This has created an alarming situation for soil and water conservation. Increased soil loss and runoff pose a threat to various reservoirs built for various uses and have increased hazards of erosion and floods in the Indus and Ganga basin regions. © 1978 Dr. W. Junk b.v. Publishers.

title: STABILITY OF SPOIL BANKS AND HOLLOW FILLS CREATED BY SURFACE MINING.
source: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
authors: Huang Y.H.
abstract: This report describes work accomplished under a research project entitled ″Slope Stability of Spoil Banks from Surface Mining″ . A spoil bank is a sidehill bench formed by depositing the overburden materials removed from above a coal seam. The objectives of this research were twofold: first, to study the failure of spoil banks in Eastern Kentucky, so as to ascertain the causes of failure and the necessary preventive measures; and, secondly, to develop a practical method for determining the most appropriate slopes to be used for spoil banks under various conditions.

title: POLICY ALTERNATIVES FOR RECLAIMING SURFACE MINED LANDS.
source: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
authors: Greenbaum M.; Harvey C.
abstract: Recently enacted surface mining controls express congressional concern with the potential for environmental damage. But how to implement the new statutes while preserving congressional intent remains a controversial issue. Resolution is left largely to federal agencies and the affected states. This paper addresses the issue of how best to internalize the external costs created by surface coal mining.
