Section II is an examination of the inherent difficulties of operationalizing a Pigouvian solution. Section III is a review of an example of actual regulation and policy based on the case of Eastern Kentucky; and Section IV offers suggestions as to the advantages and disadvantages of alternative policy tools.

title: Land use and national coal surface mining policies.
authors: Anderson M.; Harper J.
abstract: The prime cropland provisions of Public Law 95-87 are the only ones which can potentially cause major disturbances in production, and then only in the Midwest, particularly in Illinois. Even in Illinois, the known reserves under unprotected lands are several hundred times greater than current yearly production. While thousands of acres will be reclaimed under the Abandoned Mine Fund provisions, this must be viewed as a very long term program to address the damages of over a century of virtually unregulated mining. Future development plans of mine operators will have to be compatible with land use regulations, or delayed mine openings or expansions could adversely affect production.- from U.S.Govt. Reports Announcements, 4, 1980

title: Surface mining and fish/ wildlife needs in the eastern United States. Proc. symposium held at Morgantown, West Virginia, 3-6 Dec. 1978.
authors: Samuel D.E.; Stauffer J.R.; Hocutt C.H.; Mason W.T.
abstract: The report describes a state-of-the-art overview on surface mining in the eastern US and the fish/wildlife relationships; best methods for measuring mining impacts; the effects of mining on the biota; mined land reclamation techniques for fish/wildlife benefits; and opportunities for improving fish/wildlife habitat on mined lands. Information is provided by the mining industry, conservation groups, and state and federal agencies. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 23, 1979

title: IMPACT OF COAL UTILIZATION IN TEXAS UNDER THE NATIONAL ENERGY PLAN.
authors: Kaiser W.R.; Cooper H.B.H.; Gautam S.; Mabray J.; Saleh D.
abstract: The authors discuss that the National Energy Plant goal is to double coal consumption by 1985 where the intent is to completely phase out natural gas as a boiler fuel by 1990. At the same time coal consumption is to be doubled while environmental quality is to be maintained by implementing the stringent 1977 Clean Air Act Amendments and the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977.

title: New Standards for strip mining: social, economic and environmental costs now considered.
authors: Gonnefoy L.
abstract: The policy behind the Surface Mining and Reclamation Act of 1977 was to balance coal production with environmental standards. At present mine operators are phasing in an interim programme of reclamation while the final regulations are prepared. Mine operators have tried to avoid meeting all the requirements of the interim programme but court cases brought by environmental groups have been decided in favour of maintaining strict compliance.-T.O'Riordan

title: PROGRESS REPORT ON THE COAL VALLEY MINING PROJECT.
authors: Thurston D.; Latimer R.
abstract: Luscar Sterco commenced construction of the mine at Coal Valley, Alberta, in August, 1976. It is designed to produce approximately 2. 5 million clean short tons of steam coal annually - 2. 0 million tons per year being committed to Ontario Hydro and 0. 5 million tons per year being committed to Neptune Terminals for sale on the export market. The project involves constructing a heavy-media coal preparation plant, erecting a 42-cubic-yard dragline, constructing a shop/office complex, and developing three surface mining zones and associated facilities.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF THE WABCO 353FT TWIN ENGINE ELEVATING SCRAPER.
authors: Hurst C.
abstract: The development of the WABCO 353FT Twin Engine Elevating Scraper for surface mining applications is an example of advancements being made in mining equipment technology. The 353FT optimizes the benefits of the various scraper configurations available by combining the ability to work under adverse conditions, due to its all-wheel drive, with large capcity and the self loading feature of an elevating scraper. Two Detroit Diesel 12V-71T, turbocharged engines drive identical Allison planetary powershift transmissions with variable-input-power torque converters and hydraulic retarders. The tractor engine, equipped with N75 injectors, is rated at 525 brake horsepower (391. 6 kW) at 2100 rpm. The scraper engine, with N70 injectors is rated at 500 brake horsepower (373. 0 kW). The 12V-71T is a 12-cylinder, two-stroke engine. The throttles of both engines are simultaneously controlled through the use of a single throttle pedal which operates two air throttle/cylinders. A second throttle pedal, which controls the tractor engine only, can be used when power from the scraper engine is not required, such as in tight turn situations. Traction sensing differentials automatically maintain torque to the wheels with the best traction. The scraper cutter is driven hydraulically, the elevator electrically.

title: ENERGY OUTLOOK: COAL AS A FUEL.
authors: Gambs G.
abstract: The author states that the United States should produce 1. 0 to 1. 3 billion tons of coal annually by 1985 to prevent the nation from becoming overwhelmingly dependent upon foreign crude oil and refined products. The author cites the following problems which he claims will prevent this goal from being reached: 1. Clean Air Act of 1970, 2. Federal Mine Safety Act of 1969, 3. Federal Leasing Regulations, 4. Transportation Facilities, 5. Technical Manpower, 6. Mine Labor, 7. Equipment Availability. The United States is fortunate in having one of the world's largest reserves of coal. Total measured and indicated reserves of coal in beds over 28 inches thick and under less than 1000 feet of overburden totaled 434 billion tons as of January 1, 1974. Of these reserves, 297 billion tons were considered underground reserves and 137 billion tons capable of being mined by surface mining. But unless a commitment is made to coal by the Government which will remove the restrictions already in place and prevent other restrictions from being placed on the industry, this coal will not be mined, in the author's opinion.

title: STATE PROBLEMS IN IMPLEMENTING THE FEDERAL SURFACE MINING LAW.
authors: Bowling K.
abstract: The author discusses some of the problems encountered in preparation of an acceptable state plan that will lead to designation of the regulatory authority.

title: ASSESSMENT OF INITIATING SYSTEMS AND THEIR PRACTICAL EFFECT ON BLASTING RESULTS.
authors: Poole G.
abstract: The merits of various systems for designed initiating columns of explosives in surface mining activities are discussed with special reference to the quarrying and open-cast mining industries, and a comparative analysis of the practical results which can be expected from each system is made. The importance of the safety considerations involved is discussed.

title: COMPUTER-BASED TOOL PROVIDES ENGINEERING AID IN COAL RESERVE EVALUATION AND MINE PLANNING.
authors: Gillette J.
abstract: The Surface Mining Simulation System (SMSS) is a set of 16 related mathematical models - with associated equipment, investment and operating cost data - which may be selectively used to simulate the mining of a specific coal deposit. The system allows the engineer to use whatever data available for description of a mining deposit, supplies missing data (in the form of regional averages), and produces information on the best equipment selection, the investment required, the operating costs which would be incurred across years of mining operation, and the profit which would be realized.

title: STEEP SLOPE MINING AND THE SURFACE MINING CONTROL AND RECLAMATION ACT OF 1977.
authors: Sawaryinski T.
abstract: The author comments on the impact of the Surface Mining Control and Reclamation Act of 1977 on steep slope coal mining operations and reclamation.

title: An assessment of overburden stability in the in-situ gasification of texas lignite
source: Journal of Pressure Vessel Technology Transactions of the ASME
authors: Thompson T.W.; Edgar T.F.; Gray K.E.
abstract: In-silu gasification can he competitive with shaft mining for the exploitation of coal at depths too deep for surface mining. The lignite deposits in Texas may be well suited to this process because of their high reactivity, comparatively high field permeabilities and closeness to industrial demand centers. Controlled operation of a gasification facility demands a knowledge of the likely behavior of the overburden and other surrounding rocks. Fracture or collapse of the roof rock can lead to excessive gas loss, water influx arul subsidence effects. The overburden in much of Texas is weak and poorly compacted. Karly roof collapse seems inevitable, and substantial upward caving may occur. Subsidence could be significant if high extraction ratios are used. © 1978 by ASME.

title: ENERGY THEORY SERIES 7: OIL SAND.
authors: Vakabayashi T.; Nakamura E.
abstract: Oil sand structure is explained and oil sand deposits in Alberta, Canada, are discussed. Characteristics of bitumens from oil sands of Canada and Venezuela are tabulated. Also discussed are recovery methods including surface mining and in-situ recovery and methods of refining.

title: FRONT SHOVEL WORKS NARROW BENCHES ON CONTOUR JOB.
authors: Mason R.
abstract: Maneuvering equipment efficiently on narrow benches encountered in contour stripping is a big problem. But Pratt Mining Co. , Kingston, WV, is solving it with a newly purchased hydraulic front shovel. The shovel can dig out overburden and parting from essentially one position, thus relieving congested traffic on the narrow benches, and can also operate close to the outslope without spilling material down the slope - a practice prohibited by surface mining regulations. Pratt Mining adopted contour stripping to maximize recovery of the high quality metallurgical coal and to minimize overburden removal. The easy maneuverability of the hydraulic front shovel makes it effective for both stripping overburden and removing coal.

title: MINERAL OCCURRENCES OF THE SOLOMON ISLANDS: REGIONAL GUIDE TO FURTHER EXPLORATION.
authors: Takeda T.
abstract: Most of the known mineral occurrences are suitable for either open pit or surface mining method, and are located on or not very distant from the coast. Guadalcanal has discoveries of significant hydrothermal mineralization in the uplifted and eroded core of the deep-seated 'Basement Complex'. Similar discoveries have been made on New Georgia Island.

title: SAVE WATER - TURN TO SURFACE MINING OF COAL.
authors: Corbett D.
abstract: The paper presents technical and legislative arguments for the use of surface mining method of energy production to provide water storage.

title: INDUSTRIAL HYGIENE PROGRAM FOR A SURFACE MINING OPERATION.
authors: Davis S.C.; Balzer J.L.; Raymond M.A.
abstract: Utah International Inc. has established an industrial hygiene program which is designed to respond to the special concern of the mining industry and to the changing regulatory environment.

title: SCRAPERS TAKE ON DRAGLINE JOBS.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: This article describes how scrapers are beginning to compete with draglines for removing overburden in a significant departure for surface mining. Two examples given to illustrate the successful use of scrapers in removing the overburden above the coal seam are Fuel Dynamics' operations at the company's Kansas and Washington mines. High-speed scraping and the synchronization of scraper operations are highlighted.

title: HOW TO SELECT EQUIPMENT FOR OPEN-PIT COPPER MINING.
authors: Wimpfen S.
abstract: Guidelines based on mine experience are presented for selecting the type, size and combination of open-pit equipment for copper mining that can help obtain the lowest capital and operating costs for a specific deposit. The principles described are generally also applicable in other types of surface mining.

title: COAL MINE SUBSIDENCE NEAR SHERIDAN, WYOMING.
authors: Dunrud C.R.; Osterwald F.W.
abstract: Studies of coal mine subsidence features in a 30-sq mi area 3-12 mi north of Sheridan, Wyo, indicate that the long-range surface effects of mining thick coal beds underground beneath weak overburden less than about 200 ft thick are greater than the effects of well-planned surface mining practices with proper reclamation and revegetation. Coal resource recovery also is higher and more efficient in most surface mining operations. Subsidence depressions, cracks, pits, and troughs above underground mine workings can render the surface unusuable for development because of the hazard to people and structures. Fires may start by spontaneous ignition in abandoned coal mines if air and water under the right conditions reach surface mine highwalls or underground workings through subsidence cracks, pits, or troughs.

title: UPDATE ON SURFACE MINING LEGISLATION.
authors: Cook C.; Green E.
abstract: This article is a continuation of the history of the surface mining legislation commencing subsequent to the sustaining of President Ford's veto by the House of Representatives on June 10, 1975.

title: SURFACE MACHINES OF THE 80's - WHAT WILL BE DIFFERENT.
authors: Anon
abstract: Trends expected to take place during the next decade in the design of surface mining machines are outlined here. Although no dramatic change in surface mining machine design is expected in the 1980's, there are indications that advances will be made toward increasing machine productivity and reducing maintenance costs. Some will come in the form of size. Mining shovels will become larger, to more effectively match the growing size of haul units. Dragline booms are expected to become longer, to more efficiently cast spoil with an eye to the future, and mandatory, reclamation costs.

title: HIGHLIGHTS OF SURFACE MINING IN 1977.
authors: Anon
abstract: The topics covered are equipment trends and these specific mineral commodities: coal, precious metals, copper, iron ore, phosphates and uranium.

title: WHAT'S IN THE SURFACE MINING RULES.
authors: Lusk B.
abstract: The author discusses the key features of the Federal regulations controlling surface mining and reclamation operations, which were published by the U. S. Office of Surface Mining Reclamation and Enforcement. Some of the problems that mine operators must deal with in the face of the new legislation are examined, and a listing of the numerous funds available for research and reclamation is given. Performance standards that coal operators must meet are briefly analyzed.

title: NEW MINING IDEAS ABOUND IN 1978.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The United States' coal industry is participating in a record number of projects involving new operating and equipment principles for improving productivity as well as health and safety in coal mining. Presented here are some of the trendsetters that should influence the direction of mining in the next few years. New concepts and advances in both underground and surface mining, as well as some new processes now being developed for coal preparation are highlighted. One of these is the Battelle hydrothermal coal process for leaching of mineral and organic sulfur compounds from coal.

title: KEYSTONE PREDICTS RAPID EXPANSION.
authors: Nielsen G.
abstract: An industry-wide survey by The Keystone Coal Industry Manual is discussed and accompanied by tables showing new coal mines, as well as their development and expansion through 1987. The survey shows that new coal production capacity from mines that area currently expanding and developing, combined with production from planned mines, will total about 644 million tpy by late 1987. Although the majority of the new mines will be underground, surface mining will account for the larger share of the production.

title: RESERVES AND RESOURCES OF SURFACE-MINABLE COAL IN ILLINOIS.
authors: Treworgy C.; Bengal L.; Dingwell A.
abstract: Surface mining accounts for nearly 50% of recent coal production in Illinois, In previous publications, the Illinois State Geological Survey reported that over 20 billion tons of coal in Illinois were potentially strippable. A current estimate, which takes into consideration the present economic and environmental factors, shows that Illinois has 6 billion tons of surface-minable coal in the ground. The amounts of strippable reserves are large in western Illinois and especially in southwestern and southern Illinois, which are more attractive for surface mining because land costs are lower, the heating value of the coal is higher, and the tonnage recoverable per acre is greater. The southwestern and southern Illinois deposits are and will continue to be the major sources of surface-mined coal in the state.

title: Effects of acid mine wastes on aquatic ecosystems
authors: Parsons J.
abstract: The Cedar Creek Basin (39th N parallel 92nd W meridian) was studied for the period June 1952 through August 1954 to observe the effects of both continuous and periodic acid effluent flows on aquatic communities. The acid strip-mine effluent contained ferric and ferrous Fe, Cu, Pb, Zn, Al, Mg, titratable acid, and elevated H ion concentration, and was toxic to many of the aquatic organisms. In the areas of Cedar Creek, subjected to continuous acid flow, planktonic and benthic species had become adapted to the severe conditions and varied in abundance and diversity. No fishes were observed in the continuous acid effluents area. Downstream, where periodic mineral acid conditions changed drastically during an excessive effluent flow, planktonic and benthic communities had high diversity but low density. The populations of fishes were variable in this stream reach. The chemical basis of water quality variability was shown to be time-related, and statistically related to the aquatic communities. Physical, chemical and biological conditions of acid lakes formed by surface mining were reviewed. In addition to apparent physical and chemical differences in lakes, due in part to variable solar absorbance due to suspended oxides of Fe, chemical variability related to organic composition was reviewed. It is quite probable that degradation of such lakes can be reversed. © 1977 D. Reidel Publishing Company.

title: PRODUCTION CAPABILITY OF SURFACE AND UNDERGROUND COAL MINING MACHINERY.
authors: Knight H.E.
abstract: After a brief review of the United States' past coal output from underground and surface mines, the author discusses the production capabilities of today's mining machines used in conventional underground mining (including continuous mining machines) and in surface mining (including draglines for earth moving). Truck and shovel, scrapers or front-end loaders for overburden removal care not covered. Scheduling, maintenance, government regulations, new technology and some other important factors that influence the production capabilities of underground and surface coal mining machines are analyzed.

title: HEAVY SURFACE EQUIPMENT - INDUSTRY PROBLEMS AND SOLUTIONS.
authors: DeMao P.R.
abstract: The author discusses a number of problems that the mining industry must deal with in its use of heavy surface mining equipment, and then offers possible solutions to these problems. The paper deals primarily with the largest mobile excavating equipment used in various mining and earthmoving operations in the world today, including walking electric draglines, large stripping and loading shovels, and large blast hole drills. Applications of this equipment in surface coal mining, hard rock minng such as iron, aluminum, copper and other ores, as well as in phosphate mining are examined.

title: RECLAIMING SURFACE MINED LAND IN WEST KENTUCKY.
authors: Powell J.; Barnhisel R.I.
abstract: During the 1950s, surface mining of coal in western Kentucky increased to the point that production exceeded that from underground mining. Consequently, the Kentucky general assembly adopted legislation that regulated the surface-mining industry and set particular reclamation standards. This paper presents the current state-of-the-art of reclaiming surface-mined lands in the western Kentucky coal fields. A summary is given of five years of field experimentation and observations made while reclaiming thousands hectares of surface-mined coal spoils in western Kentucky.

title: EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING UPON SHALLOW AQUIFERS IN THE EASTERN POWDER RIVER BASIN, WYOMING.
source: Wyo Univ Water Resour Res Inst Water Resour Ser
authors: Davis R.W.; Rechard P.A.
abstract: This is a progress report on activities and results obtained from a continuing monitoring and study program evaluating the effects of surface mining upon shallow aquifers in the AMAX Belle Ayr mine area of the Eastern Powder River Basin. It primarily discusses events during 1976.

title: PHYSICAL PROPERTIES OF WESTERN COAL WASTE MATERIALS.
authors: Backer R.; Busch R.; Atkins L.
abstract: The Bureau of Mines investigated the typical physical and chemical properties of coal waste materials from the western part of the United States. The results are compared, in so far as possible, with the properties of waste materials from eastern coal operations. The authors found a disparity of mines and preparation plants among western U. S. coal operations and dissimilarities with typical operations in the East. The relatively cleaner product from the predominance of surface mining and the occurrence of thicker seams in the West reduces the amount of coal preparation required and the size of the waste piles. Because of the abundance of land available for waste disposal, many of the piles are low and extended over large areas. New concepts relating statistical shear strength data to liquifaction potential are presented. The somewhat limited data indicates that western coal sludge is coarser with higher permeabilities and shear strengths than the eastern deposits.

title: REQUIREMENTS FOR ROLL-OVER PROTECTIVE STRUCTURES AND FALLING OBJECT PROTECTIVE STRUCTURES FOR SURFACE COAL MINES AND SURFACE AREAS OF UNDERGROUND COAL MINES.
source: US Dep Inter Mesa Inf Rep
authors: Hollop E.
abstract: The adopted standards include regulations currently employed by the Corps of Engineers, Department of Defense, State of California, Occupational Safety and Health Administration, Department of Labor, and the Bureau of Reclamation, Department of Interior. The regulations describe the type of equipment involved, retrofit time table, equipment excluded, Society of Automotive Engineers (SAE) test requirements, and other acceptable effective specifications. The development of MESA's ROPS and FOPS regulations and the appropriate adopted standards are presented in this report. Accident statistics gathered from the mining industry which point out the need for ROPS and FOPS on surface mining equipment are included. Appendices to the report give the adopted standards and MESA's regulations covering ROPS and FOPS.

title: An environmental guide to western surface mining. Part two: impacts, mitigation and monitoring.
authors: Moore R.; Mills T.
abstract: The manual assembles information about the effects of surface mining in the Western US on fish and wildlife resources and recommends ways to mitigate these effects through carefully planned lease and permit stipulations. Chapter 1 describes the content of the manual and provides guidance to the reader in how to use it most efficiently. Chapter 2 introduces the reader to the regional ecology. The distribution of minerals, and the surface mining techniques likely to be used within the three major geomorphic regions. Chapter 3 provides a detailed list of impact activities associated with surface mining and traces the way in which these activities are evaluated with respect to various ecosystem components. Chapter 4 contains discussions of how the various mine-related effects may be mitigated at high, medium, and low levels of effort. It also provides an evaluation of existing stipulations which have been commonly used toward these same objectives. Chapter 5 contains a conceptual approach to development of a site-specific monitoring program and provides recommendations for monitoring of individual ecosystem components. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 23, 1979

title: U. S. BUREAU OF MINES MINING RESEARCH PROGRAMMES.
authors: Prast W.
abstract: The U. S. Bureau of Mines is carrying out a number of mining research programs, the objectives of which are in general to increae efficiency, safety and productivity in U. S. mines - particularly coal mines. In this article details of the various programs currently underway are given, covering almost all aspects of coal mining and including surface mining, oil shale mining and metal/non-metal mining.

title: BUREAU OF MINES OIL SHALE R & D PROGRAM.
authors: Utter S.
abstract: The Program - Advancing Oil Shale Mining Technology - is part of the Bureau's Energy Research and Development Program that began in 1974. The goals of the program are to (1) provide the technology to produce oil shale/shale oil while maintaining environmental quality, and (2) provide baseline data to assist government and industry in the sound planning and managing of the oil shale resource. The program is divided into Extraction, Environment, Special Studies, and Program Management. The major efforts and hence the major funding are in Extraction and Environment. Under Extraction, studies of surface mining, underground mining, and modified in-situ extraction systems are being conducted. Under Environment, work on waste management is being done. A data bank of all available information about oil shale resources, mining and in-situ extraction systems is being assembled under Special Studies.

title: GEORGIA WAY - AN ALTERNATIVE TO DETAILED FEDERAL SURFACE MINING AND LAND RECLAMATION LEGISLATION.
source: Proc Counc Econ AIME Annu Meet
authors: Darby S.
abstract: Surface mining and land reclamation programs are influenced by many variables, and these primarily determine mineral policies of a particular state or region. The author identifies various factors that can influence the quality of surface mined land reclamation programs and illustrates the desirability of developing, by Congress, flexible, nonrestrictive federal legislation on this subject. The article questions the need for several different federal laws to regulate the various types of surface mining when this can be accomplished with one broad, flexible overall act. An alternate approach for drafting surface mining and land reclamation legislation is suggested.

title: Respiratory status of surface coal miners in the united states
authors: Fairman P.; Obrie R.J.; Amandus H.E.; Shoub E.P.
abstract: The United States Public Health Service examined 1438 surface coal miners to determine the prevalence of coal workers pneumoconiosis (CWP), chronic bronchitis, and ventnatory impairment among them. Four percent (fifty-nine individuals) owed some roentgen graphic evidence of pneumoconiosis, but only seven miners had films interpreted as CWP of category or greater (according to the UICC/Cincinnati classification system). Moreover, most of the affected miners had worked in underground coal mines for prolonged periods. Significant decrements in pulmonary function to increasing exposure to surface mine dust were demonstrated only in the forced vital capacityof smokers. Increased prevalence of chronic bronchitis with increasing exposure was found in all smoking categories. However, significant airway obstruction was an uncommonimding in nonsmoking miners. Employment in surface mining was not likely to cause either the development of CWP or clinically significant respiratory impairment. © 1977 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: SAFER AND SPEEDIER HAUL ROADS.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The tonnage capacity and weight of haulage trucks used for surface mining of coal has been climbing rapidly, evolving from the 15 and 20-ton carriers to today's super trucks that can haul as much as 300 tons of coal or overburden. The quality of the haul roads, however, has simply not kept pace with such advancements in truck capacities. The author discusses some new design criteria for haul-road construction that will provide better lines of vision for the vehicle operator, increase the operating speeds of trucks, and reduce haulage costs as well as the number of accidents. Some special safety features for haul roads are also cited.

title: ONAKAWANA LIGNITE DEPOSITS COULD BE USEFUL ENERGY SOURCE FOR ONTARIO.
authors: Anon
abstract: Onakawana Development Ltd was formed in June 1972. It is a subsidiary of Manalta Coal Ltd, which has six surface mining operations in Alberta and Saskatchewan. The company's proposal for developing a mine at Onakawana is presented.

title: Mined land reclamation in Colorado.
source: Geologic Factors in Land Use Planning House Bill 1041 Proc Govenor S 3rd Conference on Environmental Geology Aspen Co Sept 1975
authors: Rold J.
abstract: The author effectively refutes three myths about mining in Colorado - that strop mining has scarred a large proportion of the state, that the state has no control over surface mining and it has no control over mining on federal lands in Colorado. Effective use of existing recclamation legislation should provide for multiple-sequential land use for the optimum benefit of the community and the landowner. -Nick Pinder

title: BETTER WAYS TO BUILD HOLLOW FILLS.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: Two surface mining techniques rapidly becoming popular in the steep-sloped regions of Appalachia, mountain top removal and contour mining using haulback, are discussed. With these two techniques, the trend is to store initial cuts in the hollows. New specifications that can lead to useful, more stable and less costly fills are explained. Also discussed briefly is a new, possibly better way of removing mountaintops, which involves mining across the ridges.

title: SHOVELS COME BACK IN THE WEST.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: Electric power shovels, serving as both stripping and mining units, are making a strong bid to take over a large percentage of the surface mining activities in the West of the U. S. This is especially true in the Powder River Basin of Wyoming and Montana where topography and pit geometry favor the shovel/truck team. The trends in the use of electric power shovels are analyzed, and their economics discussed. Approximately 50% of the medium-size electric power shovels sold this year went to the western coal mines, and 1978 is expected to equal or better that figure.

title: TOTAL UTILIZATION OF A LAND RESOURCE.
authors: Reiss I.
abstract: Meadowlark Farms pioneered the concept of surface mining as an interim land use. The author elaborates on the concept that coal is a legitimate crop in a long term land use program.

title: MAPCO'S MARTIKI MINES LOOKS FOR FULL PRODUCTION IN 1977.
authors: Anon
abstract: One of the newest and most modern surface mining operations in the East is gathering steam at Mapco Inc. 's Martiki mine in anticipation of yielding 2. 7 million tons (3 million st) of coal annually. The coal property located in Martin County about 16 km (10 miles) southwest of Inez, Ky. was acquired by Mapco in 1973 from Pocahontas Land Co. , a subsidiary of the Norfolk and Western Railroad. The 73-km**2 (18,000-acre) site is Mapco's first venture in surface mining, although two deep mines have been in operation in western Kentucky since the company entered the coal business in 1971. Using three Marion 201-M 15-m**3 (20-cu yd) shovels, the Martiki mine's production target in 1976 was 1. 5 million tons (1. 7 million st). In 1977, when the full equipment complement of the three 20-cu yd shovels, two 151-M 13-m**3 (15-cu yd) shovels, and a Marion 8200 dragline will be reached, the mine is expected to produce approximately 3 million tons.

title: OIL SANDS IN SITU PROJECTS CONTINUE AT IMPRESSIVE RATE.
authors: Malden M.
abstract: In-situ research and pilot-plant recovery projects that are aimed at exploiting the massive in-place reserves of Alberta's four major tar sands deposits are reviewed. With reserves estimated at 950 billion bbls of oil in place, the 10. 8 million acres of Athabasca, Cold Lake, Peace River and Wabasea oil sands deposits contain about 74 billion bbls which are covered by less than 150 ft of overburden and thus considered suitable for economic surface mining. The remaining and much bigger part of Alberta's oil sands reserves are covered by a far greater overburden and must be recovered through in-situ recovery techniques.

title: LANDSAT IMAGERY FOR SURFACE-MINE INVENTORY.
authors: Anderson A.; Schultz D.; Buchman N.; Nock H.
abstract: A band-ratio method is presented for measuring distributed surface areas proved to be both temporally and geographically extendable. This study has demonstrated the feasibility of strip-mine inventory and monitoring with Landsat multispectral data to within 2 to 3 hectares. The average accuracy of classification is greater than 92 percent for Landsat images from 1973. Using band-ratioing techniques it is possible to extend signatures over a large geographic area and temporally to other Landsat images within the same orbit. The procedures developed are now being incorporated into a comprehensive State monitoring and inventory program to provide, in a rapid and inexpensive manner, accurate inforamtion on the location, size, and condition of areas affected by surface mining.

title: COST MODEL FOR REMOTE INSPECTION OF GROUND SITES.
authors: Maxim L.; Cullen D.
abstract: A simple model is developed to assess the cost/effectiveness of remote sensing for inspection of ground activities with application to the inspection of surface mining operations. The model considers both single and multiple tier systems (those in which additional inspection is conducted if a higher order tier indicates a violation), possible trade-offs between alpha and beta errors, the worth of technological improvement, an certain fixed cost aspects of manned inspection. An interesting conclusion of this analysis is that (with current cost factors) satellite and aircraft inspection systems can be cost/effective even with relatively high (0. 15-0. 25) alpha and beta errors.

title: HOW TO KEEP DIESEL ENGINES AT PEAK EFFICIENCY.
authors: Bly R.
abstract: Aberrations in the color, pressure and temperature of a diesel engine's exhaust are the symptoms of internal malfunctions, most of which can be easily corrected by regular checks and maintenance, as shown in this article. After suggesting the ways of examining performance and combustion efficiency of modern diesel engines used for surface mining or construction machinery, the author discusses some of the common trouble areas and offers basic guidelines for correcting malfunctions in the air restriction from plugged air cleaners, fuel delivery, valve operations and compression.

title: HAULBACK RECLAIMS NATURALLY.
authors: Anon
abstract: This article deals with truck haulback which has become a successful technique for surface mining coal throughout the Appalachian regions, and which can tie in naturally and efficiently with land reclamation. The method is likely to meet the two stringent provisions which will probably be included in the federal bill on surface mining: The requirement that surface mined land be returned to the approximate original contour, and the requirement that no spoil be pushed over the mining bench on the slopes below. The single-cut haulback mining method as well as the two-direction haulback method and the multi-seam haulback mining method are highlighted.

title: Control of vibration and noise resulting from surface mine blasting
authors: Kerulis F.
abstract: After an outline of noise and vibration produced in surface mining, control procedures are outlined. The following reommendations are given. Particle velocities below 2 in. per second greatly reduce the possibility of structural damage as well as noise propagation. Delay caps of greater than eight ms should be used in association with a sequential blasting machine under controlled conditions. Adequate burden and stemming should be utilized to prevent the premature escape of by product gases. Minimization of the height of exposed faces should reduce the effects of air blast caused by face movement. Detonation cord should be buried by one to two ft. of dirt or sand, or low energy detonation cord should be used. Blasting should be restricted if weather conditions are likely to cause down range focusing of air blast waves. Blast frequency should be minimized. Blasting should be timed to coincide with the highest ambient noise level of the immediate area. Notification of residents of blasting times should minimize the element of surprise. Public relations efforts should be increased to educate the general public in blasting procedures and in resultant vibrations and noise effects.

title: PLANNING OF A NEW SURFACE MINE - WESTERN COAL.
authors: Graham R.J.
abstract: There are five geological provinces in the western states from which 100 percent of the lignite and sub-bituminous coal comes. Part of just one province, the Northern Great Plains, has recoverable reserves of lignite and sub-bituminous and bituminous coal which account for 44 percent of the nation's total. Most of western coal is low in sulfur and, therefore, in demand by utilities who must comply with the Clean Air Act. It lies in thick seams appropriate to surface mining methods. With a majority of coal reserves available in the West, several new mines are in planning stages. The article looks briefly at some of the aspects of mine planning which must be considered.

title: TOUGH STRIP MINING STATUTE IS ASSURED.
authors: Poe E.
abstract: It is generally agreed that a strict Federal surface mining law will soon become reality. The author attempts to assess the consequential impact of the proposed strip mining statute on the U. S. coal industry, and discusses some of the pertinent provisions of the scheduled new law, as first approved on the House side of the Capital. This surface mining legislation sets minimum standards to be followed by the states in setting up mandatory strip mining control programs.

title: KNIFE RIVER KEEPS AHEAD IN RECLAMATION.
authors: Anon
abstract: Knife River Coal Co. 's land reclamation efforts at its Beulah, N. D. , mine are highlighted. The company has been leveling spoil piles left by surface mining starting seven years previous to any North Dakota law which required reclamation of mined land. The Beulah mine now has between 200 and 300 acres restored for use as farm land. Scrapers are used to return the topsoil over the leveled spoil material.

title: MINING ENGINEERING'S ANNUAL REVIEW OF COAL AND INDUSTRIAL MINERALS - 1.
authors: Saperstein L.W.; Terchick A.A.; Matoney J.P.; Ramani R.V.; Wilson E.b.; Murray R.E.
abstract: Six-part review contains articles on surface mining, underground mining, coal preparation, coal utilization, health and safety, and research and development.

title: SPACE PHOTOGRAPHY-A VALUABLE TOOL FOR SURFACE MINE PLANNING.
authors: Brumbaugh F.
abstract: Three Skylab investigators have concluded after a study of surface mine area photographic imagery that much can be gained from this medium when used to monitor surface mining and reclamation activities. Given the ever-increasing demand for coal, improved means are needed for the overall planning, management and enforcement of laws governing the surface coal mining industry. Space photography is discussed as one new tool that can help the surface coal mining industry meet these needs. The Skylab findings are detailed.

title: MULTI-SEAM SURFACE MINING IN WEST.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: While some Western U. S. coal mining companies have been surface-mining multiple coal seams for some time, others, now planning to use this type of mining, will have to face some new and more complicated problems. The author discusses the use of computers and plotters for spoil diagramming, the sequencing of mining equipment in a multi-seam operation, as well as drilling, blasting and coal handling.

title: UNDERGROUND MINING REVIEW.
authors: Beattie G.
abstract: Underground mining will soon be called upon for increased production to meet the world's demand for minerals. Adaptation of surface mining techniques has improved underground productivity significantly. The ability to improve mines which are unable to reduce their labor intensive methods still exists. However, dramatic increases in the cost of energy are upsetting the energy, capital, labor relationships. This situation increases the importance of research work directed toward development of continuous mining methods to replace the cyclical method so long in use in the underground hard rock industry. The impact of the labor shortage in mining will continue to increase in severity.

title: SURFACE COAL MINING - 1976.
authors: Eadie G.
abstract: Although no radically new piece of equipment was developed during 1976 that will change the surface mining industry, there are several experiments of interest. The environmental clout has generated interest in reclamation equipment development. The handling of topsoil has taken a new dimension for many operators who have needed help in meeting legal reclamation requirements. Purchase lead time required has been reduced for equipment. The technology advances in surface mining in 1976 were those brought about by the pressure of production demands.

title: COAL MINING.
authors: Anon
abstract: Coal mining is presently one of the most hazardous industries in the United States, although vast improvements have occurred in recent years through research, improved equipment design, and mining techniques, inspection, education and training. Accident rates have decreased markedly in areas where workers are aware of the hazards and where they are trained to recognize and control the hazardous conditions. Although many mines now have safety records that are equal to those found in other industries, an all-out effort is underway to further improve the work environment of America's miners. Both underground and surface mining are discussed.

title: FABRICATION OF LARGE SURFACE MINING MACHINERY.
authors: Learmont T.
abstract: Semi-automatic welding in the shop and manual welding in the field play a major role in fabricating wheel excavators, stripping shovels and walking draglines. Flux cored arc welding, with and without gas shielding, is employed extensively.

title: COAL SURFACE MINING RECLAMATION COSTS IN THE WESTERN UNITED STATES.
authors: Persse F.H.; Lockard D.W.; Lindquist A.E.
abstract: The Bureau of Mines estimated reclamation costs for 13 surface coal mines in nine States west of the Mississippi River. With the exception of the Pacific Coast coal province, at least one mine in each of the western coal provinces was studied. Estimated costs are presented in four categories which represent the four phases of mined-land reclamation: (1) Design, engineering, and overhead; (2) bond and permit fees; (3) backfillling and grading; and (4) revegetation. Total reclamation costs ranged from 860 to 7,200 per acre, from 6 to 84 cents per ton, and from 4 to 35. 3 mills per million Btu. A mine in the NOrthern Great Plains coal province (Region D) showed the highest per acre cost whereas mines in part of the western region of the Interior coal province (Region A) experienced the greatest per ton and per million Btu cost.

title: Mining Exhibition report.
abstract: A survey of some of the hydraulic equipment for use in all types of mining extraction covering both underground and surface mining that was exhibited at the International Mining Exhibition, U.K. in October 1977.

title: STRIP MINING OF COAL: ENVIRONMENTAL SOLUTIONS.
source: Strip Min of Coal Environ Solutions
authors: Doyle W.S.
abstract: In the past strip mining was generally conducted with little regard for its effect on the environment. This has resulted in erosion and water pollution and left areas esthetically scarred and unusable for agriculture, grazing or recreational use. This book, based on 19 government reports issued from 1967 through 1974, describes coal surface mining land use and methods, land reclamation methods and sediment and erosion control. Acid mine drainage, its sources, prevention and correction as well as the mechanism of recovery of acid strip mine lakes are discussed. Specific studies on revegetation, use of spoil amendments and the effects of acid mine drainage are included. One chapter describes the Federal Republic of Germany's approach to the problem of reclamation of strip mined lands. The final two chapters discuss reclamation costs. A complete list of the cited reports is given at the end of the book. This is followed by a list of state agencies to be contacted regarding strip mining and land reclamation.

title: STEMMING THE SLIDE IN PRODUCTIVITY IS A JOB FOR BOTH MACHINERY MANUFACTURER AND MINE OPERATOR.
authors: Anon
abstract: A survey is presented of some of the new equipment and new techniques available from U. S. and British manufacturers that could help raise the productivity of U. S. coal mines. Longwall mining, the backbone of underground coal mining in Europe, will see a solid growth in the U. S. in the years ahead. In surface mining, there appears to be no new factor in the immediate future that could produce a spectacular increase in output. New equipment and methods focus on the following areas of technical interest: Use of shield supports, particularly in soft floors; application of NCB/Dosco In-Seam Miner; nucleonic sensing devices for longwall shearers; underground communication systems; dust control for longwall machines; and instrumentation techniques for strata control.

title: LAND AND NATURAL RESOURCE INFORMATION AND SOME POTENTIAL ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF SURFACE MINING OF COAL IN THE GILLETTE AREA, WYOMING.
authors: Keefer W.R.; Hadley R.F.
abstract: An integrated program of geologic, hydrologic, geochemical, and related studies by the U. S. Geological Survey in central Campbell County provides basic information about the land and its resources, including characteristics of the landscape, properties of rocks and surface materials, depth and thickness of coal, streamflow, depth to ground water, quality of ground water, sediment yield, concentrations of trace elements in soils, rocks, coal, vegetation, and water, and current land use. The data are used to analyze and predict some of the potential environmental effects of surface mining, such as the extent of land disturbance, nature and degree of landscape modification, and disruption of surface-water and ground-water systems. Refs.

title: COAL RESERVES IN MARYLAND - POTENTIAL FOR FUTURE DEVELOPMENT.
authors: Weaver K.N.; Coffroth J.M.; Edwards J.
abstract: After a brief historical review of coal development in Maryland, the authors discuss in detail the five coal basins of western Maryland, which include 11 commercially exploitable coal seams. The estimates of the recoverable reserves in each of the five basins are given, and the potential for future coal development is assessed. The total recoverable coal reserves for western Maryland are put at 854,900,000 tons of coal having fairly high BTU and sulfur content. Of this total, an estimated 100 million tons could be recovered by surface mining methods.

title: REHABILITATION OF MINING AREAS WITH PARTICULAR REFERENCE TO THE RE-ESTABLISHMENT OF PLANT GROWTH.
source: Pap Presented at the Semin on Landscaping and Land Use Plann as Relat to Min Oper
authors: Lothian T.
abstract: Plant growth is likely to prove the most suitable and satisfactory material to stabilize and cover quarry faces and worked-out surface mining sites. The careful selection of plant species is of paramount importance to the success of any attempts to revegetate these sites. Various techniques are recommended and attention is drawn to different factors which will adversely affect plant growth.

title: GUIDE TO STATE PROGRAMS FOR THE RECLAMATION OF SURFACE MINED AREAS.
authors: Imhoff E.; Friz T.; LaFevers J.
abstract: During 1975 inquiries of agencies in each State and review of State statutes and related administrative codes revealed that 38 States have established programs requiring the reclamation of surface mined lands. Results of analyses of these programs and ancillary data are presented in: a table (matrix) which has been designed for the notation and elaboration of information pertaining to the mined-area reclamation programs of the 50 States; a primer on surface mining activities and related reclamation practices and problems; and a listing of types of non-Federal governmental controls applicable to reclamation. A general trend is seen in State programs toward the requiring of an integration of land-use planning and nine planning, with increased local governmental involvement. Refs.

title: TYRES FOR THE MINING INDUSTRY.
authors: Anon
abstract: The manufacture of pneumatic tires for mobile vehicles used in underground and surface mining operations poses many specialized problems and challenges. Equally, operators have developed many systems and techniques to reduce tire costs and optimize productivity with safety. Examined in this article are the applications of rubber technology to heavy earthmover tires, such as those used on large capacity haulage trucks, wheeled loaders and bulldozers. The information is chiefly derived from visits and discussions with many of the major tire companies supplying the mining industry, but open pit and underground operations worldwide have also contributed part of the information.

title: HYDRAULIC MINING AT KAISER RESOURCES UNLOCKS NEW COAL SEAMS.
authors: Overend M.
abstract: Within five years, Kaiser Resources Limited, at Sparwood, B. C. , has turned a 32 million accumulated loss into a 71 million profit in 1975. The Sparwood operation is a combination of surface mining, conventional underground mining, and a new development in underground technology, hydraulic mining. Production is about 6 one-half million tons of metallurgical coal a year, most of which is sold under long term contracts to Japan. The balance goes to Eastern Canada, Korea, Mexico and Italy.

title: TIMELY MASSEY PURCHASE GETS ST. JOE INTO COAL.
authors: Anon
abstract: This article describes St. Joe Minerals Corp. 's acquisition and subsequent modernization and expansion of A. T. Massey Coal Co. Massey's production has grown from 4. 9 million tons in 1971 to 9. 2 million in 1975 and is projected at 16 million tons in 1980. The company will continue to broker an additional 5 to 6 million tons of coal annually. Over one-third of Massey's production and two-thirds of the brokered coal is low and medium-volatile coking coal. Less than 20% of Massey's production comes from surface mining. The operations of the coal preparation facilities are also discussed.

title: The effect of coal surface mining on the water quality of mountain drainage basin streams
source: Journal of the Water Pollution Control Federation
authors: Minear R.A.; Tschantz B.A.
abstract: Six small watersheds ranging from 1.7 to 11 sq km (0.7 to 4.3 sq mi) within the New River Basin of the Cumberland mountains of Northern Tennessee have been monitored weekly and simultaneously for water quality between January and December 1975. Three watersheds were undisturbed by mining activity and served to establish bench mark data. The other three watersheds represented varying stages of coal mining activity, ranging from initiation of surface mining in one watershed to essentially complete stripping three years ago and current deep mining activity in another. Distinct differences are observed for the variables pH, alkalinity, sulfate, calcium, magnesium, iron manganese, total solids, and suspended solids among the disturbed watersheds. In contrast to the undisturbed watershed stream constituent concentrations which were quite uniform from stream to stream and from sample to sample.

title: Overview of international health safety extraction research and development in coal mining
authors: Yancik J.
abstract: The major coal producing countries have a long history of research efforts directed toward improving coal mining techniques and equipment and improving ways to protect the miners from health and safety hazards. These R&D efforts for the most part concentrate on underground mining, where the magnitude and degree of exposure to hazards are many times greater than in surface mining. Most of the major R&D institutes are listed and pertinent information, where known, is given as to their size, programs and funding. The data is from personal contacts and the Bureau's mining research files unless otherwise noted. A brief discussion of R&D efforts in the top six coal producing countries accompanies the table.

title: SALINE AND SODIC SPOILS - WHAT ARE THEY AND HOW ARE THEY RECLAIMED?
authors: Barth R.C.
abstract: Spoils classified as saline or as sodic are frequently generated by surface mining in the western United States; these have chemical properties which can be detrimental to plant growth. However, with proper management of such spoils, reclamation is possible without incurring high costs. When spoils surfaces are saline or sodic, it is suggested that expert help be obtained. Experts can make detailed recommendations suited to particular situations.

title: OVERVIEW OF NEW SURFACE MINING METHODS OF STEEP SLOPES IN THE APPALACHIAN REGION.
authors: Lusk B.
abstract: The purpose of the study is to develop a mining system that will recover a maximum amount of coal with minimum surface disturbance. Longwall stripping will also give mining companies a third alternative in situations where conventional underground or surface mining methods are not particularly adaptable.

title: SURFACE MINING.
authors: Aiken G.
abstract: Legislation, mining engineering education, and equipment technology are discussed.

title: COAL RESEARCH PROJECTS IN MINING AND PREPARATION PROLIFERATE AS GOVERNMENT STEPS UP FUNDING.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The United States' coal industry is participating in numerous projects designed to increase productivity and safety in coal mines. An overview of the leading innovations coming, many of which are federally sponsored, is presented. These include: new equipment for improving safety, speedier mining techniques, speedier coal haulage, improved surface mining methods, and new coal preparation techniques. The Bureau of Mines has been given the lead role in planning and implementing the long-range R&D program in coal extraction and preparation that would probably involve 500 million in the next five years.

title: KENTUCKY COAL RESERVES: EFFECTS ON COAL INDUSTRY STRUCTURE AND OUTPUT.
source: Univ Ky Inst Min Miner Res Rep IMMR
authors: Anon
abstract: The quantity and quality of land with coal reserves in a region act as the long run limit to industry output and are a primary determinant of industry structure. The present reserve base in Kentucky seems quite large relative to current output rates, and exhaustion appears to be a very distant problem. Nevertheless, the effects of the land constraint on the Kentucky coal industry structure and growth prospects over the next decade may be considerable. This report includes a survey of the conceptual links between the land factor and the coal industry. Output growth in Kentucky during the 1955-1972 period is examined from an industry structure point of view. Changes in output are described in terms of changes in average mine size and number of mines. These structural variables are also compared with the same statistics for the nation and for the states of West Virginia and Illinois. This comparative analysis yields some insight into changes in the relative ranking of Kentucky coal lands. The impact of surface mining technology on the Kentucky coal industry is stressed.

title: TECHNOLOGICAL INNOVATIONS ABOUND IN COAL MOUNTAINS OF APPALACHIA.
authors: Anon
abstract: This article reviews some of the technical innovations which have been adopted by the Appalachian coal operators. Included among these are high-speed tunneling machines for coal mines, longwall shields, shortwall equipment, continous haulage systems, underground diesels, methane drainage, new surface mining techniques, and improved coal preparation equipment.

title: MONITORING OF ENVIRONMENTAL EFFECTS OF COAL STRIP MINING FROM SATELLITE IMAGERY.
authors: Brooks R.L.; Parra C.G.
abstract: A large variety of camera/film/filter combinations has been reviewed for this study. The investigation includes determining the applicability of satellite imagery for detection of disturbed acreage in areas of coal surface mining, and the much more detailed monitoring of specific surface mining operations including: active mines, inactive mines, highwalls, ramp roads, pits, water impoundments and their associated acidity, graded areas and types of grading, and reclaimed areas. Techniques have been developed to enable mining personnel to utilize this imagery in a practical and economic manner. To corroborate the photo interpretation results on-site observations were made.

title: Predicting the reclamation of land after surface mining in the Central Chernozem Region
authors: Kirillova T.B.; Ovchinnikov V.A.
abstract: A methodology is proposed for forecasting the area of land likely to be disturbed by surface mining activities and the portion of the disturbed land subject to rehabilitation for various land uses (farming, woodland, ponds, outdoor recreation, built up areas, etc.). The Central Chernozem Region includes not only peat bogs, sand and clay quarries, chalk and limestone pits and phosphate mines, but also the large iron ore operations of the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly, destined to become some of the leading iron ore producers of the Soviet Union. Iron ore, chalk and limestone pits and associated spoil banks now account for 20% of all disturbed land in the region, and their share is expected to grow to 40%. The total land area disturbed by surface mining in the Central Chernozem Region is expected to grow from 27,200 hectares in late 1970 to 63,000 hectares by 1990, or an increase of 2.3 times. According to the forecast, 46,400 hectares of the long term disturbance will be subject to reclamation, with 16,300 hectares for farming uses, 18,500 for woodland, 8,500 for ponds, and 3,200 for outdoor recreation, built up areas and other miscellaneous uses.

title: A venture into reclamation
authors: Balzer J.; Crouch D.; Poyser R.; Sowards W.
abstract: Details on the land reclamation program carried out by Utah International Inc. at their Navaho mine near Farmington, New Mexico, are presented. The mining activities at this desert site are based on conventional surface mining methods. The earliest land reclamation efforts, which were based on ash disposal from the local power plant, are reviewed, and the result of soil surveys and cooperative studies of possible reclamation methods are discussed. The use of test plots, irrigation and other planting techniques is also considered.

title: COAL SURFACE MINING RECLAMATION COSTS - APPALACHIAN AND MIDWESTERN COAL SUPPLY DISTRICTS.
authors: Evans R.J.; Bitler J.R.
abstract: Reclamation costs were estimated for 20 coal surface mining operations in the Appalachian and Midwestern Coal Supply Districts (these two districts were divided into three multi-State regions). The cost data were obtained through onsite observations, interviews with mining company personnel, and the authors' cost estimating procedures. The cost data are presented in terms of dollars per acre, dollars per ton of coal produced, and dollars per cubic yard of overburden moved during backfilling. The reclamation process is divided into three cost categories: Premining planning, backfilling, and revegetation. The average total reclamation costs for the three regions are 2. 77 per ton of coal produced and 8168 per acre. As the result of comparisons of reclamation costs by region, by mining method, by slope, and by size of operation, the most important reclamation cost difference is between area mining methods (1. 73 per ton) and contour mining methods (3. 81 per ton).

title: Environmental protection and beekeeping
authors: Engelhardt W.
abstract: The impoverishment of the West German landscape is discussed from the point of view of the beekeeper. The author reviews the increasing utilization of space for residential buildings, industrial plants and traffic facilities at the cost of agricultural and natural areas, the large scale disturbance of ecosystems and advance of monocultures, and the serious decrease of the number of different plant and animal species. Possibilities for the enrichment of landscape are mentioned, such as the recultivation of surface mining areas and reorganization of worked sand and gravel pits, the creation of new ecosystems within the framework of field clearing, and planning for the use of forests that considers not only wood production but also recreational uses and functions important to the beekeeper.

title: CAN SURFACE MINING BE COMPATIBLE WITH URBANIZATION?
authors: Coates W.E.
abstract: The compatibility or social acceptability of surface mining in and near urban areas is investigated at two points in time: (1) during the active extraction period and (2) after completion of extraction. Those features which make the typical surface mining operation quite dissimilar to normal urban uses are examined with respect to the objections usually raised by neighboring, nonextractive land owners. Means of amelioration available to the operator to mitigate the adverse impacts causing the objections are examined. Compatibility versus urbanization is investigated in terms of after-use potential. The consideration of extractive operations as ″interim″ land uses is investigated in a variety of site situations. Variations in time of after-use planning, with respect to the age of the operation and ″futuristic″ after-use potential, are investigated through case-study examples and schematic-study proposals.

title: FUTURE FOR PITS AND QUARRIES IN ONTARIO.
authors: Jewett G.
abstract: The seemingly endless array of arguments for and against the surface mining of aggregates are reduced to a relatively few key issues that are reviewed in this paper. There is no known ″elixir vitae″ for the malady. Government's role is seen as one of factilitating a free exchange of viewpoints and ideas between informed representatives of concerned agencies, followed by the development of a provincial policy that must be the framework within which individual cases will be resolved. Some of the alternatives that have been proposed are reviewed.

title: Hydrological impacts associated with coal mining
authors: Rechard P.
abstract: The extent and types of hydrologic impacts caused by the surface mining of coal are examined with regard to the influence of mine location, characteristics of the area and mining techniques used. Special attention is given to the studies carried out in the semiarid Eastern Powder River Basin of Wyoming. The possible hydrologic impacts of surface coal mining are examined with regard to the water requirements for use onsite and the impact of mining of the overall hydrologic cycle. Consideration is given to alterations in surface water runoff patterns, effects on alluvial valley floors, stream channel erosion, and creation of lakes and ponds in water short localities.

title: AVAILABILITY OF COAL IN ENERGY CRUNCH.
source: AAPG Bulletin American Association of Petroleum Geologists
authors: Potter C.
abstract: The coal reserves in the United States are well known, both as to geologic age and geographic distribution. The largest reserves must be obtained by underground mining methods (about 327 billion tons in the east; 22 billion tons in the west), with approximately 35 billion tons obtainable from surface mining in the western United States and 10 billion tons from the eastern states. The economics of coal mining have been traditionally controlled by the quality of the coal, the cost of production, and the cost of transportation. Environmental considerations have upset the usual supply and demand pattern, and may cause further serious readjustments in mining and marketing practices.

title: Pseudo-Mining Subsidence through Lowering of the Water Table.
authors: Nendza H.
abstract: Deformation of the surface caused through lowering of the water table, such as occurring in surface mining of lignite deposits, often appear as those that are caused by mining subsidence. They are designated as pseudo-mining damages. It has been acertained by means of investigating models that deformations of the surface, overlaying a geologic fault which creates different water tables, are similar in the scope and occurence to those induced by mining.

title: POSEIDON STORY.
authors: Anon
abstract: Starting with the 1969 discovery of a nickel deposit, located about 167 mi northeast of Kalgoorlie, the Poseidon Ltd has developed two mines - one underground, the other a surface mine - and put on stream on 8/28/1974 a 1-million tonnes/yr sulfides flotation concentrator. Paper describes the geologic setting of the deposit; its mineralization; and underground and surface mining methods. Ore treatment process and its flowsheet are described.

title: ATHABASCA TAR SANDS.
authors: McConville L.
abstract: Monographic description of Athabasca tar sands begins with the official definition of tar sands as ″sand containing a highly viscous crude hydrocarbon material not recoverable in its natural state through a well by ordinary production methods″ . Paper is divided into several chapters discussing: geology and history of development of the deposit (proved reserves of crude bitumen in place are estimated to amount to about 900 multiplied by 10**9 bbls); commercialization of a deposit based on example of the Great Canadian Oil Sands, Ltd (GCOS) (present production of 55,000 bcpd of oil from 140,000 tpd of oil sands); existing and planned surface mining and refining projects (flowsheet of GCOS; plant is shown); recovery by in-situ methods; and future outlook.

title: SURFACE MINING AND RECLAMATION, 3RD SYMPOSIUM, PAPERS, VOLUMES 1 AND 2, 1975.
authors: Anon
abstract: Forty-one papers and four titles by various authors are presented. The topics discussed are: Federal coal leasing, pollutant discharge elimination, environment, surface mining, reclamation, revegetation, arid zone hydrology, coal mine spoils, preplanning, overburden materials, ecology, sulfur forms, watersheds, water chemistry, groundwater quality, photogrammetry and computer applications, drills, revegetation equipment, rehabilitation base-line data, sediment erosion control, soil losses, reclamation costs, economic system analysis, horizontal haul method, soil conservation plant materials, fertilizers lime, and mulch, forage grasses, noise, soil development, and land reclamation. Individual papers are indexed separately.

title: RESEARCH AND APPLIED TECHNOLOGY SYMPOSIUM ON MINED-LAND RECLAMATION, 2ND, PAPERS, 1974.
authors: Anon
abstract: Twenty-five papers by various authors are presented. The topics discussed are: Mining and reclamation, controlled placement, surface and strip mining, revegetation, coal-leasing, federal and state permitting, ecology and restoration, mineral resource development, social and economic impacts of coal mining, sediment yield, hydrologic study of surface mined areas, groundwater quality, overburden properties, soil reconstruction, hydroseeding, pine breeding on acid spoil, all-season seeding, revegetation, surface mining technology, British reclamation experience and coal-mined land reclamation in Poland. Individual papers are indexed separately.

title: STATE-OF-THE-ART: SAND AND GRAVEL INDUSTRY.
authors: Newport B.
abstract: This report presents an overview of the sand and gravel industry in the United States and its relationship to the environment. The fate and effects of sediment generated by this surface mining activity on the benthic, planktonic, and fish communities of our waterways are discussed in detail. Problems of the sand and gravel industry, types of operations, status of current treatment technology, and legislation affecting the industry are reviewed.

title: EUBOEAN MAGNESITE MINING AND DEADBURNING IN GREECE.
authors: Anon
abstract: Surface mining and deadburning (calcining) operations of the Scalistiri Group that are located on the island of Euboea, north of Athens and which produce 200,000 tonnes/year of MgO are described. Flowsheet of the magnesite ore treatment plant is shown.

title: WEIPA BAUXITE.
authors: Anon
abstract: Australia has now become the world's largest producer of bauxite, and total production is still rising. Only 20 years ago, the country'S output was virtually negligible. Much of this rapid progress can be attributed to the high-grade discoveries at Weipa, in the Cape York peninsula area, the site of what is already the world's greatest single bauxite producer, with further excellent prospects for increases in production. Weipa has also proved to be the cornerstone for the very rapid development of a substantial proportion of Australia's own domestic aluminum industry. Geology of the orebody estimated to contain 520-million tons grading between 52 and 60% Al//2O//3 that cover a 73 sq mi area and of further 230 sq mi areas estimated to contain some 1,700-million tons of bauxite with grades of between 45 and 58% Al//2O//3 is described. Surface mining operations are removing an average 3 ft of overburden and are using wheel mounted, diesel operated, front end loaders that deliver straight to the haul trucks. Grade control, beneficiation, calcining plants, as well as railway and port facilities are described.

title: STEERING SYSTEMS FOR OFF-HIGHWAY TRUCKS.
authors: Anon
abstract: Article describes the factors involved in the design of steering systems for the large-capacity motor trucks, around 200 tons, that are now in use in surface mining.

title: MINERALIZATION MODELS FOR MINE PLANNING AND EVALUATION.
source: Int Symp on the Appl of Comput and Math in the Miner Ind 12th Annu Proc Pap Colo Sch of Mines Golden Sect H
authors: Perry J.; Phillips D.; Shearer L.
abstract: In order to evaluate a mineral deposit, a three dimensional model of the distribution of mineral values is required. For Surface Mining Systems this generally necessitates a regular block model with suitably chosen block size, bench interval and datum. This paper describes the sequential development of computerised methods for constructing such models from drill hole data for three stratiform deposits, each requiring different treatment. The methods have been developed at Roan Consolidated Mines Limited, in Zambia to deal with particular deposits encountered. In each case geological, mining and data processing staff have been involved in design and control.

title: WHAT'S AHEAD FOR RUSSIAN MINING?
authors: Zaharlev G.
abstract: Future Soviet mining growth lies in expansion of surface mining which will provide 75-80% of total output by 1980.

title: Operational compliance with noise, blasting and dust controls
authors: Schaudies F.
abstract: Noise pollution control in the area of surface mining has been, up to the past year, a slowly developing science. It is, however, becoming a rapidly growing issue because of more rigid enforcement of the present noise standards set forth in the U.S. Federal Mine Health and Safety Act of 1969. It is possible, and even probable, there will be an even greater degree of enforcement along with more stingent revisions of the present law. This paper examines some of the revisions that may have a great impact on operational compliance, particularly blasting and dust control.

title: Ecology and the problems of rehabilitating wastes from mineral extraction
source: Proc Roy Soc London Ser A
authors: Goodman G.T.
abstract: With the growing demand for minerals in the United Kingdom, it is likely that there will be a marked increase in the area of land affected by deep and surface mining and associated industries, e.g. ore concentration plant, smelters. Improving technical knowledge of how to revegetate inexpensively, land disturbed by mining helps to ensure that mineral extraction is not inhibited by nor necessarily inhibitory to other valid uses for land. Revegetation is important because experienced experienced planners have found in practice that revegetation appears to restore to a derelict or disturbed site the greatest flexibility of potential re use for the widest range of subsequent developments. Traditionally, three approaches approaches to revegetation appear to have been used: accept site conditions as they are, and plant with species known to tolerate harsh conditions, e.g. ecological 'pioneer' species; improve the soil as a medium for plant growth by incorporating, for example, NPK fertilizer, lime and organic matter; use geological knowledge to pre plan excavations so that toxic wastes are buried below the rooting zone. A combination of all three seems most desirable and involves careful species selection together with predictive physicochemical physicochemical analysis of those site conditions which which may inhibit plant growth.

title: IN WEST VIRGINIA HILLS. . . IT'S HAULBACK MINING ALL THE WAY.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: This Princess Susan coal mine of Charleston, W. Va. operation is an excellent example of surface mining performed together with reclamation work, in natural sequence and without spoil pushed over the hill or highwalls left behind.

title: IMPACT OF THE RAILROAD INDUSTRY ON MINING.
authors: Graves T.
abstract: As a case-in-point of the impact of a modern, well organized transportation of coal by rail over long distances by means of unit trains on the economics of surface mining, the boom in the Wyoming's mining industry is described. Coal activity on the Union Pacific is currently centered around the once near ghost town of Hanna, Wy. The coal rush along Union pacific Railroad lines in this area actually began taking on boom proportions in 1972 with the start up of a new strip mining operation, expansion of another mine and the addition of five new unit train operations. Today, the rich coal fields of Wyoming are being tapped to serve the elejctric utilities for boiler fuel hundreds of miles eastward from the nearby Continental Divide.

title: WANTED: NEW SYSTEMS FOR SURFACE MINING.
authors: Michaelson S.
abstract: Recent and current productivity trends in US surface mining are discouraging: they show the industry to be noncompetitive in comparison with other industries both in the US and abroad. Extensive research on productivity and costs, as witnessed in the US nonferrous, metallic surface mines, shows that on the average 10% of cost if attributable to breaking rock, 16% for shovel loading, and close to 45% is accounted for by ore and overburden haulage. The average industry-wide stripping ratio is estimated at about 2:1. Obviously, then, the stripping ratio (3 tons moved for 1 ton of ore) has the greatest potential for improving the productivity and reducing ore cost. The next, greatest target for productivity improvement is the haulage system. Paper discusses potential techniques in that direction.

title: MATERIALS IMPROVEMENTS IN SURFACE MINING EQUIPMENT.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Weston W.; McKean M.
abstract: The four basic material requirements for mining equipment are suggested by the authors who then proceed to discuss some of the ways these requirements are met by improved materials, with particular reference to surface mining equipment. A review of excavating and drilling machinery is given along with developments in design. Foreign inclusions in the material are singled out as the biggest single problem resulting in a substantial reduction in the physical properties of the steel used in surface mining equipment.

title: Determination of an Economic Size of a Producing Facility. Theoretical Fundamentals, Influence on Costs, Practical Application to a Surface Mining Operation.
authors: Kellermeyer W.
abstract: Success of an industrial operation is determined by its proper size and parameters such as productivity of the crew, productive facilities, raw materials, as well as planning, organization, and management. The theoretical fundamentals are examined and their application is illustrated on the example of a complex, surface mining operation.

title: UNIQUE APPROACH TO GET OIL SHALE OUT OF THE GROUND.
authors: Smith C.
abstract: Paper describes the geology of the Piceance Creek Basin, Colo. , oil shale deposit and presents a proposed surface mining system after partial removal of the overburden. Theoretical financial calculation for production of 500,000 bpd is included.

title: NEW USES FOR BUCKETWHEEL EXCAVATORS.
authors: Griffin T.
abstract: Surface mining today is faced with a twin challenge: accelerating the rate of removal of massive quantities of overburden and ore; and replacing comparable high volumes of overburden in the mined-out portion of the pit. It is against this background, coupled with increased demands for fossil fuels worldwide and legitimate environmental concerns, that the role of bucketwheel excavators and reclaimers has been raised to new prominence. As an innovative use that may mean low cost and a high volume article describes the application of bucketwheel excavators for removal of overburden and mining of an ore deposit with simultaneous replacement of overburden in the exploited parts of the open pit.

title: ADVANCES IN HARD ROCK MINING - ACHIEVEMENTS AND EXPECTATIONS.
authors: Janelid I.
abstract: Paper analyzes the importance of rock excavation in world wide, underground and surface mining of ores and industrial minerals. The pertinent statistics show that the ratios of the volume of rock excavated in underground and surface mining to the volume of ore were 1 to 5 and 1 to 1,1 respectively. Impact of rock excavation on the total costs of mining necessitates intensive research and development work in areas of: drilling; drifting and raising; rock drills; blasting; loading and transportation; as well as in rock mechanics. Recent Scandinavian achievements are reviewed.

title: Reclamation in steep slope surface mining
authors: Hamilton L.
abstract: Today's complex methods of mining coal on the steep slopes require millions of dollars of equipment and precise timing in order to maintain production and protect the environment. Recently, the West Virginia Department of Natural Resources established some administrative guidelines that would make steep slope operations comply with proposed U.S. requirements. This new steep slope mining theory has been labeled 'controlled placement' of spoil. Controlled placement involves the placement of spoil in steep areas where its condition can be completely stabilized and revegetated. This covers the head of the valley fill, mountain top removal, haulback, over the shoulder, block cut and any other methods where the overburden is technically delivered, hauled or compacted so that there are no adverse after effects when mining has been completed. This paper further describes the application of this technique to steep slope mining and discusses some of the results that have been obtained to date.

title: RECLAMATION PROBLEMS IN SURFACE MINING.
authors: Grandt A.
