abstract: Paper discusses the reclamation of surfaced mined coal lands in the Unites States in the 1970's from several aspects, namely, reclamation requirements, policies and techniques. In particular the legislation in effect, topsoiling, grading, water supplies, and climate are examined.

title: OPEN PIT URANIUM MINING.
authors: Graves J.
abstract: Surface mining at Anaconda's Jackpile-Paguate mine, located between Albuquerque and Grants, N. M. , begins with the delineation of the ore bodies through surface drilling and geophysical probing. Assay information is fed into a computer for the determination of ore-to-low grade for reserve calculation purposes, and the blocked-out areas are mined using conventional blasting, stripping, and loading techniques.

title: TRANSPORTATION FOR COAL.
authors: Anon
abstract: Comprehensive study of various techniques for coal transportation is divided into following chapters: mechanical, hydraulic, pneumatic options in deep-mine transport; haulage trucks for carry coal in surface mining; overland conveying, inclusive of coal-slurry pipeling; railroad-transportation; and using waterways to ship coal.

title: Inspiration's design for clean air. I
authors: Dayton S.
abstract: A detailed description of the major design and operating factors involved in the Inspiration Consolidated Copper Co.'s new $54 million electric smelter and double absorption sulfuric acid plant are presented in this first of a two part article. The new plants, which both contain some of the largest componentry of their type anywhere, are expected to yield many benefits in spite of their high cost. The smelter, equipped with a Norwegian Elkem 51 mva furnace and five Belgian siphon converters of Hoboken Overpelt design, started phasing into the production line in May 1974 as a replacement for an older, reverberatory, Pierce Smith converter installation handling a green charge. Coupled to the new smelter (which handles 1,500 tpd of copper concentrates and copper precipitates of Inspiration and toll origin) is a 'showcase' 1,330 tpd Lurgi acid train fed from an elaborate collection system that 'dry cleans and launders' electric furnace and siphon converter offgases. The new project places Inspiration first among western US copper smelters in the race to meet the Environmental Protection Agency's 90% sulfur recovery goal for stationary plants. The replacement system will enable mothballing of the present smelter as a reserve asset. The major topics of discussion are: How Inspiration settled on the new system; fitting the new facilities to the existing system; about the world's largest electric copper furnace; the enriched exit gas dividend; slag and matte tapping; sealing of the siphon convertors; how copper conversion is handled; gas handling; cold gas cleaning; making acid in a quality plant; and waste heat recovery in the steam plant. The second part of this series will present a profile of Inspiration mining and processing from ore to finished copper rod.

title: OIL SHALE: A SOLUTION TO THE ROADBLOCK.
authors: Livingston C.
abstract: The roadblock to development of United States oil shale resources is neither technology nor economics. Rather, the central issue is the fact that an area as vast as that underlain by the Green River Formation of Colorado, Utah, and Wyoming simply cannot be developed by using conventional concepts of mine layout. The problem is not one of developing a single oil shale mine or even a series of oil shale mines. Rather it is one of developing the natural resources of a vast area encompassing sodium and aluminum minerals, natural gas, water resources, land, and forests, as well as oil shale. Paper critically reviews the three approaches to the oil shale development that are being pursued, to wit: underground mining; in situ retorting; and conventional surface mining. A new proposed complex technique that should be planned on a regional basis and which is described in detail, would encompass; a new blasting technology, mining method and layout; materials handling systems; as well as a method for land reclamation and water resource development.

title: LAND REHABILITATION: PROMPT PASSAGE OF FEDERAL RECLAMATION LAW RECOMMENDED BY FORD FOUNDATION STUDY.
authors: Box T.
abstract: No issue associated with the current energy debate is more in the center of conflict between exploitation and conservation than is the surface mining of coal. Indeed, restoration of a landscape disturbed by surface mining, in the sense of duplicating former conditions, is not possible. In order to avoid the confusion caused by the vague terminology, the panel on surface mining of the National Academy of Sciences has issued following definitions: ″Restoration″ implies that the conditions of the site at the time of disturbance will be duplicated after the action. ″Reclamation″ implies that the site is habitable to organisms that were originally present, or others that approximate the original inhabitants. ″Rehabilitation″ as used in this report implies that the land will be returned to a form and productivity in conformity with a prior land use plan including a stable ecological state that does not contribute substantially to environmental deterioration and is consistent with surrounding aesthetic values. In light of the above definitions, special ecological problems of western coal lands, relationship of surface mining to environment, and recommendations for rehabilitating western land are discussed.

title: ARIZONA: COAL MOVES ON NATION'S FIRST 50-kv ELECTRIC RAILROAD.
authors: Bellas R.
abstract: Arizona's most extensive proved coal reserves are in the northeastern part of the state in Black Mesa, a 3200-sq mi area in portions of Apache, Navajo and Coconino Counties. Proved reserves, established by Peabody Coal Co which in the mid-1960s began exploration in the area are considered to be approximately 2 billion tons. One of the operating units, the Kayenta mine has coal deposits similar to those at the adjacent Black Mesa mine, and the surface mining methods are similar. Two pits are now worked. Diesel-electric haulers move the coal from the pits to a 2700-tph conveyor which feeds the coal to two 1000-tph crushers. The 2-in. size product is taken from a storage hopper and loaded onto a three-flight conveyor system which carries the coal 6 one-half mi across the mesa to storage silos at the railroad loading point. The Black Mesa & Lake Powell Railroad, built by International Engineering Co, Inc, a subsidiary of the Morrison-Knudson Co, was built expressly for this mining operation and is completely automated. Each train comprises three electric locomotives pulling 73 cars, each of 122-ton capacity. There are three train trips daily, six days a week, with non-stop unloading at the generating station. An engineer rides the train only to prevent a possible malfunction of electronic controls.

title: WYOMING: PRODUCTION SEEN DOUBLING BY 1976.
authors: Glass G.
abstract: Wyoming's coal industry is rapidly emerging from its depression era of the late 1950s. The sharpest upturn in production began in 1969 and shows no sign of stopping. From that year, production tripled from 4. 6 million tons annually to 13. 6 million tons in 1973. Because production forecasts cannot keep pace with recent developments, it is only safe to say that Wyoming coal mining activity is accelerating at unprecedented rates and that surface mining accounts for most increases in annual tonnage. Coal-related developments and existing and proposed mines within Wyoming are shown on state's map. Efforts of the individual mining companies are described. Developments in coal gasification are outlined.

title: NEW MEXICO: STATE STILL BOASTS NATION'S LARGEST SURFACE COAL MINE.
authors: Bellas R.
abstract: History of the development by the Utah International, Inc (UI) of the Navajo surface mine in the Four Corners area of New Mexico is briefly described. The leases covering 31,000 acres are estimated to contain a minimum of 1. 1-billion tons of coal. The coal seams lie 10 to 120 ft beneath the surface. Coal grade averages between 9000 and 10,000 Btu, and the sulfur content is about 0. 6%. Ash varies on the high side, about 18-20%, but the disposal problem is simplified by a short haulback to the pit area, where the ash is buried. The mine which uses conventional surface mining methods is producing 25,000 tpd of coal. Mining activities of other companies are described.

title: NORTH DAKOTA: PROPOSED COAL GASIFICATION COMPLEX WILL TAP LIGNITE RESERVES.
authors: Conrad C.
abstract: Under present plans the state's four existing coal-fired generating plants, having a capacity of 750 Mw, will eventually be increased to 2320 Mw. Estimated coal consumption of these four expanded plants will be 27. 1 million tons of coal annually. Biggest news in the history of the North Dakota lignite industry was approval on Feb 19 1974, of a plan to divert 17,000 acre-feet of water annually from Lake Sakakawea for a coal gasification plant. The lake lies north of the Garrison Dam on the Missouri River. Michigan Wisconsin Pipe Line Co of Detroit was given the go-ahead for one plant, although three have been proposed. Construction of the plant, costing up to 500 million, is expected to begin in 1979. The North American Coal Corp will supply 10 million tpy of coal for gasification which would, on the average, require surface mining 800 acres annually. Based on an estimated plant life of 30 years, this would require surface mining 24,000 acres, compared with the total of 7000 acres surface-mined in the state since records were first kept in 1884. Michigan Wisconsin will build the plant using the Lurgi gasification process. North Dakota gas will be carried by a pipeline extending across North Dakota from Alaska. The Nordth Dakota lignite has more than a 30% water content - 2% on the surface - and a heat value of about 6800 Btu per lb. In comparison, subbituminous coal yields about 9000 Btu per lb. (North Dakota's coal deposits are exclusively lignite. )

title: An aerial-photographic analysis of the environmental impact of clay mining in New Jersey
authors: Garofalo D.; Wobber F.
abstract: Black and white, color and color-infrared photography at 1:20,000 scale or larger provide useful data for monitoring the environmental effects of surface mining as demonstrated following a study of surface clay mining in New Jersey. Investigations using high-altitude color and color-infrared photography at scales of 1:80,000 to 1:120,000 provide an efficient technique for inventorying large-surface mining operations or for rapid statewide mining studies. © 1974.

title: SURFACE MINE OF THE FUTURE.
authors: Cornforth C.
abstract: If the industry is not all but abolished under federal legislation, a fantastic, exciting future is ahead for surface mining, particularly in the West. To accomplish that goal even larger, than presently available, excavators (boom-, and bucket wheel type) tractors, scrapers, and motor trucks will be needed, source of which are described. Techniques for land reclamations are discussed.

title: Digging into mine waste
abstract: In the U.S., mining activities now affect approximately 13 million acres, or about 0.5% of the total U.S. land area. Of this total, 7 million have been undercut, 3 million disturbed by surface mining, and 3 million given over to mining related waste accumulations. The subject of mining related environmental pollution is discussed and some of the possible remedial measures for the reparation of environmental damage are considered. Because of aquifer and stream disruption, both coal and hard rock mines give rise to water pollution from mine drainage, both acid and alkaline. The polluting effects of solid waste production through disposal of mine tailing after mineral values are extracted, such as land slides, air pollution through dust blowoff, and smoldering from spontaneous combustion, are also discussed. Some of the more effective methods of restoring environmental damage and meeting Federal pollution control standards are reviewed.

title: RESEARCH AND APPLIED TECHNOLOGY SYMPOSIUM ON MINED-LAND RECLAMATION, PAPERS, 1973.
authors: Symp
abstract: During recent years significant progress has been achieved in developing the technology necessary to restore to productive uses the land disturbed during surface mining. Papers presented at the Symposium cover not only the standard reclamation topics of grading, soil amendments, plant materials, and planting methods, but also preplanning the mining operation and mine operating procedures. In many cases a more productive land use can be attained through reclamation, and papers presented at the final session are devoted to utilization and management of mined-land. Individual papers are provided with bibliographic references.

title: EQUIPMENT NEEDS TO MEET THE CHLLENGE OF SURFACE MINING OF COAL AND URANIUM IN THE DECADE AHEAD.
authors: Ritchie M.
abstract: This paper focuses on the 1975-1985 period in attempting to demonstrate the equipment requirements in the coal and uranium industries for that period. In the coal industry, it appears that both stripping and mining equipment needs will grow at a rate of 10-12%/year in the future. This equipment will not be radially different from that used today even though some increases in size will probably occur in some equipment lines. The emphasis will be upon improvement in present generation machinery. The same may also be true in the uranium industry. Growth rates on the order of perhaps 50%/year will be experienced as the utility industry continues to install plants using nuclear fuels. It appears that ost of the equipment will besimilar to that used today.

title: Mined-land reclamation studies on bighorn sheep range in Alberta, Canada
authors: Etter H.M.
abstract: Several ecological factors combine to make the amount and quality of winter range of great importance for the maintenance of Bighorn Sheep (Ovis canadensis) herds in the Province of Alberta, Canada. Increased resource development activities, particularly surface mining, have posed new problems of land-use and reclamation in the sub-alpine forest zone. Solutions to these problems are being sought in reclamation studies at Luscar, Alberta, with emphasis upon winter sheep-range as an important land-use objective. Hydro-seeding trials have facilitated the selection of promising plant species and varieties for revegetation of mined-land. © 1973.

title: SIMILKAMEEN PROJECT.
authors: Anon
abstract: Similkameen Mining Co formed in 1967 by the Newmont Mining Corp owns in the vicinity of Princeton, B. C. two main orebodies: the Ingerbelle and Copper Mountain whose total reserves amount to about 76-million tons with a grade of 0. 53% Cu and an average ratio of 2. 2 tons of waste to one ton of ore. These orebodies are separated by the deep canyon of the Similkameen river. Paper describes the surface mining operations and equipment used as well as the flotation mill, designed to treat 15,000 tpd of ore. Unusual feature of the project consists of a suspension bridge over the Similkameen Canyon, built to accommodate tailings-, and reclaim water pipelines.

title: DRAMATIC MODERNIZATION PROGRAM IMPROVES OVERALL PRODUCTION AT JEFFREY MINE.
authors: Li T.
abstract: Title property, owned and operated by Canadian Johns-Manville Ltd. and located 100 m east of Montreal in the city of Asbestos, Que. accounts for approximately 37% of current Canadian production of chrysotile asbestos and about 13% of world production. Believed to be the world's largest asbestos mine, the oval-shaped open pit measures more than a mile at its widest point and is 900 ft deep. Paper describes the steeply dipping ore body and technical innovations involved in the conversion from underground to surface mining that has taken place in the 1960s. New drilling and blasting techniques and haulage of ore and waste in 100 t capacity diesel-electric trucks are outlined. Modernization of ore treatment technique comprises asbestos fiber recovery techniques and fluid bed dryers.

title: SURFACE MINING COAL VIA LONGWALL METHOD.
authors: Anon
abstract: Paper describes the scope of a study being carried out by the West Virginia Surface Mining & Reclamation Assn. of Charleston, W. Va. that has as its purpose to demonstrate that surface longwall mining of shallow-lying coal seams, 100 ft or less below the surface, will help in controlling acid mine drainage through immediately sealing the exposed coal seam from the air before acid can form. Furthermore, it is expected that the surface over the mined area will settle without shearing, causing minimal environmental disturbance.

title: Effect of Gravitational Forces on Development of the Static Groundwater Table.
authors: Kyziol S.
abstract: Paper postulates that the formation of a statical groundwater level in the mines depends also of pulling forces, being exerted by the overlying rock strata. This phenomenon should be taken under consideration in plan of surface mining exploitation because the groundwater table may be lowered on account of the removal of overburden.

title: WESTERN ENERGY STRIPS THE 25-FT ROSEBUD IN SOUTHEASTERN MONTANA.
authors: Cornforth C.
abstract: Western Energy Co. of Butte, Mont, a wholly owned subsidiary of Montana Power Co. , has reserves of 850-million tons of low sulfur (0. 7%S), sub-bituminous coal (8. 0% ash, averaging 8700 Btu), located near Colstrop, 100 mi east of Billings, Mont, the surface mining operation of the 25-ft thick Rosebud seam producing at present over 5-million tpy of coal (with a 1977 target of 12-13 million tpy) are described.

title: WOODSREEF ASBESTOS.
authors: Anon
abstract: Barraba asbestos mine and mill, located in north eastern part of New South Wales and operated by the Chrysotile Corp. of Australia Ltd, wholly owned subsidary of Woodreef Mines Ltd. has total reserves of 90-million tons of ore thus placing the deposit among the six biggest asbestos mines in the free world. Surface mining, and ore treatment methods at the rate of 5,800 tons/mo. are described.

title: SCOOP ON SHOVELS, LOADERS, AND DRAGLINES.
authors: White L.
abstract: Based on information derived from American manufacturers of bucketed surface mining equipment, the paper presents new developments in the design of shovels, draglines, and front-end wheel loaders. Other topics include: ways to obtain better equipment, the relationship of Federal regulations to cost increases, and the competitiveness of the big new front-end loaders with shovels in pit production.

title: Limiting Characteristic Data of Steel-Cable-Reinforced Conveyor Belts.
authors: Lachmann H.
abstract: In surface mining operations at the lignite district of Cologne, West Germany, steel-cable-reinforced conveyor belting with an ultimate tensile strength of 5400 kp/cm (over 100 tons/cm of width) is being used. Should conveying be introduced on a larger scale in the future to relieve transportation of bulk materials by road, rail, or water, much larger installations would be needed. Paper analyzes the limitations involved in construction of this type of belting, weight of belts, vulcanization techniques, required width of the belt for various tensile strength, as well as in drives, and concludes that the ultimate tensile strength of 10,000 kp/cm (about 200 tons/cm of width) appears to be the limit.

title: BULGARIAN NON-FERROUS METAL MINING IN FULL DEVELOPMENT.
authors: Derlipanski D.
abstract: Today non-ferrous metal mining and metallurgy is a rapidly expanding industry in Bulgaria holding an important position in the national economy. This fact is proven by statistics which show that between 1947 and 1971 the production of llead-zinc-, and copper ores has increased from 96,000 and 25,000 tons to 4,451,000 and 9,509,000 tons respectively. Paper includes a map showing the Bulgarian non-ferrous metal ore deposits and main mining and metallurgical centers. Lead-zinc ore bodies are mined by underground methods whereas surface mining prevails in copper mining. Metallurgical developments are reported.

title: TAILINGS REMOVAL PROJECT OPENS NEW HORIZONS FOR RESLURRYING PROCESS.
abstract: Mill tailings from the copper ore treatment plant operated in the Philippines by the Atlas Consolidated Mining and Dev. Co are pumped 16 mi away from shore into the ocean. Since the pipeline is of service approximately 10% of the time the tailings have to be temporarily impounded. Lack of suitable space for a new tailing pond led to adopting the Marconaflo process for reslurrying the tailings in a deep pond. Paper discusses many other potential applications of the process in vat or heap leaching, surface mining etc.

title: Significance of wathering in a pennsylvanian sandstone to pollution from strip mines
authors: Grube W.E.; Smith R.M.; Jencks E.M.; Singh R.N.
abstract: WE discuss here some of the factors relevant to the formation of acid in the spoil heaps that result from surface mining of the Upper Freeport coal in northern West Virginia. The coal is overlaid by the Lower Mahoning sandstone<sup>1</sup>, a uniform, quartzose, channel-fill sandstone that can be 30 to 50 feet thick. Pyrite (FeS<inf>2</inf>) is the chief acid-forming species in the sandstone<sup>2</sup>. © 1972 Nature Publishing Group.

title: CONQUISTA, CONOCO-PIONEER U//3O//8 VENTURE, ON STREAM.
authors: Anon
abstract: Development of the uranium ore mining and milling complex at Fall City, Tex, producing over 600,000 t/yr of ore and 1. 5 million lb of U//3O//8, from small and scattereed deposits by surface mining, required careful planning and versatile equipment because of the wide range of operating conditions encountered.

title: CONQUISTA MINES WIDE-RANGING SOUTH TEXAS URANIUM DEPOSITS.
authors: Anon
abstract: The Conquista Project - a uranium mining and milling complex owned jointly by Continental Oil Co. and Pioneer Nuclear, Inc - began processing uranium ore near Falls City, Tex. , in February 1972. Mine output from open pits will total 600,000 tpy of ore, from which uranium will be extracted by acid leach, solvent extraction, concentration, and precipitation. Surface mining techniques and milling 2000 tpd of ore are described. Flowsheet of the mill is shown.

title: MINING GUIDEBOOK.
authors: Anon
abstract: Mining Guidebook discusses recent developments in: initial planning; continuous, longwall, and conventional mining; roof control; haulage and hoisting; ventilation fundamentals; mine drainage and acid mine water treatment; surface mining; coal preparation and unit-train loading; maintenance engineering; efficient power designs; purchasing and warehousing; and safety.

title: MERITS OF OPEN PIT VS. UNDERGROUND MINING IN BUTTE.
authors: Hannifan M.K.
abstract: Paper describes development of mining in the Butte, Mont. mineral district over the past 25 yrs, characterized by block caving (1947-1962), vein stoping (1880 to present) and surface mining (1955 to present) and analyzes the first and third method from viewpoints of cutoff grade, outstanding reserves, and cost of mining. (Block caving was discontinued in 1962 because of interference with surface mining in the same area. ) Potential novel methods (open pit with high discard ratio offset by leach dump credits or underground low grade-high efficiency) are mentioned.

title: ACID MINE DRAINAGE WORKSHOP.
authors: Ahmad M.
abstract: Proceedings contains: presented papers; examination of problems and/or technologies encountered during field trips; and discussion. Among topics covered were: rate of pyrite oxidation and acid production in the field; deep mine sealing; hydrological approach to control acid pollution; the legal framework of acid mine drainage control; acid mine drainage abatement in surface mining; and reclamation of land and of toxic spoilbanks.

title: SHORTWALL: A WAY TO BOOST PRODUCTION.
authors: Zachar F.
abstract: For ecological reasons greater emphasis as before is being placed in this country on the underground coal mining vs surface mining. This poses economical problems since the productivity in underground mining has been going down, thus raising the cost of production. It would appear that a solution may be found in converting, hitherto most popular room-and-pillar mining system, to the shortwall (about 150 ft long face) system that permits a better utilization of mechanical equipment (continuous coal miners, self advancing, hydaulic steel supports, conveyors etc) as well as improving the ventilation and dust control.

title: Land application of solid waste
authors: Jackson G.B.; Myrick H.N.
abstract: The above beneficial aspects of land application of solid waste can be utilized most effectively in reclaiming stripped surface soils near abandoned surface mining operations. The adaptation of the environment in this manner toward the treatment of a suitable solid waste represents a least cost approach in order to obtain maximum waste treatment with maximum future land benefits. In this instance, suitable wastes become environmental assets rather than environmental polluters.

title: WHEN ARE WE GOING TO MINE OIL?
authors: Herkenhoff E.
abstract: Precarious state of energy supply in this country calls for examination of hitherto unexploited sources of fuels. Paper points out that there exist 383 shallow(less than 900 ft deep) oil fields plus deposits of oil sand and oil shales all of which could and should be exploited by surface mining combined, wherever necessary, with hot water processing. Preliminary economics for a domestic operation are analyzed.

title: CURRENT DRILLING AND BLASTING PRACTICES IN OPEN PIT MINES.
authors: Bauer A.
abstract: Among the recent trends in drilling and blasting practice in surface mining, as reviewed in the paper, the growing popularity of large rotary drills, replacing the percussive drills, has been noted. Hole sizes range up to 15-in. 30-in. diam holes have been tried in materials that freeze or set like concrete during winter (tar sands in Canada). ANFO and slurries predominate in open pits; slurries, however, have continued to expand in usage and applications. Effect of good blasting fragmentation on performance of power shovels is stressed.

title: Are Landowners Underpaid or Overpaid for Surface Mining Mineral Rights? Real Investment Values and Original Market Prices of Land in Eastern Kentucky
source: American Journal of Economics and Sociology

authors: ANON
abstract: Aloe Coal Co of Imperial, Pa, is producing 60,000 t/mo of coal by surface mining. In order to reduce cost of mining as well as to speed up land reclamation the company entered into a contractual arrangement with the City of Pittsburgh, whereby the former is paid for picking up an average of 700 tpd of solid refuse, transporting it over a distance of 18 mi, spreading and compacting it in mined- out open pits. In order to prevent water pollution, the refuse is placed over an impervious clay lining.

title: Survey of crawler dozers and wheel frontend loaders
authors: JONES DC
abstract: Originally considered as '%'service'%' machines in strip mining of coal, these tractor units have experienced rapid growth in recent years in both application and size, even to the extent of replacing older type machines. Paper reviews the types of commercially available machines and cites in tabulated form selected data on crawler tractors and rubber wheel front end loaders used in surface mining.

title: EXCAVATORS
authors: RUMFELT H
abstract: The development, capabilities and relative merits of the big excavators used for surface and strip mining are surveyed in this article. Along with his discussion of shovels, draglines, and bucketwheel excavators, the author considers the future of these machines and of surface mining itself. He also discusses the possible influence of environmental regulation on surface mining and points out some improvements which would make surface excavators more economical to operate.

title: Environmental side effects of rising industrial output, (Studies in Social and Economic Process)
authors: VAN TASSEL ED AJ
abstract: The complex of problems involved in dealing with environmental pollution was the subject of a research seminar held at Hofstra University, School of Business. Some of the problems considered are- % water pollution and expanding production in the steel, paper, chemical, and petroleum industries; nonindustrial water pollution; thermal pollution; disposal of atomic wastes; air pollution and the expanding consumption of fuels; solid waste disposal problems; harmful side effects of pesticide use; and the environmental effects of surface mining and mineral waste generation.

title: Mining and ecology in the arid environment, Proceedings, Mar 22- 27 1970, Tucson, Ariz
authors: PETERS ED WC
abstract: Proceedings contains 21 papers discussing following groups of topics- perspectives facing the mining industry in title region from the viewpoint of environmental engineering; air pollution control with emphasis on fumes emission; management of water resources; land reclamation with emphasis on surface mining and tailings disposal; control and design of mining operations; and evaluation of quality environment. Minutes of discussions and bibliographic references are included.

title: PRODUCTION POTENTIAL OF COPPER DEPOSITS ASSOCIATED WITH PERMIAN RED BED FORMATIONS IN TEXAS, OKLAHOMA, AND KANSAS
source: U S Bur Mines Rep Invest 7422
authors: STROUD RB; MCMAHAN AB; STROUP RK; HIBPSHMAN MH
abstract: Bureau of Mines studies of copper-bearing Permian red beds, which extend from north-central Texas through western Oklahoma to south- western Kansas, indicate heretofore undefined commercial possibilities for low-grade, medium- volume, surface mining operations. Potential orebodies are indicated containing 0. 5 to 1. 5% copper in zones 6 to 12 in. thick. Cost analysis studies indicate a commercial operation is feasible for a hypothecated 1000 tpd ore mining and milling complex where a maximum of 60 ft of overburden can be removed in mining a seam of shale 12 in. thick containing 1. 2% copper.

authors: PEIRCE HW; KEITH SB; WILT JC

Black Mesa coal field, containing some 20 billion t of coal within 1700 ft from the surface is being developed for surface mining of good quality coal to be pipelined to Mojave power plant in Nevada. Oil, natural gas and helium deposits occur in the northeastern Plateau province. Production since 1954 amounted to 9. 3 million bbl of oil, 8. 5 and 5. 5 billion cu ft of naturalgas and helium respectively, but the potential is still largely untested. Uranium ores will need a considerable amount of exploration.

Article describes some of the latest techniques developed for the efficient use of explosives and blasting procedures in surface mining.

Since World War II, track-or rubber- tire mounted front end loaders have found increasing use in coal mining, and for the last several years, they have been playing a vital role in contour mining. title: Surface Mine Planning Adaptations for the Integration of Autonomous Haulage Systems: A Review
authors: Chimbwanda T.B.; Bettencourt T.; Risso N.; Bheemasetti T.V.; Anani A.; Momayez M.
keywords: autonomous haulage systems | haul road design | human–machine interface | mine planning
abstract: Autonomous haulage systems (AHSs) have become increasingly important as mining operations seek to improve productivity and remove workers from hazardous environments. The systematic integration of this technology requires not only operational change management but also a deeper understanding of mine planning implications. The existing literature describes AHSs and implementation guidelines with a focus on operational safety and autonomous system architecture, but it does not systematically address required planning-level adaptations. This study aims to identify how surface mine planning frameworks must evolve to accommodate autonomy in open-pit metal mining operations. A systematic review was conducted using the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) methodology, with emphasis on identifying the principal aspects of AHSs that must be considered in mine planning strategies. Findings reveal major shifts in workforce dynamics, communication infrastructure, and haul-road geometry, and show that road-width and load-channelization questions remain site-specific research needs rather than settled design rules. This study highlights the need for (i) mine planning frameworks that treat AHSs as a constraint on pit geometry, haul-road structural and functional design, fleet selection, production scheduling, road-maintenance strategy, and economic and social evaluation; (ii) human–systems integration and improved human-autonomous collaboration; and (iii) empirical validation of workforce transition strategies for more effective and safe deployment.

title: Geochemical, geochronological and textural evidence from bentonite and K-bentonite layers within the no. 3 coal seam, Haerwusu Mine, Jungar Coalfield, Ordos Basin
authors: Hao H.; Jiu B.; Huang W.; Shang Z.; Wang Z.; Qin B.; Huang L.; Zhao Y.; Chen H.
keywords: Bentonite | K-bentonite | North China Craton | Provenance | Zircon geochemistry
abstract: Altered volcanic ash layers, such as bentonite and K-bentonite, provide key insights into tectonic evolution, coal seam correlation, and the enrichment of critical metals (e.g., REE, Li, and Ga) in coal-bearing sequences. In this study, we report for the first time the discovery of a composite interval of bentonite and K-bentonite layers with a cumulative thickness of ∼1.5 m within the No. 3 coal seam of the Haerwusu surface mine, located in the Jungar Coalfield, north China. This finding is highly significant given the typical prevalence of thin tonsteins in these Carboniferous-Permian strata. This study aims to clarify the magmatic origins and tectonic implications of the bentonite and K-bentonite. An integrated in-situ study of zircon U-Pb geochronology and trace element geochemistry was performed on altered volcanic ash samples. Zircons from both the bentonite and K-bentonite samples yielded consistent Early Permian ages (283.5 ± 4.8 Ma for bentonite; 286.0 ± 5.4 Ma for K-bentonite), indicating contemporaneous volcanic activity. Zircon trace element systematics revealed pronounced negative Eu anomalies (Eu/Eu* = 0.1–0.52) and positive Ce anomalies (Ce/Ce* = 1.09–178), with U/Yb ratios (0.3–2.2) and Nb/Yb ratios (0.002–0.01) plotting within the continental arc field. These geochemical signatures consistently indicate felsic magmatism with a significant continental crustal contribution, generated under high oxygen fugacity conditions characteristic of subduction-related magmas in an active continental margin. Our results suggest that the volcaniclastic components of both bentonite and K-bentonite layers were likely linked to subduction-related volcanism along the northern margin of the North China Craton. Variations in trace element concentrations between the two rock types are interpreted to reflect varying proportions of terrigenous detrital input and localized diagenetic modification, rather than distinct magmatic sources or complex fractional crystallization processes. These findings offer useful insights into the late Paleozoic tectonic evolution of the northern North China Craton (NCC) margin and highlight the utility of zircon trace element geochemistry in resolving provenance controversies in altered volcanic-sedimentary sequences.

title: Evaluation of coal mine methane inventory methods using aircraft-based approaches in the Bowen Basin, Australia
authors: Harris S.J.; Krautwurst S.; Hacker J.; Lunt M.; Borchardt J.; Bai M.; Boesch H.; Brain T.; Burrows J.P.; Chakravarty S.; Field R.A.; Fisher R.E.; France J.L.; Gerilowski K.; Huhs O.; Junkermann W.; Kelly B.F.J.; Kumm M.; Lanoisellé M.; Lieff W.; McGrath A.; Murphy A.; Röckmann T.; Salmon Z.; Schindewolf J.; Thoböll J.; van der Veen C.; Bovensmann H.
abstract: Australia uses a blend of IPCC Tier 2 and 3 bottom-up approaches to estimate and report fugitive coal mine methane (CH<inf>4</inf>) emissions. To date, Tier 3 reporting for underground coal mines, which predominantly relies on direct measurements of ventilated air, has not been systematically assessed against top-down atmospheric measurements. Tier 2 coal core-based emission factors and Tier 3 model guidelines for estimating surface (open-cut) mine emissions similarly lack verification. Here, an in-situ and a remote sensing aircraft-based approach were used to quantify CH<inf>4</inf> emission rates from 17 coal mines in the Bowen Basin, Australia. When compared to bottom-up mean annual reported estimates, airborne estimates from underground mines showed a non-significant mean positive bias of 0.28 t h<sup>−1</sup> (p = 0.28,n = 8 estimates) and good agreement (normalised root mean squared error (NRMSE) = 0.20). When aggregated, top-down measured emissions from all underground mines were within 8 % of bottom-up reported totals. In contrast, aircraft-based estimates from surface mines showed a significant mean positive bias of 3.7 t h<sup>−1</sup> CH<inf>4</inf> (p = 0.001,n = 10 estimates) and poor agreement (NRMSE = 0.86). In aggregate, top-down emissions from all surface mines were 3.6 times the bottom-up totals. Alignment between airborne top-down and measured vented underground coal mine emissions increases confidence in Australia’s Tier 3 direct monitoring methods, while the difference between top-down and bottom-up surface mine emission estimates suggests core-based methods require review. Given that surface mines in the Basin alone account for ∼ 38 % of national production, the contribution of coal mining to Australia’s CH<inf>4</inf> emissions may exceed the reported ∼ 19 %.

title: Comparative assessment of the vertical distribution of respirable particulate matter in surface coal and metal mines using unmanned aerial vehicle mounted low-cost sensor
authors: Penchala A.; Patra A.K.; Mishra N.; Pradhan D.S.; Thota B.
keywords: Chromite dust particles | Coal dust particles | Low-cost air sensors | Multiple path particle dosimetry | Occupational health risk | Unmanned aerial vehicle
abstract: Assessing respirable particulate matter (PM) concentration along the vertical depth of the surface mine provides important information on exposure risks, source contributions, and dispersion dynamics. This study investigates the variation of PM<inf>10</inf>, PM<inf>2.5</inf>, and PM<inf>1</inf> mass concentration at different vertical depths in two 130 m deep surface mines (coal and metal). Using a low-cost PM sensor mounted on an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV), a total of 54 vertical flights were conducted from the pit bottom to the pit top. Analysis of UAV measurements revealed a significant variability in airborne PM levels at different depths. Coal and metal mines have shown elevated PM levels at the pit bottom and minimum concentrations at the pit top. Higher PM concentrations were reported in the coal mine compared to the metal mine, due to the greater amount of material (coal and overburden) being handled. Both mines have shown a decreasing PM concentration profile, with a higher fall in the metal (24–73%) compared to the coal mine (6–57%) for a similar vertical depth. This can be attributed to the high-density metal particles having a quicker settling tendency than the finer and less dense coal dust particles. Health risk assessment of miners due to inhalation of mining-generated PM indicated that the deposited mass of PM per unit lung area varies between 0.04 and 0.12 µg m<sup>− 2</sup>. The findings of this study provide information for estimating exposure to different working groups and for forecasting PM concentrations under scenarios of mine expansion.

title: Porosity–Height Relationship of Unsaturated Soil–Rock Mixtures Based on Field and Laboratory Investigations
authors: Shrivastava S.; Deb D.
keywords: Compaction behavior | Dump material | In situ density | In situ porosity | Shear strength | Soil–rock mixtures | Triaxial shear test
abstract: The stripping ratio increases as the surface mine gets deeper, causing an increase in the height of waste dump slopes. This threatens stability since dumps are composed of soil–rock mixtures, mostly in an unsaturated state. In this research, field and laboratory studies were carried out on soil–rock mixtures to estimate in situ porosity, a key factor influencing shear strength of these materials, and consequently, the stability of waste dumps at various dump heights. Sand replacement methods in the field and standard Proctor test and consolidated drained triaxial shear tests in the lab were performed to establish the porosity–height relationship curves. It was found that the porosity decreases with height, as described by a negative exponential distribution with an exponent termed the “pseudo-pore mechanical compaction coefficient,” which determines the shape of the curve. The proposed relationship was then utilized to evaluate the compaction of soil–rock mixtures at a preresidual state. The parameters of the porosity–height relationship were also assessed for lightly, partially, and fully compacted dump slopes.

authors: Watson D.H.; Renner J.F.; Hunter E.A.
keywords: autonomous recording units | disturbance-dependent birds | passive acoustic monitoring | surface mine reclamation | working lands
abstract: Introduction: Working lands can provide habitat for declining disturbance-dependent birds, such as Bachman's Sparrow (Peucaea aestivalis) and Northern Bobwhite (Colinus virginianus), but it remains unclear whether restoration following intensive land use (e.g. surface mining) yields habitat comparable to less intensive land uses (e.g. timber production). Objectives: We evaluated effects of land use both in working lands (recently replanted surface mine reclamation site and recently replanted timber production site) and reference sites explicitly managed for wildlife (recently restored young pine savanna and mature pine savanna) and understory vegetation characteristics on relative abundance of disturbance-dependent birds within upland pine (Pinus spp.) communities in southeastern Georgia, United States. We hypothesized that the mine reclamation site would support similar bird species but in lower relative abundances than other land uses. Methods: We conducted daily acoustic surveys using autonomous recording units (ARUs) and measured vegetation surveys once per point from May to June 2024. We used Royle-Nichols models, an adapted occupancy model, to estimate relative abundance for eight bird species. Results: Land use influenced relative abundance for all species and explained more variation in relative abundance than measured understory vegetation characteristics. The mining reclamation site supported most disturbance-dependent species and, in some cases, equal or higher relative abundances, particularly for Northern Bobwhite and Common Nighthawk (Chordeiles minor). Responses across timber production and savanna sites varied by species. Vegetation effects were generally weaker and species-specific, suggesting that land use history and associated habitat legacies play an important role in structuring these bird communities. Conclusion: Working lands, including reclaimed mines, can provide habitat for disturbance-dependent birds, and ARUs are effective for evaluating these patterns across land uses.

title: Enhancing safety in surface mine blasting operations with IoT based ground vibration monitoring and prediction system integrated with machine learning
authors: Aruna M.; Vardhan H.; Tripathi A.K.; Parida S.; Raja Sekhar Reddy N.V.; Sivalingam K.M.; Yingqiu L.; Elumalai P.V.
keywords: Ground vibration | IoT-based monitoring | Machine learning | Safety enhancement | Safety net | Surface mines
abstract: Monitoring and predicting ground vibration levels during blasting operations is essential to safeguard mining sites and surrounding communities. This study introduces an IoT-based ground vibration monitoring device specifically designed for limestone mining operations, combined with machine learning algorithms to predict ground vibration intensity. The primary aim is to provide an efficient predictive tool for anticipating hazardous vibration levels, enabling proactive safety measures. A comparative analysis with the industry-standard Minimate Blaster indicates high accuracy of the IoT device, with percentage errors as low as 0.803% across multiple blasts. The study also employed Support Vector Regression (SVR), Gradient Boosting Regression (GBR), and Random Forest (RF) algorithms to predict Peak Particle Velocity (PPV) values. Among these, the Random Forest model outperformed the others, achieving an R<sup>2</sup> score of 0.92, Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.21, and Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) of 0.31. These findings underscore the reliability and predictive accuracy of the IoT-integrated Random Forest model, suggesting that it can significantly contribute to enhancing safety and operational efficiency in mining. The research highlights the potential of IoT and machine learning technologies to transform ground vibration monitoring, promoting safer and more sustainable mining practices.

title: The Impact of and Cut-Off Criteria for Auxiliary Consumables in Quantifying the CFP of Hard Coal: A Case Study of Typical Coal Mines in China
authors: Gu E.; Liu X.; Yu W.; Tian X.; Duan M.; Wang E.; Feng T.; Chen B.; Zhang Y.
keywords: auxiliary consumables | carbon footprint of product | cut-off criteria | hard coal | life cycle assessment | sustainable supply chain
abstract: Accurate carbon footprint quantification for hard coal products is essential for the development of low-carbon and sustainable supply chain emissions management. A significant challenge lies in handling the numerous auxiliary consumables used in mining, whose contributions to upstream emissions are often unclear. This study addresses this gap by calculating the cradle-to-gate carbon footprint of hard coal from typical surface and underground mines in China using a life cycle assessment. Confronted with the challenge of accounting for thousands of consumable types, this study demonstrates that economic cost is an ineffective criterion for identifying high-impact items. In contrast, consumable weight shows a strong correlation with emissions and provides a robust basis for cut-off decisions. CFP quantification results obtained using this method show that upstream emissions from other auxiliary consumables (OACs), except for fuel and explosives, account for a significant proportion of the total CFP: 1.64 ± 0.50% (1.02 ± 0.31 kg CO<inf>2</inf>e/t) in a surface mine and 11.63 ± 3.17% (2.91 ± 0.87 kg CO<inf>2</inf>e/t) in an underground mine. Based on three years of requisition data and an emission analysis, a reference list of the OACs that need to be included is provided, which can serve as a reference for determining the cut-off criteria for and system boundary of the carbon footprint of hard coal products and thus promote the better development of sustainable supply chains.

title: Assessment of vertical distribution of respirable particulate matter at a large-scale surface chromite mine using low-cost sensors and unmanned aerial vehicle
source: Measurement Journal of the International Measurement Confederation
authors: Penchala A.; Patra A.K.; Mishra N.; Taksal P.A.
keywords: Low-cost PM sensor | Random forest machine learning model | Surface chromite mine | UAV monitoring | Vertical distribution
abstract: Understanding particulate matter (PM) accumulation, dispersion, and transport within and above surface mines is crucial for protecting the health of mine workers and nearby communities. However, such assessments are often limited by measurement challenges. This study presents an advanced method that combines low-cost PM sensors with an unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV) to monitor real-time airborne PM of different sizes within and above a 130 m deep large-scale surface chromite mine. Results showed higher PM concentrations near active mining operations, followed by a gradual decline within 8–20 m of vertical height. Mean PM mass (PM<inf>1</inf>, PM<inf>2.5</inf>, PM<inf>10</inf>) concentrations recorded in-pit (54, 67, 128 µg m<sup>−3</sup>) were significantly higher than the out-pit values (48, 57, 83 µg m<sup>−3</sup>), indicating 11–35 % reduction in the vertical direction. Finer particles were more dominant at higher altitudes with UAV-to-source ratios of 0.9 (PM<inf>1</inf>), 0.8 (PM<inf>2.5</inf>), and 0.5 (PM<inf>10</inf>). A decision tree-based random forest model trained using realistic and site-specific input features performed with reasonable accuracy (R<sup>2</sup> ≥ 0.85; RMSE ≤ 0.11) in predicting PM at higher altitudes. Vertical depth of the mine was found to be the most important parameter (40 %) in explaining the variability of PM concentration in the vertical direction. The outcomes of this study provide detailed measurements of size-resolved PM mass concentrations associated with major mining activities across the vertical depth of the surface mine. The findings serve as a critical basis for evaluating the exposure risks faced by different mine worker groups and adjoining communities.

title: Optimization of borehole diameter to improve rock fragmentation in open-pit limestone mine bench blasting
authors: Ye H.; Yu M.; Shi B.; Yu Y.; Shang F.; Dong Y.; Lei T.; Li N.; Wang Q.
keywords: Borehole diameter | Jointed rock mass | Rock blasting fragmentation | Rock mass damage
abstract: Blasting fragmentation distribution in open-pit mines directly affects the efficiency and cost of subsequent production, so controlling the reasonable distribution of rock blasting fragmentation is one of the main objectives of surface mine bench blasting. Taking a limestone mine as an example, numerical simulation tests and field bench blasting tests with different borehole diameters were conducted to optimize the rock blasting fragmentation distribution. The results of numerical simulation indicate that there is an exponential functional relationship between the cumulative volume proportion of the limestone blasting fragments and dynamic damage value of the numerical model. When the borehole diameter changes from 90 to 190 mm and the powder factor remains constant, there is a cubic functional relationship between the average fragmentation size of rock blasting and the borehole diameter, and quadratic functional relationships between the big block rate, powder ore rate, and the borehole diameter, respectively. The attenuation rate of explosive stress waves during blasting with larger borehole diameters is faster than that with smaller borehole diameters. A borehole diameter of 115 mm yields the most significant stress superposition effect in the inter-borehole region. The results of field bench blasting tests show that compared to the 140 mm borehole diameter, the 115 mm borehole diameter blasting can decrease the proportion of fragments larger than 900 mm and powder ore (0–5 mm) by 52.91% and 33.85%, respectively, and increase the proportion of fragments sized 20–40 mm by 71.40%.

title: Investigation of Insect Diversity in the Restoration Area of Yimin Surface Mine in Inner Mongolia
authors: Zhang Y.; Yang Y.; Shi R.; Li X.; Yan H.; Bai X.; Gao S.
keywords: diversity of insect assemblage | ecological restoration | Yimin Surface Mine | α-diversity | β-diversity
abstract: Elucidating the relationship between changes in insect assemblage structure and diversity and the number of years of ecological restoration will help us evaluate the effectiveness of ecological restoration. Our objective is to investigate the response of the structure and diversity of insect communities in the ecological restoration area of Yimin Surface Mine in Inner Mongolia to different restoration years (1 year, 4 years, 7 years) by monitoring in 2018, 2021, and 2024. A total of 1282 insect specimens were collected using sweep-netting methods, representing 70 species from 46 families across 8 orders. The results demonstrated that as restoration progressed, insect taxa significantly increased from 25 to 55 species (p < 0.01), with key functional groups (Coleoptera and Lepidoptera) showing marked richness enhancement. α-diversity indices (Shannon–Wiener and Margalef) significantly increased, while the Simpson dominance index decreased, indicating a more homogeneous species distribution. β-diversity analysis revealed reduced compositional dissimilarity among plots during later restoration stages, reflecting enhanced assemblage stability. The trophic structure shifted from phytophagous dominance to stabilized proportions across all feeding guilds, signaling food web maturation and ecosystem development. Overall, local ecological restoration projects had a significantly positive effect on insect survival and biodiversity development. Our research addresses a gap in faunal assemblage studies of coal mine rehabilitation zones.

title: Policy support and the combination of artificial guidance with natural restoration can effectively restore the surface mine ecosystem in South China
authors: Peng Y.; Xia L.; Liu Y.; Yang R.; Zheng C.; Xie M.
keywords: Mine Landscape Restoration Index | Policy support | Restoration effect | Restoration measure | Surface mining
abstract: Assessing the effectiveness of ecological restoration policies in mining areas is vital for optimizing governmental investments and balancing financial expenditures with environmental recovery. Dongting Lake, China's second-largest freshwater lake, holds significant ecological importance in southern China, faces ecological challenges from legacy mines, yet the success of restoration efforts remains unclear. This study evaluated 170 abandoned surface mines (10 types) around Dongting Lake (2000–2023) using the Mine Landscape Restoration Index (MLRI) from remote sensing. Through MLRI time series analysis, four restoration types were identified, and their proportions and changes in MLRI values were statistically analyzed to assess the overall ecological restoration effect of the abandoned surface mines. The effectiveness of various restoration measures and policies was further compared to assess their practical impact. The effectiveness of ecological restoration policies was assessed, and the effectiveness of different restoration measures was compared to clarify the practical impacts of policies on the ecological restoration of surface mines and the applicability of restoration measures. Results indicate that 72.94 % of the mines have been significantly rehabilitated, with 105 achieving over 50 % restoration. The number of mine sites with ecologically significant restoration areas greater than 50 % is 15.48 % higher in artificially supported natural restoration than in artificially supported ecological reconstruction. Policy support has been instrumental in driving ecological recovery, with artificially supported natural restoration proving more effective than artificial ecological reconstruction. This study underscores the importance of policy support and the combination of artificial guidance with natural restoration in the ecological restoration of mining areas.

title: Application of Humate-Containing Agent for Sorbing Trace Metals in Simulated Solutions and Surface Waters from Tunnels at the ‘Degelen’ Site
authors: Dyussembayeva M.; Shakenov Y.; Kolbin V.; Tashekova A.; Aidarkhanov A.; Dzhusipbekov U.; Nurgalieva G.; Bayakhmetova Z.; Duisenbay D.; Aksakalova U.
keywords: heavy metals | humates | natural pH | Semipalatinsk Test Site | sorption | sorption capacity | tunnel water treatment
abstract: This article presents the potential use of a humic agent called ‘Superhumate’, obtained from weathered coal from the Shubarkol deposit in Kazakhstan. The experiment was conducted using model solutions and surface mine water samples from the “Degelen” site at the Semipalatinsk Test Site. The adsorption of heavy metals and toxic elements using the “Superhumate” agent was carried out under dynamic conditions using a chromatographic column. Tests were conducted at a natural pH range of 5–8 (mine waters) and with a model solution at pH 1.7. Assessing the sorption efficiency of this preparation revealed that at pH 1.7, the agent does not adsorb elements such as Cd, Cu, Pb, and Zn. Under dynamic experimental conditions, using the preparation for mine waters at natural pH levels (pH 5–8), elements such as Be, Sr, Mo, Cd, Cs, Zn, and U were efficiently adsorbed at levels of 60–95%. The sorption efficiency of Pb ions was found to be almost independent of pH. The experimental results obtained with mine water samples indicate that alkaline solutions have the highest sorption efficiency, with pH ≥ 7, which is attributed to the solubility of the agent.

title: Application of machine learning algorithms for prediction of Blast-induced Ground Vibration in View of Stiffness Ratio, Energy Coverage and Scaled Distance
authors: Agan Y.; Hudaverdi T.
keywords: Adaptive-network-based fuzzy inference system (ANFIS) | Blasting | Gaussian process regression (GPR) | Ground vibration | Support vector machine (SVM)
abstract: The purpose of this research work is to predict blast induced ground vibration in surface mine by using classical and machine learning algorithms. For the purpose of minimizing blast-induced ground vibration to acceptable levels, the level of vibration must be predicted. Blast-induced ground vibration is defined peak particle velocity (ppv) in the ground. All data used to estimation were obtained by observing real blasting operations. After the measuring of the peak particle velocity, models of the prediction were created using independent site parameters. Most of the data is used to train the model, while remaining part is used for testing. The models were created using independent blasting parameters proportionally. Thus, more parameters are included in the models without complicating the models. A thorough validation process was conducted utilizing a diverse set of nine error criteria. Artificial intelligence models have been found to outperform traditional methods in predicting ground vibration. The mean absolute error values were found to be 1.42, 1.54, and 1.78 for ANFIS, GPR, and SVM, respectively. A similar situation is observed for other error criteria as well. ANFIS appears to be the most effective model for predicting ground vibration.

title: Prediction of Rock Fragmentation for Surface Mine Blasting Through Machine Learning Techniques
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Series D
authors: Raj A.K.; Choudhary B.S.; Deressa G.W.
keywords: Machine learning | Mining | Rock blasting | Rock fragmentation | Surface mines
abstract: Blasting is essential in mining for rock fragmentation, significantly impacting downstream processes, overall productivity, and the efficiency of resource extraction. This study uses machine learning models, including decision tree regressor, random forest regressor, support vector regressor, and Extreme gradient boosting machine to predict the blast outcomes, specifically the mean fragmentation size. Field data collection involved assessing rock properties, performing pre-blasting measurements, and analyzing post-blast results through digital images of muckpiles and fragmentation distribution using Fragalyst software. The observed mean fragmentation size ranged from 0.15 m to 0.81 m, with an optimal size of 0.34 m, based on the maximum productivity of a 5 cum excavator bucket used in the study. The aim of this study is to identify the most accurate and reliable machine-learning model based on the key blast design parameters for mean fragment size prediction. The analysis of rigorous model training and Shapley feature importance revealed uniaxial compressive strength and specific charge as the key factors affecting rock fragmentation efficiency. Among the models used to predict fragmentation sizes against testing values, extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) exhibits the best performance, followed by random forest regressor, support vector regressor, and decision tree regressor. The coefficient of determination values for these models are 0.818, 0.677, 0.674, and 0.473, respectively, with corresponding mean squared errors of 0.0031, 0.0037, 0.0055, and 0.0086. Thus, XGBoost is identified as the best model for the dataset, demonstrating superior performance in predicting fragmentation outcomes.

title: Considering Uncertainty for Estimating Shear Strength Parameters of Intact Rock Using Statistical Methods
source: Journal of Analytical and Numerical Methods in Mining Engineering
authors: Mohammadi M.; Maraji M.F.
keywords: Hoek Brown Failure Criterion | Mohr Coulomb Failure Criterion | Shear Strength Parameters | t Distribution | Uncertainty
abstract: Summary One of the most critical steps in the design process of a rock structure by the limit equilibrium method is to determine the shear strength parameters. Because the prediction of these parameters is always accompanied by uncertainty. In such cases, if the range in which the actual shear strength parameters are located is obtained, the results are more reliable. Hence, in this paper, an applied technique based on probabilistic methods is developed. In the first step, by developing an innovative method for two widely used failure criteria, consist of Mohr-Coulomb and Hoek Brown, statistical samples of shear strength parameters are generated and latter, using the t distribution in which the shear strength parameters are located with confidence 95% are determined separately for the two failure criteria. The available data from the previous research are used for the case study. The results of the case study indicate that the prediction of shear strength parameters with the presented method is more accurate than the conventional methods. Introduction Stability analysis of rock structures in mining and civil structures, such as surface mine walls, dams, or rock slopes, is very necessary and important. Because the instability of each of them will cause damage and costs. Shear strength parameters are required for stability analysis. Estimation of shear strength parameters is a critical and vital step in the design and analysis of rock structures. Because the prediction of these parameters is always accompanied by uncertainty. In practice, for determining the shear strength parameters, two failure criteria consist of Mohr-Coulomb and Hoek-Brown, are widely used. The two criteria results are crisp values. Studies show that these results are affected by the uncertainties due to the heterogeneity of the rock or the mathematical relationship of the failure criterion. On the other hand, to estimate the shear strength parameters, at least the results of 5 triaxial stress tests are needed for determining these parameters based on regression. If the number of samples (number of tests) changes or the ultimate strength of one of the samples changes due to the influence of lateral stress in the experiments, the shear strength parameters vary by the regression of the results. In the past decades, some studies reported the determination of the equivalent parameters of shear strength based on the Hoek- Brown criterion [1-5]. According to Brown, the determination of exact equivalent shear strength parameters is a challenging point due to the inherent uncertainty of rock as well as the failure criterion [6]. In such cases, if the range in which the actual shear strength parameters are located is obtained, the results are more reliable [7-10]. Hence, in this paper, an applied technique based on probabilistic methods is developed. In the first step, by developing an innovative method for two widely used failure criteria, consisting of Mohr-Coulomb and Hoek-Brown, statistical samples of shear strength parameters are generated, and later, using the t distribution in which the shear strength parameters are located with confidence 95% are determined separately for the two failure criteria. The available data from the previous research are used for a case study (Table 1) [11]. Methodology and Approaches The conventional method for determining the shear strength parameters is based on the regression of the results of at least 5 groups of data obtained from samples subjected to triaxial stress, according to the Mohr-Coulomb or Hoek-Brown criteria. But in practice, if there are two different groups of triaxial test results of the same type of rock, in the regression of the test results, the shear strength parameters are also changed, and the results are not reliable. Hence, in the first step, using an innovative method, groups of different triaxial test data are generated for the desired rock, and then the cohesion and internal friction angle are determined for each group, and finally, statistical samples of the shear strength parameters are predicted. By generating statistical samples (from shear strength parameters), the range in which the real shear strength parameters are located is determined using the t distribution. Therefore, the obtained result has the highest level of certainty, and the uncertainty is reduced. Results Figure 1 shows the shear strength parameters based on the developed method and the conventional method. According to the figure, the developed method is superior concerning the conventional method. This is because of the statistical samples that were produced to determine the range in which the real parameters are located are taken from the conventional method. In other words, if the conventional method is used, the results in Figure 1 may be used in the analysis. But by utilizing the developed method, shear strength parameters are determined with higher certainty and in a more realistic range.

title: Construction of Key Technology System for Mine Ecological Restoration Under System Perspective
authors: Jiang S.Y.; Tan L.P.; Feng C.; Wang J.J.; Fan X.Y.; Li X.Y.
keywords: 3S technologies | geological disaster prevention | mine ecological restoration | soil remediation | technical system | vegetation re‐greening | water restoration
abstract: Mine ecological restoration has experienced a long-term development process in China，in which various technologies have been constantly developing and integrating. Based on the related theoretical research and field program，the technical system of mine ecological restoration was constructed，and the characteristics of key technologies were specifically grasped. In this research，the environment，including natural elements and the spatial environment，is the object of mine ecological restoration，which requires further long-term investigation and monitoring. Therefore，natural element restoration technology，space environment restoration technology，and environmental survey and restoration monitoring technology should be considered when establishing technical systems. The research showed that：① In mine natural element restoration，where soil and water are important，traditional technologies like pollution abatement with physical，chemical，and biological methods have been extensively used. Meanwhile，artificial soil reconstruction and multi-technology joint remediation became the main study focus in soil restoration and artificial wetlands have been gradually constructed as a new method in water restoration，covering water system restoration and pollution control. ② The two tasks of space environment restoration were geological disaster prevention and vegetation re‐greening. Major technologies of the former were applied to surface mine slope treatment and mining subsidence area control，the latter of which could be divided into three technical links：vegetation selection，construction，and maintenance. Although many technologies are valid，a few frontiers need to be further pursued. ③ The mine environmental investigation and restoration monitoring were based on 3S technologies，containing GIS，GPS，and RS，all of which are developing rapidly but still have a large space for integration and innovation.

title: Rock mass classification for estimating the drilling rate in a surface mine using rock mass drillability index
authors: Ghosh S.; Behera C.; Mishra M.K.
keywords: Drilling rate | Drilling time optimization | Rate of penetration | Regression analysis | Rock drillability index
abstract: Accurate determination of drilling rate in surface mines is influenced by not only the mechanical parameters of the drilling rig but also the rock properties. The primary mechanical parameters include the rotational speed, thrust force, and air flushing pressure while the rock properties include uniaxial compressive strength (UCS), tensile strength, elastic modulus, hardness, discontinuities characteristics etc. This study has attempted to quantify the geological and geotechnical characteristics of a chromite deposit using rock drillability index (RDi) by dividing the working area into ten zones. Thereafter, considering the varied geo-mechanical properties of the deposit and the net time invested for drilling, site-specific empirical relations were formulated correlating the rock drillability index with drilling rate; Schmidt hammer rebound number with uniaxial compressive strength with correlation coefficients of 0.95 and 0.97 respectively. Lastly, a new rate of penetration model was proposed by incorporating the rock drillability index and the mechanical specifications with a correlation coefficient of 0.86. Thus, this study has successfully executed rock mass classification and justified the performance efficiency of the proposed model by its comparison with a universal model. Finally, the ten zones were grouped according to their drilling rates and quantified in terms of their drillability for optimization.

title: Acid Leaching of Rare Earth Elements from Coal Ash Obtained from a Mongolian Surface Mine
authors: Jamiyansuren B.; Myagmarsuren B.; Khongorzul N.; Baatar B.
keywords: acid leaching | alkaline pre-treatment | coal ash | Rare Earth Elements | REEs from secondary sources
abstract: Rare earth elements (REEs) are crucial for various renewable and clean technologies, increasing the importance of their recovery from secondary sources. This study determines if REE content and recovery from coal samples, and their ash, could be obtained from a Mongolian coal mine deposit in sufficient quantities for reuse. 9 different coal samples were examined and the highest REE concentrations were found in samples 3, 7, and 4. Upon burning, REEs in the coal ash samples significantly increased in all three samples. Direct acid leaching further improved REE recovery (S3); moreover, when alkali pre-treatment and 1M hydrochloric acid leaching were used, REE recovery was increased even further (sample 7). These findings characterize coal ash at this mining site, and indicate that it could serve as a viable secondary source of REEs, using optimized leaching methods to enhance the effectiveness, for potential industrial applications in Mongolia.

title: A case of mixed connective tissue disease following occupational silicosis: A potantial association
authors: Hasanlı Y.S.
keywords: autoimmune | mixed connective tissue disease | silicosis
abstract: Mixed connective tissue disease is a rare autoimmune rheumatological disorder of unclear etiology. Its association with silicosis is even rarer, but it is an intriguing relationship worthy of investigation. We present the case of a 45-year-old male patient who was diagnosed with silicosis after seven years of working in a quartz surface mine. Three years following his silicosis diagnosis, he developed rheumatological complaints and was subsequently diagnosed with mixed connective tissue disease. This case highlights the association of silicosis and mixed connective tissue disease. While rare, the available literature suggests that silica particles may contribute to the development of the disease.

title: Experimental study on freeze-thaw damage characteristics and mechanical properties of fractured rock mass of surface mine slope in cold region
source: Meitan Xuebao Journal of the China Coal Society
authors: Tian S.; Zhao Y.; Si H.; Zhu C.; Li Q.
keywords: fracture mode | fractured rock mass | freeze-thaw cycle | frost heave force | rock slope
abstract: There are numerous large-scale rock slopes in the surface mines of China, which are easily affected by multiple factors such as complex geological topography and natural, engineering disturbances, thereby resulting in frequent landslide disasters. Especially in northwest China, the landslides in surface mines occur frequently due to the complicated topographical and geological structures, harsh climate and environment, as well as long-term engineering disturbance, which seriously threaten miner’s life and property safety. From the perspective of macro-micro damage evolution of characteristic slope rock masses, this study conducted the freeze-thaw test, the frost heave force evolution test, and the uniaxial compression test of fractured rock masses in the potential landslide area, based on the actual engineering geological and environmental characteristics of high-steep rock slope at an surface mine in Xinjiang province. Where multi-faceted research approaches including engineering field investigation, theoretical analysis and laboratory experimental research were adopted, and the theories and methods of rock mechanics and soil mechanics were integrated. Through these tests, the mass loss, wave velocity attenuation and frost heave force evolution characteristics of fractured rock masses with different inclinations (0°, 25°, 50°, 75°) were analyzed under different freeze-thaw cycles, and the strength and aging characteristics of fractured rock masses under different load conditions, along with the evolution of their mechanical properties under different freeze-thaw cycles were revealed. On this basis, combined with the synchronous acoustic emission test, the final rock fracture mode, the morphology and macro-micro propagation mechanisms of cracks during the rock deformation and failure process were expounded. The results show that under the action of freeze-thaw cycles (0, 10, 20, 30 times), the saturation mass of rock masses increased first and then decreased, while the P-wave velocity showed a decelerated decay. The evolution of frost heave force could be divided into five stages: the incubation stage, the heaving stage, the stabilization stage, the secondary heaving stage and the melting stage. Moreover, the generation of frost heave force, the time required to reach peak and the peak values were all positively correlated with the fracture inclination. The peak values of frost heave forces of rock samples with crack inclinations (0°, 25°, 50°, 75°) are 3.68, 3.88, 4.04, 4.13 MPa, respectively. The frost heave effect resulted in a decreased strength of rock masses due to the repeated tensioning action, which was a major cause of slope instability in this cold region. The stress-strain relationship of rock masses under uniaxial compression and the trend of crack volume strain were roughly the same, which could be divided into five typical stages: the microfracture closure stage, the elastic deformation stage, the yield stage, the crack acceleration stage and the post-peak stage. The compressive strength and elastic modulus of rock masses decreased linearly with the increase of freeze-thaw cycles, while increased linearly with the increase of fracture inclination. According to the final fracture morphology of rock samples and the Gaussian mixture model-based classification of microcracks, the tensile fracture was the predominant microfracture mode of rock samples (up to 54.2%), followed by the mixed mode (up to 42.3%). With the increase of freeze-thaw cycles (20–30 times), the proportion of mixed-mode microcracks increased and that of shear cracks decreased. Moreover, the macroscopic failure mode was the mixed tensile–shear failure.

title: Using Overall Equipment Effectiveness as a Driver for Improving the Productivity of Continuous Mining Systems
authors: Pavloudakis F.; Roumpos C.; Agioutantis Z.
keywords: Availability | Coal | Mining equipment | Reliability | Utilization
abstract: The gradual depletion of mineral deposits with favorable stripping ratios and ore grades, combined with the increased demand for raw materials used in digital and energy technologies, makes unavoidable the transition to the exploitation of deeper deposits with a high degree of technical difficulty. The mines developed for the exploitation of these deposits must effectively utilize the installed equipment to keep their production costs as low as possible. Using digital technologies to record and process equipment operating parameters enables the determination of several key performance indicators that can be used in decision-making processes. In this framework, the objective of this article was to demonstrate how the proven concept of overall equipment effectiveness (OEE) can be the driver for improved production performance in surface mines equipped with continuous mining machines. For this purpose, the lignite surface mine of South Field, located in the region of Western Macedonia, Greece, was used as a case study to investigate numerous parameters that affect the availability, utilization, and performance of continuous mining equipment. According to the results obtained from the analysis of the mine operation records for the period 2015–2020, the low OEE values achieved were related to the reduced availability as a result of frequent failures caused by the excavation of the hard rock inclusions of the overburden, as well as the reduced utilization, as a result of the multi-layered structure of the lignite strata that is dealt with frequent changes of the digging faces and the lack of personnel due to the ongoing restructuring in the context of lignite phase-out. Nevertheless, it was proved that OEE could be successfully used for the improvement of mine productivity by supporting decisions such as planning the annual maintenance of bucket-wheel excavators, managing the operators and maintenance personnel, and deciding about the remaining life span of equipment because of the energy transition.

title: Integrated smart dust monitoring and prediction system for surface mine sites using IoT and machine learning techniques
authors: Tripathi A.K.; Aruna M.; Parida S.; Nandan D.; Elumalai P.V.; Prakash E.; Isaac JoshuaRamesh Lalvani J.S.C.; Rao K.S.
keywords: Dust pollutants | IoT technology | Machine learning models | Miner's safety | Mining industry
abstract: The mining industry confronts significant challenges in mitigating airborne particulate matter (PM) pollution, necessitating innovative approaches for effective monitoring and prediction. This research focuses on the design and development of an Internet of Things (IoT)-based real-time monitoring system tailored for PM pollutants in surface mines, specifically PM 1.0, PM 2.5, PM 4.0, and PM 10.0. The novelty of this work lies in the integration of IoT technology for real-time measurement and the application of machine learning (ML) techniques for accurate prediction based on recorded dust pollutants data. The study's findings indicate that PM 1.0 pollutants exhibited the highest concentration in the atmosphere of the ball clay surface mine sites, with the stockyard site registering the maximum levels of PM pollutants (28.45 µg/m<sup>3</sup>, 27.89 µg/m<sup>3</sup>, 26.17 µg/m<sup>3</sup>, and 27.24 µg/m<sup>3</sup>, respectively) due to the dry nature of clay materials.
