title: Brackish Water in Unsaturated Confining Beds at a Texas Lignite Mine
authors: Dutton A.R.
abstract: Deposits of low permeability are hydrologic barriers between reclaimed land and juxtaposed aquifers and should limit the impact of mining on ground‐water quality. Clay‐stone and mudstone in argillaceous facies of the Calvert Bluff Formation (lower Eocene, Wilcox Group) function as confining beds in the East Texas Basin. In the subsurface and at the outcrop, water in argillaceous deposits is brackish to saline. Samples of vadose water from the outcrop of confining beds at the Big Brown lignite mine in Freestone County, Texas, have a chloride concentration of up to 3,500 mg/l and total dissolved solids of up to 8,000 mg/l. Ground‐water composition evolved from Eocene sea water by seven‐ to nine‐fold dilution with rain water. Ion exchange, pyrite oxidation, and calcite dissolution further modified water composition. The amount of recharge through the vadose zone where confining layers crop out is probably negligible over an extremely long time. Meteoric flushing in reclaimed land at the surface mine is many times greater than that in unmined mudstone deposits, and the chemical composition of vadose water in reclaimed land is changed by further dilution and water‐rock reactions. Copyright © 1985, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Morphometry of coal and bentonite surface mine and livestock impoundments in the Northern High Plains.
authors: Rumble M.A.; Anderson M.T.; Hawkes C.L.
abstract: Mining for coal and bentonite has resulted in water impoundments which, along with livestock watering impoundments, can provide habitat for aquatic and wetland organisms, waterfowl and other terrestrial wildlife.-from Authors

title: Results of a tree species trial on a recontoured surface mine in southwestern Virginia.
authors: Torbert J.L.; Burger J.A.; Lien J.N.; Schoenholtz S.H.
abstract: Five pine and 10 hardwood species were planted on a reclaimed, return-to-contour, strip-mine site. A systemic herbicide was sprayed on half of each of 4 experimental blocks prior to the 2nd growing season. After 3 growing seasons, this treatment resulted in increased survival of black locust Robinia pseudoacacia (90% survival and a 10-fold increase in height), black alder Alnus glutinosa, sycamore Platanus occidentalis and cottonwood Populus deltoides. As a group, the pines outperformed the hardwoods. Loblolly Pinus taeda and Virginia pine Pinus virginiana were the fastest growing; survival of each was significantly higher on the sprayed plots.-from Authors

title: Systematic variation of iron disulfide occurrences in the Permo- Pennsylvanian Waynesburg coal at a surface mine near Morgantown, West Virginia.
source: 9e Congres International De Stratigraphie Et De Geologie Du Carbonifere Washington Et Champaign Urbana 1979 Compte Rendu Vol 4
authors: King H.; Renton J.
abstract: The abundance, size, shape, and maceral association of the iron disulfide minerals within the Waynesburg coal were studied. At the mine of study, the coal appears in two 1.5 m-thick benches. Pyrite was the most abundant iron disulfide mineral in the upper bench; marcasite was the most abundant one in the lower bench. Microscopically, iron disulfide occurrences were classified into five categories: 1) framboids, 2) euhedral aggregates, 3) isolated euhedra, 4) cleat and fracture fillings, and 5) irregular shapes. Framboids, euhedral aggregates, and isolated euhedra were the dominant morphologies in the upper bench; irregularly shaped marcasite dominated the lower bench.-from Authors

title: Comparative techniques used to evaluate Thematic Mapper data for land cover classification in Logan County, West Virginia ( USA).
source: Landsat 4 Science Characterization Early Results Vol 4 Applications Symposium Greenbelt February 1983
authors: Brumfield J.; Witt R.; Blodget H.; Marcell R.
abstract: Several digital data processing techniques were evaluated in an effort to identify and map active/abandoned, partially reclaimed, and fully revegetated surface mine areas in the central portion of Logan County. The TM data were first subjected to various enhancement procedures, including a linear contrast stretch, principal components and canonical analysis transformations. At the same time, 4 general procedures were followed to produce 6 classifications as a means of comparing the techniques involved. Preliminary results show that various feature extraction/data reduction techniques provide classification results equal or superior to the more straightforward unsupervised clustering technique. -from STAR, 23(13), 1985

title: Potential Effects on Ground Water of a Hypothetical Surface Coal Mine in Indiana
authors: Banaszak K.
abstract: The possible mine will remove a gently, less than 50 feet per mile, westerly dipping Springfield coal from an area covered by glacial till and some channel sands and gravel. The area is flat, with less than 20 feet of relief in a square mile. The channel sands and gravels, the till and the bedrock are capable of yielding ground water at 5 to 75,3 to 10, and 1 to 10 gallons per minute (gpm), respectively. The ground water in the drift and the shallow bedrock is calcium‐bicarbonate type, contrasting with the sodium‐bicarbonate type in the deep bedrock. The surface mine will feature selective handling of overburden. The probable hydrologic consequences of the mine will be 1) a short‐term, areally limited dewatering, 2) an increase in dissolved solids, 3) a change in ground water chemistry in some areas to a calcium‐bicarbonate sulfate water, 4) an increase in ground water storage, and 5) a new integrated surface water system. The proposed ground water monitoring system will include seven monitoring wells in the glacial material and one in the bedrock. The primary effort in ground water monitoring to the west of the mine will be to detect changes in the quality of the ground water, whereas to the east, changes in both quality and quantity will need to be monitored intensively. Copyright © 1985, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: SURFACE MINE ELECTRICAL DISTRIBUTION SYSTEMS.
authors: Alexander J.
abstract: The review covers UK criteria for power system design and installation with a discussion of each point and the methods of calculation.

title: Final comparison of TM and MSS data for surface mine assessment in Logan County, West Virginia.
source: Landsat 4 Science Investigations Summary Proc Vol 2 1983
authors: Witt R.; Blodget H.; Marcell R.
abstract: A variety of classifications during both raw and transformed MSS and TM data sets from September 4, 1982 were performed for the Logan County, West Virginia study area. The object was to compare the utility of TM and MSS data for delineating small, irregular ground features, particularly surface mines, and also to test data reduction/transformation techniques (band selection, canonical analysis, and principal components) in relation to a traditional means of unsupervised classification. Statistical results demonstrate that, on the average, the TM classifications yielded an overall 0.53 factor of improvement.-from STAR, 22(20), 1984

title: APPRAISAL OF THE CORRECT TRANSPORT SYSTEM FOR A SURFACE MINE.
authors: Bullivant D.
abstract: In general, the objective of any mining operation is to extract the ore from the ground and transport it to the process plant at the minimum cost. It can be argued that the winning of the ore does add value to the product, but certainly the transportation aspect is only a pure cost factor and therefore must be achieved in the most economic way. Off-road trucks represent a very flexible means of handling material within a surface mine and this feature has made them the most widely-used method of transportation.

title: Habitat use by Red-tailed Hawks in surface-mined areas
authors: Mindell D.; Samuel D.
abstract: Habitat use by 4 radio-tagged red-tailed hawks (Buteo jamaicensis) was monitored during 708 transmitter-days in coal surface-mined areas in northern West Virginia and southwestern Pennsylvania in 1977 and 1978. Mean cumulative home range size for the 3 adults was 316.8 ha (3.2 km<sup>2</sup>). Red-tailed hawks showed significant (P<0.005) tendencies to elect certain habitats over others. Descending order of habitat electivity was: 1) woods edge with open area not surfacemined. 2) woods edge with surface-mined area. 3) deciduous woods, 4) open area not surface-mined, and 5) surface-mined area. Red-tailed hawks' flexibility in niche requirements allowed them to exploit reclaimed area. Recommendations for surface mine reclamation are given. © 1984 Science and Technology Letters.

title: DESIGN OF SURFACE MINE BLASTS - A MICROCOMPUTER PACKAGE FOR FIELD USE.
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: Ghose A.K.; Samaddar A.B.
abstract: In the search for optimum design of surface mine blasts, several empirical and computer models have been proposed. The paper examines the outline of an interactive model which utilizes theoretical as well as empirical relationships to arrive at an optimum design strategy. An interactive microcomputer package developed for field application is reported.

title: Influence of wetlands and coal mining on stream water chemistry
authors: Kelman Wieder R.; Lang G.E.
abstract: Comparisons of stream water chemistry over a 2 yr period in East Fork, which drains an entirely forested watershed, and Big Run, which drains a forested watershed 8 % of which is occupied by Big Run Bog, indicated that Big Run Bog had no effect on stream water H<sup>+</sup> or Cl<sup>-</sup> concentrations, but with increasing stream discharge the wetland was a source of Ca<sup>++</sup> Mg<sup>++</sup>, K<sup>+</sup>, Na<sup>+</sup>, NO<inf>3</inf><sup>-</sup>, and SO<inf>4</inf><sup>-</sup>, and a sink for Fe<sup>+ +</sup>. Further comparisons with Tub Run, which drains a forested watershed, 13 and 12% of which is occupied by Tub Run Bog and an abandoned, unreclaimed coal surface mine, respectively, suggested that Tub Run Bog removes H<sup>+</sup>, Ca ++, Mg<sup>++</sup>, Fe<sup>++</sup>, and 50<inf>4</inf><sup>-</sup> from inputs of acid mine drainage. Wetland areas on the landscape contribute to the regulation of stream water chemistry in ways that are different from upland areas, and wetlands may have considerable applied potential for minimizing the impact of the mine drainage on stream water quality. © 1984 D. Reidel Publishing Company.

title: HYDROGEOCHEMICAL ASPECTS OF SURFACE MINE RECLAMATION IN THE NORTHERN GREAT PLAINS.
source: Transactions of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers
authors: Groenewold G.H.; Koob R.D.
abstract: Studies of several coal-mining sites in western North Dakota have resulted in the development of a hydrogeochemical model which accounts for the observed chemical characteristics of subsurface water in undisturbed settings. Critical hydrogeochemical processes include sulfide oxidation, gypsum precipitation and dissolution, carbonate mineral dissolution and cation exchange. The hydrogeochemical model is equally applicable to undisturbed and spoils landscapes and that the major species of concern in this region are sodium and sulfate. This research indicates that the major source of sulfate is sulfides in the overburden and that the solubility of sulfate in groundwater in these settings is largely controlled by the sodium/calcium ratio.

title: Aggregation of surface mine soil by interaction between VAM fungi and lignin degradation products of lespedeza
authors: Rothwell F.
keywords: Aggregate stability | Glomus clarum | Lespedeza cuneata | Minesoil aggregation | VAM fungi
abstract: The external mycelium of a vesicular-arbuscular mycorrhizal (VAM) fungus was effective in aggregating a sandy loam minesoil. The polysaccharide nature of the soil binding agent on hyphal surfaces and on the surfaces of sand particles in contact with the hyphae within the aggregate was demonstrated with the periodic acid-Schiff reagent staining reaction. A possible stabilizing mechanism for macroaggregates was proposed that involves a coupling reaction between glucosamines in the hyphal walls of the fungus with phenolic compounds released during lignin degradation of sericea lespedeza root tissue. © 1984 Martinus Nijhoff/Dr W. Junk Publishers.

title: Within-Tree Distributions and Seasonality of Immature Stages of the Bronze Birch Borer, Agrilus Anxius (Coleoptera: Buprestidae)
authors: Loerch C.R.; Cameron E.A.
abstract: Distributions of immature stages of the bronze birch borer, Agrilus anxius Gory (Coleoptera: Buprestidae), infesting young European white birch, Betula pendula Roth, were studied on a surface mine reforestation site in Pennsylvania. Eggs of A. anxius were common on boles of trees from mid-June through mid-August, in clusters of up to 14 eggs. Almost 70% of the eggs were in crevices in the dark triangular patch at branch origins. Larvae were present throughout the year. Fourth instars comprised 93.1% of the overwintering population. Vertical distributions of eggs, larvae, and pupae along the bole were random relative to available surface area. Consequently, each stage was more abundant on the lower half than on the upper half of trees. Eggs and first instars were concentrated on the northeast, or shaded, side of trees. Second and third instars were distributed randomly around the bole. Fourth instars overwintered and pupated primarily on the south-west aspect. © 1984, Entomological Society of Canada. All rights reserved.

title: ROCK REINFORCEMENT DESIGN FOR SURFACE MINE BENCH INSTABILITIES.
authors: Seegmiller B.
abstract: Horizontally stratified lithologies of certain open pit or strip mines create unique stability problems for mine operations. Slope instabilities may occur when a sandstone unit overlies a shale unit and ground water drains into the mine along the lithologic contact. Large sandstone blocks fail in a toppling mode and cause safety and cleanup problems. Use of rock reinforcement including chain link fencing, roof bolt mats, rock bolts, rock anchors, and shotcrete offers a possible solution.

title: CROSS-PIT SPREADER SELECTED BY COMPUTER FOR NEW SURFACE MINE.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The Texas lignite fields are becoming receptive ground for innovative mining schemes. North American Coal Corp. is considering using a team consisting of bucketwheel excavators and cross-pit spreader to strip upper strata at one of the two pits at a new multi-seam mine to be located on a 38,000-acre tract east of Dallas. A large-scale software program was used to select the cross-pit spreader for this surface mine.

title: Derivation of a diggability index for surface mine equipment selection
authors: Scoble M.; Muftuoglu Y.
abstract: This paper reports on research aimed at developing techniques to predict the influence of ground conditions on excavating equipment performance. The work was conducted in operating British surface coal mines and presents a technique for diggability assessment in that mining and geotechnical environment. A diggability index is proposed which consideres both ground conditions and excavating equipment capabilities. This is supported by reference to back-analysis of several mine excavating case studies. © 1984.

title: Surface Mine Pit Retention
source: Journal of the Air Pollution Control Association
authors: Cole C.; Fabrick A.

title: HOW ONE ENGINEER AND COMPUTER WORKSTATION DESIGN A SURFACE MINE.
authors: Chironis N.
abstract: The article deals with how a 4-million-tpy stripping operation at the Lee Ranch mine near Grants, N. M. was developed with the MINEMAP mine planning system. The system creates a mine model, graphics and mine plans to the level of detail involving ramps, roads, buildings, sumps and services.

title: WIDCO'S PROGRAM FOR UCG COMMERCIALIZATION.
authors: Paul R.
abstract: This paper describes the Tono Project, WIDCO's underground coal gasification (UCG) technology development program which is, a phased series of laboratory, field laboratory, and increasingly larger field tests leading to a commercial development. This unique approach to the commercialization of the UCG technology centers around the controlled retracting injection point (CRIP) gasification system. The Tono Project was intiated in 1979 to assess the potential for developing the unminable coal resources of the state of Washington via the UCG technology. Phase I of the program was to determine the role of the UCG in the total development of a coal resource through a total economic coal utilization (TECU). The second phase of the program was to identify potential sites within the Washington where a successful commerical-scale UCG development might be established. The third phase was to identify site-specific conditions which effect the UCG process at the Tono test site through a site characterization study conducted by Sandia National Laboratory. This paper describes the programmed full-scale field gasification test experiment which will be operating by 1986. The first commercial modules would be installed from the coal face exposed at the base of the final highwall in the surface mine, and would access and recover the coal from the area designated as the buffer zone.

title: SURFACE COAL MINING - AN APPROACH TO PRIME FARMLAND REQUIREMENTS.
authors: Sorrell S.
abstract: To obtain a negative determination for prime farmlands in its approved lignite surface mine permit application, Phillips Coal Co. conducted a soils mapping and historic land use survey. In addressing the justification for topsoil substitute materials, the company relied on results of a geochemical evaluation to demonstrate improved drainage, trafficability, and fertility. The reclamation plan incorporated these elements plus indicator species, existing vegetation, and wildlife needs.

title: Classifying aquatic resources: a quantitative approach.
authors: Rumble M.
abstract: Twenty-seven water quality parameters from 41 coal and bentonite surface mine and livestock ponds were used to show how quantitative, multivariate procedures could be used to classify aquatic resources. Data were subjected to polar ordination to define the groups of ponds based on water quality criteria, followed by analysis of variance and discriminant analysis to estimate the classification functions and coefficients.-from Author

title: Monitoring strip mining and reclamation with Landsat data in Belmont County, Ohio.
authors: Witt R.G.; Schaal G.M.; Bly B.G.
abstract: Two data sets from 1976 and 1979 were processed to classify level-1 land covers and three strip mine categories in order to examine change over time and assess reclamation efforts. The two classifications were compared with aerial photographs. Results of the accuracy assessment show that both classifications are approximately 86% correct, and that surface mine change detection (date-to-date comparison) is facilitated by the digital format of Landsat data. -NASA abstract E83-10209

title: Prairie pond morphometry and aquatic plant zonation - northern High Plains.
authors: Bjugstad A.; Rumble M.; Olson R.; Barker W.
abstract: Before US Public Law 95-87, surface mine and livestock ponds on the northern High Plains had uniquely different physical features. Surface mine ponds varying in age from 12 to 25 years for bentonite clay and coal, respectively, had smaller surface areas, greater water depths, and steeper basin slopes than livestock ponds. Livestock ponds were richer than surface mine ponds, floristically, with 106 plant species compared to 76 on surface mine ponds.- Authors

title: Water regime control in mines and quarries in the USSR coal industry
authors: Gazizov M.
abstract: The paper briefly reviews the mine water problems associated with coal mining industry in the USSR. Statistics regarding quantities of water discharged from surface and underground coal mines are given together with the pumping heads, range of water problems at a coal face and the quality of mine water. Ground water control systems are described which include surface preventive measures, surface mine water control techniques and underground mine dewatering methods. Recommendations for further investigations for solving a variety of mine water control problems are included. © 1983 Springer-Verlag.

title: POST-MINING NEUTRALIZATION OF ACIDIC SURFACE MINE LAKES.
source: Research Report University of Illinois at Urbana Champaign Water Resources Center
authors: Brugam R.; Carlson M.; Chakraverty S.; Lusk M.
abstract: Twenty core samples and 54 surface sediment samples were taken from surface mine lakes in Missouri, Illinois, and Indiana to determine the rates of neutralization of acid mine lakes. Sediment samples were analyzed for diatom microfossils, selected chemical elements, and the radionuclide, lead-210. Chemical analyses of lake sediment showed that the sediment is a sink for heavy metals.

title: The distribution of Desmognathine larvae (Amphibia: Plethodontidae) in coal surface mine impacted streams of the Cumberland Plateau, USA
authors: Gore J.
abstract: Hatchling desmognathine larvae and pre-metamorphic larvae of Desmognathus fuscus were found in 16 of 78 low order streams from coal surface mine impacted areas of the Cumberland Plateau. Although larvae were found to be surviving in a wide range of pH values, they were limited in range by high concentrations of dissolved solids (probably metal salts) in combination with acid conditions. The loss of shading (tree removal) resulted in increased turbidity and siltation which probably eliminated preferred habitat. I suggest that many species of the desmognathine complex, some of which are considered rare and protected, can be used as effective indicators of surface mine impacts, particularly heavy metal contamination and other effects associated with low pH conditions. © Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: Hydrology of the Ferron sandstone aquifer and effects of proposed surface- coal mining in Castle Valley, Utah.
source: US Geological Survey Water Supply Paper
authors: Lines G.C.; Morrissey D.J.
abstract: A three-dimensional digital-computer model was used to simulate ground-water flow in the Ferron sandstone aquifer in the Emery area. Discharge from the proposed surface mine is predicted to average about 0.3 cubic foot per second during the 15 years of mine operation. Dewatering of the mine would affect the potentiometric surfaces of all sections of the Ferron sandstone aquifer, but the greatest effects would be in the upper section. -from Authors

title: Habitat evaluation procedures for planning surface mine reclamation in Texas.
authors: Rhodes M.; Cloud T.; Haag D.
abstract: The objective of the study was to demonstrate HEP as a tool for planning surface mine reclamation activities. Emphasis was placed upon a comparison of the relative impact and wildlife habitat development potential of several reclamation alternatives typically considered for large surface mine projects. -from Authors

title: Decomposition of tall fescue ( Festuca elatior var. arundinacea) and cellulose litter on surface mines and a tallgrass prairie in central Missouri, U.S.A.
authors: Wieder R.K.; Carrel J.E.; Rapp J.K.; Kucera C.L.
abstract: Compared to other studies of litter decomposition in temperate grasslands, losses of ash-free mass from fescue litter were rapid. In addition, <sup>14</sup>C-labelled fescue litter (initial C:N = 14.2) decomposed more rapidly than unlabelled fescue litter (initial C:N = 25.9), reflecting the influence of initial N content on decomposition. Decomposition of fescue and cellulose litter on non-vegetated mine sites was slow, probably because of low exogenous N inputs and harsh environmental conditions that characterize barren spoil. Regression models of remaining ash-free mass as a function of C:N, C:P, and N:P ratios increased progressively in complexity from non-vegetated mine to vegetated mine to tallgrass prairie sites, reflecting differences in the structure and function of the decomposer communities. Significantly less ash-free mass, <sup>14</sup>C, and N was lost from fescue situated over very acidic (pH = or < 4.5) spoil than from fescue situated over moderately acidic (pH = or > 5.0) spoil. Current reclamation practices, such as liming, fertilization, and mulching, could have conflicting effects on organic matter accumulation and N and dynamics in surface mine spoils.-from Authors

title: CHARACTERIZING UNSATURATED HYDRAULIC CONDUCTIVITY OF WESTERN KENTUCKY SURFACE MINE SPOILS AND SOILS.
source: Soil Science Society of America Journal
authors: Ward A.; Wells L.G.; Phillips R.E.
abstract: A large-scale laboratory infiltrometer system was used to determine infiltration characteristics of 'reconstructed' surface mine spoil and soil horizons. Soil water characteristic curves were determined using the Brooks-Corey and the Gardner procedures and developed based on desorption tensiometer data. Unsaturated hydraulic conductivity values were determined using the 'plane of zero flux' procedure and compared with predictions resulting from models described by Campbell, Burdine, and Mualem for situations involving reconstructed soil and spoil materials.

title: INFILTRATION THROUGH RECONSTRUCTED SURFACE MINED SPOILS AND SOILS.
source: Transactions of the American Society of Agricultural Engineers
authors: Ward A.; Wells L.; Phillips R.
abstract: The research described was carried out to determine hydraulic characteristics in the surface horizons of reconstructed surface mine spoils and soils from Western Kentucky; and to evaluate the effects of initial soil moisture conditions, profile bulk density, and rainfall intensity on infiltration through these reconstructed profiles.

title: Geophysical techniques applied to surface mine design in stratified deposits
authors: Elkington P.; Scoble M.; Brown J.; Muftuoglu Y.
abstract: Geophysical techniques have been traditionally associated with exploration for metalliferous and hydrocarbon deposits. However, they also offer potential for the evaluation of geo-technical parameters associated with mineral deposits in mine design. Such geotechnical evaluate not only deposit quality and dimensions but also to characterise rock mass quality, geological structure and groundwater regime. This paper gives a short review of the both surface and borehole measurements which offer application to surface mine design. Reference is made to experience with actual mine case studies. These are predominantly in coal deposits where, in recent years, the techniques have found increasing usage. Many of the techniques covered, however, offer potential application to surface mine design for metal and indutrial mineral deposits, particularly those of a stratified nature. © 1983 Elsevier Science Publishers B.V.

title: COAL MINING AND THE ENVIRONMENT.
authors: Luder O.
abstract: This paper reports on the progress of the NCB's North East Leicestershire, United Kingdom, project which shows how, with the aid of environmental consultants, the quest for coal and the interest of conservationsists need not be incompatible. The following reports are discussed in some detail: effects of reclamation record; method of selection (visual impact, noise, landscape, agriculture, traffic); surface mine complex design.

title: Forage yield and quality on Kentucky surface mine spoils.
authors: Henry D.
abstract: The suitability of several forage species for use in pasture and hay production on surface-mined land was studied in the eastern and western coal fields of Kentucky. A mixture of KY31 tall fescue Festuca arundinacea and Interstate sericea lespedeza Lespedeza cuneata was used as a standard for comparison. Species tested alone or in mixtures included Caucasian bluestem Bothriochloa caucasica, Kaw big bluestem Andropogon gerardii, Cheyenne Indiangrass Sorghastrum nutans, Blackwell switchgrass Panicum virgatum, Chemung crownvetch Coronilla varia and Appalow (dwarf) sericea lespedeza Lespedeza cuneata. A mixture of Blackwell switchgrass and Interstate sericea lespedeza, harvested twice, produced 435 kg/ha more forage than the control mixture in eastern Kentucky. In western Kentucky, all species seeded alone or in mixture produced more forage than the control mixture. Chemung crownvetch was significantly higher in protein, dry matter digestibility, and yield than the two sericea lespedeza varieties.-from Author

title: Surface mine drainage using large diameter pumpwells
authors: Atkinson T.; Dow R.
abstract: Pumpwell drainage systems used in large surface mines involve considerable investigation and engineering design if they are to be economically effective. Such systems must be compatible with the method of mining adopted and must be fully integrated with mining operations at the planning stage. The security of the mine is often largely dependent on the continuous and effective operation of the pumpwell system and extremely reliable systems are essential. Often this involves large capital and operating expenditures that can have a significant effect on the viability of a project, thereby justifying the in-depth considerations that are needed. The organisation of the operations requires high levels of technical competence and managerial skill. Often innovation and occasionally improvisation are essential ingredients in the design and operation of pumpwell mine drainage systems. The whole subject crosses the boundaries of geology, hydrology, mechanical and electrical engineering as well as mining engineering. © 1983 Springer-Verlag.

title: Mammalian community characteristics on surface mine lands in Pennsylvania
authors: Brenner F.J.; Kelly R.B.; Kelly J.
keywords: Mammalian communities | Natural succession | Reclamation | Surface mines | Vegetative structure
abstract: Mammalian communities were studied on 10 surface mines over a four year period. The size and composition of these communities varied among the different areas. The size, composition, and spatial distribution of these mammalian communities were related to the structure of the plant community, and native plant species were of greater importance in determining size and composition of these communities than were those used in reclamation. © 1982 Springer-Verlag New York Inc.

title: White-tailed deer movement and distribution about surface coal mines in West Virginia, USA
authors: Knotts R.; Samuel D.
abstract: Deer movements around surface coal mines were investigated in Preston Country, West Virginia, USA. Seventy-two deer crossings were counted on 29 surface mines with only 8% found on highwalls with more than 20% rock or stone. Thus, although slope was important, the percentage of dirt on the highwall determined use as a crossing location for deer. The average distance between all deer crossing was 209.7 m but the distance between the end of the highwall and the nearest highwall crossing was 248.7 m indicating reluctance of deer to cross mines when they could walk around them. Winter snow track counts showed fewer deer within 90 m of the top edge of the highwall. Four land bridges traversed the highwall and were heavily utilized by deer, especially in March, April, May, October and November. The surface mine bench was used as a fawn bedding area, but little feeding occurred on this portion of the mine. © 1982 Science and Technology Letters.

title: NOISE AND VIBRATION CONTROL FOR SURFACE MINES.
source: Information Circular United States Bureau of Mines
authors: Johnson B.; Seibel R.; Siskind D.
abstract: This publication summarizes the inhouse and contract research and development projects inducted since 1974 by the Bureau of Mines for the control of noise and vibrations from surface mine blasting.

title: Habitat: a rational approach to assessing impacts of land use changes on fish and wildlife.
authors: Schamberger M.
abstract: Habitat is a predictive tool for use in wildlife management and impact evaluation studies, and provides quantitative information for decisionmakers. Ecological concepts and modeling approaches yield the Habitat Evaluation Procedures (HEP), a habitat-based approach to environmental inventory and assessment. Habitat models for selected species are used to develop site indices, which are combined by use of the HEP to determine an index of habitat availability for selected species. Presents a hypothetical application of the approach to a surface mine study.-Author

title: Seed size influence on germination and plant growth of Kobe lespedeza and other species used for surface mine revegetation.
authors: Gabrielson F.C.; Cross E.A.; Bradshaw D.K.; Carter O.C.
abstract: Seed size effects differed with substrate and soil amendments (lime and fertilizer), but overall selection for the largest (heaviest) 60-75% seeds of a given species increases plant density and biomass. Fertilizer interacted with low cation exchange capacity substrates to reduce plant density. Lime modified the effect. - from Authors

title: A temporal approach to monitor surface mine reclamation progress via Landsat.
source: Proc National Conference on Energy Resource Management Baltimore 1982 Vol 2
authors: Davis A.L.; Bloemer H.L.; Brumfield J.O.
abstract: Small-scale breakdown in the reclamation process was detected using an unsupervised classification technique with eight-year temporal Landsat imagery coverage. -from STAR, 21(15), 1983

title: MOBIL ENTERS THE US COAL MARKET.
authors: Carter R.A.
abstract: Highlights are given of the Caballo Rojo, the Powder River Basin's newest surface mine which represents Mobil Oil Corp. 's first venture into U. S. domestic coal production, construction, mine planning and site environmental factors are briefly discussed. Mobil has set up a sophisticated land reclamation and wildlife protection program for the Caballo Rojo coal mine.

title: LANDSLIDES IN FUSHUN WESTERN SURFACE MINE.
authors: Wu J.
abstract: From 1927 to 1982 some 50 landslides occurred in Fushun Western Surface Mine. According to the engineering geological conditions and landslide situations, the slopes in this mine can be divided into the following six sections: south collapse rock, western slope, north-western slope, smooth face in the middle part of the south slope, eastern part of the south slope, and eastern part of the north slope. According to their specifications, slopes are classified as the following 5 types: arc landslide, flat landslide, flat-arc landslide, wedged or polyhedron landslide, and landslides not parallel to the bench inclination.

title: STUDYING THE PRODUCTION SYSTEM OF SURFACE MINES BY USING A COMPUTER SIMULATION METHOD.
authors: Wang S.
abstract: A description is given of fundamental concepts, steps to be followed, simulation methods, and random variables. Finally, an example is given of the simple loading, drainage, and transportation systems of a surface mine.

title: SAMPLERS PINPOINT SURFACE DUST.
authors: Heimbach J.A.; Scott M.D.
abstract: This article tells how to set up an air-quality network around a surface mine to monitor suspended particulates. Included are highlights of federal and state regulations.

title: SURFACE MINE ELECTRICAL POWER SYSTEM DESIGN.
source: Transactions of the Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Section A Mining Technology
authors: Atkinson T.
abstract: The steps in surface mine electric power system design are discussed in logical order for strip mines, terrace mines and open-pits, attention being paid to voltage regulation, fault-level calculations, earthing systems, transient voltage problems and system layout. The problems of production losses and their prevention, diversity calculations and weak power systems are highlighted.

title: CONTINUOUS SURFACE MINE MATERIALS HANDLING SYSTEMS.
authors: Brady T.M.; Goris J.M.; Martin T.W.; Frizzell E.M.
abstract: This paper presents a review of three ongoing research projects dealing with continuous materials handling systems in open-pit mines in the USA. The systems include mine-run-rock conveyors, high-angle conveyors, and movable in-pit crushers. These material handling systems are being evaluated and applied to mining systems primarily to reduce the dependency on diesel fuel and to reduce mining costs.

title: WHAT CAUSED SURFACE MINE PRODUCTIVITY TO DECLINE - A CASE STUDY.
authors: Herhal A.; Cook F.
abstract: Surface coal mine productivity in the Illinois basin peaked in 1967 at about 45 tons per man-day (manshift). Since then, surface mine output has exhibited a drop to less than 20 tons per man-day. The article is a case study of a large midwestern, union surface mine.

title: GAMMS RAYS, LASER AID SURFACE MINE.
authors: Jackson D.
abstract: A Wyoming mine uses a hand-held gamma ray scintillometer to help loader operators detect a parting. A laser guides coal haulers through a narrow crossover dump.

title: Coal surface mine land reclamation costs ( USA).
authors: Misiolek W.S.; Noser T.C.
abstract: In the light of a lack of consistency in prior reclamation cost estimates and apparent methodological problems, attempts to develop an economic method for estimating costs of land reclamation for large-scale ore mining operations in the USA. The mine simulation approach is extended to include relevant opportunity costs. The cost impacts of federal reclamation regulations in different regions are also compared.-K.Turner

title: Characteristics of bird communities on surface mine lands in Pennsylvania
authors: Brenner F.; Kelly J.
keywords: Bird communities | Natural succession | Surface mines | Vegetative structure
abstract: A variety of species was observed as either visitors, permanent, or summer residents on surface mines with different ecological adaptations. Passerine species were the most prevalent of the 25 families represented. Bird communities as well as individual species were correlated with the structure and species of vegetation on the mines. The composition of the bird communities changed in response to successional vegetation stages from grassland to forest communities. © 1981 Springer-Verlag New York Inc.

title: The impact of surface mine reclamation on headwater streams in Southwest Virginia
authors: Matter W.J.; Ney J.J.
keywords: benthic invertebrates | fish | streams | strip mining | water quality
abstract: Recovery of headwater streams following the cessation of mining and the application of terrestrial (vegetative) reclamation techniques was assessed by comparison of water quality and aquatic biota in two such systems (reclaimed four to seven years) with that of an unimpacted stream and of streams draining mine areas which were abandoned without reclamation. Alkalinity, hardness, sulfate, and conductivity were elevated in the reclaimed mine streams as were fine-particle suspended solids and sediment. Overall water quality was comparable to streams draining unreclaimed lands. Benthic invertebrate and fish populations were significantly lower in abundance in the reclaimed mine streams than in the reference stream and showed less taxonomic richness and stability; they were similar in these respects to the biota of the unreclaimed mine streams. Continued sedimentation from mined areas and haul roads affected stream habitat and appeared to be the major factor limiting biotic recovery. These findings emphasize that terrestrial reclamation does not assure lotic restoration. Water quality criteria merit consideration in the refinement of reclamation procedures for mined lands. © 1981 Dr. W. Junk B.V. Publishers.

title: Evaluation of hydraulic coal transport system concepts for surface mines.
authors: Roberge J.; Stoukidis M.; Rubin L.; Burnett M.
abstract: The objective of the programme was to develop concepts for in-pit hydraulic transport systems for surface coal mines that will permit significant increases in coal extraction and pit haulage productivity as compared to truck haulage. Large particle coal transport was demonstrated to be the most desirable for central and western United States surface mines. Three conceptual hydrotransport systems, including a centrifugal pump, jet pump and ventilated inducer system, were developed for each of two currently active mining operations. General and site specific design parameters were developed for each of the conceptual hydrotransport systems. A detailed economic comparison of capital and operating and maintenance costs for each of the hydrotransport systems was made with the existing truck haul operations. An increase in haulage productivity of approximately 19% was demonstrated for the central surface mine, while that of the western surface mine increased by more than 180%. Included in this report is a bibliography containing over 600 citations pertinent to hydraulic transport of coal. (from authors' abstract)

title: A summary of fish and wildlife information needs to surface mine coal in the United States. Part 3. A handbook for meeting fish and wildlife information needs to surface mine coal: OSM Region I.
authors: Hinkle C.; Ambrose R.; Wenzel C.
abstract: This volume is specifically for the states of Maine, Vermont, New Hampshire, Massachusetts, Connecticut, New York, Rhode Island, Pennsylvania, New Jersey, Delaware, Maryland, West Virginia and Virginia. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 14, 1982

authors: Hinkle C.; Ambrose R.; Wenzel C.
abstract: This volume is specifically for the states of Nebraska, Iowa, Kansas, Missouri, Oklahoma, Arkansas, Texas and Louisiana. -from US Govt Reports Announcements, 14, 1982

authors: Hinkle C.; Ambrose R.; Wenzel C.
abstract: This volume is specifically for the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin, Michigan, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio.-from US Govt Reports Announcements, 14, 1982
