keywords: Occupational dust exposure | Opencast coalmining | Respiratory health
abstract: Objectives-To identify whether there is evidence of pneumoconiosis and other respiratory health effects associated with exposure to respirable mixed dust and quartz in United Kingdom opencast coalmines. Methods-A cross sectional study of current workers (1224 men, 25 women) was carried out at nine large and medium sized opencast sites in England, Scotland, and Wales. To characterise a range of occupational groups within the industry, full shift measurements of personal exposures to respirable dust and quartz were taken. Up to three surveys were carried out at each site, covering all four seasons. For the purposes of comparisons with health indices these groups were further condensed into five broad combined occupational groups. Full sized chest radiographs, respiratory symptoms, occupational history questionnaires, and simple spirometry were used to characterise the respiratory health of the workforce. Logistic or multiple regression techniques were used to examine relations between indices of exposure and respiratory health. Results-None of the group geometric mean dust concentrations, based on 626 valid dust samples, exceeded 1 mg.m<sup>-3</sup>, and 99% of all quartz concentrations were below 0.4 mg.m<sup>-3</sup>, the current maximum exposure limit. The highest quartz concentrations were experienced by the rock drilling team and drivers of bulldozers (used to move earth and stone from layers of coal). There were clear differences in mean respirable dust and quartz concentrations between occupational groups. These were consistent across the different sites, but depended in part on the day of measurement. The variations between sites were not much greater than between days, suggesting that differences between sites were at least partly explained by differences in conditions at the time of the measurements. The prevalence of radiographic small opacities profusion category ≤ 1/0, based on the median of three readings, was 4.4%. Five men had category 2 pneumoconiosis and two men (including one of these five) had progressive massive fibrosis category A. From regression analyses, the relative risk of attaining a profusion of category ≤ 0/1 was estimated to be doubled for every 10 years worked in the dustiest, preproduction opencast jobs, after allowing for age, smoking, and site effects. Risk was not associated with time worked in any other occupation within the industry, nor with previous employment in underground mining or other dusty jobs. Symptoms of chronic bronchitis were present in 13% of the men. Frequency of chronic bronchitis was influenced by years worked in dusty jobs outside opencast mining, but not by time spent in occupations within the industry. Asthmatic symptoms were reported by 5% of the workforce, close to the mean frequency found in adult men. No positive associations were found between asthma and occupational exposures. Lung function on average was close to predicted values and showed no relation to time worked in opencast occupations. Conclusions-Frequency of (mostly mild) chest radiographic abnormalities is associated with working in the dustier, prepreduction jobs in the industry. Although some of these mild abnormalities may be non-occupational (due to aging or smoking), the association with exposure indicates a small risk of pneumoconiosis in these men, and the need to monitor and control exposures, particularly in the high risk occupations.

title: Textural and mineralogical characteristics of SPM in coal mines
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Jamal A.; Ratan S.; Dhar B.B.
abstract: The ultimate goal of air pollution assessment and control effort is to mitigate the effect of pollutants on environment. The effects may be on health, various other biological and systems, and physical quality of environnent. The severity of impact of airborned suspended particulate matter nay depends upon its physico-chemical properties. Opencast mining operation often generates high percentage of airborned Suspended Particulate Matter (SPM) which gets dissipated into the atmosphere around the mine and leads to serious disruption to the quality of the life. To this paper, a study of air quality monitoring in terms of SPM in an opencast coal mine has been presented. Among the various mining activities drilling, coal crushing and handling operations and movement of dumpers on the haul roads are the main sources of dust generation in an opencast coalmine. The concentration of SPM is variable throughout the year. It shows wide variation in summer and winter seasons in mining area. The mineral constituents present in the SPM also vary considerably.

title: Restoration of the Ackton opencast coal site, West Yorkshire
source: Coal International Mining and Quarry World
abstract: This short article describes the restoration of a site which was scarred by spoil heaps from underground mining and from subsequent opencast mining operations. The reinstatement of the site resulted in a prestigious environmental award for Miller Mining.

title: Coal geology, chemical and petrographical characteristics, and implications for coalbed methane development of subbituminous coals from the Sorgun and Suluova Eocene basins, Turkey
authors: Karayigit A.I.; Eris E.; Cicioglu E.
abstract: The Sorgun and Suluova basins contain a thick and laterally extensive Lower Eocene coal seam. The stratigraphy of both basins comprises basement rocks, the Yozgat Granitoid of Pre-Eocene age in the Sorgun basin and Jurassic-Cretaceous limestones in the Suluova basin, overlain unconformably by the coal-bearing Lower Eocene Celtek Formation and by transgressive units of Middle-Upper Eocene age. In the Sorgun basin the Artova Ophiolitic Complex tectonically overlies the transgressive units. Neogene and Quaternary deposits cover all the older units unconformably in both basins. The single coal seam is located at the base of the Celtek Formation and reaches a thickness of 6 m in the open-cast mine at Sorgun and 8 m in boreholes in the Suluova basin. Some coal is produced by opencast mining, but most is produced by underground mining methods. A total of 75 coal samples was collected from both basins and analysed chemically and petrographically. The coals are characterized by a relatively low moisture content (0.7-9.3 wt% on an air-dried basis) and variable ash yields (2.4-67.8 wt% on an air-dried basis) and huminite contents (28.4-89.6 vol%). Measurements of the mean random reflectance of ulminite (mainly eu-ulminite A) vary between 0.46 and 0.60% (0.53% average). These reflectance values and the chemical analyses show that the rank is subbituminous A or transitional to high-volatile bituminous C coal according to the ASTM classification. The coalbed methane potential of both basins is at present unknown. No borehole has been drilled to explore for this resource and no gas capacity value has been obtained for the coal seam and bituminous shales. The methane explosions which have occurred during coal production in the underground mines imply that both basins may have been an important potential for coalbed methane.

title: Variation in the concentration of heavy metal contents in minespoil dumps and its relation to vegetational establishments
source: Journal of Surface Science and Technology
authors: Pandya S.; Patil M.; Kharat R.
keywords: Atomic Absorption Spectroscopy | Heavy metal contents | Minespoil dumps | Vegetational establishment
abstract: With a view to utilisation of enormous minespoil dumps from increasing opencast mining, for vegetational establishments, characterisation of these materials have been undertaken with special reference to nutrients and heavy metals. Pb, Mn, Fe, Cu, Co, Ni, Cr, B and Cd in the soil and also in the grains of 13 different crops in different seasons have been determined before and after cropping using an Atomic Absorption Spectrophotometer. Addition of ameliorating material, i.e., lime sludge from pulp and papermills have shown interesting results in the stabilisation of overburden material for cropping. © 1996 Indian Society for Surface Science and Technology,.

title: Flooding concept for the residual holes of opencast mining
authors: Luckner L.; Eichhorn D.
abstract: Reclaiming of the water resource systems in the mining regions of Lausitz (Lusatian) area of the former East Germany required flooding of the remaining opencast lignite mines which finished their production after the reunification of Germany. This flooding was regarded as a transient state between achieve mining and a restored land scape which follows mining. A number of urgent decisions had to be taken, as each day's delay meant further acidification of the water. This shown that overcoming water shortages in the area under discussion caused by groundwater mismanagement over decades requires region-wide management of groundwater and surface water resources.

title: Rational exploitation of non-renewable resources through opencast mining for a fast expanding Indian cement industry vis-a-vis sustainable development
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Paul P.; Selvarajan M.; Imran M.
abstract: India is blessed with considerable mineral endowment which, if utilized in optimal manner can go a long way in accelerating industrial growth and thereby the economic development of the country. Minerals and mineral based industries, namely steel, cement and many others have been one of the major contributors for the progress of a country. Sustainable growth of the mining of the raw materials in the mineral sector is closely linked with rational exploitation through advanced techniques keeping in view environmental aspects as well. The present paper highlights state-of-the art of the opencast mining techniques which would rationalize the mineral exploitation and also bring in the much-needed mineral conservation. The magnitude and significance of the environmental degradation caused by opencast mining with proper abatement measures have also been discussed.

title: Making the solution stick
abstract: In the former Soviet Union, productivity at mines is hit hard by the sticking and freezing of coal to the surfaces of chutes and bunkers, and the loss of coal during transportation. For some years now NIIOGR, a Russian opencast mining research institute, has been studying the use of polymer compositions to prevent such things happening.

title: Mapping geological features of the Jharia coalfield from Landsat-5 TM data
authors: Chatterjee R.S.; Roy J.; Bhattacharya A.K.
abstract: False Colour Composite 754, the principal component imagery and edge enhanced imagery of Landsat-5 TM data have been found useful in delineating the regional geological features, viz, the curvilinear coal bands and sandstone ridges, faults, fractures and dolerite dykes of the Jharia Coalfield of Bihar, India, covering an area of about 480 km<sup>2</sup>, where many parts are inaccessible to direct field mapping due to extensive opencast mining operations. The features, their occurrences and spatial dispositions, as deciphered from satellite data, are found to match significantly well with selective field maps. © 1996 Taylor & Francis Group, LLC.

title: Opencast contracts a consultant's view
authors: Walton G.
abstract: Contractual claims on opencast sites are inherent in the risk attached to the operations. To resolve such problems, several issues need to be explored, in particular the risk areas in opencast mining. The risk areas may be divided into geological constraints, geotechnical constraints, operational constraints, timing, changes in requirements, environmental restrictions and market.

title: Model for Kovin lignite deposit suction cutterwheel dredging
source: Prace Naukowe Instytutu Gornictwa Politechniki Wroclawskiej
authors: Pavlović V.; Lazić A.
abstract: The Model for suction cutterwheel dredger Kovin UCW-450 operation was developed as programming support for operation of the suction cutterwheel dredger engaged in lignite deposit "Kovin" in Kovin. In its structure the model represents an integral parts of a research program at the Department for Opencast Mining of University of Belgrade Faculty of Mining and Geology in the areas of working out mathematical models of mineral material deposits and modelling of technological processes and procedures of opencast mining systems. The Model was developed as an application for lignite deposit "Kovin" concrete conditions as support in optimization of operation technological parameters and course of dredger advance during dredging.

title: From wasteland to wonderland: Opencast mining, regeneration and the English National Forest
authors: Cloke P.; Milbourne P.; Thomas C.
abstract: In this paper we examine the outcomes of restructuring within the British coal mining industry in the English countryside and an attempt by the Countryside Commission to regenerate an area of the rural East Midlands through a forest project of sustainable development. In this particular area, deep-mine coal production has collapsed resulting in high levels of unemployment and large parcels of derelict land, while an expansion of opencast coal (and other mineral) extraction has led to considerable landscape despoliation. We examine critically the Countryside Commission's project of the National Forest in this area, involving the planting of thirty million trees over an area of almost 200 square miles. The Forest is seen as an example of sustainable development, bringing together economic growth - based around timber production and the encouragement of tourism and 'green' business -and environmental enhancement. However, the National Forest will be planted on private land, some of which is controlled by major mineral companies, with relatively little public ownership of this so-called 'national asset'. The paper draws on recent research carried out by the authors which has explored a series of important land use conflicts surrounding the sustainability of the Forest alongside on-going processes of opencast mining within its boundaries and also tensions associated with public access within a privately-owned forest. Copyright © 1996 Elsevier Science Ltd.

title: Evaluation of land use potential for quarrying area around Ramganjmandi (Kota, Rajasthan), India
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Sharma D.K.; Saharan M.R.; Parihar S.K.
abstract: Large opencast mining leads to problems of land degradation and calls for quarry planning, particularly reclamation and post-quarried land use aspect of secondary utilisation mined out areas effectively. The problem becomes more complex as quarrying operations approach more densely populated areas and forest areas. The aim of the present study is to outline appropriate potential, secondary use for quarried land for which two approaches, first based on logical study of natural and cultural parameter, and second approach is computer-aided and uses a model to decide the priorities for the best suited quarried land uses. A case study of Satalkhedi Laxmipura area in Ramganjmandi, Kota (Rajasthan), India, has been presented.

title: Effects of topsoiling on rates of erosion and erosion processes in coal mine spoil banks in Utrillas, Teruel, Spain
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Nicolau J.M.
abstract: Runoff production and soil erosion, produced by energetic Mediterranean storms, are amongst the first environmental impacts of opencast mining activity and amongst the main limiting factors in achieving self-sustaining reclaimed landscapes in Teruel. This paper aims to understand the geomorphological response of topsoiled and overburden-covered banks. This is considered essential in improving soil management and designing accurate erosion control plans. Runoff and erosion rates were recorded after every rainfall in permanent plots for one year in both overburden and topsoiled banks. In the same way experiments were conducted with a portable rainfall simulator to follow the response evolution throughout time. Grass communties control topsoiled bank evolution, leading to an improvement in the hydric characteristics of the topsoil during ecological succession. Physical-chemical soil properties condition the erosion processes in overburden-covered banks. No improvement in infiltration rate nor in erodibility has been recorded 6 years after the slope banks were constructed.

title: The prediction of opencast backfill settlement
source: Proceedings of the Institution of Civil Engineers Geotechnical Engineering
authors: Hills C.W.W.
abstract: With ever-increasing demands on land use, large areas of land are being considered for development, which owing to past mining activities are covered by substantial depths of fill materials. This paper examines the problem faced, with the development of land infilled with opencast mining backfill, in predicting the behaviour of the fill upon development. To be able to design foundations suitable to withstand the movements that occur within opencast backfill or to design a backfilling operation that produces land suitable for development, a means of predicting backfill settlement is required. The information required to make accurate predictions includes the timing of backfilling operations, the compactive state and type of backfill, and the inundation of the backfill. This information will be available in most cases where development is planned, as a scheme of controlled backfilling will generally be undertaken. The resultant monitoring scheme, carried out to ensure controls are being met during backfilling, will provide the information necessary to enable settlement predictions to be made. From the analysis of a considerable quantity of data collected from the monitoring of backfilling operations and backfill movement at a range of opencast coal sites located within the UK, a computer program has been developed, enabling opencast backfill settlement predictions to be made taking into consideration the factors mentioned above. To demonstrate the validity of the approach, a case study is carried out from a real site from which a comparison between predicted and actual settlements can be made.

title: Environmental dust analysis in opencast mining areas
authors: Merefield J.; Stone I.; Jarman P.; Rees G.; Roberts J.; Jones J.; Dean A.
abstract: An atmospheric dust database has been set up for the western end of the South Wales Coalfield. This, the first of its kind in the UK, comprises dust data from British Standard 1747 four-way directional gauges, a window ledge sampler and an experimental frisbee deposit gauge. X-Ray diffraction was used to characterize the dust on the basis of mineralogy. Scanning electron microscopy was used to examine particle size and shape and an energy dispersive X-ray analysis system was used to locate coal particles. For 18 months, a total of 15 directional and three frisbee gauges were used to collect dust on and around the Ffos Las opencast coal site in South Wales, UK. Additionally, two more directional gauges have been installed in the Brecon Beacons and at Exeter in south-west England to provide data from outside the coal mining area. Processed data from the X-ray diffractograms, along with the weather data from an onsite weather gauge, are input to a geographical information system (ArcInfo), where they can be manipulated statistically. Rose diagram plots for the area can thus be presented, giving the mineralogical contents of dust from the four directions of each sampling station, set in a spatial context. A series of these plots introduces the temporal element. This new dust data technology already shows considerable potential for use in nuisance complaints, planning applications, site licence renewals and for the implementation of future European environmental protection legislation. © 1995 The Geological Society.

title: Influence of geological structures in slope stability analyses for opencast mining and quarry excavations
source: Geological Society Engineering Geology Special Publication
authors: Cojean R.
abstract: The influence of structural features on slope stability in rock masses is analysed, with particular reference to opencast mining and quarrying. Various failure mechanisms are illustrated at different scales. The primary importance of the method of modelling rock masses is highlighted, with discussion about the need to emphasize either the continuous or discontinuous properties of the rock masses. The choice of mechanical parameters for the joints, as well as the rock material, is significant and a slight variation may alter the mode of failure of the slope. There is therefore a need for further investigation into the geological description and mechanical analysis of rock masses. In many instances, sound judgement by an experienced engineering geologist is required to identify the relevant features of the rock mass and to assess the mechanical behaviour that may operate.

title: Opencast mining in Coal India Ltd
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Mishra R.
abstract: Coal India Limited has vigorously pursued and succeeded in adopting and absorbing state-of-the-art technologies in opencast mines. Shovel dumper system remains the main technology although a few open pits use walking draglines for stripping operations. Electric rope shovels up to 20 cu.m. bucket capacity are working successfully with standard thyristor control while a wide range of hydraulic excavators are proving their worth in selective mining and medium hard strata conditions.

title: Flora and vegetation on dumps of uranium mining in the southern part of the former GDR
authors: Sanger H.
keywords: Bioindication | Dumps | Ecological characteristics | Flora | Uranium mining | Vegetation
abstract: From 1946 to 1990 an intensive uranium mining had been carried out with underground mining and also with opencast mining by the Wismut enterprise in the southern pan of the former GDR. The mining activity lead also in the surroundings of Ronneburg to a permanent growth of devastated areas, among others in the form of dumps and tailings. These areas form by reason of mining-specific contaminations, extrem biotops which demand high claims on the pioneer organisms during the phase of natural first settlement. From 1990 to 1992 vegetation mappings were carried out on 15 dumps of the Thuringia mining area according to Braun-Blanquet (1964). The utilization of the computer prograrnm Flora D (Frank and Klotz 1990) enabled the ecological characterisation of the dumps. On the 15 investigated dumps found were 498 higher plants, belonging to 65 families. One hundred species are species with a high dominance. The number of species per dump fluctuates between 11 and 282. Pioneer plants occur on the berms mostly in the second year after stoppage of the dumping, on the slopes after five to ten years. After nearly ten years the first step of settlement seems to be finished. Among the mechanisms of spreading dominate wind-And burdock spread. According to the form of life forms the dump species are predominantly henlicryptop- hytes, further therophytes, geophytes and phanerophytes.

title: Die Trauermücken des Sächsischen Bernsteins aus dem Untermiozän von Bitterfeld/Deutschland (Diptera, Sciaridae)
authors: Röschmann F.; Mohrig W.
abstract: The Sciarid flies from Saxonian Amber of Lower Miocene of Bitterfeld/Germany (Diptera, Sciaridae) From the Saxonian amber of the lower Miocene of the opencast mining area in Bitterfeld there are specified 32 species of sciarids of 6 genera. The genus Succinosciara MOH. & RÖSCH. gen. nov. with the typespecies Succinosciara acuminata spec. nov., the subgenus Protolycoriella MOH. & RÖSCH. subgen. nov. with Lycoriella (Protolycoriella) gigaspina spec. nov. as the typespecies and additional 12 new species are described and drawn. 14 of the species from Saxonian amber are also known from Baltic amber. Copyright © 1995 Wiley‐VCH

title: Cainozoic of the Konin area with special emphasis on the stratigraphy of Quaternary deposits
authors: Stankowski W.; Biedrowski Z.; Stankowska A.; Kolodziej G.; Widera M.; Wilkosz P.
abstract: A characteristic geological feture of the Konin region is the shallow occurrence of the Mesozoic rocks. The palaeorelief is marked by vast, valley-type depresions of erosional origin, as well as by grabens. Tectonic activity took place in that area not only in the Tertiary but also during the Quaternary period. Thick Tertiary series were deposited during the period between the Eocene and the Miocene. Within the Quaternary sediments, series of three cold periods have been distinguished: the South Polish Glaciation, the Middle Polish Glaciation and the North Polish Glaciation. Similarly, series of two warm periods, those of the Great Interglacial and of the Eemian Interglacial have been encountered. Rapid transformations in the relief, as well as in the geological structure and water conditions, have been the result of Tertiary coal opencast mining. -from Authors

title: Polish lignite mine provides major source of power
abstract: This short feature describes the Belchatow opencast mining operation in Poland. The pit supplies coal for a 4320 MW power plant which produces 20% of the country's energy. -Author

title: Prediction of subsoil subsidence caused by opencast mining
source: Land Subsidence Proc International Symposium the Hague 1995
authors: Konderla H.; Hawrysz M.
abstract: Attempts were made to formulate the correlation between the subsidence of the soil mass exposed to opencast mining and the parameters characterizing the development of the depression and the geological structure of the seam. The process of soil surface subsidence was analysed, making use of the results from geodetic and piezometric measurements carried out in one of Poland's brown-coal mines. A simple model was proposed for the prediction of superficial displacements produced by the dewatering of the soil mass. The subsidence and rise of the soil surface, recorded in the course of geodetic measurements, reflect both the effect of seam dewatering and the effect of mining operations. -from Authors

title: Soil factors affecting tree growth on former opencast coal land
authors: Scullion J.; Malinovszky K.
keywords: opencast mining | soil properties | tree growth
abstract: The growth of three tree species (Alnus glutinosa, Betula spp. and Quercus spp.) was related to soil factors on two restored opencast coal sites in South Wales, UK. The main factors favouring tree growth were greater soil depth and organic content. Factors limiting growth included poor site drainage and high magnesium levels. Whilst all species were related to most of the above factors, soil depth was of particular importance for Alnus glutinosa and Betula spp., whilst site drainage had the greatest influence for Betula spp. Soil‐tree associations tended to be closer on the older of the two sites. Combinations of soil depth, percentage clay and percentage organic content in a multiple regression predicted around 40 per cent of the growth variation in Alnus glutinosa, between 6.9 and 32 per cent of that for Betula spp. and between 14.5 and 32.6 per cent of that for Quercus spp. Growth prediction for Betula spp. improved to 40.9 and 34.8 per cent when a site drainage factor was included in the regression. The development of such predictive relationships might contribute to the planning of site reinstatement for tree planting after opencast mining, and to a better ‘matching’ of tree species to site characteristics. Copyright © 1995 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

title: Engineering geomorphological mapping and opencast mining in unstable mountains - a case study
source: Transactions Institution of Mining Metallurgy Section A
authors: Hearn G.
abstract: The application and value of rapid geomorphological mapping techniques in the assessment of slope instability and erosion hazards in the remote and mountainous area of Ok Tedi mine, Papua New Guinea, are reviewed. It is believed that this mapping is the first to have been systematically applied to any mining operation in remote mountainous terrain. Rock avalanches and landslides are features of the area around the mine and represent potential hazards to mine operations. In 1989 an avalanche with an estimated volume of 70 000 000 m<sup>3</sup> occurred in close proximity to the mine and promoted a multidisciplinary geotechnical study of the entire mine operational area. The assessment of landslide hazard and geomorphological mapping formed integral parts of the study and were carried out at rates of 0.6-0.75 km<sup>2</sup> per week. They yielded various documentation for geotechnical management. This documentation, together with the conclusions reached and recommendations made, played an important role in the geotechnical assessment of slopes in the mine operational area. -from Author

title: Mineralogy and provenance of airborne dust in opencast coal mining areas of South Wales
authors: Merefield J.R.; Stone I.; Rees G.; Roberts J.; Dean A.; Jones J.
abstract: Fugitive dust from opencast mining is a contentious issue. It has often been perceived to be a significant contributor to ambient levels of airborne particulates, even though no reliable means of dust fingerprinting has been available to regulatory authorities. To address this need, dust has been collected continuously for an eighteen month period in and around Ffos Las opencast coal mine in South Wales, over an area covering some 250 square kilometres. Samples have been analysed for mineral content by X-ray diffraction (XRD), and particle shape, size and geochemistry by scanning electron microscopy (SEM) with EDAX energy dispersive X-ray analysis. By this means it has proven possible for the first time to fingerprint dust from different sources, such as on-site and immediately off-site of the opencast coal workings, and elsewhere in the region. The results show calcite and dolomite to occur over the entire study area, indicating a significant regional component present in airborne dust in the Ffos Las locality. Local sources are recognised by an increase in clay minerals such as chlorite and kaolinite over non-clay minerals such as quartz. Chlorite being detected on-site and occasionally near-site, characterises dust derived from Ffos Las opencast coal workings. Local dust generation, however, is not restricted to Ffos Las opencast site. Dust arising from quarrying, road developments and ground cover in residential properties can make a substantial contribution to the dust flux in this area. This new dust data technology has proven particularly effective and will be of considerable use in the implementation of future environmental protection legislation in Europe and world-wide.

title: Mining simulation of a new type continuous surface miner
authors: Xichun X.; Fei C.; Qiguang W.; Chong C.
abstract: A new type of continuous surface coal miner (csm) and mining simulation tests carried out for designing it are introduced in this paper. The tests provided a reliable basis for determining the main technical parameters and the structure of the new machine. Emphasis was put on the test rig, the coal and rock mass specimens, and the system and contents of test and data processing. The continuous surface miner is a new type of opencast mining equipment. In order to determine the technical parameters and basic structure of its working device, we have carried out a series of cutting and loading experiments upon the drum with various parameters of helical vane and pick arrangement in rock and coal specimens of different height on a mining simulation test rig, and measured seven parameters. The results of this project have been adopted in the design of this machine.

title: High-power inverters optimize mammoth excavator
authors: O'Connor R.
abstract: Inverters are used to optimize the performance of excavators used in digging coal at opencast mining sites. The dc technology controlling the travel-and boom-slewing motions of such excavator lacks the fine control necessary to provide maximum output when the excavator is operating on variable terrain. With respect to this problem, a new system that improves performance and reduce downtime is used. The use of SIMOVERT P inverters that combines the V/F method and vector control technique showed a promising performance. The control of these inverters is fully digitized. This system is specifically integrated to the No. 292 excavator.

title: Opencast operations at Optimum Colliery, South Africa
authors: Rutten O.; Bornebroek H.; Rossouw P.
abstract: The Optimum Colliery is one of South Africa's major opencast coal mining operation under the Division of the Trans-Natal Coal Corporation, Limited. The coal were initially mined using underground mining procedures. However, due to the proven success of an opencast mining enterprise, the entire production at Optimum Colliery was altered to opencast extraction. Four walking draglines consisting of Marion models 8000, 8200-12A, 195 and 7450 were employed for stripping. Three rope shovels and four wheel loaders as well as 12 bottom-dump coal haulers and five rear-dump trucks were used for coal loading and hauling.

title: Opencast mining for coal in the People's Republic of China
authors: Zhang Y.; Zhang D.
abstract: The opencast coal mining in the People's Republic of China (PRC) has shown the benefits of this method of mining over conservative underground mining. Opencast mining provide high production, shorter construction terms, minimal cost, increased labor productivity, lesser unit investment, higher coal recovery and enhanced working conditions and better safety record. However, there are many consideration that must be taken into account when applying opencast mining technique in the PRC. These include ground water resources and human resources, which are particularly significant factors in remote areas such as the Inner Mongolian Autonomous Region.

title: Mining and the environment - an agenda for action
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: De P.
abstract: The phenomenon of environmental and ecological damage has been threatening the country more and more by every passing day, substantiated as it is by the late or non-arrival of the monsoon. This paper seeks to point the major areas of concern in terms of the immediate and the long term fall outs of the mining at a place - be it an underground or an opencast mining activity-and suggest some effective and practically implementable remedial measure. What is being tried to be outlined in this paper is an immediate agenda for action that shall help unite development to environmental safeguards by practically sound and technologically feasible management of natural resources.

title: Digging in
authors: ANON
abstract: Ground engineering works required during the improvement of the A55 North Wales Coast Road, U.K., are described. These included piling through soft alluvial material, crossing disused lead mines, negotiating opencast mining works and installing retaining walls and barette foundations. Details of the methods adopted and construction difficulties encountered are included. (D.W.Taylor)

title: Early-diagenetic deformation structures in the overburden of the bełchatw brown-coal mine (central poland): A predictive tool regarding engineering-geological conditions during exploitation
authors: Van Loon A.J.; Brodzikowski K.
abstract: This chapter focuses on the early-diagenetic deformation structures in the overburden of the belchatów brown-coal mine. Optimization of open-cast mining, including removal of the overburden, requires good planning that should be based on reliable prediction of the working conditions. Investigations made in this framework, in connection with opencast mining of unconsolidated sediments, tend to focus on the characteristics of the sediments with respect to: (1) their workability by mining equipment (excavators, conveyor belts, etc.), (2) the dewatering of the material, and (3) the stability of the mine's slopes. Such analyses are traditionally based on lithology, the vertical succession of layers with different lithology, and the physical mechanical parameters of all lithological units. The choice of the most appropriate system depends on the specific purpose of the investigation and on the geological characteristics of the study area. In the case of the Belchatów mine, the classification should, obviously, be aimed at a system that would be helpful for developing measures to solve (or, if possible, prevent) engineering-geological and mining problems. © 1994, Elsevier Science B.V. All rights reserved.

These included piling through soft alluvial material, crossing disused lead mines, negotiating opencast mining works and installing retaining walls and barette foundations. Details of the methods adopted and construction difficulties encountered are included. -D.W.Taylor

title: Conservation of mineral nitrogen in restored soils at opencast coal mine sites: II. The effects of inhibition of nitrification and organic amendments on nitrogen losses and soil microbial biomass
authors: WILLIAMSON J.; JOHNSON D.
abstract: Soils stored in stockpiles during opencast mining operations accumulate significant quantities of ammonium (of the order of 200 μg NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>‐N g<sup>−1</sup> soil) within the predominantly anaerobic cores of mounds. Upon stockpile dismantling and land restoration, this NH<sup>+</sup><inf>4</inf>‐N is rapidly oxidized to NO<sup>−</sup><inf>3</inf>‐N, which is readily lost from newly restored soil ecosystems by leaching and denitrification. Experiments were set up to examine how these significant reserves of mineral N might be conserved in such situations. Application of the nitrification inhibitor dicyandiamide was successful in minimizing NO<inf>3</inf><sup>−</sup>‐N lost by leaching, though large concentrations of NH<inf>4</inf><sup>+</sup>‐N were detected in drainage waters. Straw incorporation decreased nitrate leaching by up to 40%; biomass C was some 40% greater in straw‐amended than in unamended soils after 14 weeks, though biomass N was similar in both. Addition of nitrogen‐free organic materials (glucose, starch and cellulose) produced different results, with glucose amendment showing the greatest reduction in nitrate leaching in the short term (due to an apparent stimulation of denitrification) whereas addition of cellulose resulted in the most effective conservation of nitrogen over 14 weeks; this was due, at least in part, to uptake of mineral N by the soil microbial biomass. Copyright © 1994, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: The effect of different post‐restoration cropping regimes on some physical properties of a restored soil
authors: Davies R.; Younger A.
abstract: Abstract. The aggregate stabilities of a soil restored after opencast mining and an undisturbed soil were measured over a complete cropping year from the time of ploughing a grass ley in autumn. This was to examine the effects of various post‐restoration cropping regimes on soil aggregate stability and soil porosity. A wet sieving technique and a mild dispersion method were used to determine indices of soil macro‐ and micro‐aggregate stability, respectively. Air filled porosity at field capacity and crumb porosity were also determined. Removal, storage and restoration decreased macro‐ and micro‐aggregate stability. After restoration, the different grass managements i.e. cutting for silage and grazing, had similar effects on soil aggregate stability and maintained greater aggregate stability than the arable regimes. The pattern of fluctuation in soil macro‐aggregate stability over the year was similar under all crops at both sites, but at the restored site there was a decline in stability, and differences in the air filled porosity at field capacity developed between cropping regimes. Micro‐aggregate stability was less at the restored than at the undisturbed site and showed no seasonal variation or difference between cropping regimes. However, a difference in crumb porosity between cropping regimes did develop. Copyright © 1994, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Selection criteria for the application of continuous mining and transport methods in opencast mines
authors: Kutschera S.
abstract: Continuous mining and transport methods are gaining increased interest for medium and large size opencast mining operations. This trend is fueled by the fact that belt conveyor systems feature significantly lower operating costs than commonly used truck haulage, especially when applied for high capacity or longer distance transport tasks. This paper highlights some criteria essential for a proper selection of the mining and transport method. It discusses most recent trends in design and application of continuous operating mining and transport equipment. It further compares commonly used methods such as shovel-truck operations with systems comprising continuous operating equipment. Systems such as mobile or semimobile crusher-belt conveyor, bucket wheel excavator round-the-pit-conveyor-spreader, and bucket wheel excavator-cross pit spreader are briefly introduced.

title: Creative conservation and opencast mining
authors: Gough J.
abstract: Creative conservation was largely a disregarded concept in Britain until the introduction of Town and Country Planning Regulations in 1988. Since then, the applicants and mineral planning authorities together have slowly realized the effects of the Environmental Impact Statement and what is expected of it. Some examples of the implementation of creative conservation in opencast mining are presented.

title: Some trends of problem solving of mineral deposit mining at great depths
source: Fiziko Tekhnicheskie Problemy Razrabotki Poleznykh Iskopaemykh
authors: Zubkov A.
abstract: Geomechanical situation while mineral deposit mining at great depths with account of regularities of variation of initial depth stresses and three-dimensionality of exhausted strippings is considered. The assumption is drawn on the existence of four mechanisms of rock displacement in the dependence of geological conditions of mineral deposit mining. A variant of combined mining of extended ore bodies is suggested. It is noted, that the study on strength properties of great depth deposits and the strain-stressed state of the open cut structural elements is necessary to conduct while extended ore bodies opencast mining.

title: The Impact of Storage of Soils during Opencast Mining on the Microbial Community: A Strategist Theory Interpretation
authors: Harris J.; Birch P.; Short K.
abstract: The microbial community in a soil stripped and stored during opencast coal mining was analyzed. There were significant effects of soil disturbance on the microbial community: in particular, there were large decreases in the total microbial biomass, as determined by ATP analysis, and numbers of fungal propagules as a result of the store construction process, but there was no significant effect on the numbers of bacteria. During the subsequent months of storage there was a flush in the numbers of bacteria, with gram‐negative bacteria showing an increase of nearly 700% in comparison to the control. During this time there was a steady accumulation in the amount of ammonium in the deepest part of the soil store, indicating the onset of anaerobiosis. These changes may be interpreted in terms of lifestyle strategy theory (Grime 1979). The bacteria exhibit behavior typical of R‐strategists, or ruderal species, taking advantage of the nutrients made available by the death of fungal biomass during store construction. Fungi respond as C‐strategists, or competitors, and they are severely affected by store construction‐and unable to persist deep in the anaerobic part of the store. In contrast, anaerobes, S‐strategists or stresstolerators, are able to survive under the same conditions. These changes have serious implications for the restoration of systems using stored topsoil as a resource. The microbial population has been altered in terms of its size and composition. Many of the fungi required for adequate breakdown and incorporation of organic matter will be absent, and the soils will be generally poor in microbial biomass. This will lead to inadequate nutrient cycling and poor soil structural stability, two factors essential for the restoration of a self‐sustaining ecosystem. Copyright © 1993, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Land reclamation and restoration of natural ecosystem: A case study from opencast mines of North Eastern Coalfields of India
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Singh G.; Sinha D.K.
abstract: Coal mining authorities of North Eastern Coalfields have been facing serious challenges of reclamation of the mine lands and restoration of natural ecosystem as a result of opencast mining operations on densely forested hills in Assam. Having regard to present operations, locations of opencast mining and particularly importance of Assam Coal and Its potential use in steel industry and environmental restoration/reclamation measures taken by the NEC authorities, it is justified to continue present opencast mining operations. This case study attempts to present sincere efforts being carried out in environmental restoration by NDC authorities. Background of mining, geology, climate and ecology in the region and also lmpacts of opencast mining operations have been described in this paper. Slope stability and aspects of control of soil wash off are also dealt with particularly civil engineering and mechanical measures such as terracing, bamboo barricading in the slopes, stone-barriers at the toe of dumps, revetment and retaining walls, check-dams in the channels and valleys and gully-plugging etc. Vegetation restoration through plantation of various selected species including turfing/transplantation etc are also presented. Soil quality aspects of in-situ soils dealt with. Vegetation results obtained have been quite successful with survival of diverse species at the rate of over 90%. The aspects of restoration of natural ecosystam restoration in this region of subtropical climate have also been described. © 1993, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Biological reclamation of surface mined land without soil grafting: A working model
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Ghosh R.; Ghosh D.N.
abstract: Opencast mining needs excavation. This, in most cases, mixes the topsoil with subsoil and overburden materials. The excavated mass when occurs in dump, gets washed and losses its topsoil component. Even if any amount is retained, it looses its biolife due to occurring at this displaced place over years. This causes severe loss and hence scarcity of topsoil in mining areas. This, aided by lowering of water table (due to mine water pumping) has caused extensive degraded lands in opencast mining areas. A techno-economically feasible procedure for greening this category of wastelands, without soil grafting has been recommended after thorough field experiment. © 1993, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Determination of the working zone of a dragline bucket - a graphical approach
authors: Pathak K.; Dasgupta K.; Chattopadhyay A.
abstract: A dragline is used extensively to remove the overburden in opencast mining operation. The transport efficiency of the dragline depends largely upon the dragging, hoisting and swinging operations with proper bucket suspension. The working zone of the dragline bucket may be determined considering its swinging, dragging and hoisting movement at different planes. In this paper a graphical approach for determination of the bucket path profile of a standard dragline has been indicated considering the simple three period duty cycle in each operation.

title: Chances for developments in belt conveyor technology in open pit mines
authors: Hager M.
abstract: The advantages of belt conveyors for lignite transportation in open pit mines are elucidated. The mobile belt conveyor has proved successful as the only possible system for large mass flows, such as those that are conveyed under the conditions of deep opencast mining. Neither trains nor dumper trucks can be employed in a technically and economically efficient way. Some developments are discussed that have been made in the field of belt conveyor technology outside the mining of lignite, and which could be the starting point for more detailed projects. These include plants with a particularly large conveyor length, particularly large lifting heights and with curved conveying routes.

title: Reliability, production and control in coal mines. Proceedings of an international conference, Wollongong, New South Wales, September 1991
source: Reliability Production and Control in Coal Mines Proceedings of an International Conference Wollongong New South Wales September 1991
authors: Hargraves A.
abstract: A collection of 64 papers presented at this conference. The only constraint on effective competition between underground mining and opencast mining in Australia is the reliability of underground systems currently at only 40% although individual components reach 95%. The papers come primarily from Australia, the former USSR, China and the USA. -K.Clayton

title: Effects of subsoiling and associated incorporation of fertilizer on soil rehabilitation after opencast mining for coal
authors: Scullion J.; Mohammed A.R.A.
abstract: A trial was set up in South Wales in 1980 on land replaced in 1972 after opencast coal mining, to assess the effects on soil rehabilitation of regular subsoiling, through an established sward, with and without incorporation of a ‘semi-organic’ fertilizer into subsoiling slots. Treatments were assessed on the basis of yield, soil structure indices, root and organic contents and earthworm population densities. Apart from yields, data are for the eighth year of the experiment (1987), 18 months after the fourth programme of treatments. Treatments did not markedly affect productivity, although it tended to be higher with subsoiling and fertilizer incorporation. Subsoiling had little effect on root and organic content, but fertilizer incorporation increased the latter, particularly at depth. Earthworm population densities were markedly higher on subsoiled areas, the increase in the deeper burrowing species Aporrectodea caliginosa being largest. Fertilizer incorporation increased abundance of Lumbricus rubellus, but had little effect on other species. Subsoiling reduced surface wetness, but did not result in any significant improvement in structure. Fertilizer incorporation reduced clay dispersion at depth and, with subsoiling, also increased pore space. Treatment responses in term of soil structure were not large, but the incorporation of fertilizer did markedly accelerate structure rehabilitation at depth. Subsoiling alone contributed to land rehabilitation by controlling surface wetness and encouraging an increase in earthworm populations. © 1991, Cambridge University Press. All rights reserved.

title: Alluvial mining in the USSR
authors: Bogdanov E.I.; Politiuk V.I.
abstract: This report concerns continental alluvial placer deposits of precious metals and tin. Alluvial placers constitute the bulk (more than 80%) of the entire stock of genetically different placer deposits prospected in the USSR. More than 40% of these alluvial placer deposits are located in permafrost areas. In the USSR, the main method of alluvial placer mining is that of opencast mining. The bulk of placer gold in the USSR, about 86%, is obtained with methods wherein independent simultaneously operating earthmoving, hauling and processing machines are used. The rest of placer gold output is obtained using dredges. -from Authors

title: Classification and quantification of erosion phenomena, of transport and sedimentation in basins affected by mining in New Caledonia
authors: Danloux J.; Laganier R.
abstract: The topical perturbations (cyclone and multiannual drought) which condition the hydrological regime of New Caledonia rivers and the different phases of opencast mining are compared with the suspended load variations, measured in the Pouembout and Ouenghi catchments. In addition, the analysis of air photography and satellite imagery demonstrates fluvial and coastal geomorphological changes (creation of the Thio meanders, evolution of the Thio and Ouenghi deltas). This study shows that evolution of the exploitation conditions leads to a decreasing number of pollution causes, while alluviation continues. -from English summary

title: The effect of cultivation on structure in soils affected by opencast mining for coal
source: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
authors: Scullion J.; Mohammed A.; Ramshaw G.
keywords: Cultivation | opencast mining | soil structure
abstract: Two grassland sites, reinstated after opencast mining for coal, were used to assess the effect of cultivation on structure rehabilitation. In general, cultivation had an adverse effect over a range of porosity and aggregate stability indices. This effect tended to be more marked in macro‐ rather than micro‐aggregate stability, in the upper rather than the lower half of the tillage layer and at higher intensities of cultivation. Some tillage responses persisted after two years. Cultivation effects were partly explained by mixing of soil within the tilled layer. However, results indicated some direct physical destruction of aggregates and a large reduction in aggregate stability. Data available did not point to any clear cause of this reduction in stability. Nevertheless, there was some evidence that cultivation may have disrupted the stabilisation of aggregates by organic matter, without influencing overall organic content. Net structural responses to cultivation are a balance of adverse and beneficial effects. In replaced soils this balance is negative. For this reason, tillage should be restricted where structure rehabilitation is a priority. Copyright © 1991 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

title: Ancient copper mining at Wadi Amram, Israel: an archaeological survey
source: Bulletin Peak District Mines Historical Society
authors: Willies L.
abstract: Extensive underground workings for copper minerals in the soft Kurnub Sandstone (Lower Cretaceous) were examined at three sites. Pottery scatters at surface on Sites 33 and 75 suggest Egyptian New Kingdom workings. At Site 38 similar workings were found, whilst surface and underground pottery and other finds underground suggest the workings were reopened and worked at intervals from the 1st and 2nd to the 7th and 8th centuries AD, with the possibility of further minor working or exploration in late medieval (Mamaluk) times. At site 38, three or four periods of mining, not all necessarily widely spaced in time, were observed. Despite much covering of the original working floors by sand, it was evident that many artefacts remain in place. There is evidence of opencast mining. It is possible to suggest simple beneficiation methods such as hand picking and winnowing appropriate to the ore, though little direct evidence was found. The findings complement previous work done both on mining remains, and particularly on copper smelting in the nearby Timna Valley. -Author

title: Opencast coal production and the planning system
source: Occasional Papers in Minerals Planning Duncan of Jordanstone College of Art University of Dundee
authors: Cromie S.
abstract: This research concentrated on testing the hypothesis that in relation to mineral resources exploitation, planning authorities were being forced into a "policy vacuum', arising from the conflict between their traditional concern for environmental protection, and the requirement that they should assess the case for "need' on individual opencast mining proposals. The principal methodology employed (outlined in the appendix) centred on a questionnaire survey of selected planning authorities. Following a brief introduction, the author considers the historical development of opencast coal mining, reviews mining authorisation procedures, highlights the planning considerations and the availability of policy and advice, suggests some of the implications for planning authorities, and draws conclusions on the themes emerging from the change in authorisation procedure initiated by the recommendations of the 1981 Flowers Commission. -P.Hardiman

title: UK opencast mining equipment in the 1980’s
source: International Journal of Surface Mining Reclamation and Environment
authors: Adams J.N.
abstract: Opencast coal mining in the UK is currently one of the most profitable mining operations in the world. This level of profitability has been sustained throughout the 1980’s, a decade during which the UK mining Industry has experienced a prolonged strike during 1984 followed by significant internal re-structuring, and operated through a transitional period of planning legislation culminating in the Housing and Planning Act 1986 and Minerals Planning Note 3, May 1988. The summary outlines the background environment of the decade during which time the excavating and haulage equipment being selected by opencast mining contractors has changed significantly to meet the challenge of an increasingly competitive business. © 1990, Taylor & Francis Group, LLC. All rights reserved.

title: Shallow coal: a hidden resource for urban regeneration
authors: Grimshaw P.
abstract: An ironic legacy of the Industrial Revolution is the large amounts of shallow coal buried under its factories and houses. As these areas become ripe for redevelopment there is an opportunity to reclaim the land by the process of opencast mining. The article describes five areas: Bilston, in the West Midlands; Wednesbury, Rotherham and Tinsley Park in Yorkshire; and Merthy Tydfil in Wales where over 10 million tonnes of coal have been mined and 653ha of land reclaimed for after-use as shops, airports, housing or industry. -A.Gilg

title: Deforestation and soil degradation in Sierra Leone: the role of forest removal and upland erosion in a rural catchment under multiple uses
source: International Journal of Ecology Environmental Sciences
authors: Bomah A.; Sama S.
abstract: In Sierra Leone, the most important human activities in rural areas include shifting cultivation, brush firing, opencast mining, commercial forest harvesting of firewood and timber and suburban development. The inherent characteristics of land attributes which are more visible expressions of land degradation were measured in a typical catchment in the eastern part of the country to explain the variation of soil erosion taking place. Human activities in the catchment are leading to degradation the most important of which is soil erosion. All the land attributes studied operate simultaneously in the degradation processes. This is because the farmers indiscriminately clear and cultivate these lands paying no attention to the land attributes and management strategies. This is a result dampens the predominant role of any one attribute in land degradation. -from Authors

title: Technology upgradation, new technology and R&D in Coal India
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Narayanan M.; Misra B.
abstract: For the next several years, coal India's proposed strategy is development and adoption of new technologies, and commercialisation of technologies established with R&D work. The major areas where work on the strategy has been taken up are coal exploration, shaft sinking, mine development, mine construction, underground mining, opencast mining, coal handling, coal beneficiation, coal combustion, slurry pipeline transport, environmental management, and The areas for further R&D work are an in-seam seismic survey, detection of sub-surface cavities in abandoned underground workings, evaluation of hydrogeological parameters by geophysical methods, and stochastic modelling of the structures of the coal fields for assessing exploration work.

title: Environmental aspects of opencast mining with reference to the Rother Valley Country Park
authors: Brook C.; Cresswell P.
abstract: The environmental aspects which affect open-cast coalmining are broadly those which arise during the period of working the site and those relating to the restoration and after use of the land. The paper considers both these aspects and relates to the working of the Meadowgate opencast coal site and its restoration as the Rother Valley Country Park. This country park provides a wide range of outdoor leisure activities, at the same time incorporating extensive flood protection works, and demonstrates how an opencast restoration can be designed to improve the environment and maximise the benefit to the public.

title: The Lausitz "bottle' clay - a ceramic accompanying raw material of brown coal open cast mining in the past and future
authors: Lincke L.; Kliemt A.; Gedai L.; Heinrich R.
abstract: The Lausitz "bottle'-clay is the raw material base to produce bricks. At the end of our millennium the today used "bottle'-clay deposits will be mined or will be overdredged in connection with coal mining. So, the mining of "bottle'-clay in connection with brown-coal mining is necessary to maintain the brick production after the year 2000. Today that would be already possible in the "bottle'-clay deposits in the east field of the brown-coal opencast mining Nochten. Extensive prospection and projection work is necessary to prepare that combined mining. -English summary

title: Use of quantitative complex interpretation of bore-hole measurements for tips of opencast mining
authors: Zwingmann A.; Wein R.
abstract: The possibilities of geophysical bore-hole measurements and the direct deduction of soil-physical data to investigate tips are discussed at one example. An estimation of results allows to suppose possible use of them with higher exactness. -English summary

title: Changes in the microbial community and physico‐chemical characteristics of topsoils stockpiled during opencast mining
authors: Harris J.; Birch P.; Short K.
abstract: Abstract. Experiments on the effects of stockpiling soil on an opencast coal mine in Derbyshire showed that there were significant changes in the microbial community. Numbers of aerobic bacteria in stored soils ranged from 0.5 to 12.8 ± 10<sup>7</sup> colony‐forming‐units (CFU)g<sup>‐1</sup> with the smallest values being in the deepest parts of the oldest stores, whereas an adjacent undisturbed soil contained 6.6 ± 10<sup>7</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup>. There was a greater effect on the numbers of fungal spores, which ranged from 0.1 to 6.7 ± 10<sup>5</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup> soil, all less than the 10 ± 10<sup>5</sup> CFU g<sup>‐1</sup> recorded for the undisturbed control soil. The number of fungal spores in the deepest part of the older soil stores was only 1/100 of the number in the undisturbed soil. This was mirrored by the biomass values, as determined by adenosine triphosphate (ATP) assay. Values of ATP ranged from 0.38 to 13.13 nmol g<sup>‐1</sup> as compared to 5.8 nmol g<sup>‐1</sup> in the undisturbed soil. All three of these microbiological properties decreased in value with both age and depth of storage. Neither anaerobic nor spore‐forming bacterial numbers were greatly affected by storage. The pH values tended toward neutrality in the deeper parts of the soil stores, and there was less organic matter in the older stores. Copyright © 1989, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Environmental assessment for opencast coal mining
authors: Coppin N.
abstract: Provides a discussion of the background to an examination of the assessment of environmental impacts both in the short and the long term. It describes the procedural aspects of environmental assessments for opencast mining and details technical aspects before considering the benefits to be achieved. -from Land & Minerals Surveying

title: A review of the bureaucratic, political and legislative problems encountered in the reclamation of the plateau tinfields of Nigeria
authors: Alexander M.J.
abstract: In most countries today, consent given by government for opencast mining activities usually includes strict regulations governing the restoration and reclamation of the area once mining operations have ceased. Even in the developed countries of Europe and North America, such legislation is frequently of relatively recent origin and requires strong political willingness for enforcement. In countries such as those in Africa, where mineral resources were often first exploited by the colonial powers, the introduction and enforcement of reclamation legislation has proved extremely difficult. This paper examines the problems the authorities on the Jos Plateau of Nigeria have encountered in attempting to implement the reclamation clauses of the Minerals Act introduced in 1946 in the laws of Nigeria. Commercial opencast tin mining was begun on the Jos Plateau by the Niger Company in 1904. From the outset, whilst all mining activities were controlled by legislation governing granting of leases and compensation rates for loss of land, no requirement for the restoration of land after tin extraction was placed on the mining companies. Thus, with the introduction of non-retrospective legislation in the 1946 Minerals Act, only mining operations started after the date of enactment were covered by the restoration and reclamation clauses. Unfortunately, neither the legislation requiring restoration nor the operation of the Reclamation Unit established to deal with reclamation of sites worked before 1946, can be considered to be a success. The reasons for the almost complete failure of this legislation is examined in some detail, and it is argued that the lack of success of the policies is attributable primarily to political rivalries both within the State legislatures and between the State and Federal Governments. In recent years economic problems have added to the difficulties facing those involved in attempting to reclaim the "devastated" areas of the Plateau. With the temporary, economically-enforced lull in reclamation activities, it is suggested that a major reappraisal of reclamation strategy is required in order to ensure that maximum benefit is obtained from the derelict mined areas. © 1989.

title: Shear strength characteristics of sandstones of an opencast mining block, Jharia coalfield, India
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Gupta K.K.; Kumar S.; Singh T.N.; Singh D.P.
abstract: Application of a non-linear failure criterion and non-linear regression analysis (NLRA) determine the material constants and other curve defining constants which give shear strength characteristics more precisely. A Fortran computer program I3XIER was developed for carrying out NLRA. The program J3XIER was developed for highly jointed/broken rock. Triaxial data of eleven tests conducted on sand-stones occuring in a rockmass in an opencast mining block in Jharia Coalfield were analysed by I3XIER. A sample input/output and a sample plot are presented. Shear strength characteristics of the rockmass were required for conducting slope stability analysis. A 140 m section of the strata will be affected when the open pit will reach a depth of about 120 m.

title: Opencast mining noise
authors: Walker A.
abstract: Coal occurs in seams of varying thickness overlain and interleaved by layers of soil and other materials, loosely described as overburden. It is largely the removal, storage and replacement of the overburden which gives rise to most of the environmental consequences of opencast coaling, including noise. In this feature three aspects of the issue of environmental noise are considered: Sources of Noise; Noise Criteria; and the Control of Noise.

title: Ballymoney lignite project. Hydrology and environmental assessment
authors: Finlayson D.
abstract: This article discusses the role of hydrology in environmental assessment, against the background of studies carried out into the feasibility of opencast mining of lignite at Ballymoney in Northern Ireland. These studies were carried out for Mekatharra (NI) Ltd, a subsidiary of Meekatharra Minerals of Syndey Australia, during 1987 and 1988. The work was to establish the base feasibility, costs and output characteristics of the development as a possible source of fuel for a 450MW minemouth power station, as a potential element in the development of generating capacity in Northern Ireland. Other alternatives then being considered by the Department of Economic Development (DED) in Northern Ireland included a lignite mine at Crumlin, being supported by BP Coal Ltd, and further development at Kilroot power station on the East Antrim coast. Hydrotechnica Ltd were also responsible for hyrological studies of the Crumlin project.

title: Mining technology - an overview
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: Banerjee A.
abstract: According to the author, the provisions of the Land Acquisition Act should be suitably amended to provide a corporate incentive to the mining industry to plan the mines with a view to bring about a change in the environment management concepts with particular reference to reclamation of mined land. Unless this is done, no amount of legislative measure alone will be able to place the large scale opencast mining in coal, lignite and other minerals, in a position to make a meaningful contribution to the economy despite introduction of the latest hardware. The present trend if carried forward to the 21st century, which starts only 12 years from now, will retard economic growth.

title: New crusher system for working with mobile plants
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Snell D.
abstract: A new type of crushing machine, a continuous crusher, has found application to opencast working in recent times. The crushing machine is a combination of a crusher and a feeder and has the possibility of working a complete crushing plant at ground level. According to design, the horizontal crusher can be loaded horizontally by loading shovels or it can be equipped with a loading bunker lying at the most 3 m above ground and which can be reached without a ramp. There are currently about 30 plants of this type in operation. Of these, one third stands in quarries, a third is used in large coal and oil shale opencast mining fields and a third is working in recycling building materials from building and industrial demolitions.

title: Application of deep diaphrach walls for groundwater control in opencast lignite nining in the German Democratic Republic
authors: Mielcarek W.; Braunkohlenkombinat V.
abstract: In the German Democratic Republic, about 95% of highly saturated lignite deposits, mined by opencast mining methods, are drained by dewatering wells. However, in order to reduce the surface water inflow to an excavation through sub-soil and to minimize the number of dewatering wells and to effect financial and material savings deep impermeable diapaphragm walls are being increasingly used. In order to meet the requirements of modern opencast mining technology, these diaphragm walls are some 100m deep and extend for a continuous length of several kilometers. Consequently, the well known technique of constructing diaphram walls by the discontinuous pile and section method has been replaced by the newly developed continuous leading pile method. As a result of research and development, this new method of excavating deep trenches utilises a horizontally rotating twin screw shaft device. This technique can excavate a trench in soil from the surface to its final depth by continuously advancing in a lateral direction. Two further technical modifications to this device have been carried out to improve its operational efficiency. The paper describes the application of deep diaphragm walls in the control of groundwater in opencast lignite mining. © 1988 Springer-Verlag.

title: REVIEW OF BLAST DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS IN QUARRYING AND OPENCAST MINING PART 2 INITIATION AND COMPUTERIZED DESIGN.
authors: Ball M.
abstract: With the development of modern drilling equipment capable of drilling blast-holes cleanly and accurately and advanced surveying equipment for the precise determination of quarry face profiles, blasting design is simpler and more predictable. The use of computers may also predict blast results and permits adjustments to blast patterns and choice of explosives without recourse to implementing these in the field. In spite of these modern aids to blast design, safe blasts need not necessarily follow accurate measurement and computer-aided design. It is a combination of these factors with understanding on the part of the operator which will ultimately lead to safe and efficient blasts. The computer aided design method SABREX is described.

title: Opencast mining in Great Britain
authors: Anon
abstract: Since the beginning of the 1980s British Coal's opencast coal production in Great Britain has been maintained at about 14Mt/y, a rate of output which has met the requirements of the market without causing undue disturbance to the environment. Opencast coal recovery methods allow seams of only 100mm-150mm to be worked profitably in association with thicker coal seams. However, difficulties in finding sites, the role of opencast in balancing the quality of deep-mined coal, and public hostility all combine to make opencast mining an activity beset with controversy. Colliery Guardian's review of opencast mining is based on the revised edition of the Opencast Executive's explanatory brochure. Production costs are given.

title: Recent developments in explosives techniques: Testing and safety aspects of non-permitted explosives
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Bhattacharyya M.
abstract: With growing emphasis on large-scale opencast mining, the need for efficient and, as far as possible, hazard free explosives has become inevitable. The explosives industry in India, since its beginning in 1958, has been developing continually to keep pace with this growing need of the country, and with the infrastructural facilities, CMRS have always encouraged the indigenous development of explosives. As a result of all these efforts, India is now self sufficient in meeting its requirement of explosives. Explosives showing satisfactory performance under the regular tests and not required to be put through the safety tests in respect of their incendivity are designated as non-permitted explosives. Such explosives are suitable for use in opencast mining of coal, rock and other minerals and in underground metaliferrous mine workings.

title: A REVIEW OF BLAST DESIGN CONSIDERATIONS IN QUARRYING AND OPENCAST MINING.
authors: Ball M.
abstract: Good blasts are the result of the correct choice of explosives, and good blast design. The diameter, length and inclination of blast holes, drilling pattern, type, quantity and utilization of explosives, rock type, firing sequence and delay timing all have an effect on the efficiency of the overall operation. If the highest overall efficiency and highest safety standards are to be achieved, all blasts must be properly designed and recorded for future reference. This paper reviews the basic factors leading to good design and discusses the role of computer-aided design and in particular the SABREX computer blast model.

title: NALCO - an epoch in mine development
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Mohanty D.; Misra S.
abstract: The discovery of over 1000 million tonnes of bauxite deposits on the east coast of India in the mid seventies has placed the country in the forefront on the world bauxite map. National Aluminum Company Limited (NALCO) was formed to exploit and utilize the rich bauxite resources with the following units: a bauxite mine to raise 2.4 million tonnes per year of bauxite; an alumina plant to produce 800,000 tonnes per year of coarse alumina; an aluminum plant of 218,000 tonnes capacity per year; a captive power plant with an installed capacity of 600 MW; and port facilities. The state-of-art technology, meticulous planning, efficient project management, prudent manpower selection and careful training at NALCO mines have given us a quantum jump and now, the Indian mining industry can take-off to be a forerunner in the field of opencast mining.

title: Opencast mining machinery and productivity at Neyveli Lignite Mines
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: Sundaramurthy T.
abstract: The problems associated with mining lignite at Neyveli, India, the mining and auxiliary equipment used and the special modifications incorporated in them, the transportation facilities, the method used to dispose off the overburden and achievements of the organization, are discussed. Lignite mining conditions are examined. The continuous method of mining is discussed as are capacity and size changes in mining equipment.

title: TECHNOLOGICAL UPGRADATION AND MODERNISATION OF METALLIFEROUS MINES IN INDIA.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Choudhuri S.
abstract: The emergence of the public sector as the prominent leader in the core sector and demand for bulk production and productivity improvements has brought about major changes in the technological profile of mining industry especially after the sixties. The first technological upgradation and modernization was adopted by the iron ore mines of NMDC and Hindusthan Steel Ltd. (presently SAIL) for opencast mining and by Hindusthan Copper Ltd. in respect of underground mining for the Khetri copper complex. Other mining enterprises have followed suit. The author reviews these developments.

title: LATEST TECHNIQUES IN COAL AND ROCK DRILLING.
authors: Anon
abstract: The proving of coal reserves, the extraction of overburden in opencast mining, the drivage of underground gate-roads and the fixing of roof bolts for support depend, to a large extent, on the use of rock drills and associated equipment. The drilling equipment chosen by any drilling contractor is based upon the contractor's experience and the economic environment in which it is operating. It is utilized to achieve the most cost effective means of drilling a borehole, while maintaining the quality of the end product, i. e. , the borehole and the geological information obtained from it.

title: Some physical features of soil after opencast mining
authors: King J.A.
abstract: Abstract. The soil of a restored opencast site in Northumberland is described and compared with the surrounding undisturbed soil. The most serious change in the soil was increased bulk density at the surface of the subsoil (0.3 m depth). Only a small overall reduction in pore space occurred, at the expense of continuous macropores. More of the pore space in the restored soil occurred as fine fissures as opposed to biotic channels, and the restored soil was weaker because of subsoiling and a loss of stability in microstructures. These changes are discussed in relation to root exploration, water movement and land management. Copyright © 1988, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Changes in earthworm populations following cultivation of undisturbed and former opencast coal-mining land
authors: Scullion J.; Mohammed A.R.A.; Ramshaw G.A.
