abstract: Earthworm response to a single cultivation sequence was assessed. Cropping and management of cultivated land was similar to that of non-cultivated areas. Effects were measured in a trial on recently replaced opencast mining land. A subsequent survey investigated responses to cultivation on both replaced and undisturbed land at periods since cultivation ranging from 1.5 to 7.5 years. On undisturbed land, adverse effects of cultivation, if any, were short-lived, with numbers of all species, but particularly deep-burrowing species, having recovered or increased after 3 years. However, on replaced land the initial adverse effect appeared to be larger, and recovery from this effect was delayed until at least 5 years after tillage. Different species present (Lumbricus terrestris/ Aporrectodea longa, Lumbricus rubellus/festivus, Aporrectodea caliginosa/Octalasion tyrtaeum and Allolobophora chlorotica) also varied in the extent of the initial reduction and in their rate of recovery. Reasons for different responses to cultivation and implications for the management of replaced land are considered. © 1988.

title: The development of mining and its influence on changes of relief in the Walbrzych Coal Region
authors: Wojcik J.
abstract: Out of all the components of the natural environment of the Walbrzych Coal Region, relief was the most affected by the development of mining of rock raw materials. Hard coal mining brought about the biggest changes in the relief. The extraction of this raw material resulted in the formation of many mine dumps, settling ponds, and crowded urban and industrial structures near Walbrzych and Boguszow-Gorce. Hard coal mining caused ground settlement which had led to the formation of small hollows in the ground, the so-called subsidence basins. Maximum values of ground settlement amount to over 12 m in that area. Opencast mining of rock raw materials resulted in smaller changes of relief. -from English summary

title: Post glacial history of the Nant Helen opencast site South Wales: implications for land restoration
source: Occasional Paper University of Keele Department of Geography
authors: Chambers F.; Lageard J.; Elliot L.
abstract: A proposal to extend opencast mining at Nant Helen Colliery, South Wales, threatened both archaeological sites and a large expanse of upland mire on Mynydd y Drum. Excavations of two cairns and a length of post-medieval trackway were conducted there by the Clwyd-Powys Archaeological Trust in the summer of 1987. These were accompanied by palaeoecological work to ascertain both the post-glacial environmental history of Mynydd y Drum and the contemporary environmental setting of the two cairns. Evidence suggests that the most dramatic impact upon local woodland was in the early Bronze Age. The evidence for former extensive deciduous woodlands on Mynydd y Drum now offers British Coal a wider range of land restoration goals, for consideration when the opencast mining ceases. -from Authors

title: The conservation and amenity value of ball-clay ponds in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, UK
authors: Friday L.E.
abstract: Opencast mining is the principal method by which ball-clays are extracted from heathland in the Isle of Purbeck, Dorset, UK. An understanding of the substitute habitats so created is required if the environmental impact of this mode of extraction is to be assessed. This paper investigates the conservation and amenity value of the water bodies arising from 18th and 19th century workings in the Isle of Purbeck. The 16 ball-clay ponds studied varied widely in chemistry and supported a range of freshwater habitats and biotas. Several species of special conservation interest occurred and the ponds had a diverse dragonfly fauna. The acidic heathland ponds represent a habitat of local and diminishing distribution in lowland Britain. The more enriched, circum-neutral ponds supported fish populations of varying quality, some of which may have a considerable amenity value. Collectively, these ponds make a positive contribution to the ecological and landscape diversity of the Isle of Purbeck. © 1988.

title: Earthworms and structure rehabilitation in subsoils and in topsoils affected by opencast mining for coal
authors: Stewart V.I.; Scullion J.; Salih R.O.; Al-Bakri K.H.
abstract: Because soil structure seems to benefit from the period under grass in a normal rotation, it is widely assumed that grass roots are primarily responsible (Strutt, 1970). Due credit is also given to efficient drainage, adequate inputs of organic matter, lime and microbial activity. However, it is not clear whether the earthworm is a passive exploiter or a causal agent of structure improvement. When the pressures of production end up in severe soil structure deterioration, or when massive soil disturbance and stockpiling ends up in soils restored with little residual structure, experimental evidence suggests that the role of the earthworm is crucial. Evidence will be presented to show how earthworms, in association with all the other factors normally held to be responsible, initiate the development of water-stable, soil granulation. However, evidence will also be presented which shows how certain features of modern agriculture are, to some extent at least, antagonistic to earthworms. In utilizing degraded land, it may be necessary to farm initially for the benefit of the earthworm rather than for yield. This approach must be maintained despite the fact that, in the early stages, it may result in a phase of greater waterlogging and susceptibility to poaching. © 1988 A B Academic Publishers.

title: Thematic mapping of the abandoned mining hazard: A pilot study for the South Wales Coalfield
source: Geological Society Engineering Geology Special Publication
authors: Statham I.; Golightly C.; Treharne G.
abstract: The Department of the Environment and the Welsh Office jointly sponsored a South Wales Desk Study into the feasibility of producing thematic maps of the Mining subsidence risk for planners. A method was to be developed and tested for a 25 km<sup>2</sup> Pilot Area centred on Ebbw Vale. The study was started by collecting geological and mining data for the Pilot Area and compiling this information on a map. It was then intended to prepare the mining subsidence map from this map by back analysing subsidence incidents to determine the hazardous areas. This simple approach could not be followed for two reasons. First, the record of mining was incomplete and it was therefore necessary to define 'worked' seams and areas from the total historical record and not only from the surviving mine plans. Secondly, insufficient subsidence incidents were discovered in the Pilot Area to carry out meaningful back analysis. The study was extended to collect all readily available records of subsidence incidents throughout the Coalfield. A total of 388 were traced, mainly dating from 1960. About threequarters were collapses through superficial materials and were either close to the outcrop or above mine entries, the remaining 25% propagated to the ground surface through rock. The upper limit of migration was typically 8 times the extracted height where the dip was shallow, incrasing to as much as 18 times for steep dips. Selected grout contracts and opencast mining sites were also examined to gain information on the present condition of old workings and to study the 'reputations' of the various seams for voids. The results of the coalfield study were applied to the Pilot Area to produce a 1: 10 000 scale Development Advice Map, 'Mining Subsidence for use by developers and planners'. The map is zoned to show areas where specialist advice is necessary to support a planning application and it also shows all mine entries traced by the desk study. The method of production is general for the South Wales Coalfield and further maps could be prepared, using the Coalfield Study, quickly and cheaply.

title: Environmental planning and mineral development: The case of Hemerdon Mine
source: Geological Society Engineering Geology Special Publication
authors: Jones A.R.
abstract: In 1981 a planning application was submitted to mine tungsten and tin at Hemerdon, near Plymouth, close to the edge of Dartmoor National Park. Considerable concern was expressed about the possible environmental damage which could result from this major opencast mining and waste disposal operation. Against this are set the potential benefits to the local and national economy. After a public inquiry in 1982 the Secretary of State refused permission but indicated improvements to the visual aspects of the processing plant and waste disposal area which would be regarded more favourably in a new submission. A revised plan was submitted in 1985 which, while still not satisfying objectors, was passed by Devon County Council, subject to conditions.

title: OPENCAST MINING - A SUCCESS STORY.
authors: Cotgrove P.; Weavers P.
abstract: In the UK, opencast mining of all vested coal is carried out under the auspices of British Coal represented by the Opencast Executive in England and Wales and by Scottish Area north of the border. As in any manufacturing or extractive industry productivity is the cornerstone, and opencast mining is no exception. This review covers economics, plant capacity, manpower reductions, product quality and mining costs.

title: Reducing Risk of Accidents Thanks to the Improvement of Materials Handling in the Quarrying Industry.
authors: de la Rupelle G.
abstract: Quarrying and opencast mining inevitably involves the loading, transport, unloading and crushing of the excavated materials. Extraction of such materials is essential to satisfy the basic needs of a modern economy and is therefore inevitable. It must, however, be conducted in such a way as to minimize environmental nuisances such as noise, dust, vibration and disfigurement of the landscape and to ensure that the workforce enjoy the best possible safety standards and working conditions. Prevention has a major part to play, both in protecting the environment and avoiding accidents to the workforce within the site. Realistic preventive legislation tailored to the industry and taking account of the state of the art is necessary to provide mine and quarry operators with guidance in these important areas. In order to prevent nuisance and accidents, one must choose good loading, transport and crushing plant and maintain it in accordance with good working practices.

title: Typical mining methods proposed for working a large complex opencast mining block in the Jharia Coalfields
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Ghosh S.; Sinha P.; Mozumdar B.
abstract: The Jharia Coalfield has one of the highest concentrations of seams containing the only metallurgical coal reserve in the country. The coalfield has been exploited by both opencast and underground methods of mining over many decades. The latter largely consisted of bord and pillar working in multi-section, multi-seam operations without much forethought of the subsequent liquidation of the coal pillars. With the demand of coking coal rising, the only practicable method of exploiting these pillars is to go for large-scale opencast mining. This calls for new as well as modified methods of opencast mining. This paper presents some typical mining methods proposed to exploit coal by opencast mining under these conditions.

title: Casting of overburden by directional blasting
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Ali S.
abstract: The importance of opencast mining in Indian mining industry is examined. It is shown that casting of overburden by directional blasting can be used successfully to reduce costs in excavating and handling large volumes of overburden. The advantages and the factors affecting directional blasting are examined. The effects of air drag, size of fragments and initial velocity on casting factor are also examined. Ballistic tables and nomographs available for designing directional blasts are mentioned.

title: GROUND WATER CONTROL FOR OPENCAST MINING.
authors: Cashman P.M.
abstract: There are two broad elements to the control of groundwater at opencast mines, namely, the control of water ingress to the site and the collection and subsequent disposal of effluent from the site. In this paper, the author examines slope stability; site investigation, 'heave' and effluent control.

title: OPENCAST TECHNOLOGY.
authors: Couzens K.
abstract: Within British Coal today, opencast mining is the responsibility of the Opencast Executive and, in Scotland, of Scotland Area management. Opencast mining is a low-cost source of domestically produced energy for the British economy, most of the 14 million tonnes a year costing not more than POUND 1 a gigajoule to extract. Because opencast coal is often low in chlorine and ash content, it can be used for blending, which makes some otherwise unsaleable deep-mined coal acceptable to customers. Since the introduction of opencast mining operations in the UK some 460 million tonnes of coal have been produced which could not have been covered by traditional deep mining methods.

title: SEALING WALLS IN OPENCAST MINING.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Strzodka K.; Fischer M.; Mielcarek W.
abstract: Lignite seams that do not immediately lie at surface level are mostly covered by interstratified coarse-grained or fine-grained layers. In most cases these layers are water-bearing and therefore must be drained before mining operations can begin. The article reports experience with sealing walls at the Ruedersdorf, Jaenschwalde and Berzdorf mines in the German Democratic Republic.

title: The influence of nitrogen and early drainage on production from grazed and cut grassland restored after opencast mining
source: Journal of the Science of Food and Agriculture
authors: Baker A.; Younger A.
keywords: drainage | grassland | nitrogen | Opencast restoration
abstract: A review of past and present grassland management on land restored from opencast mining suggests that the most noticeable changes have been increased nitrogen fertiliser use and earlier installation of permanent under‐drainage. A programme of research is described which aimed to examine the effect of early drainage on perennial ryegrass (Lolium perenne S23) grown for grazing, frequent cutting or silage production on sites previously opencast mined for coal, and to consider how these options affected both the short‐term productivity and the long‐term restoration of the soil. The results demonstrate that satisfactory herbage production is possible on restored land provided moderate levels of fertiliser are applied. Grass was utilised at high levels of intensity with no detrimental effects on sward or soil. Highest yields were obtained when grass was cut for silage, and under this regime early drainage led to a significant increase in herbage production each year of the study. When grazing was practised, drainage only led to increased total herbage production in wet years although benefits were seen in spring and in the overall sheep carrying capacity of the land. Clover inclusion in the cut swards only increased yield when less than 200 kg N ha<sup>−1</sup> year<sup>−1</sup> was applied. Copyright © 1987 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd

title: OPENCAST TECHNOLOGY.
authors: Couzens K.
abstract: British Coal's opencast mining operations are in one sense a continuation of the oldest coal mining activities in Britain when, in mediaeval times and earlier, coal was dug from surface outcrops or seams near the surface.

title: GIANT EXTRACTION MACHINES FOR OPENCAST MINES: PART II.
authors: Wild J.
abstract: Without doubt some of the most spectacular stripping machines used in opencast mining operations in the world are those constructed by the Vitkovice Steel works situated in Czechoslovakia. A number of these machines are constructed in excavator or stacker form with walking undercarriages and linked by long-distance conveyors.

title: GEOLOGICAL ASPECTS OF OPENCAST MINING.
authors: Kelly D.
abstract: Prospecting policy and practice can be summed up under five headings: the finding of coal potential; the proving of coal reserves; presentation of the data upon which the decision to proceed can be made; production of contract documents which form the legal basis of the relationship between the National Coal Board and an appointed contractor; and provision of a back up service on operational sites. Each is discussed in more detail.

title: GIANT EXTRACTION MACHINES FOR OPENCAST MINES: PART I.
authors: Wild J.
abstract: Opencast mine operators are required to mine deep and to deal with great quantities of groundwater as a result of the steadily deteriorating overburden to coal ratio. Under the present conditions 69% more overburden had to be removed in 1980 than 20 years earlier. Hence larger and more efficient digging and dumping machines are developed and opencast mining techniques that will result in shorter hauling distances are applied. The equipment employed, such as bucket ladder and bucket wheel excavators plus dumping machines, like overburden conveyor bridges bridges and spreaders all of matching capacity, is described in the article.

title: PWH/PAURAT C-MINER: A NEW MACHINE FOR CONTINUOUS MINING OF HARD MATERIALS IN OPENCAST MINES.
authors: Sagner R.
abstract: Although the continuous-Miner of PHB Weserhuette AG and Paurat GmbH represents a new opencast mining technique, its subassemblies comprise components well proven in opencast and underground mining. The flexible concept of the continuous-Miner provides a broad scope for versatile opencast duty in conjunction with conveyor system and truck haulage. Combining three operations - 'cutting', 'crushing', 'loading' - the continuous mining machine can selectively remove thin seams of hard materials. Compared with conventional surface miners, its numerous advantages and low operating costs make this machine an economic and technical enrichment of the opencast sector.

title: LONG-TERM PLANNING FOR THE REHABILITATION OF OPENCAST WORKINGS.
source: Journal of the South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Wells J.
abstract: An account is given of the planning required for the rehabilitation of land that is to be disturbed by opencast mining, and of the preparation of rehabilitation plans for submission to the Inspector of Mines. The plans include the provisions that are to be made to allow for climatic conditions, land use, vegetation and wildlife, surface-water resources, geology and ground water, soils, land capability, rehabilitation method, location of discard dumps and slurry ponds, pollution control, and costs. Monitoring of the operation is the only way that the rehabilitation plan can be improved, and both monitoring and planning are essential when provision is being made for the closure of a mine.

title: (Geology of coal deposits. 1. Fundamental problems).
authors: Petrescu I.
abstract: There are seven main chapters in the multi-authored book. 1) Chemical composition, physical and technical properties of coal. 2) Coal petrography, 3) Classifications of coals, 4) The main types of coals. 5) Origin of coal and coal deposits. 6) Special problems referring to the biostratigraphy of the main formation periods of coal deposits. 7) Principles of economic geology regarding the coal deposits: a) prospecting and exploration; b) coal reserve estimation; c) hydrogeology; d) underground and opencast mining; e) underground gasification. Both worldwide and Romanian aspects are covered.-M.A.Bass

title: A phytosociological study of a mid‐altitude heath in County Durham, Northern England
authors: Hughes J.; Huntley B.
abstract: A phytosociological survey of Hedleyhope Fell, a mid‐Durham heath, was carried out. Much of the Fell is rank Nardus grassland, with damper Juncus and Eriophorum patches. Disturbed areas to the west are covered by poor Agrostis/Trifolium/Festuca grasslands. The eastern end of the Fell forms a locally valuable area of heathland. 115 relevés were taken and 131 species of plant recorded. Classification by two‐way indicator species analysis suggested the delimitation of 19 noda. The principal ordination axes, produced by detrended correspondence analysis, emphasised the importance of soil moisture gradients, organic/mineral soil gradients and levels of disturbance in determining the vegetation. The Fell, at 300 m, falls between the lowland heaths of southern England and the upland mires of the north. Indeed, its vegetation contains some assemblages and species characteristic of both habitats. The heaths of central, mid‐altitude County Durham are found where the coal measures lie close to the surface and so this habitat type has suffered extensively from opencast mining activity in the recent past. Proposed opencast sites, if they go ahead, will destroy the Fell. Copyright © 1986, Wiley Blackwell. All rights reserved

title: Geoveterinary aspects of Pb, Zn, Cu and Cd concentrations in part of the Pennines.
source: Geology in the Real World the Kingsley Dunham Volume
authors: Ineson P.
abstract: High concentrations of Pb, Zn, Cu and Cd have been reported in streams, stream sediments, soils and herbage of the South Pennines. These anomalous metal values may be due to geochemical leakage haloes over veins, contamination from active industrial pollution, opencast mining operations, reworking of spoil heaps (mine tailings) or disused smelting sites. Aerial photographic interpretations, together with geological, geochemical and botanical surveys indicate potentially toxic areas known locally as 'belland ground'. The agricultural community and veterinary surgeons have long experience of the effects such ground has on crops and livestock management.-J.M.H.

title: OPENCAST MINING OF PREVIOUSLY UNDERGROUND-MINED COAL SEAMS.
source: Journal of the South African Institute of Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Clough W.; Morris R.
abstract: The presence of bord-and-pillar workings within the No. 2 seam of the Witbank Coalfield of South Africa requires that different methods of mining should be considered, depending on the location of the workings. The paper describes some basic methods of underground mining the seam.

title: HOMOGENIZATION SYSTEM FOR RUN-OF-MINE COAL AT THE EKIBASTUZ COAL FIELD.
authors: Krueckemeier R.
abstract: This paper discusses one of the largest opencast mining operations for the excavation of bituminous coal, the Ekibastuz field in Kasachstan, USSR. Background for this large-scale stockyard order was PWH's leading position and high technology standard in erecting high-capacity terminals and stockyards as well as the high standard in the field of opencast mining technology. Four homogenization systems, each with a storage capacity of 100,000 t and a stockpiling capacity of 6000 t/h, are interlinked between the mining operation and the shipment of the coal. The reclaiming capacity per system and reclaimer amounts to 4000 t/h. The systems are run in three operating shifts at approx. 6000 working hours per year.

title: OPENCAST MINING AND THE ENVIRONMENT.
authors: Tomlinson J.D.
abstract: This article discusses the work of the Opencast Executive of the NCB with reference to noise control, noise measurement, blasting, control of ground vibrations, water pollution, dust problems and land reclamation.

title: Seismic spectroscopy in fracture characterization.
authors: Young R.P.; Hill J.J.; Bryan I.R.; Middleton R.
abstract: As part of a research project to assess fracturing in rock masses on opencast coal sites, empirical correlations are being developed which relate fracture characteristics to the attenuation of seismic signals. An experimental programme into the design of efficient blasting/fragmentation systems in opencast mining is outlined. The results show that the fragmentation efficiency of a mine blast can be quantified in terms of 3-D seismic attenuation spectra and polar anisotropy diagrams. A data case study is given to highlight the scope of the data collected and the type of multivariate statistical analysis methods used.-from Authors

title: Authorisation procedures for opencast mining.
authors: Peart J.D.; Rutherford L.A.
abstract: A review of the change in planning law which transfers development control powers over opencast mining to mineral planning authorities. Three perspectives are forwarded: 1) the planning authorities are detrimentally affected by inadequate staffing, and the lack of any national policy for either energy or opencast coal; 2) the National Coal Board are concerned that the new procedures are too slow, and 3) the environmental lobby has been outmanoeuvred and should press for the more comprehensive legislation available in the USA.-A.Gilg

title: COAL EXPORT POTENTIAL FROM INDIA'S EAST COAST.
authors: Bordia S.
abstract: On April 1, 1984, India had surplus coal stocks of about 20 mt stored near coal mines and this surplus is likely to increase as newer and bigger opencast mining projects are commissioned. India can therefore plan to export 10 mt of steam coal from coal regions near the eastern sea coast. This paper presents a brief outline of the export plan, involving coal basins to be developed, the mining system to be employed, the transportation system from coal mines to ports, port facilities to be developed, capital investment required and expected earnings from the coal exports.

title: QUALITY PROFILE OF A BLAST.
source: Journal of the Institution of Engineers India Mining Engineering Division
authors: Murari K.
abstract: Mechanization is necessary for a higher output in opencast mining. To produce several thousand tons of ores a day of a mine-run, the bench height must be increased. Drilling patterns are chosen in such a manner that blasting is done either weekly or fortnightly. In this paper a method of predicting the quality of the broken rock mass is described and its application in openpit mines indicated.

title: Problems of Flue Gas Gypsum Disposal as Exemplified by the Rhenish Lignite District.
authors: Bloss W.
abstract: As can be judged at present, it does not seem possible for the gypsum and cement industries to absorb the expected quantities of flue gas gypsum arising from coal-fired and lignite-fired power stations. Based on the need to develop new applications for these quantities, a disposal scheme for lignite-fired plants is proposed which consists of using the gypsum in combination with lignite ash as a filling material in opencast mining.

title: A strategy for nature conservation.
abstract: Describes the wildlife resources of Wigan, Lancashire, and the key wildlife sites. The threats and pressures are outlined, ranging from opencast mining to intensive recreation use. Then presents the strategy, which is divided into 1) protection and enhancement of existing interest - policies on waste tipping, land reclamation and effective management; 2) creation of wildlife areas - ecological planting, land reclamation and urban nature parks; 3) environmental awareness - wildlife surveys and interpretation.-R.Land

title: (Pursuing the phenomena associated with opencast mining by means of earth- remote sensing).
authors: Plachy S.
abstract: Investigates mining characteristics, using multispectral and multitemporal methods. The area investigated was 200 km<sup>2</sup> of brown coal mining round Teplice (Teplitz). It uses a AFA-39-M Camera and MSP-4 interpretation. Orthophotographs were used at 3 dates eleven years apart. The 'digikart' system was used to quantify the area devastated. Four classes of objects were chosen. Methods of expressing the results are compared and their reliability evaluated. -D.J.Davis

title: DUMPTRUCKS FOR QUARRYING AND OPENCAST MINING.
authors: Anon
abstract: The article covers articulated trucks, safety factors, noise reduction, tire care, rolling resistance, technical innovations, truck productivity and the market situation in the UK.

title: PLANT AND EQUIPMENT USED IN OPENCAST MINING AND ASSOCIATED ACTIVITIES.
authors: Brook C.; Thornley F.
abstract: The NCB Opencast Executive produces low-ash high-quality coal for industrial markets. Opencast sites vary in workable reserves from a few thousand tonnes up to several million tonnes. A discussion is given on the following: the three basic working methods (the motor scraper, the dragline, and the face shovel/dump truck); a description of practices in site working; environmental considerations (blasting, noise, dust, and water pollution); disposal points for the mined coal; and future prospects.

title: AIR PHOTOGRAPHS FOR INVESTIGATING NATURAL CHANGES, PAST USE AND PRESENT CONDITION OF ENGINEERING SITES.
source: TRRL Laboratory Report Transport and Road Research Laboratory Great Britain
authors: Dumbleton M.
abstract: Air photographs can play an important part in the investigation of engineering sites because they provide an overall view which can reveal surface features, ground conditions, and evidence of past use and natural changes which may be of importance in site development. Historical series of available air photographs can often allow the history of past use and natural change to be followed in detail over the last 35 years or more. The Report reviews the availability of air photographs and gives details of some 20 major sources and collections for the UK. The interpretation of air photographs is discussed, and illustrated by two case studies in which historical series of available photographs allowed the construction and demolition of brick works, the excavation and filling of clay pits, and the progress of opencast mining and restoration to be followed in detail. In addition, examples are given of the successful use of air photographs in the investigation of a wide range of engineering problems.

title: The application of soil survey data in opencast coal sites in Scotland
authors: Gauld J.H.; Brown K.W.M.
abstract: A commitment by the National Coal Board Opencast Executive to restore opencast coal areas to agricultural use as efficiently as possible recognizes the need for continual improvement in techniques. The Department of Agriculture and Fisheries for Scotland, as agents to the National Coal Board Opencast Executive, share a similar objective. Both organizations appreciate the need for a comprehensive soil survey, but experience has shown that general-purpose maps and reports are not always adequate for use in opencast mining operations. A soil survey of a proposed site at Keirsbeath is described and, on the basis of results from the use of improved survey methodology, and computer techniques to analyse the data, interpretative maps have been produced. The procedures, together with an examination of soil quantities available for restoration, and of critical moisture levels in soil stripping, are an improvement with significance for the planning and development work stage. A scheme of soil operations has been presented and the relevance of soil data to the forthcoming restoration and rehabilitation stages is discussed. © 1983.

title: Water and soil guideline for mining.
authors: Lawrence J.; Smith D.
abstract: Covers mining of unconsolidated alluvial and coastal sediments and offshore mineral and petroleum deposits; rock quarry mining, non-metallic opencast mining and underground and opencast hardrock metallic and coal mining. The guideline is divided into four sections set in the context of management planning. These are: 1) a description of the statutes which cover prospecting and mining; 2) the potential impacts on water and soil resources; 3) the minimisation or avoidance of these impacts; and 4) mining operations which require special attention from a water and soil viewpoint.-from Editors

title: Morphogenetic approach to man-made landforms due to opencast mining of porcelain clays and silica sands, around Seto City, Aichi Prefecture, central Japan.
authors: Moriyama A.
abstract: Landforms of mining fields are generally characterized by disordered distribution of large mining hollows such as honeycombs. Each hollow consists of steep cliffs, step-like benches, abandoned roads and settling basins in the bottom of hollows. The Mizuno Gravel Bed which is called the 'surface layer' by mine workers is excavated and transported to the abandoned mining fields or the upper part of valleys to make flat or rolling surfaces. New machines such as large bulldozers, power-shovels and loader shovels have greatly exaggerated the landform transformation. Present detailed features such as height and width of bench cliffs, benches and roads of mining fields seem to be provided by the capacity and function of these heavy machines and dump cars. -from English summary

title: SEISMIC REMOTE SENSING OF ROCK MASSES FOR THE OPTIMIZATION OF EXCAVATION EFFICIENCY.
source: IEEE Transactions on Geoscience and Remote Sensing
authors: Young R.P.; Hill J.J.
abstract: A seismic remote sensing technique and the associated microprocessor-based instrumentation are described, as part of three phases of a research project into the design of efficient blasting/fragmentation systems in opencast mining. The experimental program outlined involves the remote assessment of rock quality before and after a blast, together with the monitoring of the associated ground vibration and excavation process in order to assess blast fragmentation efficiency. An overview of the experimental program and instrumentation is given together with preliminary results from phase three of the research.

title: DEVELOPMENT TRENDS IN THE CONSTRUCTION OF SPREADERS FOR OPENCAST MINE DUMPS: PART 2. CROSS-PIT-SPREADERS.
authors: Weiss A.
abstract: Direct haulage of overburden over the shortest distance across the open pit to the mine area where the useful seams were already exploited represents the oldest and most economic method of exposing deposits by application of opencast mining techniques. For increased digging heights, the method of continuous overburden transport by means of conveying bridges was introduced. These systems require an additional travel path at the dumping side and their design needs to be exactly tailored to the geometric dimensions in a specific mine. For exposal of deeper seams in large opencast mines, extensive application of the 'around-the-pit' method is made.

title: OPENCAST MINING - THE CUMBRIAN SCENE.
authors: Mck. Guyan J.
abstract: Following the explosion in oil prices in 1973 the Plan for Coal 1974 required the Opencast Executive to expand production from around 6/7M tonnes to 15M tonnes. Cumbria's share was approximately 1M tonnes. Subsequent to 1974 six sites have been authorized. These are Low Close Extension, Outgang, Oughterside, Foxhouse, Moresby and Keekle and Pica with production continuing from all but Outgang which is currently undergoing restoration.

title: TOTAL SYSTEM CONCEPT IN PLANNING AND IMPLEMENTATION OF INTEGRATED DEVELOPMENT OF IRON ORES, FLUXES & INFRASTRUCTURAL FACILITIES REQUIRED FOR IRON AND STEEL INDUSTRY IN INDIA.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Khuntia G.
abstract: Some aspects of planning the Indian iron and steel industry are reviewed to cover principal raw materials and their conservation; quality control practices; traffic and power requirements; application of computers in opencast mining; provision of adequate capital; corporate organization for planning and monitoring the performance and development of mineral reserve base. It is shown that a time bound program for development and growth of mines producing principal raw materials for iron and steel industry has to be worked out. The main objective should be to supply adequate raw materials with highest productivity utilizing existing capacities and for providing additional capacities in time to produce maximum raw materials with minimum production cost.

title: Analysis of mineral wear processes with particular reference to open-cut mining equipment.
authors: Besser D.
abstract: Abrasive wear process are marked by high intensities of wear. Such wearing processes can be classified in three large groups, the most complex group being that of 3-body wear in which two solid bodies are moving against each other under the influence of mineral abrasives. Influential factors affecting such processes were analyzed in the laboratory, and the results obtained were confirmed by those obtained for lignite opencast mining equipment. (English abstract)

title: Environmental problems of coal production in the federal republic of of germany with particular reference to to the Ruhr
authors: Petsch G.
abstract: In 1979 it was noted that the production of deep-mined coal in the Federal Republic of Germany, including the Ruhr area, has risen once again. Since the beginning of the sixties the convenient source of both energy and raw material, oil, has been responsible for the falling levels of coal production in the Ruhr, to almost one half of peak production in 1956. Not much would have been needed to give up the entire troublesome and expensive process of deep coal mining in the Federal Republic in favour of the then cheap and bountiful oil. Only lignite managed to maintain a more or less steady annual production rate due to the direct conversion into electricity of a major part of its production at the site of extraction. Since the limitations and uncertainties governing the supply of crude oil have now been clearly exposed, the illusions about oil have begun to fade, and as a result confidence in our indigenous supplies of energy and raw material resources has been restored. What, however, are the implications of this revival of home-produced energy and raw material, which are not without problems both when produced and when consumed for the region in which they are extracted and brought to the surface, and where, to a large extent, the processing takes place? The region benefits from employment and investment, and in turn offers its resources (labour, land, water, air) inasmuch as past development has left them available for future development. But is the region to be covered with even more 'honourable' scars? In 1980, 87 million tonnes of deep mined coal were produced in the Federal Republic of Germany which resulted in roughly the same amount of minestone (spoil). Approximately 600 km<sup>2</sup> of densely populated area in the Ruhr district was already acquiring artificial drainage due to subsidence. Coking plants and old coal-based stations fired with deep mined coal pollute air and water. Lignite production in 1980 in the Federal Republic of Germany - which was almost entirely obtained by opencast mining - amounted to 130 million tonnes. To achieve this an additional 445×10<sup>6</sup>m<sup>3</sup> of overburden had to be shifted. Already in 1977 in the Rhineland between Cologne, Dusseldorf and Aachen (Aix-la-Chapelle), 522 km<sup>2</sup> of mainly good agricultural land was acquired under compulsory purchase order for lignite mining. Villages, roads, rail and waterways were and continue to be re-routed and re-sited. The direct conversion of lignite into electricity produces emission and spreads pollution. Now, it is not only the people of the Ruhr area, the largest industrial conurbation in Europe, that have become sensitive to the impact of mining upon their environment. In all industrial countries it has been learned that those things which cannot be replaced, i.e. environment, are not always being valued by the free market at a price which represents the value they may have for the individual and possibly should have for all of us. Today the need for mining is hardly being questioned any more but people are voicing their opinion as to what is a just price to be paid. The citizen of the Ruhr, for instance, no longer accepts that the specific environmental impacts caused by deep coal mining, which produces a commodity wanted by the entire nation, should be borne solely at the place where it is produced and by the people who happen to live there. He demands that such burdens are borne by everybody who enjoys the benefits. Clear political ideas must be developed and made know as to how much we value home-produced energy sources, what proportion of the resulting burdens the country is willing to bear and how they are to be distributed fairly. There are many methods and technical means by which the burdens of the mining and industrial regions can be minimised, by which damage can be repaired and derelict areas reclaimed. The application of such means must be safeguarded by early planning and sufficient finanacing so that the exploitation of one resource will not result in other resources being lost. © 1982 Science and Technology Letters.

title: The design of a microprocessor-based instrument for the seismic interrogation of rock masses
authors: Hill J.J.; Young R.P.; Gabell D.D.
abstract: This paper describes a microcomputer-based instrument which is used for the recording and spectral processing of seismic signals obtained in opencast mining. Various types of vector attenuation spectra can be computed and displayed. The instrument is used to evaluate indirectly the brokenness of rock masses prior to blasting. © 1982.

title: Effects of stockpiling topsoils associated with opencast mining 1. Chemical properties and the growth of ryegrass and white clover.
authors: Widdowson J.; Gibson E.; Healy W.
abstract: Two stockpiles were studied: one at Mataura, formed from Mataura silt loam (recent soil), was associated with opencast lignite mining; the other at Lorneville near Invercargill, formed mainly from Makarewa silt loam (gleyed recent soil), was associated with opencast mining of ceramic clays. Ryegrass yields in soils from the top of the stockpiles were similar to those in unstored topsoil from under pasture. Yields from the lower part of the stockpile were higher than those at the surface because of high levels of mineral N that had accumulated under anaerobic conditions. -from Authors

title: Land drainage and restoration of land after NCB opencast mining ( UK).
authors: Bragg N.
abstract: So far the work has been aimed at identifying the problems of reinstated soils and how these affect drainage design. The physical soil examinations have indicated that the soils on reinstated sites are very different from their undisturbed neighbours. The monitoring of drainage on sites of differing age from reinstatement indicates that where a true control is established there are significant differences between the worked and unworked land. -Author

title: Effects of stockpiling topsoils associated with opencast mining 2. Physical properties.
authors: McQueen D.J.; Ross C.W.
abstract: Physical properties of 2 topsoil stockpiles associated with opencast mining were studied in the Mataura and Lorneville areas, Southland. In both cases, stockpiling resulted in increased bulk density and mechanical strength and decreased porosity, especially macroporosity. These changes are attributed to the influence of earthmoving equipment rather than the 'overburden' effect of stockpiling. The major effect of stockpiling on soil physical conditions appears to be soil compaction which occurs during formation of the pile. -from Authors

title: TECHNO-ECONOMIC FEASIBILITY OF OPENCAST MINING.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Jinarajan G.
abstract: Some technological, operational and economic aspects of opencast coal mining are considered with special reference to the conditions prevailing in Indian mines. It is shown that purely viewing from a technical angle the scope for opencast mining is vast but each project requires a thorough economic analysis.

title: DEVELOPMENT OF RESPONSE SPECTRA TECHNIQUES FOR PREDICTION OF STRUCTURAL DAMAGE FROM OPEN-PIT BLASTING VIBRATIONS.
source: Transactions of the Institution of Mining and Metallurgy Section A Mining Technology
authors: Walker S.; Young P.; Davey P.
abstract: Structural damage from blasting vibrations has been a major problem associated with opencast mining and quarrying operations for many years. Investigations have shown that there are many inadequacies in the conventional method that is used to limit the amounts of explosive and distances to local buildings. A more rational method of predicting damage is based on response spectra techniques, which were originally developed in the field of earthquake engineering. These techniques have been adapted for use in opencast mining and the results of the research to date show that the conventional methods, based on peak particle velocity measurements, can result in overrestrictive site blasting practices.

title: COMBINED MINING SYSTEMS FOR OPEN PIT MINES.
authors: Franke R.
abstract: Production rates in opencast mines will have to be increased in the future, especially in the energy sector. Reactions for this development are an increased demand for coal, oil-sand and oil-shale, the steadily growing share of opencast mining operations as opposed to a decreasing share for underground mining, and the increase of the overburden-to-pay mineral ratio. Various possible combined opencast mining systems are presented and explained by practical examples.

title: Coal and the environment.
abstract: Produced by the Commission on Energy and the Environment, contains the following chapters: the coal industry: decline and renaissance; prospects for coal; framework of environmental control; deep mining; subsidence; spoil: dereliction and pit closures; opencast mining; coal markets; transport, handling and storage; conversion to substitute fuels; combustion technology; combustion residues; sources, quantities, control and effects; environmental effects of burning coal in urban areas; and the planning process reconciling the interests.-from CEGB Digest

title: Shifts in US coal production: trends and implications.
authors: Davis J.
abstract: In the last 20 yr coal's importance has revived. The distribution of resources is described with particular reference to greater emphasis on opencast mining, the new significance of low sulphur coals, and increased production W of the Mississippi. Employment has increased as output revived, but not in proportion to the extra output because of gains in productivity. Massive mining developments have had an environmental impact which has stimulated much conservation activity. Changes in location of production and the nature of the market means that coal tends to move by rail or water, or sometimes by rail/water combined. Transport issues are therefore important. The future of coal in the USA seems assured. -D.G.Price

title: Trends in Opencast Mining at Increased Diesel Prices.
source: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Kutschera S.
abstract: Cost comparisons between conventional truck haulage and systems consisting of small truck fleets, semi-mobile crushers and belt conveyors show lower operating costs for the latter. Pipeline transport using semi-mobile crushers and semi-mobile mills for grain size reduction could be another solution. Lurgi centrifugal mills, characterized by high capacity, very small dimensions and low capital cost, represent an alternative. German open-pit technology with bucket wheel excavators, shiftable belt conveyors and spreaders operating in conjunction with draglines could be the answer for large strip mines.

title: Environmental impact of iron ore mining and control
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Jain N.
abstract: The pollution due to opencast mining in general and iron ore mining in particular is dealt with under the following headings: Air pollution; Water pollution; Noise; Vibrations; Visual intrusions. Suggestions about pollution control measures are given.

title: EXTRACTION OF PILLARS IN THICK COAL SEAMS DEVELOPED IN MULTI-SECTIONS.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Kejriwal B.
abstract: This paper presents a critical review of the current mining practices and the available technological solutions for extracting thick coal seams developed in multi-sections. The methods considered include opencast mining; hydraulic mining; extraction by multi-slice longwall with or without sublevel caving; total underwinning (integral caving) by one slice longwall; and, sublevel caving from galleries.

title: PRECLASSIFYING with Mobile Screen Units in Mobile Crushing Plants.
authors: Sieburg S.; Kelleners W.
abstract: Preclassification is becoming an ever-growing necessity in opencast mining systems to meet demands with regard to the end product and output. Optimum economy in crushing and screening plants is first brought about by mobility for which, according to the application, crawler mountings, independent transport crawlers, raft-type walking mechanisms, wheel mountings or rail mountings are employed. The authors present in two examples, with conveying capacities of 2000 and 2800 t. p. h. , two preclassifying screens (circular and linear vibrating screens) in mobile units.

title: DEVELOPMENTS IN MINING CABLES.
authors: Brown R.
abstract: MEPR (Medium Ethylenepropylene Rubber) was developed for trailing cable use. The characteristics of this compound are given. The electrical properties at high voltages have been proven in opencast mining, where mechanical robustness is a requirement.

title: OPTIMUM - SECOND DRAGLINE ON ITS WAY.
source: South African Mining and Engineering Journal
authors: Anon
abstract: Gencor's Optimum Colliery, near Hendrina in the Eastern Transvaal is erecting a second dragline. The company intends to concentrate entirely on opencast mining.

title: OPENCAST MINING OPERATIONS IN CUMBRIA.
authors: Anon
abstract: Since 1958 five sites have been work out and restored for agricultural usage, and four sites are currently in production. Two more sites will be coaling by the end of 1981.

title: Opencast Coal Mining.
authors: Chapier G.; Simand R.; Delorme H.
abstract: This paper briefly reviews the history of France's opencast coal mines ad analyzes various aspects of the opencast mining method. Special emphasis is placed on the comparatively low cost of opencast mining operation. Finally, details are given of the opencast mining practice at the Houilleres de la Loire with particular reference to the thorough and careful land reclamation conducted by this French coal producer at nine mine sites since 1969.

title: The agricultural impact of opencast coal mining in England and Wales
authors: Tomlinson P.
abstract: Opencast coal mining in England and Wales can cause a wide range of environmental problems which are increasingly public issues due to the planned expansion in output and the impact this may have on agriculture and landscape. Opencast mining is reviewed on a county by county basis to identify the variations in the disturbance caused. A detailed review of restoration techniques and the agricultural quality of the restored land is presented, and the role of Planning Authorities is discussed. Significant variations in the impact of opencast operations are identified, especially in relation to the potential for derelict land reclamation and the grade of agricultural land affected. The latter is generally lower grade 3 and below, although in certain areas operations are entering land of higher agricultural and scenic quality. The quality of restoration, while good, still has scope for improvements, such as reducing soil compaction and the subsequent management of the land by the farmer. The impact on agricultural productivity is difficult to assess, but it appears to be only slight in those cases where recent restoration techniques were used and when lower grade agricultural land is taken. © 1979 Science and Technology Letters.

title: Opencast mining and landscaping
authors: Niemann-Delius C.
abstract: This paper covers the influence on the environment through opencast mining operations. The effect on the natural surroundings, which still exist when the mine is closed down, is dealt with in particular. Described in this context are the methods of landscaping and the possibilities and criteria for the selection of subsequent applications for the area, which is shown by means of examples.

title: Gosselies 1 Opencast Coal Mine.
authors: Frenay C.; Cazier J.
abstract: For many years in Great Britain and in France relatively shallow deposits of coal - either massive or consisting of a series of seams - have been worked by opencast methods. With this method in mind, a reassessment has been carried out of the carboniferous strata in the Belgian province of Hainaut, in which the coal seams crop out at certain places or are covered by a small thickness of overburden. In October 1980, work was started at a first site at Gosselies and Thimeon (now Charleroi and Pont-a-Celles) at the point where the E 41 and A 54 highways intersect. This site, known as ″Gosselies 1″ , covers an area of 45 hectares and will be worked at depths not exceeding 30 meters. The authors describe the opencast mining method employed and the mining operations which are scheduled to last approximately 28 months.

title: OPENCAST MINING OF BROWN COAL IN EASTERN EUROPE.
authors: Chugh Y.
abstract: A European technique using bucketwheel excavators, bucket chain excavators, and mobile conveyors bridges may be an alternative for the large lignite mines planned in North Dakota and Texas.

title: MINING THICK COAL SEAMS IN THE SOCIALIST REPUBLIC OF ROMANIA.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Covaci S.; Oncioiu G.
abstract: In accordance with the plan for the development of the coal industry, Romania's coal production will exceed 37 million tons by 1980. In the Romanian Socialist Republic, both low grade coals and lignite required as fuel for the energy industry, and high-quality bituminous coal for the iron and steel industry, are mined. The main coal basins bearing thick seams are Oltenia for lignite and the Jiu Valley for bituminous coal. In the Oltenia coal field exploitation is undertaken both by opencast mining in the Rovinari-Jilt region and by underground methods in the Motru region. This article highlights thick seam mining in the major coal and lignite mines in Romania, and surveys some improvements in mining technologies used at the coal face.

title: PRODUCTION RECORDS TUMBLE AT SISHEN IRON ORE MINE.
source: South African Mining and Engineering Journal
authors: Anon
abstract: Iscor's opencast mining operation has been producing high grade iron ore since 1953, but real growth has only come in the past seven years. Production has increased steadily and in the past few months tonnage records have been broken.

title: Geophysical reconnaissance to assess a site affected by shallow opencast mining
source: Bulletin of the International Association of Engineering Geology Bulletin De L Association Internationale De Geologie De L Ingenieur
authors: Booth A.; Cox D.; Hall J.
abstract: La condition physique du sol d'un chantier de construction a été étudiée. Le terrain avait été exploité par endroits et les trous de faible profondeur qui en résultaient avaient été comblés de remblai. Pour fixer l'emplacement des maisons, et pour faciliter l'étude de leurs fondations, il fallait d'abord faire un plan de ces trous remblayés. On traça, à partir des résultats des essais séismiques et des contrôles d'impédance électrique du sol, des courbes d'égale vitesse de propagation des ondes et d'égale résistivité électrique, et on compara avec l'expérience et avec le témoignage des archives d'activité minière. Il est en général possible de localiser, à partir des résultats de cette étude, les zones qui sont composées de matériaux peu compactés. On put répérer les régions qui pouvaient poser des problèmes pour la construction, ce qui permit de faire une étude efficace et plus économique. Les maisons sont actuellement en cours de réalisation.

title: Asset stripping (UK).
abstract: As open cast mining has expanded in scale in recent years, public opposition has become more vocal. One notable consequence has been the setting up of the Opencast Mining Intelligence Group and their report 'A reassessment of opencast coalmining' is discussed by the author. -from Author

title: What will be the price for energy tomorrow?. I. Coal price.
authors: Ippolito M.
abstract: Traces the evolution of the coal industry in the developed world and looks to opencast mining in the southern continents as the sources of cheap supplies in the future, even when transport costs are taken into full consideration.-H.Clout

title: Sedimentary structures in Quaternary ironsands at Waikato North Head, New Zealand
source: New Zealand Journal of Geology and Geophysics
authors: Christie A.B.
abstract: Opencast mining at Waikato North Head, Franklin County, South Auckland, New Zealand, has exposed the sedimentary structures in Late Quaternary titanomagnetite ironsands of two units of the Kaihu Group: the Waiuku Blacksand Member (Hood Formation) and the Entrican Dune Member (Mitiwai Formation). The Waiuku Blacksand Member consists of a series of alternating, steeply cross-laminated and horizontally laminated sand units, which are sometimes separated by units of mud. The very large scale of the cross-laminated sets (up to 12 m thick), their orientation, grain size and internal features suggest an eolian origin. Some of the horizontally laminated units are topset beds associated with the foresets of the cross-laminated units, whereas others are of either interdune stream-lake, or beach origin. Mud units may represent soils, loess, or interdune swamp and lake deposits. The Entrican Dune Member consists of large migrating dunes which were stabilised in this area by afforestation in 1935. Internally, they are composed of large and very large sets of steeply inclined, cross-lamination (foresets) and large sets of horizontal lamination, or low angle crosslamination (topsets). © 1979 Taylor and Francis Group, LLC.

title: Brown coal opencast mining and landscaping in the rhineland
authors: Kausch P.
keywords: Brown coal | Land reclamation | Opencast mining
abstract: The brown coal deposits in the world form an important reserve of energy and raw material, which can also be widely used economically in the present state of opencast mining techniques. Rhenish brown coal mining with its high values of production and productivity proves also that brown coal deposits, though low in energy, are economically exploitable if, for the mining of this coal, necessary preconditions are fulfilled. These are large‐scale mining fields and the use of an appropriate opencast mining technique which includes reclamation and landscaping after mining. the measures necessary for this and the technical development have been carried out by mining Rhenish brown coal on an economical basis. Thanks to the rich deposit reserves, to the high level of development of the opencast mining technique as well as to new or further development of refining processes, Rhenish brown coal mining will also be able in the future, to contribute considerably to securing the supply of energy and raw material. Copyright © 1979 John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.

title: Investigation on the methods of forecasting changes in the physicogeographical environment on the basis of the Konin area.
authors: Kozacki L.; Stankowski W.
abstract: Discusses the prediction of changes that will result from a major opencast mining development in Tertiary and Quaternary sediments. Changes in relief, groundwater levels and the pattern of revegetation are covered.-K.Clayton

title: Analysis Results for Building an Opencast Mine for the Exploitation of the ″Djurakov Do″ Bauxite Deposit.
authors: Jujic D.
abstract: Both opencast and underground methods were considered for mining Yugoslavia's Djurakov Do bauxite deposit, and it was concluded that opencast mining would be more attractive from economical and other standpoints. The deposit was divided into five blocks, each with differant mining characteristics, in order to facilitate the evaluation. Several opencast design variations were developed for the selection of an optimum design with specific parameters.

title: OPENCAST MINING MACHINERY FROM EAST GERMANY.
authors: Sealy T.
abstract: An earlier article dealt with the important brown coal mining industry in the German Democratic Republic (DDR) and outlined the current operations and future plans for the industry. In this follow-up article, the type of machinery manufactured in East Germany for strip mining operations is considered and examples are given of th use of such machinery outside the DDR. The machinery covered includes conveyors and bucket ladder excavators.

title: The archaeology of the Coal Measures and the Magnesian Limestone escarpment in Co. Durham: a preliminary survey.
authors: Turnbull P.; Jones R.F.J.
abstract: The first systematic study of the poorly understood lowland areas of the county used information from tithe maps, OS records, and vertical air photographs, with some follow-up field walking. Many new sites were revealed; buildings and industrial monuments are also listed. Recommendations are made for meeting the threats from opencast mining and stone quarrying and appendices treat the vegetational history, the place-names, and comparative landscape histories of three individual parishes.-from British Archaeological Abstracts

title: Determining topographic surface on contour plans in recultivation.
authors: Dimov L.
abstract: Discusses the rational shaping of the surface of embankments and fills on land affected by opencast mining. Possible approaches to the problem of planning suitable surfaces are given: analytical, graphic-analytical and graphic. A detailed examination is made of the graphic method of vertical planning with the aid of projected contours on 1:2000 and 1:5000 topographic plans. -from Abstracts of Bulgarian Scientific Literature

title: Limits of environmental protection considered from the viewpoint of the opencast mining and quarrying industry
authors: Goeke H.
abstract: Based on the conceptions of environment and environmental protection, the author takes a look at the need for protective measures. The limits of environmental protection are equated to the limits of what the world of human industrial activity can be expected to tolerate, and a note of warning is sounded against one-sided loading of the demands imposed. The importance of the pit and quarry industry is outlined. Various environmental problems associated with interventions in the landscape and with pollutant emissions are discussed, and licensing procedures are explained.

title: Groundwater control in opencast mining of a lignite deposit in southern Greece.
source: In Proc Siamos 78 Int Symp on Water in Mining and Underground Works Granada Spain Sep 18 22 1978 Granada Spai
authors: Spiliotis G.
abstract: This paper describes the method adopted for the protection of the northern part of the Megalopolis lignite mine, against hazards resulting from inundation due to groundwater inflow. The groundwater is confined in a karstic aquifer below the floor of the opencast mine and the respective hydrogeological conditions are described. Also included are descriptions of field examination by pumping tests, and the interpretation of the test results. Finally, the paper deals with the design of a pumping system for the protection of the mine, and the economical data concerning the installation and the operation of this sytem. (A)

title: BUTTERWELL.
authors: Batchelor M.
abstract: Contract opencast mining accounts for an important part of U. K. coal output. This article deals with a new opencast operation at Butterwell in north-east England, which provides a good example of such a contract, being a multi-seam mine using modern excavation and haulage equipment. The contract for mining at Butterwell involves the productionof 12 million tonnes of coal over 10 years. The geology of the coal seams, initial operations at the mine, as well as future plans are outlined.

title: OPENCAST COAL MINING IN THE UNITED KINGDOM AND ITS ROLE IN THE MINING INDUSTRY.
authors: Davidson D.
abstract: The author examines the trends in opencast coal mining in the U. K. and shows how the whole concept of opencast mining in that country has radically changed over the past 30 years. The future availability of opencast reserves in Great Britain is also discussed in terms of both technically workable and economically workable deposits. Finally, a brief description of the production techniques employed in opencast mining is given.

title: Opencast Mining of Coal in the Blanzy Basin of the Houilleres du Centre et du Midi.
authors: Cochon R.
abstract: The Blanzy basin, part of the Houilleres du Centre et du Midi, is the biggest opencast mining site in France, producing 700,000 tonnes of coal per year. This article examines in detail the equipment used at the mine: motorscrapers used for overburden removal, hydraulic shovels, tire loaders, dump tracks, and then deals briefly with auxiliary operations, environmental problems, and costs.

title: FLUX GRADE LIMESTONE DEPOSITS OF JAGGAYYAPETA AREA, KRISHNA DISTRICT, ANDHRA PRADESH.
authors: Natarajan V.; Rajagopalan Nair S.
abstract: A total of 134 million tonnes of flux-grade limestones, including 47 million tons of easily workable limestone, are estimated to exist in the area under study. The deposits lend themselves to easy, economical and largely mechanized opencast mining. The proven reserves alone could meet the needs of proposed steel plants in the southern part of India, since these limestones possess the necessary chemical and physical characteristics for use in blast furnaces. The geology of the area is also covered.

title: SCHEME OF DEVELOPING SEAMS BELOW WATER-LOGGED WORKINGS.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: Gulati A.K.; Singh A.K.
abstract: Several disasters have occured in the past in Indian coal mines in which the old water-logged workings existed that had been exploited by opencast mining and inclines up to shallow depths. Therefore, an efficient system for proving the width of safety pillars in the old workings and of dewatering these has become a must. One of such systems, based on advance boring and adopted by the Sudamdih Incline Mine, is examined in detail here.

title: PRODUCING COAL.
authors: Rawlinson R.
abstract: In the U. K. 's Plan for Coal, it is envisaged that of the 150 million tons potential demand for coal in 1985, opencast mining would produce 15 million tons, the remaining 135 million tons to be obtained by deep mined output. If, as at present, 6. 75 million tons continue to be mined by shortwall and other similar systems, then the remaining 128. 25 million tons will have to be obtained from longwall mechanized faces. The author examines the areas for improvement of coal face equipment, and reviews some recent development in power loader design and practice, armored face conveyors, powered supports, and automatic steering of power leaders. The Advanced Technology Mining (ATM) concept is also considered.

title: Some of the World's Major Opencast Mining Operations.
authors: de Coussemaker P.
abstract: The author first presents a brief review of the world's major opencast mining operations, then examines the reasons for which this type of mineral exploitation is elected. Inconveniences and shortcomings of opencast mining are also discussed, along with various techniques and equipment employed, which include drilling, blasting, loading, transport and crushing. The use of computers in large-scale opencast mining is also considered.

title: SNATCHILL EXPERIMENT.
authors: Anon
abstract: The article reports on an experiment to furnish data on settlement and its effects on houses built on land recently restored after ironstone extraction by opencast mining. The experiment is being conducted on dwellings that have been constructed with conventional foundations on adjoining plots that have been afforded differing ground treatments.

title: Study of the Future Supplies of the Iranian Smelters with Iron Ores.
source: Erzmetall Journal for Exploration Mining and Metallurgy
authors: Bassir S.
abstract: Expansion plans of the Iranian steel industry are briefly outlined. Main problems here involve the selection of smelting method and suitable locations for smelters. The country's rich natural gas deposits would favor a direct reduction of iron ore, which could make a decisive breakthrough with the help of the forthcoming expansion in Iran. The choice of optimal flow of transportation warrants special consideration because the transportation costs play a decisive role in the supply of smelters with iron ore. Exploration activity is reviewed, Iran's major iron ore deposits are presented in tabular form, and opencast mining plans and extraction methods are dealt with.

title: LIGNITE MINING IN GERMANY INVOLVES VAST RECLAMATION/RELOCATION WORK.
authors: Anon
abstract: The Federal Republic of Germany has considerable coal resources, some of which are recovered by opencast mining methods. Some 62,000-million tons of brown coal in the Republic are largely concentrated (55,000-million tons) in the area of Cologne, Aachen, Duesseldorf. Under present technical and economic conditions, it is estimated that about 35,000-million tons of the deposit can be recovered. Although it is of relatively low thermal value, the brown coal is very suitable for conversion to electrical energy in thermal generating plants.

title: OPENCAST MINING PAVES THE WAY FOR TELFORD NEW TOWN.
authors: Anon
abstract: The new town of Telford is reaching the third stage of development, having been established by Government decision in 1968. Much of the work to date has included the preparation of land and the provision of services for the projected township of 220,000 people in the 21st century. Telford is unique, not only for the way in which the reclamation of the derelict land has been tackled, but for several large areas scheduled for domestic housing where the derelict land has been reclaimed as a result of opencast coal mining by the NCB. In this way valuable tonnage of steam raising coal for power stations has been won and the pitfallen land with chartered and unchartered shafts has been consolidated thus providing instant building land for houses or the construction of orbital roads.

title: Decreased Output and Aging of Drainage Filter Wells.
authors: Folkens K.
abstract: The optimum design and rating of the drainage filter wells in lignite opencast mining are making steady progress thanks to ever better methods of analytical ground-water hydraulics. However, practical advantages of these advances are called into question, or at least limited, when the optimum design does not also result in a trouble-free operation of the wells. To deal with such problems, investigations were undertaken by the Freiberg Mining Academy, and were partly based on the already available research results concerning water management, particularly water supply and treatment. Initial results of these investigations are reported.

title: LEAD AND COPPER OCCURRENCES IN BHAGALPUR DISTRICT, BIHAR.
authors: Prasad U.
abstract: Lead and copper occurrences in the Bhagalpur district of Bihar, India, have been noted in nine areas. The mineralization has been observed in the pockets of tremolite-actinolite schist and hornblende-schist, and is indicated by the presence of malachite and azurite stains and occasional grains of galena. These mineralized pockets vary in size from 20 m. multiplied by 4. 5 m. to 300 m. multiplied by 25 m. Given the ever-increasing demands for base metals in India, the author feels that these small pockets should be exploited. Further, the exploitation of some of the smaller pockets, which would involve the opencast mining on a small scale, is considered to be economical, if done while prospecting these deposits.

title: OPENCAST MINING CATCHES ON IN SOUTH AFRICA.
authors: Holz P.
abstract: Anglo Power Collieries in the Anglo American Corp. Group are partially converting their Arnot Colliery to an opencast operation. At Arnot Colliery site, technicians are currently assembling the largest dragline unit in South Africa - a Bucyrus Erie 1570 W model. The dragline with its 285-ft boom will be capable of moving 1,620,000 cu ft of overburden per day in a sidecasting operation. It will ship 115 cu ft of overburden for every ton of coal mined.

title: Hydrological effects of urbanization: report of the sub group on the effects of urbanization on the hydrological environment, of the Coordinating Council of the International Hydrological Decade
authors: McPherson M.B.
abstract: Among the numerous studies undertaken by the International Hydrological Decade (IHD) was an investigation initiated in 1965 by the Working Group on the Influence of Man on the Hydrological Cycle and supported by the Food and Agricultural Organisation (FAO), charged with agricultural and urbanization aspects of the subject. The Coordinating Council in 1970 decided to form a Subgroup on the Effects of Urbanization on the Hydrological Environment, supported by Unesco, to assist the Working Group and to investigate more intensively industrial and urbanization aspects. In 1972 the IHD secretariat circulated to all national committees for the IHD a questionnaire on research and development needs. Responses are summarized in this report, and the respondents were among the participants at an International Workshop on the Hydrological Effects of Urbanization held in Warsaw, Poland, in November, 1973. A draft of Part I of this report, 'International Summary', was reviewed at the Workshop and the many invaluable observations and suggestions made by the participants were taken into account in the final publication. Part II of this report contains 'Case Studies' for Subgroup members' countries, and includes information collected in the Federal Republic of Germany, the Netherlands, Sweden, the United States of America and the Union of Soviet Socialist Republics. Part III is a group of 'Illustrative Special Topic Studies' prepared by individual members and associates from their countries, covering such subjects as urban runoff; effects of lignite mining on the urban water cycle; effects of industrial waste water and sludge on the self purification of rivers; some aspects of solid waste disposal; waste water dilution in rivers, lakes and reservoirs; synthetic detergents and water quality; effects of opencast mining on the water balance of an area; and the effects of urbanization on polder areas. One of the major findings of this report is that the field of urban hydrology is almost devoid of modern research investment and there has been relatively little study to date of the effect of urban man upon natural hydrological conditions, in spite of the significant economic and environmental importance of urban settlements in nearly every nation.

title: EFFECT OF OPENCAST MINING ON THE WATER BALANCE OF AN AREA.
authors: Kuprianov V.V.; Obraztsov I.N.
abstract: The effect of opencast mining on the various water balance elements of river basins may extend far beyond the limits of the areas under construction as a result of drainage from the opencast mining. The resulting lowering of level (or head) of subsurface water may cover areas from a dozen up to tens of thousands of square kilometers. At the same time, the drainage of opencast mining is usually accompanied by drainage water discharge into the river network which can increase river runoff. The paper describes research results on the effect of iron ore excavation on runoff within the Kursk Magnetic Anomaly. Observational data from hydrological stations have been used together with material from expeditionary investigations.

title: Opencast Mining with Bucket-Wheel Excavators - Another 100,000-m3 Excavator at Rheinbraun.
authors: Anon
abstract: Another excavator was recently taken into service in the Frimmersdorf opencast mine of the Rheinische Braunkohlenwerke AG. Its maximum stripping capacity is 112,000 m**3 a day for the overburden and 110,000 tons a day for lignite. The construction time was 43 months. The technical design of this excavator is described, and the significance and further trends in this opencast mining technique are explained.

title: Opencast Mining of Lignite: Operation of Belts Without Supervision.
authors: Thiede H.
abstract: With the exception of the loaders in the vicinity of the central conveyor depot, all the drive stations on the lines of conveyor belts in the Frimmersdorf opencast mine have been running for more than one year without any operators. During this period, the task of monitoring the installation has been assumed by two motorized groups of checkers, who drive along the line of the conveyor belts every two hours, and by automatic control devices. The author describes the experience gained and the assessment of tests with various control systems.

title: Delineation of opencast working limits and optimum depth
source: J Inst Eng India Mining Met Div
authors: RAINA MN
abstract: Unit cost of production by opencast mining is a function of opencast depth. In delineating the optimum depth and the most economic surface working limits, detailed technoeconomic evaluation is obligatory. In this paper, analytical, graphical and graphical- analytical method, being simple, quick and fairly accurate, should be the preferred method of analysis for speedy schematization of opencast mining in case of deposits of varied geological features.

title: OPENCAST COAL MINING TECHNIQUE IN THE U.S.S.R.
source: Journal of Mines Metals and Fuels
authors: RAINA MN
abstract: This paper is an attempt at the presentation of the opencast coal mining technique as it prevails in the Soviet Union, one of the leading coal producing countries in the world today. Considering the phenomenal development in the coal mining industry of that country, production from opencast mining accounted for about 24% of total coal production during the year 1967. With the increased application of the soviet equipment in India, a brief survey of the Soviet machines, mechanization and technique should be of interest. Soviet practice of application of excavation and other equipment is dealt with in some detail with special reference to their operating parameters.
